questions.title: The sliding window pattern
questions.prompt: Explain the sliding window pattern. Describe a problem where it applies, walk through how the window expands and shrinks, state the time and space complexity, and say when the pattern does NOT work.

expectedConcepts.label: Works on contiguous subarrays/substrings
Left and right pointers expand/shrink
O(n) because each element enters and leaves once
Extra space is O(1) or O(k) for a hash map of counts
Edge cases: empty input, window larger than array
Compared with O(n^2) brute force or limits with negatives

questions.modelAnswer: Sliding window maintains a contiguous range [left, right] and a running summary (sum, counts in a hash map). Move right to expand; while the window violates the constraint, move left to shrink. Example: longest substring without repeating characters. Each index is added and removed at most once, so time is O(n); space is O(1) or O(alphabet/k) for the count map. It needs a monotonic property — shrinking must never make a valid window invalid — so it fails for sums with negative numbers, where prefix sums + hash map are used instead. Edge cases: empty input, k larger than n.
researchContext: Fixed-size windows (max sum of k elements) vs variable-size windows (smallest subarray with sum ≥ S).
Key invariant: shrinking the window must move it toward validity; with negative numbers that monotonicity breaks.
Typical state: running sum, frequency map, count of distinct elements.
Complexity argument: amortised analysis — each pointer moves at most n times.

questions.title: Binary search complexity
questions.prompt: Explain how binary search works, why its time complexity is logarithmic, what its space complexity is for iterative and recursive versions, and what preconditions and edge cases matter.

expectedConcepts.label: Requires sorted / monotonic input
Halves the search space each step
O(log n) time
O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive stack
Overflow in mid, off-by-one, empty array

questions.modelAnswer: Binary search works on sorted (more generally, monotonic) data. Compare the target with the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain it. After k steps n/2^k elements remain, so it finishes in about log2(n) steps: O(log n) time. Iterative uses O(1) extra space; recursive uses O(log n) stack. Pitfalls: computing mid as (lo+hi)/2 can overflow — use lo + (hi-lo)/2; off-by-one loop bounds; duplicates when you need the first/last occurrence; empty arrays.
researchContext: Generalisation: binary search on the answer (e.g. minimum capacity to ship packages in D days).
Loop invariant thinking avoids off-by-one bugs: decide whether hi is inclusive or exclusive.

questions.title: DFS versus BFS
questions.prompt: Compare depth-first search and breadth-first search. Explain the data structure each uses, their complexity on a graph, and give one problem where each is the better choice.

expectedConcepts.label: DFS uses a stack/recursion, BFS a queue
BFS explores level by level; shortest path in unweighted graphs
O(V + E) time
Space: BFS frontier width vs DFS depth
Visited set to handle cycles
DFS for topological sort / cycle detection / backtracking

questions.modelAnswer: DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack; BFS explores neighbours level by level using a queue. Both run in O(V + E) with an adjacency list and need a visited set to handle cycles. Memory: BFS holds the frontier (can be wide), DFS holds the current path (can be deep — risk of stack overflow). Use BFS for shortest path in an unweighted graph (minimum moves in a grid); use DFS for topological sort, cycle detection, connected components and backtracking.
researchContext: Grid problems: treat cells as nodes, 4-directional neighbours as edges.
Iterative DFS avoids recursion depth limits.
Bidirectional BFS for large search spaces.

questions.title: Heaps and priority queues
questions.prompt: Explain how a binary heap supports priority-queue operations. Cover the array representation, insert and extract operations, their complexity, and how building a heap from an array can be linear.

expectedConcepts.label: Complete binary tree stored in an array
Heap property: parent ≤ children (min-heap)
Insert = append + sift up; extract = swap root + sift down
Build-heap is O(n)
O(n) storage, in place
Compared with sorted array / balanced BST

questions.modelAnswer: A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array: children of index i are 2i+1 and 2i+2. The heap property (min-heap: parent ≤ children) means the minimum is at index 0, so peek is O(1). Insert appends and sifts up; extract-min moves the last element to the root and sifts down — both O(log n) because the tree height is log n. Bottom-up heapify is O(n) because most nodes are near the leaves and sift down a short distance. Compared with a sorted array (O(n) insert) or balanced BST (O(log n) everything but more overhead), heaps are compact and cache-friendly. Uses: Dijkstra, top-k, merging k sorted lists, schedulers. It needs no extra space beyond the array itself: O(n) storage, and heapsort works in place with O(1) extra space.

questions.title: Dynamic programming state definition
questions.prompt: Walk through a dynamic programming problem of your choice. Define the state precisely, give the recurrence, the base cases, the evaluation order, and the time and space complexity. Mention how you could reduce memory.

expectedConcepts.label: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Explicit state definition
Recurrence / transition
Base cases
Complexity = states × transition cost
Rolling array / memory optimisation
Top-down memoisation vs bottom-up tabulation

questions.modelAnswer: Example: longest common subsequence of strings a (length n) and b (length m). State: dp[i][j] = LCS length of a[0..i) and b[0..j). Recurrence: if a[i-1] == b[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Base: dp[0][*] = dp[*][0] = 0. Fill row by row. Time O(nm), space O(nm), reducible to O(min(n,m)) by keeping only the previous row. Top-down memoisation is easier to write; bottom-up avoids recursion depth and enables the memory optimisation.

questions.title: How a hash map works
questions.prompt: Explain how a hash map achieves average constant-time lookups. Cover hashing, collisions, load factor and resizing, and when performance degrades.

expectedConcepts.label: Hash function maps key to bucket index
Collision handling: chaining or open addressing
Average O(1), worst case O(n)
Load factor triggers resize/rehash
Bad hash / adversarial keys degrade performance
Compared with balanced tree maps (ordered)

questions.modelAnswer: A hash function turns the key into an integer, reduced modulo the bucket count to pick a slot. Different keys can land in the same slot: chaining stores a list per bucket; open addressing probes for the next free slot. With a good hash and a bounded load factor (entries / buckets, e.g. ≤ 0.75) buckets stay short, so lookup is O(1) on average. When the load factor is exceeded the table grows (usually doubling) and rehashes everything — O(n) once, amortised O(1). Worst case is O(n) if many keys collide (bad hash or adversarial input). Tree maps give O(log n) and ordered iteration.

questions.title: How a load balancer distributes requests
questions.prompt: Explain how a load balancer distributes requests across servers. Compare at least two algorithms, explain health checks, and discuss layer 4 versus layer 7 balancing and session affinity.

expectedConcepts.label: Round robin, least connections, consistent hashing
Health checks remove unhealthy servers
Layer 4 (TCP) vs layer 7 (HTTP)
Session affinity trade-off
Load balancer itself must be redundant
Horizontal scaling behind the LB

questions.modelAnswer: A load balancer sits in front of a pool of servers and picks one per request/connection. Round robin is simple; least-connections adapts to uneven request cost; consistent hashing keeps a key on the same server (useful for caches). Health checks take failing servers out of rotation. Layer 4 balancers route TCP connections cheaply; layer 7 balancers understand HTTP and can route by path, terminate TLS and retry. Sticky sessions simplify stateful apps but unbalance load and complicate failover — prefer stateless servers with external session storage. The balancer itself needs redundancy (pairs with failover, or anycast/DNS). Because any server can handle any request, the pool scales horizontally: you scale out by adding servers behind the balancer.

questions.title: Design a URL shortener
questions.prompt: Design a URL-shortening service like a link shortener. Clarify requirements and scale, choose an ID generation strategy, describe the data model, the read path, caching, and the main trade-offs.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements & read-heavy ratio
ID generation: base62 counter vs hash
Redirect flow 301 vs 302
Cache hot links
Key-value store, partitioned by short code
Replication / availability
Bottleneck / abuse: rate limiting, ID range allocation
Consistency of newly created links
Trade-offs: predictability vs collision checks

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: create short link, redirect, optional custom alias/expiry; ~100:1 reads to writes. IDs: a distributed counter (pre-allocated ranges per server) encoded in base62 gives short collision-free codes but is guessable; hashing the URL needs collision checks. Store code → URL in a key-value store partitioned by code, replicated. Read path: client → LB → service → cache (Redis/CDN) → DB, returning 301 (cacheable) or 302 (if you need analytics). Bottlenecks: hot links (cache), write ID allocation (ranges), abuse (rate limits, malware checks). New links should be readable immediately — write-through cache or read from primary briefly.
researchContext: 301 is cached by browsers — fewer hits but lost analytics; 302 keeps every click visible.
Analytics should be asynchronous (queue) so it never slows redirects.

questions.title: Cache invalidation strategies
questions.prompt: Explain common cache invalidation and update strategies — such as TTL, write-through, write-behind and cache-aside. Describe the consistency problems each one can cause and how you would choose between them.

expectedConcepts.label: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
TTL expiry
Write-through vs write-behind
Stale reads / race conditions
Thundering herd / stampede
Freshness vs latency vs complexity
Invalidate (delete) rather than update on write

questions.modelAnswer: Cache-aside: read from cache, on miss load from DB and populate; on write update the DB then delete the cache key. TTLs bound staleness cheaply. Write-through writes cache and DB together (fresh reads, slower writes); write-behind writes the cache and flushes asynchronously (fast but risks data loss). Problems: races where an old value is re-cached after a delete, stale reads across regions, and stampedes when a hot key expires (use request coalescing, jittered TTLs, early refresh). Choose by how stale data may be and whether write latency or durability matters more.

questions.title: SQL versus NoSQL for a workload
questions.prompt: Compare SQL and NoSQL databases for a specific workload of your choice — for example, an e-commerce order system or a high-volume event log. Justify your choice by data model, query patterns, consistency needs and scaling.

expectedConcepts.label: Names a concrete workload and its access pattern
Relational: joins, schema, ACID transactions
NoSQL types: document, key-value, wide-column
Horizontal scaling / partitioning
Consistency model
Trade-offs and flexibility

questions.modelAnswer: Orders: strongly relational (customers, orders, line items, inventory), needs multi-row ACID transactions and ad-hoc reporting — PostgreSQL fits; scale with read replicas, partitioning by time, and later sharding by customer. Event log: append-heavy, queried by key and time range, no joins, tolerates eventual consistency — a wide-column store (Cassandra) or a log system partitions writes horizontally. Trade-off: NoSQL gives write scalability and flexible schemas but pushes joins/denormalisation and integrity checks into the application.

questions.title: Database sharding
questions.prompt: Explain database sharding. Compare range-based, hash-based and directory-based sharding, explain how you choose a shard key, and describe the operational problems sharding introduces.

expectedConcepts.label: Splits data across machines horizontally
Range vs hash vs directory
Shard key choice: cardinality, even distribution, query locality
Hot spots / skew
Cross-shard queries and transactions
Resharding / consistent hashing
Complexity cost vs alternatives (replicas, vertical scaling)

questions.modelAnswer: Sharding splits one logical table across machines by a shard key. Range sharding keeps ordered scans cheap but creates hot spots on recent keys; hash sharding spreads load evenly but loses range queries; directory sharding uses a lookup service for flexibility at the cost of an extra hop. A good key has high cardinality, even access and matches the dominant query (e.g. tenant_id). Problems: cross-shard joins and transactions (scatter-gather, 2PC or sagas), hot keys, rebalancing (consistent hashing / virtual nodes), global uniqueness, backups. Try indexes, caching, read replicas and vertical scaling first.

questions.title: A rate-limited API gateway
questions.prompt: Describe how you would design an API gateway that enforces per-client rate limits. Compare token bucket and sliding window algorithms, explain where counters live in a distributed deployment, and how clients learn they are throttled.

expectedConcepts.label: Gateway responsibilities: auth, routing, limits
Token bucket vs sliding window / fixed window
Shared counter store (e.g. Redis) with atomic ops
HTTP 429 + Retry-After headers
Latency / store becomes bottleneck; local approximation
Fail open vs fail closed if store is down
Accuracy vs performance

questions.modelAnswer: The gateway authenticates the client (API key/JWT), routes to services, and checks a limit before forwarding. Token bucket allows bursts up to bucket size while enforcing an average rate; sliding-window counters smooth fixed-window edge bursts. In a multi-node deployment counters live in a shared store (Redis with atomic INCR/Lua) keyed by client+window; to cut latency, nodes can keep local buckets and sync periodically, accepting approximate limits. Throttled requests get 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers. Decide whether to fail open (availability) or fail closed (protection) when the store is unavailable.

questions.title: Message queues and scaling consumers
questions.prompt: Explain why systems put a message queue between services, what delivery guarantees consumers get, and how you scale consumers with partitions and consumer groups without breaking per-key ordering.

expectedConcepts.label: Decoupling and buffering bursts
At-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once
Idempotent consumers
Partitions and consumer groups set parallelism
Ordering holds per key within a partition
Dead-letter queues and retries
Ordering versus parallelism; lag when consumers are slow

questions.modelAnswer: A queue decouples producers from consumers: the producer returns as soon as the message is stored, bursts are buffered, and each side can be deployed and scaled independently. Most brokers give at-least-once delivery, because a consumer can crash after processing but before acknowledging, so consumers must be idempotent, for example by deduplicating on a message ID. To scale, logs such as Kafka split a topic into partitions, and a consumer group assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the number of partitions; adding consumers beyond that leaves some idle. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so you pick a partition key, such as the order ID, that keeps related messages in order while spreading load; a skewed key creates a hot partition. Changing group membership triggers a rebalance that pauses consumption. If consumers are slower than producers, lag grows as a backlog; messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue after limited retries.

questions.title: Design a scalable notification service
questions.prompt: Design a notification service that sends push, email and SMS notifications to millions of users. Cover the API, user preferences, fan-out, retries, deduplication, third-party provider limits and monitoring.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements: channels, priority, preferences
Queue per channel / priority
API → validation → preferences → queue → workers → provider
Fan-out for broadcasts, horizontal workers
Retries with backoff, DLQ
Idempotency keys / deduplication
Provider rate limits
Delivery speed vs cost vs duplicates

questions.modelAnswer: API accepts {user/segment, template, data, priority, idempotency key}. It validates, checks user preferences and quiet hours, renders templates and enqueues per channel and priority (high-priority OTPs never wait behind marketing). Channel workers call providers (APNs/FCM, email, SMS) within their rate limits, retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, and send permanent failures to a DLQ. Broadcasts fan out in batches by partition. Dedup by idempotency key in a short-TTL store. Track sent/delivered/failed metrics per provider, and fail over to a secondary provider. The trade-off is between delivery latency, provider cost and duplicates: retries and provider failover improve delivery but can send a message twice, which the idempotency key limits.

questions.title: Idempotency in HTTP APIs
questions.prompt: Explain what idempotency means for HTTP APIs. Say which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition, why it matters for retries, and how you would make a POST payment endpoint safe to retry.

expectedConcepts.label: Same effect whether called once or many times
GET, PUT, DELETE idempotent; POST not
Retries after timeouts can duplicate work
Idempotency key stored with the result
Race between concurrent duplicates; key expiry

questions.modelAnswer: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. By HTTP semantics GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not. It matters because clients retry after timeouts without knowing whether the first request succeeded — a retried payment could charge twice. Fix: the client sends an Idempotency-Key; the server stores key → result in a table with a unique constraint, and on a repeat returns the stored response instead of reprocessing. Handle concurrent duplicates with the unique constraint or a lock, and expire keys after a window.

questions.title: Authentication versus authorization
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between authentication and authorization with a concrete example. Describe how sessions or tokens carry identity, and where authorization checks should happen.

expectedConcepts.label: Authentication = who you are
Authorization = what you may do
Sessions / JWT / OAuth carry identity
Authorization enforced server-side per resource
RBAC / ABAC models

questions.modelAnswer: Authentication proves identity (password + 2FA, SSO); authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action on a resource. Example: logging in to a bank app is authentication; being allowed to view only your own account is authorization. After login, identity travels as a session cookie or a signed token (JWT). Authorization must be enforced on the server for every request and every resource — checking ownership, roles (RBAC) or attributes — never just by hiding UI buttons. Broken object-level authorization is a top API vulnerability.

questions.title: Connection pooling and transaction isolation
questions.prompt: Explain why applications use database connection pools and how to size one. Then explain transaction isolation levels and one anomaly each level prevents.

expectedConcepts.label: Connections are expensive to create
Pool sizing; too large overloads DB
Read committed, repeatable read, serializable
Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, write skew
Stronger isolation costs throughput / retries

questions.modelAnswer: Opening a DB connection costs a TCP + TLS handshake, authentication and server-side memory, so pools keep a set of open connections and lend them out. Size small: roughly cores × 2-ish on the DB side and total across all app instances below the DB's max — oversized pools cause contention, not speed. Isolation: read committed prevents dirty reads; repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads (and in PostgreSQL snapshot isolation, phantoms); serializable prevents write skew. Stronger levels mean more locking or serialization failures that the app must retry.

questions.title: Modular monolith versus microservices
questions.prompt: Compare a modular monolith with a microservices architecture. When would you choose each, what operational costs do microservices add, and how would you migrate if needed?

expectedConcepts.label: Single deployable with enforced module boundaries
Independently deployable services, own data
Network calls, observability, distributed transactions
Team size / org structure drives choice
Strangler fig migration

questions.modelAnswer: A modular monolith is one deployable with strict internal module boundaries — simple deploys, in-process calls, one database, easy transactions. Microservices are independently deployable services that own their data, enabling independent scaling and team autonomy, at the cost of network latency and failures, distributed transactions (sagas), versioned APIs, and heavy observability needs. Start with a modular monolith for small teams; split a module when it needs independent scaling, release cadence or ownership. Migrate with the strangler-fig pattern, extracting one bounded context at a time.

questions.title: Retries, timeouts and circuit breakers
questions.prompt: Explain how timeouts, retries and circuit breakers work together when one service calls another. Describe exponential backoff with jitter and how retries can make an outage worse.

expectedConcepts.label: Timeouts bound waiting
Exponential backoff with jitter
Circuit breaker states: closed, open, half-open
Retry storms amplify load
Only retry idempotent / transient failures

questions.modelAnswer: Timeouts stop a caller from waiting forever and tying up threads. Retries recover from transient failures but only for idempotent operations, with a capped attempt count or retry budget. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads retries so clients don't synchronise. If a dependency is truly down, retries multiply load (retry storms, cascading failure). A circuit breaker tracks failures: closed lets calls through; after a threshold it opens and fails fast; after a cool-down it goes half-open to probe with a few requests.

questions.title: The React rendering lifecycle
questions.prompt: Explain how React renders and re-renders a component. Cover what triggers a render, the render and commit phases, reconciliation, and how effects fit in. Mention one common cause of unnecessary re-renders.

expectedConcepts.label: State/props/context changes trigger renders
Render phase vs commit phase
Virtual DOM diffing / reconciliation, keys
Effects run after commit
New object/function props; memoisation

questions.modelAnswer: A component renders when its state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context it reads changes. In the render phase React calls components (which must be pure) to produce a new element tree, then reconciles it against the previous tree — comparing types and keys — to compute minimal DOM changes. In the commit phase React applies those changes; layout effects run synchronously after, regular effects after paint, each with cleanup before the next run. Unnecessary renders often come from passing newly created objects/functions as props to memoised children; React.memo, useMemo/useCallback or restructuring state fixes it.

questions.title: Server-side versus client-side rendering
questions.prompt: Compare server-side rendering and client-side rendering. Discuss first-load performance, SEO, hydration, server cost and when static generation is the better option.

expectedConcepts.label: CSR: browser downloads JS and builds the page
SSR: server sends HTML per request
Hydration attaches interactivity
SEO and first contentful paint
Static generation / caching on CDN

questions.modelAnswer: CSR ships a mostly empty HTML page and a JS bundle; the browser fetches data and renders, so first paint waits for JS — fine for app-like dashboards behind login. SSR renders HTML on the server per request, giving fast first contentful paint and crawlable content, then hydration attaches event handlers (time-to-interactive still depends on JS). SSR costs server CPU and adds latency per request. Static generation renders at build time and serves from a CDN — best for content that changes rarely; incremental regeneration or streaming SSR sits in between.

questions.title: Browser event propagation
questions.prompt: Explain how events propagate in the browser DOM. Describe the capture and bubble phases, event delegation, and the difference between stopPropagation and preventDefault.

expectedConcepts.label: Capture → target → bubble
Event delegation on a parent
stopPropagation stops travel
preventDefault cancels browser default action
Pitfalls: stopping propagation breaks other listeners

questions.modelAnswer: An event travels from the window down to the target (capture phase), fires on the target, then bubbles back up through ancestors. Listeners run in bubble phase by default. Event delegation puts one listener on a parent and uses event.target to handle many children — efficient and works for dynamically added elements. stopPropagation stops the event from reaching further ancestors; preventDefault cancels the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form) without stopping propagation. Overusing stopPropagation breaks things like outside-click handlers.

questions.title: Frontend state management and caching
questions.prompt: Describe how you would organise state in a large frontend application. Distinguish server state from client UI state, and explain how data caching libraries handle staleness and refetching.

expectedConcepts.label: Server state vs UI state vs URL state
Colocate state; lift only when shared
Query caches: stale-while-revalidate, invalidation
Global stores for truly global state
Optimistic updates & rollback

questions.modelAnswer: Separate server state (data owned by the backend: cached, can be stale) from UI state (modal open, form inputs) and URL state (filters, page). Keep UI state local and lift it only when shared. Use a query cache (TanStack Query/SWR) for server state: keyed caching, stale-while-revalidate, background refetch, invalidation after mutations, and optimistic updates with rollback. Reserve a global store for genuinely global client state (auth session, theme) — putting server data in a global store recreates a cache badly.

questions.title: Frontend performance bottlenecks
questions.prompt: Explain the most common frontend performance bottlenecks and how you would diagnose them. Mention Core Web Vitals, bundle size, main-thread work and rendering cost.

expectedConcepts.label: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS
Bundle size, code splitting
Long tasks block the main thread
Layout thrashing / excessive re-renders
Measure with DevTools / Lighthouse / RUM
Fixes add complexity; optimise only what you measured

questions.modelAnswer: Measure first: Lighthouse for lab data, real-user monitoring for field Core Web Vitals (LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness, CLS for visual stability). Common causes: large JS bundles (code-split routes, tree-shake, drop heavy libs), unoptimised images and fonts (responsive sizes, preloading), long main-thread tasks (break up work, web workers), layout thrashing from interleaved reads/writes, and excessive React re-renders or huge lists (memoisation, virtualisation). Fix the biggest measured bottleneck, then re-measure. Every fix has a price: code splitting adds requests and loading states, and memoisation adds complexity, so optimise only what measurement shows matters.

questions.title: How languages manage memory
questions.prompt: Compare the main ways programming languages manage memory: manual allocation, reference counting, tracing garbage collection and Rust-style ownership. Give the trade-offs of each and a language that uses it.

expectedConcepts.label: Manual, reference counting, tracing GC, ownership
Mark and sweep, generational GC, RAII, smart pointers
Pauses, overhead, predictability, productivity
Leaks, cycles, dangling pointers, double free

questions.modelAnswer: Manual management (malloc and free in C, new and delete in C++) gives full control and no runtime overhead, but risks leaks, double frees and use-after-free; modern C++ reduces this with RAII and smart pointers. Reference counting (Swift, CPython, C++ shared_ptr) frees an object as soon as its count reaches zero, which is predictable, but every copy updates a counter, and cycles are never freed without help such as weak references or a cycle collector. Tracing garbage collection (Java, Go, C#, JavaScript) periodically marks objects reachable from roots and frees the rest. It handles cycles and is productive, but uses extra memory and introduces pauses, which modern concurrent and generational collectors keep short. Rust's ownership frees each value deterministically when its owner goes out of scope, checked at compile time, so there are no GC pauses or counters, at the cost of a stricter programming model.

questions.title: Static vs dynamic, strong vs weak typing
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between static and dynamic typing, and between strong and weak typing. Give examples of languages, and the trade-offs for large codebases.

expectedConcepts.label: Static: checked before running; dynamic: checked at runtime
Static/dynamic, strong/weak, type inference, implicit conversion
Refactoring, tooling and documentation vs prototyping speed
Runtime type errors; gradual typing with type hints

questions.modelAnswer: Static typing checks types before the program runs (C++, Go, Rust, Java, TypeScript); dynamic typing checks them at runtime, because types belong to values (Python, JavaScript, Ruby). Strong versus weak describes how much implicit conversion happens, and it is a spectrum: Python is dynamic but fairly strong, since "1" + 1 raises an error, while JavaScript coerces it to "11". Static types catch many bugs earlier, document intent and enable safe refactoring and autocompletion in large codebases, and type inference keeps them from being verbose. Dynamic typing is quicker for prototypes and scripts, but type errors appear at runtime and you need more tests. Gradual typing, such as Python type hints with mypy or TypeScript over JavaScript, offers a middle ground.

questions.title: Overfitting and regularization
questions.prompt: Explain overfitting in machine learning, how you detect it, and at least three ways to reduce it. Explain how L2 regularization works intuitively.

expectedConcepts.label: Model memorises training noise, fails to generalise
Gap between training and validation error
More data, simpler model, early stopping, dropout, augmentation
L2 penalises large weights
Bias-variance trade-off

questions.modelAnswer: Overfitting is when a model fits noise in the training data and performs worse on unseen data. Detect it with a held-out validation set: training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises. Remedies: more or augmented data, a simpler model, regularisation, dropout, early stopping, cross-validation. L2 regularisation adds λ·Σw² to the loss, pushing weights toward small values so the model can't rely on extreme weights to fit individual points — trading a little bias for lower variance. Too much regularisation causes underfitting.

questions.title: Classification versus clustering
questions.prompt: Compare classification and clustering. Explain supervised versus unsupervised learning, give an algorithm and a real use case for each, and explain how you evaluate each.

expectedConcepts.label: Classification is supervised (labels)
Clustering is unsupervised (no labels)
Algorithms: logistic regression/trees vs k-means/DBSCAN
Metrics: accuracy/precision/recall vs silhouette
Use cases: spam detection vs customer segmentation

questions.modelAnswer: Classification is supervised: you learn a mapping from features to known labels (spam vs not spam) with algorithms like logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees, evaluated on held-out data with precision, recall, F1 or ROC-AUC. Clustering is unsupervised: no labels, you group similar points (customer segmentation) with k-means or DBSCAN; evaluation is harder — silhouette score, cluster stability, and whether segments are useful to the business.

questions.title: Attention in transformers
questions.prompt: Explain the attention mechanism in transformers. Describe queries, keys and values, why attention is computed in parallel, what multiple heads add, and the cost as sequence length grows.

expectedConcepts.label: Queries, keys, values
Softmax of scaled dot products gives weights
Parallel over tokens unlike RNNs
Multi-head attention captures different relations
Quadratic cost in sequence length

questions.modelAnswer: Each token is projected into a query, a key and a value. A token's attention weights are the softmax of its query's dot products with all keys, scaled by √d; its output is the weighted sum of values — so each token gathers information from the tokens most relevant to it. All positions are computed at once with matrix multiplications, unlike sequential RNNs, which is why transformers train efficiently on GPUs. Multiple heads let the model attend to different relations (syntax, coreference) in parallel subspaces. Cost is O(n²) in sequence length for compute and memory, which motivates techniques such as FlashAttention, sparse attention and KV caching at inference.

questions.title: Embeddings and retrieval-augmented generation
questions.prompt: Explain what embeddings are and how retrieval-augmented generation uses them. Walk through the RAG pipeline, explain chunking, and describe common failure modes and how you would evaluate the system.

expectedConcepts.label: Vectors where similar meaning is close
Chunk → embed → index → retrieve top-k → prompt
Cosine similarity / ANN search
Grounds answers in sources, reduces hallucination
Failure modes: bad chunks, irrelevant retrieval, stale index
Evaluate retrieval recall and answer faithfulness

questions.modelAnswer: An embedding model maps text to a vector so that semantically similar texts land close together (cosine similarity). RAG: split documents into chunks, embed them, store vectors in an index; at query time embed the question, retrieve the top-k nearest chunks (approximate nearest-neighbour search), optionally rerank, and put them in the LLM prompt with instructions to answer from them and cite. This grounds answers in current, private data. Failure modes: chunks too big or too small, retrieval missing exact terms (use hybrid keyword + vector search), irrelevant context confusing the model, stale indexes. Evaluate retrieval recall@k and answer faithfulness on a labelled question set.

questions.title: Model training versus inference
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between training and inference for a neural network. Compare compute, memory, latency requirements and hardware, and mention techniques used to make inference cheaper.

expectedConcepts.label: Training: forward + backward pass, update weights
Inference: forward pass only with fixed weights
Training stores activations and optimizer state
Inference optimised for latency/throughput
Quantization, distillation, pruning, caching

questions.modelAnswer: Training runs forward passes, computes loss, backpropagates gradients and updates weights with an optimizer over many epochs; it needs memory for activations, gradients and optimizer state and is throughput-bound, usually on GPU clusters. Inference runs only the forward pass with frozen weights to make predictions; it is latency- and cost-sensitive and runs on GPUs, CPUs or edge devices. Cheaper inference: quantisation (int8/int4), distillation into smaller models, pruning, request batching, KV caching for LLMs, and compiled runtimes.

questions.title: Why LLMs hallucinate
questions.prompt: Explain why large language models sometimes produce confident but false statements. Describe how training and decoding contribute to this, and list practical mitigations for a production application.

expectedConcepts.label: Trained to predict plausible next tokens, not truth
Gaps / outdated training data
Sampling/temperature effects
Mitigations: RAG, citations, tool use, abstaining
Evaluation and human review for high stakes

questions.modelAnswer: LLMs are trained to produce likely continuations of text; fluency is rewarded, not verified truth. When the training data lacks or conflicts on a fact — or it is past the cutoff — the model can still generate a plausible-sounding answer, and sampling at higher temperature increases variety (and errors). Mitigations: ground answers with retrieval and require citations, use tools for facts and calculations, constrain outputs with schemas, let the model say it doesn't know, evaluate on a test set, and keep humans reviewing high-stakes outputs.

questions.title: How database indexes work
questions.prompt: Explain how a B-tree index speeds up queries. Describe what a composite index is, why column order matters, and the costs of adding indexes.

expectedConcepts.label: B-tree: sorted, balanced, O(log n) lookups
Avoids full table scans
Composite index and leftmost prefix
Write overhead and storage
Use EXPLAIN to verify

questions.modelAnswer: A B-tree index stores keys in sorted order in a balanced tree of pages, so the database finds a value in O(log n) page reads instead of scanning every row, and can also serve range queries and ORDER BY. A composite index on (a, b) is sorted by a, then b — it helps queries filtering on a, or a and b, but not b alone (the leftmost-prefix rule); put equality columns before range columns. Every index slows inserts/updates and uses storage, so add indexes for real query patterns and verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

questions.title: ACID transactions
questions.prompt: Explain each letter of ACID with a concrete example, such as a bank transfer. Describe how a database typically implements atomicity and durability.

expectedConcepts.label: Atomicity: all or nothing
Consistency: constraints hold
Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere
Durability: committed data survives crashes
Write-ahead log implements atomicity/durability
Bank transfer example
Stricter isolation and durability reduce throughput

questions.modelAnswer: Bank transfer of ₹500 from A to B. Atomicity: both the debit and the credit happen, or neither (rollback on failure). Consistency: constraints hold before and after — balances never negative, total money conserved. Isolation: two concurrent transfers behave as if run one after another, according to the isolation level. Durability: once committed, the transfer survives a crash. Databases implement atomicity and durability with a write-ahead log: changes are appended and fsynced to the log before commit is acknowledged, and recovery replays or undoes log records. These guarantees are not free: stricter isolation and synchronous durability reduce throughput and add latency, which is why many databases default to a weaker level such as read committed.

questions.title: What happens when you type a URL
questions.prompt: Explain what happens, step by step, between typing a URL into a browser and seeing the page. Cover DNS, TCP and TLS, the HTTP request, and rendering.

expectedConcepts.label: DNS resolution
TCP handshake
TLS handshake and certificates
HTTP request/response
Parsing HTML, CSS, JS and rendering
Caching / CDN along the way

questions.modelAnswer: The browser parses the URL, checks its caches, then resolves the domain via DNS (browser/OS cache → recursive resolver → root, TLD, authoritative servers) to an IP. It opens a TCP connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) — or QUIC for HTTP/3 — and performs a TLS handshake, verifying the server certificate and agreeing keys. It sends an HTTP GET; the request may hit a CDN or load balancer before the origin. The response HTML is parsed into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM, scripts run, further resources are fetched, then layout and paint display the page.

questions.title: TCP versus UDP
questions.prompt: Compare TCP and UDP. Explain reliability, ordering, congestion control and connection setup, and give applications that suit each protocol.

expectedConcepts.label: TCP: reliable, ordered, retransmission
UDP: connectionless datagrams, no guarantees
Congestion and flow control
Head-of-line blocking; latency
Apps: web/DB vs video calls/games/DNS; QUIC

questions.modelAnswer: TCP sets up a connection with a handshake and gives a reliable, ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission, plus flow and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams with no handshake, ordering or retransmission — lower latency and overhead. TCP suits web, APIs, databases and file transfer; UDP suits real-time voice/video and games (late data is useless), DNS lookups, and QUIC/HTTP3, which builds its own reliability over UDP to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.

questions.title: Processes versus threads
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a process and a thread. Cover memory isolation, context-switch cost, communication between them and failure isolation.

expectedConcepts.label: Processes have separate address spaces
Threads share memory within a process
Context switch cost
IPC vs shared memory synchronisation
Failure isolation: crashing thread kills process

questions.modelAnswer: A process is a running program with its own virtual address space, file descriptors and resources; a thread is an execution path inside a process sharing that memory. Threads communicate cheaply through shared memory but need synchronisation (locks, atomics) to avoid races; processes communicate via IPC (pipes, sockets, shared-memory segments). Thread switches within a process are cheaper because the address space (page tables, TLB) stays. Processes give failure isolation — a crashing thread takes down its whole process — which is why browsers run tabs in separate processes.

questions.title: Virtual memory and paging
questions.prompt: Explain virtual memory. Describe pages, page tables, the TLB, page faults, and why virtual memory helps both isolation and efficiency.

expectedConcepts.label: Virtual addresses mapped to physical frames
Pages and page tables
TLB caches translations
Page faults and swapping
Isolation, overcommit, shared libraries, copy-on-write

questions.modelAnswer: Each process sees its own virtual address space; the MMU translates virtual pages (typically 4 KB) to physical frames using per-process page tables, and the TLB caches recent translations because walking page tables is slow. If a page isn't resident, a page fault traps to the OS, which loads it (demand paging) or kills the process on an invalid access. Benefits: isolation and protection between processes, programs larger than physical RAM, shared libraries mapped once, copy-on-write after fork. Costs: TLB misses and thrashing when the working set exceeds RAM.

questions.title: Containers versus virtual machines
questions.prompt: Explain how containers differ from virtual machines. Cover isolation mechanisms such as namespaces and cgroups, image layers, startup time and security trade-offs.

expectedConcepts.label: Containers share the host kernel; VMs have their own
Namespaces for isolation, cgroups for limits
Image layers and caching
Fast startup, small footprint
Weaker isolation boundary

questions.modelAnswer: A VM virtualises hardware via a hypervisor and runs a full guest OS kernel — strong isolation, slower boot, more overhead. A container is a process tree on the host kernel isolated with namespaces (PID, network, mount, user) and resource-limited by cgroups; images are stacks of read-only layers built from a Dockerfile and cached. Containers start in milliseconds to seconds and pack densely, but share the kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape — mitigated with non-root users, seccomp, or sandboxed runtimes like gVisor/Firecracker microVMs.

questions.title: The CAP theorem
questions.prompt: Explain the CAP theorem accurately. Describe what happens during a network partition, give an example of a CP system and an AP system, and explain what PACELC adds.

expectedConcepts.label: Consistency, availability, partition tolerance
During a partition you choose C or A
CP and AP examples
Not 'pick any two' in normal operation
PACELC: latency vs consistency without partitions

questions.modelAnswer: CAP says that when a network partition occurs, a distributed data store must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, linearizability) and availability (every request to a non-failed node gets a response). Partitions are unavoidable, so 'pick two of three' is misleading — the choice only bites during a partition. CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper) refuse some requests to stay consistent; AP systems (Cassandra, Dynamo-style) keep answering and reconcile later. PACELC adds: Else, in normal operation, you trade latency against consistency.

questions.title: Consensus with Raft
questions.prompt: Explain what distributed consensus solves and how Raft achieves it. Cover leader election, log replication, majorities, and what happens when the leader fails.

expectedConcepts.label: Agree on a single ordered log despite failures
Leader election with terms and randomized timeouts
Leader appends and replicates entries
Commit after majority acknowledges; quorum
Leader failure → new election; tolerate f of 2f+1

questions.modelAnswer: Consensus lets a cluster agree on one ordered sequence of commands despite crashes, giving a replicated state machine (used by etcd, Consul). Raft elects a leader: followers that hear no heartbeat within a randomised timeout become candidates, increment the term and request votes; a majority makes a leader. Clients send commands to the leader, which appends them to its log and replicates via AppendEntries; an entry is committed once a majority stores it. If the leader fails, a new election picks a node with an up-to-date log. With 2f+1 nodes Raft tolerates f failures; a minority partition cannot commit, preventing split brain.

questions.title: Designing a good REST API
questions.prompt: Explain the principles you follow when designing a REST API. Cover resource naming, HTTP methods and status codes, pagination, versioning and error format.

expectedConcepts.label: Nouns for resources, hierarchy
Methods and status codes
Cursor vs offset pagination
Versioning and backward compatibility
Consistent error format

questions.modelAnswer: Model resources as plural nouns (/orders/{id}/items) and use methods for actions: GET reads, POST creates (201 + Location), PUT replaces, PATCH updates partially, DELETE removes. Use precise status codes — 400 validation, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 409 conflict, 429 throttled. Paginate collections; cursor pagination is stable under inserts, offset is simple but slow and inconsistent on large sets. Evolve additively and version breaking changes (/v2 or header) with deprecation notices. Return a consistent error body with a machine-readable code, message and field details.

questions.title: XSS, CSRF and SQL injection
questions.prompt: Explain cross-site scripting, cross-site request forgery and SQL injection. For each, describe how the attack works and the primary defence.

expectedConcepts.label: XSS: injected script runs in victim's browser
Escape output, CSP
CSRF: forged request with victim's cookies
SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens
SQL injection via string concatenation
Parameterised queries
No single defence suffices; strict rules can break features

questions.modelAnswer: XSS: attacker-controlled input is rendered as HTML/JS and runs in other users' browsers, stealing tokens or acting as them. Defence: context-aware output encoding (frameworks escape by default), avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and add a Content-Security-Policy. CSRF: a malicious site makes the victim's browser send an authenticated request using its cookies. Defence: SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, checking Origin. SQL injection: user input concatenated into a query changes its structure. Defence: parameterised queries/prepared statements, least-privilege DB users. No single control is enough: escaping can be bypassed through unsafe APIs, and strict CSP or SameSite rules can break legitimate features, so layer the defences.

questions.title: Layered and hexagonal architecture
questions.prompt: Explain layered or hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture. Why separate domain logic from infrastructure, how does dependency inversion enable it, and when is it overkill?

expectedConcepts.label: Domain logic independent of frameworks
Ports (interfaces) and adapters
Dependency inversion: dependencies point inward
Testability and swapping infrastructure
Overkill for simple CRUD

questions.modelAnswer: Hexagonal architecture keeps business rules in a core that knows nothing about HTTP, databases or queues. The core defines ports (interfaces such as OrderRepository); adapters implement them (Postgres repository, REST controller). Dependency inversion makes dependencies point inward — infrastructure depends on the domain, not the reverse — so you can unit-test the core with in-memory fakes and swap infrastructure. For simple CRUD apps the extra layers add indirection and boilerplate without much benefit.

questions.title: The testing pyramid
questions.prompt: Explain the testing pyramid and what goes wrong with an 'ice-cream cone' suite made mostly of end-to-end tests. When does a different shape, such as the testing trophy, make more sense?

expectedConcepts.label: Many unit, fewer integration, few end-to-end tests
Ice-cream cone: slow, flaky, hard to diagnose
Trophy: integration-heavy when logic lives in wiring
Flakiness from timing, shared state and network

questions.modelAnswer: The pyramid recommends a wide base of fast, isolated unit tests, fewer integration tests that use real collaborators such as the database, and a small number of end-to-end tests through the real UI. Higher levels give more realistic confidence but run slower, cost more to maintain and fail for more reasons. An ice-cream cone inverts this: most coverage comes from end-to-end tests, often manual or UI-driven. The suite takes hours, so feedback arrives too late; tests are flaky because of timing assumptions, sleeps, shared test data and real network calls; and when one fails, it is hard to diagnose which of many components broke. The testing trophy is a reasonable alternative for applications whose logic lives mostly in wiring, such as a web app gluing together a framework, a database and APIs: put static analysis at the bottom, then a few unit tests for real logic, and most effort into integration tests, which catch the bugs that actually happen there. The right shape follows where your bugs come from.

questions.title: Profiling a slow service
questions.prompt: A service's p99 latency doubled after a release. Explain how you would investigate, from metrics to profiling, and name common root causes you would check.

expectedConcepts.label: Start with metrics: p50 vs p99, throughput, saturation
Compare against the release diff / rollback
CPU profiling / flame graphs
GC pauses, lock contention, N+1 queries, cache misses
Distributed tracing to find the slow span

questions.modelAnswer: Confirm the regression in metrics: which percentiles moved, for which endpoints, and whether throughput, CPU, memory or queue depth changed. Correlate with the release; if impact is high, roll back first. Use distributed tracing to locate the slow span, then profile that component (sampling CPU profiler, flame graphs, allocation profiles). Tail latency often comes from GC pauses, lock contention, a new N+1 query or missing index, cache invalidation causing misses, synchronous calls added to the hot path, or retries. Fix, then verify with a load test comparing before and after.

questions.title: Batch versus stream processing
questions.prompt: Compare batch and stream processing for data pipelines. Explain latency, correctness concerns such as late events and exactly-once processing, and when you would choose each.

expectedConcepts.label: Batch processes bounded data periodically
Streams process unbounded events continuously
Windowing and event time vs processing time
Late/out-of-order events and exactly-once
Tools: Spark, Flink, Kafka

questions.modelAnswer: Batch jobs process bounded datasets on a schedule (nightly Spark jobs) — simple, easy to reprocess, but results are hours old. Stream processing handles an unbounded flow of events continuously (Kafka + Flink) with seconds of latency, using windows over event time and watermarks to handle late, out-of-order data. Exactly-once results require checkpointing plus idempotent or transactional sinks. Choose streaming for fraud detection or live dashboards; batch for reporting, backfills and heavy aggregations — many systems combine both.

questions.title: How a compiler works
questions.prompt: Explain the main stages of a compiler, from source code to machine code. Describe lexing, parsing, semantic analysis, intermediate representation, optimization and code generation.

expectedConcepts.label: Lexing into tokens
Parsing into an AST
Semantic analysis / type checking
Intermediate representation and optimisation
Code generation, register allocation, linking
Optimisation speeds code but slows builds and debugging

questions.modelAnswer: The lexer turns characters into tokens; the parser builds an abstract syntax tree according to the grammar; semantic analysis resolves names with symbol tables and checks types. The front end lowers the AST into an intermediate representation (e.g. LLVM IR in SSA form), where target-independent optimisations run — constant folding, inlining, dead-code elimination, loop optimisations. The back end selects instructions, allocates registers and emits machine code into object files, which the linker combines with libraries into an executable. More optimisation passes give faster code but slow compilation and make debugging harder, which is why debug builds skip most of them.

questions.title: Git merge versus rebase
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase. Describe what each does to history, when you would use each, and the golden rule of rebasing.

expectedConcepts.label: Merge creates a merge commit, preserves history
Rebase replays commits onto a new base
Don't rebase shared/public branches
Rebase local feature branches, merge into main
Conflicts resolved per commit during rebase

questions.modelAnswer: git merge combines branches by creating a merge commit with two parents, preserving exactly what happened. git rebase replays your commits on top of another base, producing new commits and a linear history. Use rebase (often interactive) to tidy a local feature branch before review; merge (or squash-merge) into main. Golden rule: never rebase commits others have already pulled — it rewrites history and forces them to reconcile; if you must, use --force-with-lease.

questions.title: Design an LRU cache with O(1) operations
questions.prompt: Design a least-recently-used cache that supports get and put in O(1) time. Explain the data structures, walk through get, put and eviction step by step, and discuss edge cases and how you would make it thread-safe.

expectedConcepts.label: Hash map to nodes of a doubly linked list
Move to front on access; evict from tail
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: capacity zero/one, updating an existing key
Alternatives: ordered dict, LFU, sharded locks

questions.modelAnswer: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency, using sentinel head and tail nodes to avoid null checks. get: look up the node in the map; if absent return miss; otherwise unlink it and insert it after head, then return the value - O(1). put: if the key exists, update the value and move it to the front; otherwise create a node, insert at the front and add to the map; if size exceeds capacity remove the node before tail and delete its key from the map - which is why nodes store their key. All operations are O(1) time; space is O(capacity). Edge cases: capacity 0 (never store), capacity 1, put on an existing key must not evict, and repeated gets. Alternatives: LinkedHashMap / OrderedDict give this for free; LFU evicts by frequency; CLOCK approximates LRU with less bookkeeping. For thread-safety a single mutex is simplest but becomes a bottleneck; shard the cache by key hash with a lock per shard.

questions.title: Union-find (disjoint set union)
questions.prompt: Explain the union-find data structure. Walk through find and union, path compression and union by rank or size, and their combined complexity. Give two problems it solves well and explain when you would use BFS or DFS instead.

expectedConcepts.label: Parent array; find root, union by linking roots
Path compression and union by rank/size
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: self-union, already connected, dynamic element ids
Uses (Kruskal, connected components, cycle detection) vs BFS/DFS

questions.modelAnswer: Union-find keeps a parent array where each set is a tree whose root is its representative. find(x) follows parent pointers to the root; union(a, b) finds both roots and, if different, links one under the other. Without optimisations trees can degrade to chains (O(n) per find). Union by rank or size attaches the shorter/smaller tree under the larger, keeping height O(log n); path compression makes every node on a find path point directly at the root. Together, m operations take O(m * alpha(n)) amortised, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant. Space is O(n). Edge cases: union of elements already in the same set (that is how you detect a cycle in an undirected graph), and mapping arbitrary keys to indices with a hash map. Classic uses: Kruskal's MST, counting connected components while edges stream in, detecting redundant connections, grouping accounts by shared emails. BFS/DFS are better when the graph is static and you need paths or distances; union-find cannot handle edge deletions efficiently.

questions.title: Dijkstra's algorithm and when it fails
questions.prompt: Explain Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm step by step with a priority queue. Prove informally why it is correct, give its complexity, explain why negative edge weights break it, and compare it with BFS, Bellman-Ford and A*.

expectedConcepts.label: Pop min-distance node, relax edges
Popped distance is final because weights are non-negative
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: negative edges, unreachable nodes, stale heap entries
BFS for unweighted, Bellman-Ford for negatives, A* with heuristic

questions.modelAnswer: Set dist[source] = 0 and all others to infinity, and push (0, source) into a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the node with the smallest tentative distance; if the popped distance is larger than dist[u] it is a stale entry, skip it. Otherwise relax each edge u->v: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push it. Correctness: with non-negative weights, when u is popped no other path can be shorter, because every alternative path must leave the settled set through a node whose distance is already at least dist[u], and adding non-negative edges cannot make it smaller. With a binary heap the cost is O((V + E) log V), space O(V + E). A negative edge breaks the invariant - a settled node could later be reached more cheaply - so use Bellman-Ford, O(VE), which also detects negative cycles. For unweighted graphs plain BFS is O(V + E); with 0/1 weights use a deque (0-1 BFS). A* adds an admissible heuristic to guide the search toward a single target, as in maps and games. Unreachable nodes stay at infinity.

questions.title: Topological sort and cycle detection
questions.prompt: Explain topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph using both Kahn's algorithm and DFS. How does each detect a cycle, what are the complexities, and where does this come up in real systems such as build tools or course scheduling?

expectedConcepts.label: Kahn's: in-degree zero queue
DFS post-order reversed, three colours
Time complexity
Space complexity
Cycle detection; multiple valid orders; disconnected graphs
Real uses: build systems, package managers, schedulers

questions.modelAnswer: A topological order lists every node before all nodes it points to; it exists only for DAGs. Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, enqueue all zero-in-degree nodes, repeatedly pop one, append it to the output and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, enqueuing any that hit zero. If the output has fewer than V nodes, the remainder are in a cycle. DFS version: mark nodes white/gray/black; on finishing a node (post-order) push it onto a list and reverse at the end; meeting a gray node means a back edge, i.e. a cycle. Both are O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space, though deep recursion can overflow the stack on long chains. Edge cases: disconnected components (start from every unvisited node), multiple valid orders (use a min-heap in Kahn's for the lexicographically smallest), and self-loops. Real uses: build systems and Makefiles ordering compilation, package managers resolving install order, task schedulers, spreadsheet recalculation and course prerequisites.

questions.title: Segment trees and Fenwick trees
questions.prompt: You need range sum queries and point updates on an array of a million numbers with a million operations. Explain why prefix sums are not enough, then explain a Fenwick tree and a segment tree, their complexities, and when you would need lazy propagation.

expectedConcepts.label: Prefix sums: O(1) query but O(n) update
Fenwick / BIT using lowest set bit
Segment tree: node stores aggregate of a range
Time complexity
Space complexity
Lazy propagation for range updates; non-invertible ops
Edge cases: 1-indexing, empty ranges, overflow

questions.modelAnswer: Prefix sums answer a range sum in O(1) but a single point update forces O(n) recomputation, so a million updates is 10^12 work. A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) stores at index i the sum of a block whose length is the lowest set bit of i (i & -i). Query prefix(i) by repeatedly adding tree[i] and stripping the lowest bit; update by adding to tree[i] and moving i += i & -i. Both are O(log n), memory O(n), and it is tiny to code, but it needs an invertible operation such as sum or XOR to answer arbitrary ranges. A segment tree is a binary tree where each node stores the aggregate (sum, min, max, gcd) of its range; queries combine O(log n) nodes and updates walk one root-to-leaf path, using about 2n-4n memory. For range updates (add 5 to all of [l, r]) use lazy propagation: store pending updates at nodes and push them down only when needed, keeping both operations O(log n). For static arrays with min/max queries a sparse table gives O(1) queries. Watch for 1-indexing in Fenwick trees, integer overflow on sums, and empty or reversed ranges.

questions.title: Tries for prefix search and autocomplete
questions.prompt: Explain the trie data structure and use it to build autocomplete that returns the top five completions for a prefix. Discuss insert and search complexity, memory usage, how to make top-k fast, and alternatives such as sorted arrays or ternary search trees.

expectedConcepts.label: Nodes per character with child links and end-of-word flag
Store top-k at each node or DFS with a heap
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: empty prefix, no match, unicode, case
Alternatives: sorted array + binary search, radix tree, TST

questions.modelAnswer: A trie stores strings character by character: each node has children (an array of 26 or a hash map) and a flag marking the end of a word. Insert and search are O(L) for a word of length L, independent of how many words are stored, and every node represents a prefix, so finding all words with a prefix means walking to the prefix node then exploring its subtree. For autocomplete top-5, a full DFS of the subtree can be huge for short prefixes, so precompute at each node the top 5 completions by frequency; queries become O(prefix length) and updates refresh the lists along the path. Memory is the main cost: one node per character with pointer arrays wastes space, so use hash-map children, a radix (compressed) tree that merges single-child chains, or a ternary search tree. Alternatives: a sorted array of words with binary search on the prefix range is compact and cache-friendly for static data. Edge cases: empty prefix, no matches, case folding and Unicode normalisation.

questions.title: The monotonic stack pattern
questions.prompt: Explain the monotonic stack pattern using "next greater element" and "largest rectangle in a histogram" as examples. Why is it linear time even though there is a loop inside a loop, and how do you recognise problems that need it?

expectedConcepts.label: Stack kept increasing/decreasing; pop while it violates order
Histogram: popped bar extends between new top and current index
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: equal heights, sentinel, empty stack
Brute force O(n^2), divide and conquer, recognising signals

questions.modelAnswer: A monotonic stack holds indices whose values are kept in sorted order. For next greater element, scan left to right; while the current value is greater than the value at the top index, pop that index and record the current value as its answer; then push the current index. For the largest rectangle in a histogram, keep an increasing stack of bar indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop the taller bar: its height is fixed and it can extend from just after the new stack top to just before the current index, so area = height * (i - top - 1). A sentinel bar of height 0 at the end flushes the stack. Although there is a while loop inside the for loop, each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total is O(n) amortised, with O(n) stack space. Equal values need a consistent rule (pop on >= or >) to avoid double-counting. Brute force is O(n^2); divide and conquer with a segment tree is O(n log n). Recognise it when each element needs its nearest greater or smaller neighbour: stock span, daily temperatures, trapping rain water, sum of subarray minimums.

questions.title: Finding the kth largest element
questions.prompt: Find the kth largest element in an unsorted array of n numbers. Compare sorting, a min-heap of size k, and quickselect. Give the time and space complexity of each, explain the worst case of quickselect and how to avoid it, and say which you would pick for a stream.

expectedConcepts.label: Min-heap of size k
Quickselect partitions and recurses into one side
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: duplicates, k out of range, already sorted input
Random pivot, median of medians, streams favour the heap

questions.modelAnswer: Sorting then indexing is O(n log n) time and simplest. A min-heap of size k: push each element and pop whenever the heap exceeds k; the root is the answer. That is O(n log k) time, O(k) space, and it works on a stream because it never needs the whole array. Quickselect uses quicksort's partition: pick a pivot, partition so larger elements are on one side, and recurse only into the side containing position k. Average time is O(n) because the work halves geometrically (n + n/2 + ...), with O(1) extra space if done in place, but a consistently bad pivot - e.g. first element on sorted input - gives O(n^2). Avoid it with a random pivot, introselect (fall back to a heap or median-of-medians, which guarantees O(n) worst case), and use three-way partitioning when there are many duplicates. Edge cases: k < 1 or k > n, all equal elements. For a one-off query on an array use quickselect; for a stream or when k is small use the heap.

questions.title: Running median of a data stream
questions.prompt: Design a structure that receives numbers one at a time and can return the median at any moment. Explain the two-heap approach, how you keep the heaps balanced, its complexity, and how you would handle a sliding window or very large value ranges.

expectedConcepts.label: Max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half
Rebalance so sizes differ by at most one
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: even count average, empty stream, overflow
Sliding window: lazy deletion or order-statistic tree; buckets for small ranges

questions.modelAnswer: Keep a max-heap containing the smaller half of the numbers and a min-heap containing the larger half. To add x: push it into the max-heap if it is at most the max-heap's top, otherwise into the min-heap; then rebalance by moving a top element across so the sizes differ by at most one (with the max-heap allowed to hold the extra one). The median is the max-heap top when the count is odd, or the average of both tops when it is even - beware integer overflow and decide on float versus integer division. Insertion is O(log n), finding the median is O(1), space O(n). For a sliding window you must also remove elements: heaps cannot delete arbitrary items cheaply, so use lazy deletion with a hash map of pending removals, or an order-statistic tree / two balanced multisets for O(log k) operations. If values come from a small range (e.g. ages 0-150), a counting array gives O(range) or better medians; for huge streams where exactness is not needed, use approximate quantile sketches such as t-digest.

questions.title: Merging k sorted lists
questions.prompt: Merge k sorted linked lists or arrays with N total elements into one sorted output. Compare merging one by one, a min-heap, and divide-and-conquer pairing, with complexities, then explain how the same idea is used in external sorting of data that does not fit in memory.

expectedConcepts.label: Heap holds the current head of each list
Pairwise divide and conquer merges
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: empty lists, k = 0, duplicates and stability
External merge sort: sorted runs on disk merged with a heap

questions.modelAnswer: Merging lists one at a time into an accumulator costs O(N * k), because early elements are re-scanned at every step. With a min-heap, push the first element of each non-empty list with its list index; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it to the output and push the next element from the same list. Each of the N elements is pushed and popped once at O(log k), so total time is O(N log k) with O(k) extra space. Divide and conquer pairs lists up and merges them in rounds - log k rounds each touching N elements - also O(N log k) with simple two-way merges and good cache behaviour. Edge cases: empty input, empty individual lists, ties (include the list index in the heap key for stability). The same idea powers external sorting: read chunks that fit in memory, sort each into a run on disk, then k-way merge the runs with a heap and buffered I/O. LSM-tree databases use k-way merges when compacting sorted files.

questions.title: 0/1 knapsack and its variants
questions.prompt: Explain the 0/1 knapsack problem and solve it with dynamic programming. Define the state and recurrence, explain the space optimisation to one dimension and why the loop direction matters, and contrast it with unbounded knapsack and the greedy fractional version.

expectedConcepts.label: dp[i][w] = best value using first i items with capacity w
Take or skip each item
Time complexity
Space complexity
Loop direction backwards for 0/1; zero weights; reconstructing items
Unbounded knapsack, fractional greedy, meet in the middle

questions.modelAnswer: Given n items with weight w_i and value v_i and capacity W, choose a subset to maximise value without exceeding W, each item used at most once. State: dp[i][c] = maximum value using the first i items with capacity c. Recurrence: dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c - w_i] + v_i if w_i <= c). Answer dp[n][W]. Time O(nW), which is pseudo-polynomial - fine when W is small, infeasible when W is a billion, because the problem is NP-hard in general. Space can drop to a single array of size W+1: for each item iterate c from W down to w_i; iterating backwards ensures dp[c - w_i] still holds the previous row so the item is not used twice. Iterating forwards gives the unbounded knapsack, where items can repeat. To reconstruct chosen items keep the 2D table or a decision bitmap. The fractional knapsack, where items can be split, is solved greedily by value-to-weight ratio, but greedy fails for 0/1. For large W but small n, meet-in-the-middle (2^(n/2)) or branch and bound helps.

questions.title: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n)
questions.prompt: Explain how to find the length of the longest increasing subsequence. Start with the O(n^2) dynamic programming solution, then explain the O(n log n) patience sorting approach with binary search, why the tails array works, and how to reconstruct the actual subsequence.

expectedConcepts.label: O(n^2) DP: dp[i] = LIS ending at i
tails[k] = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1
Time complexity
Space complexity
Strict vs non-decreasing, duplicates, tails is not the answer itself
Reconstruct with parent indices; related problems

questions.modelAnswer: Quadratic DP: dp[i] is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i, equal to 1 + max(dp[j]) over j < i with a[j] < a[i]; the answer is max dp[i]. That is O(n^2) time and O(n) space. Faster: maintain tails, where tails[k] is the smallest possible last element of any increasing subsequence of length k+1 seen so far. tails is always strictly increasing, so for each x binary-search the first position with tails[pos] >= x (lower_bound): replace it, or append if x is larger than everything. Keeping tails as small as possible leaves the most room for future elements; the final length of tails is the LIS length. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Caveats: tails is not itself a valid subsequence; for non-decreasing subsequences use upper_bound; to reconstruct, store for each element the index at its tails position and a parent pointer to the element at pos-1, then walk back from the last. Related problems: Russian-doll envelopes (sort by width ascending and height descending, then LIS on heights), box stacking, and longest chain.

questions.title: Edit distance (Levenshtein distance)
questions.prompt: Explain how to compute the edit distance between two strings with insertions, deletions and substitutions. Define the DP table and recurrence, walk through a small example, reduce the memory, and explain where edit distance is used and how diff tools differ.

expectedConcepts.label: dp[i][j] = distance between prefixes
Match or min of insert, delete, replace + 1
Time complexity
Space complexity
Base cases: empty string; equal strings; unicode
Uses: spell check, DNA alignment; Myers diff, Hirschberg, banded

questions.modelAnswer: Let dp[i][j] be the minimum edits to turn the first i characters of a into the first j characters of b. Base cases: dp[i][0] = i (delete everything) and dp[0][j] = j (insert everything). If a[i-1] == b[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)). Example: kitten to sitting is 3 - replace k with s, e with i, insert g. Time O(mn); since each row depends only on the previous one, space drops to two rows or one row plus a saved diagonal, O(min(m, n)). Reconstructing the actual edits needs the full table or Hirschberg's divide-and-conquer trick in linear space. If you only care whether distance is at most k, a banded DP computes only the diagonal band, O(k * n). Uses: spell correction, fuzzy search, DNA sequence alignment (with weighted costs). Diff tools usually compute a longest common subsequence with Myers' O(ND) algorithm, which is fast when files are similar. Handle Unicode by comparing code points or grapheme clusters, not bytes.

questions.title: Backtracking with N-Queens and subsets
questions.prompt: Explain backtracking as a technique using N-Queens and generating all subsets or permutations as examples. Describe the choose, explore, unchoose structure, how pruning works, the complexity, and how backtracking differs from dynamic programming.

expectedConcepts.label: Choose, explore, unchoose over a decision tree
Prune invalid partial states early
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: duplicates in input, copying the path, n = 0
Backtracking vs DP (overlapping subproblems), bitmasks

questions.modelAnswer: Backtracking explores a decision tree depth-first: at each level choose an option, recurse to explore, then undo the choice so the shared state is clean for the next option. Subsets: at index i either include nums[i] or not, giving 2^n leaves; permutations: choose any unused element at each position, n! leaves. N-Queens places one queen per row; for each column check whether the column or either diagonal is attacked using three sets (or bitmasks for col, row - col and row + col), and only recurse if safe. Pruning - rejecting a partial placement as soon as it violates a constraint - is what makes backtracking far faster than generating everything and filtering, though worst cases remain exponential (O(2^n * n) for subsets with copying, O(n!) for permutations). Extra space is the recursion depth, O(n), plus output. Edge cases: duplicates in the input (sort and skip equal siblings), forgetting to copy the current path when recording a result, and n = 0. DP applies when subproblems overlap and you need a count or optimum; backtracking applies when you must enumerate actual configurations or the state cannot be compressed.

questions.title: String matching: KMP and Rabin-Karp
questions.prompt: Find all occurrences of a pattern of length m in a text of length n. Explain why the naive approach can be O(nm), then explain the KMP failure function and Rabin-Karp rolling hashes, with complexities, collision handling and when you would choose each.

expectedConcepts.label: Naive restarts at each position: O(nm)
KMP failure (prefix) function: longest proper prefix that is also suffix
Rabin-Karp rolling hash updated in O(1)
Time complexity
Space complexity
Hash collisions: verify matches, double hashing; empty pattern
Choose: multiple patterns (Aho-Corasick), Z-algorithm, Boyer-Moore

questions.modelAnswer: Naively you compare the pattern at each of n positions, up to m characters each, so text "aaaa...ab" with pattern "aaab" costs O(nm). KMP precomputes the failure (prefix) function: for each position in the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. On a mismatch, instead of moving the text pointer back you shift the pattern to that length, so the text pointer never retreats; total time O(n + m), space O(m). Rabin-Karp hashes the pattern and each window of the text with a polynomial hash modulo a large prime; sliding the window removes the outgoing character and adds the incoming one in O(1).
