Expected time O(n + m), but because different strings can share a hash you must verify each hash match character by character (or use two moduli), so adversarial inputs can push it to O(nm). Rabin-Karp shines for many patterns of the same length or 2D matching; KMP gives guaranteed linear time. Aho-Corasick generalises KMP to many patterns at once (virus scanners, keyword filters); Boyer-Moore skips ahead and is fast in practice for large alphabets (grep); the Z-algorithm is an easy alternative to KMP. Handle the empty pattern and overlapping matches explicitly.

questions.title: Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal versus Prim
questions.prompt: Explain what a minimum spanning tree is and the cut property that makes greedy algorithms work. Walk through Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms, their complexities and data structures, and when each is the better choice. Give a real application.

expectedConcepts.label: Spanning tree with minimum total weight; V-1 edges
Cut property justifies greedy choice
Kruskal: sort edges, union-find to skip cycles
Prim: grow from a vertex with a priority queue
Time complexity
Space complexity
Sparse vs dense graphs; disconnected graph gives a forest; applications

questions.modelAnswer: A minimum spanning tree connects all V vertices of a weighted undirected graph using V-1 edges with the smallest possible total weight. Cut property: for any partition of the vertices into two sets, the lightest edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST - so greedily picking safe light edges is optimal. Kruskal: sort all edges by weight, scan them, and add an edge if its endpoints are in different components according to union-find; stop at V-1 edges. Cost O(E log E) dominated by sorting. Prim: start from any vertex, keep a min-heap of edges leaving the tree, repeatedly add the lightest edge to a new vertex. O(E log V) with a binary heap, or O(V^2) with an adjacency matrix and no heap, which is better for dense graphs. Kruskal is natural for sparse graphs or when edges are already sorted or streamed; Prim suits dense graphs. If the graph is disconnected, Kruskal naturally yields a minimum spanning forest. Applications: designing cheapest cable or road networks, approximation for the travelling salesman problem, and single-linkage clustering by removing the heaviest MST edges. Boruvka's algorithm parallelises well.

questions.title: Interval problems and greedy scheduling
questions.prompt: Explain how to solve interval problems: merging overlapping intervals, finding the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings, and the minimum number of meeting rooms. What do you sort by in each case, why is the greedy choice correct, and what are the complexities?

expectedConcepts.label: Merge: sort by start, extend current end
Max non-overlapping: sort by end, pick earliest finishing
Min rooms: min-heap of end times or sweep line
Time complexity
Space complexity
Touching endpoints inclusive vs exclusive, empty input
Alternatives: weighted intervals need DP; interval trees

questions.modelAnswer: Merge intervals: sort by start time; walk through, and if the next interval starts at or before the current end, extend the end to the max of both ends; otherwise emit the current and start a new one. O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n). Maximum non-overlapping meetings (activity selection): sort by end time and greedily pick each meeting that starts after the last chosen end. Exchange argument: the earliest-finishing meeting leaves the most room, and any optimal solution can swap its first meeting for it without losing count. Minimum meeting rooms: sort by start and keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use; if the earliest end is at or before the new start, reuse that room (pop), then push the new end; the heap's maximum size is the answer. Equivalent sweep line: +1 at each start, -1 at each end, process ends before starts at the same time, and track the maximum. All are O(n log n) time with O(n) space. Decide whether [1,2] and [2,3] overlap. If meetings have weights (maximise value, not count), greedy fails - use DP with binary search. For many dynamic overlap queries, use an interval tree.

questions.title: Amortised analysis
questions.prompt: Explain amortised analysis. Use a dynamic array that doubles when full to show why push is O(1) amortised, explain the aggregate, accounting and potential methods, and contrast amortised with average-case and worst-case bounds. Why does growing by a constant amount fail?

expectedConcepts.label: Average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence
Doubling: total copies n + n/2 + ... < 2n
Time complexity
Aggregate, accounting (credits), potential function
Amortised is a guarantee, unlike average-case; latency spikes
Growing by constant c gives O(n) amortised (n^2 total)

questions.modelAnswer: Amortised analysis bounds the total cost of any sequence of n operations, then divides by n; it is a worst-case guarantee over sequences, not an expectation over random inputs. Dynamic array: when capacity is full, allocate twice the size and copy. One push can cost O(n), but across n pushes the copies total n/2 + n/4 + ... < n, so total work is O(n) and each push is O(1) amortised (aggregate method). Accounting method: charge each push 3 units - 1 to insert, 2 saved as credit to pay for moving itself and one older element at the next resize. Potential method: define Phi = 2 * size - capacity; each cheap push raises it slightly and a resize spends it, so amortised cost stays constant. Growing by a constant c instead requires a copy every c pushes, totalling O(n^2 / c), i.e. O(n) per push. Shrinking must use hysteresis (shrink at one quarter full, not half) or alternating push/pop at the boundary thrashes. Amortised bounds still allow individual latency spikes, which matters in real-time or low-latency systems - preallocate or use incremental resizing there. Other examples: union-find, splay trees, and hash table rehashing.

questions.title: Two pointers and the three-sum problem
questions.prompt: Explain the two-pointer technique and use it to solve three-sum: find all unique triplets that add up to zero. Walk through the algorithm, how you skip duplicates, the time and space complexity, and compare it with a hash-set approach.

expectedConcepts.label: Sort, fix one element, two pointers on the rest
Move left up if sum too small, right down if too large
Time complexity
Space complexity
Skip duplicate values for fixed element and pointers
Hash set approach, k-sum generalisation, early exit

questions.modelAnswer: Two pointers works on sorted data: one pointer at each end moving inward based on a comparison, turning an O(n^2) pair search into O(n). For three-sum, sort the array, then for each index i treat -nums[i] as a two-sum target on the subarray to its right: set left = i + 1 and right = n - 1; if the sum is too small move left up, if too large move right down, and on a match record the triplet and move both. Sorting makes the moves valid because increasing left can only increase the sum. Duplicates: skip i when nums[i] equals nums[i-1], and after a match advance left and right past equal values. You can stop early once nums[i] > 0. Total time O(n^2) (the sort is O(n log n)), extra space O(1) beyond the sort and output. A hash-set approach is also O(n^2) but uses O(n) memory and makes deduplication messier. It generalises to k-sum with recursion down to two-sum, O(n^(k-1)). Edge cases: fewer than three elements, all zeros, integer overflow in other languages.

questions.title: Design a chat system like WhatsApp
questions.prompt: Design a one-to-one and group chat service for 500 million daily users. Cover requirements, real-time delivery over persistent connections, message storage and ordering, delivery and read receipts, offline users and push notifications, and how group fan-out scales.

expectedConcepts.label: Scale, latency, ordering, delivery guarantees
WebSocket gateways with a connection registry
Messages partitioned by conversation, wide-column store
Group fan-out on write vs read; large groups
Offline: store and forward, push notifications, sync on reconnect
Per-conversation sequence numbers, idempotent client ids, receipts
Hot groups, gateway reconnect storms
Trade-offs: E2E encryption limits server features; storage retention

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 1:1 and group chat (say up to 1000 members), online presence, sent/delivered/read receipts, history sync across devices, sub-second delivery, no lost messages. Clients keep a persistent WebSocket (or MQTT) connection to a stateless-ish gateway fleet; a connection registry (Redis or an in-memory service) maps user to gateway. Send path: client sends a message with a client-generated id; the chat service assigns a per-conversation sequence number, persists it to a store partitioned by conversation id (Cassandra/HBase style: partition = conversation, clustering = sequence), acks the sender, then looks up recipients' gateways and pushes. Offline recipients get a push notification via APNs/FCM and pull missed messages on reconnect using their last seen sequence number. Delivery is at-least-once with client-side dedup by message id. Groups: fan out per member on write for small groups; for very large groups store once and have members read from the group timeline. Bottlenecks: reconnect storms after a gateway deploy (jittered backoff, gradual drain), hot groups, presence updates (throttle and only send to interested contacts). Trade-off: end-to-end encryption (Signal protocol) means the server cannot search or moderate content and multi-device needs per-device keys.
researchContext: WhatsApp famously ran millions of connections per server on Erlang/FreeBSD.
Discord stores messages in a wide-column store partitioned by channel and time bucket.

questions.title: Design a social media news feed
questions.prompt: Design the home feed for a social network with 300 million daily users, where users follow others and some accounts have tens of millions of followers. Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read, explain the hybrid approach, ranking, caching and pagination.

expectedConcepts.label: Read-heavy, freshness, latency targets
Fan-out on write into precomputed timelines
Fan-out on read for celebrities
Candidate generation then ranking
Timeline cache in Redis of post ids; hydrate posts
Async fan-out workers via queue, retries
Eventual consistency, deletes and privacy changes
Celebrity write amplification; inactive users
Trade-offs: storage vs read latency; cursor pagination

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: users post, follow, and open a feed of recent ranked posts in under 200 ms; reads vastly outnumber writes. Fan-out on write: when a user posts, workers consuming from a queue push the post id into each follower's precomputed timeline (a capped list in Redis). Reads are just a cache fetch plus hydrating post bodies and authors from caches. That breaks for celebrities - one post means 50 million writes - so use fan-out on read for them: at read time merge the precomputed timeline with recent posts pulled from the few celebrities the user follows. Skip precomputing for inactive users and build their feed lazily on login. Ranking: gather a few hundred candidates, score them with a model (affinity, recency, engagement), and return a page; paginate with a cursor rather than offsets because the feed changes underneath. Reliability: fan-out is asynchronous and retried; the post store is the source of truth so timelines can be rebuilt. Consistency is eventual - a new post may take seconds to appear - but deletes and block/privacy changes must be filtered at read time. Trade-off: fan-out on write spends storage and write capacity to make reads cheap.

questions.title: Design a distributed in-memory cache
questions.prompt: Design a distributed key-value cache like Memcached or Redis Cluster serving a million requests per second. Explain partitioning with consistent hashing, replication and failover, eviction policies, hot keys, and the cache-aside pattern with its consistency problems.

expectedConcepts.label: Throughput, latency, memory budget, durability needs
Consistent hashing / hash slots with virtual nodes
Client-side or proxy routing
Primary-replica replication and automatic failover
Eviction: LRU/LFU, TTLs
Hot keys: replicate, local near-cache, key splitting
Cache stampede and stale sets; invalidation races
Async replication can lose writes; cost vs hit ratio

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: get/set/delete with TTL, ~1 ms p99, 1M ops/s, data can be rebuilt from the database so durability is best-effort. Partition keys across nodes with consistent hashing (with many virtual nodes per server) or fixed hash slots like Redis Cluster's 16384, so adding a node moves only a small fraction of keys. Routing happens in a smart client that knows the slot map, or in a proxy layer (twemproxy/mcrouter) that simplifies clients at the cost of a hop. Each shard has a primary and one or more replicas with asynchronous replication; a failure detector promotes a replica, so a few acknowledged writes can be lost - acceptable for a cache. Memory is bounded with LRU or LFU eviction plus TTLs. Hot keys (a celebrity profile) overload one shard: add a small in-process near-cache with a short TTL, replicate hot keys to several shards with suffixes, or read from replicas. With cache-aside (read DB on miss, then set), races can leave stale data: reader A misses and reads old value, writer updates DB and deletes key, A then sets the stale value. Mitigate with delete-after-write plus TTLs, leases or versioned sets, and avoid stampedes with request coalescing or probabilistic early refresh.

questions.title: Design a ride-hailing service like Uber
questions.prompt: Design the core of a ride-hailing app: drivers send location every few seconds, riders request a ride and get matched to a nearby driver. Explain geospatial indexing, the matching flow, trip state, handling millions of location updates, and failure cases like a driver going offline mid-match.

expectedConcepts.label: Location update rate, match latency, regions
Geospatial index: geohash, quadtree, H3 cells
In-memory location service, sharded by region/cell
Matching: nearby candidates, ETA ranking, offer with timeout
Trip state machine persisted durably
Avoid double-assigning a driver: lock/lease or CAS
Hot cells at events; write-heavy location traffic
Trade-offs: freshness vs cost, cell size, nearest vs optimal

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: drivers send GPS every ~4 s (with 1M active drivers that is 250k writes/s), riders get matched within a few seconds, trips must never be lost or double-assigned. Drivers connect through gateways that write their latest location into an in-memory location service sharded by region; within a region a geospatial index (geohash prefixes, quadtree or Uber's hexagonal H3 cells) maps cells to driver ids. Only the latest position matters for matching; the full trail goes to a Kafka stream for analytics and fares. Matching: on request, query the rider's cell and neighbouring rings for available drivers, rank candidates by road-network ETA, and offer the trip to the best driver with a ~10 s timeout before moving on. Reserve the driver atomically (compare-and-set on driver status or a short lease) so two riders cannot get the same driver. The trip is a durable state machine (requested, accepted, arrived, in progress, completed) in a replicated database; clients reconnect and resync from it. If a driver goes offline mid-offer the lease expires and matching retries. Hot spots like stadiums need finer cells and batched matching. Trade-offs: smaller cells mean more precise queries but more cell hops; greedy nearest-driver is fast but batch matching over a window gives better global ETAs.

questions.title: Design a video streaming platform like YouTube
questions.prompt: Design a video platform where creators upload videos and millions of viewers watch them. Cover the upload and transcoding pipeline, adaptive bitrate streaming, CDN usage, metadata and view counts, and how you keep costs under control.

expectedConcepts.label: Upload size, watch scale, startup latency, global
Resumable chunked upload to object storage
Transcoding DAG to multiple resolutions, segmented
Adaptive bitrate via HLS/DASH manifests
CDN edge caching, long tail from origin
Retryable idempotent pipeline steps; replicated storage
View counts: approximate, aggregated asynchronously
Bottlenecks: transcoding compute, egress bandwidth, viral videos
Trade-offs: encode only popular ladders, storage vs compute cost

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: uploads up to several GB, millions of concurrent viewers worldwide, playback start under 2 s, smooth playback on poor networks. Upload: the client gets a pre-signed URL and uploads in resumable chunks directly to object storage, so app servers never proxy bytes. An upload event triggers a transcoding pipeline - a DAG run by workers from a queue: inspect, split into segments, encode each segment into a ladder of resolutions and bitrates (240p to 4K, H.264/VP9/AV1) in parallel, generate thumbnails, run moderation, then publish HLS/DASH manifests. Each step is idempotent and retried. Playback: the player fetches the manifest and picks segments of different bitrates as bandwidth changes (adaptive bitrate). Segments are served from CDN edges; popular videos stay hot at the edge, the long tail falls back to regional caches and origin storage. Metadata (title, owner, status) lives in a sharded relational or document store with caches. View counts are emitted as events, aggregated in a stream processor and written periodically - approximate and eventually consistent, with fraud filtering. Cost is dominated by egress and storage: encode expensive codecs like AV1 only for popular videos, tier cold videos to cheaper storage, and place caches inside ISPs.

questions.title: Design search autocomplete (typeahead)
questions.prompt: Design the autocomplete for a search box that suggests the top queries as the user types, serving 100,000 requests per second with under 100 ms latency. Cover how suggestions are computed from logs, the serving data structure, caching, updates and filtering.

expectedConcepts.label: Latency per keystroke, QPS, freshness, personalisation
Offline aggregation of query logs into counts
Trie with precomputed top-k per prefix, served from memory
Browser/CDN caching and debouncing
Shard by prefix, replicate read-only snapshots
Rebuild and swap snapshots atomically; fallbacks
Hot short prefixes; trending freshness
Trade-offs: freshness vs cost; filtering offensive suggestions

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: suggest top 5-10 completions per prefix, under 100 ms end to end, 100k QPS, updated at least daily with a faster path for trending terms, and no offensive suggestions. Offline: stream search logs into storage, run a batch job that counts queries over a window with time decay, filters blocked terms, and builds a trie where every node stores its precomputed top-k completions. Serialise it into immutable snapshots. Online: a suggestion service loads the snapshot into memory; a lookup walks the prefix (a few characters) and returns the stored list - O(prefix length). Shard by prefix range if the trie is too big and replicate each shard; swap in new snapshots atomically and keep the old one as a fallback. Reduce load with client-side debouncing (only query after 100-200 ms of no typing), browser caching, and CDN caching of responses for short popular prefixes. Trending queries come from a streaming job that maintains short-window counts merged at query time. Personalisation (recent searches, location) is blended on top in the service. Trade-off: rebuild frequency versus cost and stability; short prefixes are extremely hot and best served from cache.

questions.title: Design a payment system
questions.prompt: Design the payment backend for an e-commerce company that charges customers through external payment providers. Explain idempotency, the double-entry ledger, the payment state machine, handling provider timeouts and webhooks, reconciliation, and why exactly-once is so hard here.

expectedConcepts.label: Correctness over latency; audit; no double charges
Idempotency keys on every request
Append-only double-entry ledger
Payment state machine: created, pending, succeeded, failed
Unknown outcome on timeout: query provider, retry safely
Daily reconciliation against provider settlement files
Transactional outbox for events
Provider rate limits/outages, hot merchant accounts
Trade-offs: strong consistency for money, availability during outages

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: never charge twice, never lose a payment, full audit trail, PCI scope minimised (card data tokenised by the provider). Every client request carries an idempotency key; the service stores key -> result in the same transaction as the payment row, so retries return the original result instead of charging again. A payment is a state machine (created -> pending -> succeeded/failed/refunded) persisted in a strongly consistent relational database. Money movements are recorded in an append-only double-entry ledger: every transaction has balanced debits and credits across accounts, so balances are derived and errors are detectable. Calling the provider: pass our idempotency key to the provider too. On timeout the outcome is unknown - never assume failure; mark pending, then resolve via provider webhooks or a status-polling job. Webhooks are verified, deduplicated and processed idempotently. Downstream events (order paid) are published through a transactional outbox so DB and messages cannot diverge. Daily reconciliation compares our ledger with provider settlement reports and flags mismatches for humans. Exactly-once is impossible across a network to a third party; we achieve effectively-once with at-least-once retries plus idempotency on both sides. Trade-off: prefer consistency over availability for money; route to a backup provider during outages.

questions.title: Design a distributed job scheduler
questions.prompt: Design a service that lets teams schedule millions of jobs to run at specific times or on cron schedules, with retries, across a fleet of workers. Explain how you store and find due jobs, assign them to workers without running a job twice, handle worker crashes and keep it highly available.

expectedConcepts.label: Timing precision, at-least-once, scale, multi-tenant
Jobs indexed by next run time, partitioned
Schedulers claim due jobs and push to a queue
Leases / visibility timeouts and heartbeats
Duplicate execution prevention: fencing tokens, idempotent jobs
Leader election or partitioned schedulers
Thundering herd at the top of the hour; noisy tenants
Scale schedulers by partition, workers by queue depth
Trade-offs: precision vs load, at-least-once vs exactly-once

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: create one-off and cron jobs, run within a few seconds of the scheduled time, retries with backoff, history, and at-least-once execution for millions of jobs from many tenants. Store job definitions in a durable database and keep a separate index of upcoming executions keyed by (next_run_time, job_id), partitioned into N shards. Each shard is owned by one scheduler instance (assigned via leader election or a lease in etcd/ZooKeeper); it scans for due rows every second, atomically marks them claimed, and pushes execution messages onto a work queue. Workers pull from the queue, take a lease with a visibility timeout and heartbeat; if a worker crashes the lease expires and the job becomes visible again. This means a job can run twice, so jobs must be idempotent, and side effects should carry a fencing token (execution id) so a zombie worker's late writes are rejected. After completion the scheduler computes the next cron time and inserts the next execution. Bottlenecks: everyone schedules at midnight or on the hour - add jitter, rate-limit per tenant, and pre-load upcoming jobs into in-memory timer wheels. Scale schedulers by adding partitions and workers by queue depth. Trade-off: tighter precision costs more polling and coordination; true exactly-once is not achievable, effectively-once comes from idempotency.

questions.title: Design a web crawler
questions.prompt: Design a web crawler that fetches a billion pages a month for a search engine. Explain the URL frontier, politeness per host, DNS and fetching, deduplication of URLs and content, handling traps and failures, and how you distribute the work.

expectedConcepts.label: Pages per second, freshness, politeness, robots.txt
URL frontier with priority and per-host queues
Fetchers with async I/O, DNS cache
Dedup URLs with Bloom filter/hash set; content with fingerprints
Partition by host hash across crawler nodes
Checkpointing frontier, retries with backoff
Crawler traps, infinite calendars, malicious pages
Bottlenecks: DNS, slow hosts, bandwidth
Trade-offs: freshness vs coverage, recrawl scheduling

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 1 billion pages a month is about 400 pages/s (plan for peaks of 1000+), obey robots.txt and per-host rate limits, prioritise important and frequently changing pages, store raw HTML for indexing. Components: seed URLs feed a URL frontier with two layers - front queues by priority (PageRank, freshness) and back queues per host, each host emitted no faster than its politeness delay. Fetchers use async I/O with thousands of concurrent connections, a local DNS cache, timeouts and size limits. Fetched pages go to object storage and a parser that extracts links, normalises URLs (lowercase host, strip fragments, sort parameters) and checks a seen-URL store (a Bloom filter in front of a sharded key-value store) before adding to the frontier. Content duplicates and near-duplicates are detected with checksums and SimHash. Distribution: partition hosts across crawler nodes by hash so each host's politeness is enforced in one place. Reliability: checkpoint frontier state, retry with backoff, and skip hosts that keep failing. Traps: infinite calendars and session-id URLs - cap URL length, depth and pages per host. Trade-off: recrawl budget - news sites daily, static pages rarely, using observed change rates.

questions.title: Design an object storage system like S3
questions.prompt: Design a highly durable object storage service storing exabytes of data. Explain the separation of metadata and data, how objects are placed and replicated or erasure coded, how you reach eleven nines of durability, handling large uploads, and the consistency model for reads after writes.

expectedConcepts.label: Durability target, availability, object sizes
Separate metadata service from data nodes
Replication vs erasure coding across failure domains
Background scrubbing and repair
Multipart uploads for large objects
Partition metadata by key prefix; scale data nodes
Strong read-after-write via metadata commit
Hot prefixes, small objects overhead
Trade-offs: erasure coding saves space but costs CPU and repair traffic

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: put/get/delete/list objects from bytes to terabytes, 99.999999999% durability, 99.99% availability, strong read-after-write consistency. Split the system: a metadata service maps bucket+key to object version, size, checksum and the location of its chunks; data nodes store immutable chunks on disks. The metadata store is a strongly consistent, partitioned key-value store (sharded by key prefix with Paxos/Raft replication). Writes: the front end streams data into chunks, writes them to data nodes in different failure domains (disks, racks, availability zones), verifies checksums, and only then commits the metadata pointer atomically - so readers see either the old or new version, giving read-after-write. Durability: three-way replication costs 200% overhead; erasure coding (e.g. 10 data + 4 parity Reed-Solomon fragments) tolerates four lost fragments at 40% overhead. Background scrubbers read data, verify checksums and rebuild lost fragments quickly - durability is really about repairing faster than failures accumulate. Large objects use multipart uploads in parallel, assembled at commit. Bottlenecks: hot key prefixes (auto-split partitions), billions of tiny objects (pack them into larger chunks), and LIST operations. Trade-off: erasure coding saves space but needs more CPU and network for reads and repairs, so hot data may stay replicated.

questions.title: Design a ticket booking system for a big concert
questions.prompt: Design a ticketing system where 2 million fans try to buy 50,000 seats the moment a concert goes on sale. Explain how you prevent overselling, hold seats while users pay, keep the site up under the spike, and treat users fairly against bots.

expectedConcepts.label: No overselling, burst traffic, fairness
Virtual waiting room / admission control
Seat holds with TTL
Atomic seat claim: conditional update / optimistic locking
Inventory in memory/Redis per event, DB as source of truth
Payment with idempotency; release on failure
Hot single event row; static assets on CDN
Bots: CAPTCHA, verified fans, per-account limits

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: never sell a seat twice, survive a 100x traffic spike at on-sale time, let buyers pick seats and pay within a few minutes, and be fair. Front door: serve everything static from a CDN and put users into a virtual waiting room - they get a signed queue token and are admitted in batches at a rate the backend can handle, which turns a stampede into a steady flow and gives a fair first-come order. Seat claim: each seat row has a status and version; claiming is an atomic conditional update (UPDATE seat SET status=HELD, holder=u, hold_until=now+10min WHERE id=s AND status=AVAILABLE) - one winner, everyone else gets a clean "taken" response. For extreme contention keep the event's seat map in Redis with atomic scripts and write through to the database as the source of truth. Holds expire automatically so abandoned carts return seats. Payment uses an idempotency key; success marks the seat SOLD, failure or timeout releases it. The event row is a hot spot, so partition inventory by section and avoid a single global counter. Bots: CAPTCHA at queue entry, verified-fan registration, per-account and per-card limits. Trade-off: the waiting room adds friction but protects correctness and fairness.

questions.title: Design a metrics and monitoring system
questions.prompt: Design a monitoring system like Prometheus or Datadog that collects metrics from 100,000 servers every 10 seconds, stores them, supports dashboards and alerting. Explain push versus pull, time-series storage and compression, downsampling, high cardinality, and alerting reliability.

expectedConcepts.label: Ingest rate, retention, query latency
Push vs pull collection
Time-series DB: series id, chunks, delta/Gorilla compression
Downsampling and tiered retention
High cardinality labels blow up series count
Shard by series hash; Kafka buffer for ingestion
Alerting evaluated independently, HA pairs, dedup
Late or missing data, gaps vs zeros
Trade-offs: resolution vs cost, metrics vs logs

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 100k hosts x ~500 series every 10 s = 5M points/s ingest, 15 days at full resolution and a year downsampled, dashboards in under a second, alerts within a minute. Collection: pull (Prometheus scrapes endpoints, easy to detect dead targets) or push via agents (works through firewalls and for short jobs); at this scale agents push to a gateway that writes into Kafka as a buffer against spikes. Storage: a time-series database identifies each series by metric name plus label set, buffers recent samples in memory, and writes immutable compressed blocks - Gorilla-style delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-encoded floats get points down to around 1.5 bytes. Shard by series hash across nodes with replication. Downsample old data to 1-minute and 1-hour rollups (min, max, sum, count) to bound storage. High cardinality - labels like user_id or request_id - multiplies series and is the classic way to break a TSDB, so enforce label limits. Alerting runs in a separate service evaluating rules on recent data, deployed as an HA pair with deduplication, and is itself monitored with a dead man's switch. Distinguish missing data from zero. Trade-off: higher resolution and longer retention cost more; per-request detail belongs in logs or traces, not metrics.

questions.title: Design a distributed unique ID generator
questions.prompt: Design a service that generates unique 64-bit IDs at 100,000 per second across many data centres, ideally sortable by time. Compare database auto-increment, UUIDs, ticket servers and Snowflake-style IDs, and explain how you handle clock skew and machine ID assignment.

expectedConcepts.label: Uniqueness, 64-bit, time-sortable, throughput
Auto-increment, UUID v4/v7, ticket server
Snowflake: timestamp + machine id + sequence
No coordination per ID; each node independent
Clock skew and NTP going backwards
Machine id assignment via ZooKeeper/etcd lease
Sequence exhaustion within a millisecond
Trade-offs: guessability, k-sorted not strictly ordered, B-tree locality

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: globally unique 64-bit IDs, roughly time-ordered for index locality, 100k/s with low latency and no single point of failure. A database auto-increment is simple but a bottleneck and single point of failure; multiple databases with different offsets complicate scaling. UUID v4 needs no coordination but is 128 bits and random, which fragments B-tree indexes; UUID v7 fixes ordering but is still 128 bits. A ticket server handing out ranges of IDs to services reduces load but is still central. Snowflake layout: 1 sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch (~69 years), 10 bits of machine id (1024 generators), 12 bits of sequence (4096 per millisecond per machine). Each generator creates IDs locally with no coordination; if the sequence overflows in a millisecond it waits for the next one. Machine ids are leased from ZooKeeper or etcd so two instances never share one. Clock risk: if NTP moves the clock backwards the generator could repeat IDs, so it must refuse or wait until the clock passes the last timestamp, and use a monotonic clock where possible. Trade-offs: IDs are only roughly sorted across machines, and they leak creation time and volume, so they are guessable.

questions.title: Design a collaborative document editor like Google Docs
questions.prompt: Design a real-time collaborative text editor where many users edit the same document at once. Explain how concurrent edits are merged with operational transformation or CRDTs, the server architecture, presence and cursors, offline editing, and how documents are stored and versioned.

expectedConcepts.label: Low-latency local edits, convergence, offline, history
Operational transformation with a central server ordering ops
CRDTs: commutative ops with unique ids
Per-document session server, sticky routing via WebSocket
Operation log plus periodic snapshots
Presence and cursors as ephemeral state
Convergence and intention preservation; reconnect resync
Hot documents with hundreds of editors; large docs
OT vs CRDT trade-offs: central authority vs metadata overhead

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: typing appears instantly locally, all replicas converge to the same text, edits survive disconnects, full revision history. Each client applies its own edits immediately (optimistic) and sends operations over a WebSocket. Operational transformation: a server holding the authoritative document per session assigns a total order to operations; when a client's op was based on an older revision, it is transformed against concurrent ops (e.g. shifting an insert position) so intention is preserved - Google Docs works this way. CRDTs (Yjs, Automerge) give every character a unique id and ordering metadata so operations commute and any replica can merge in any order without a central server - great for offline and peer-to-peer, at the cost of metadata and tombstones that need garbage collection. Architecture: route all editors of a document to the same document server (consistent hashing on document id) which orders ops, broadcasts them and appends to a durable operation log; take periodic snapshots so loading does not replay everything. Cursors and presence are ephemeral and not persisted. Offline clients queue ops and rebase or merge on reconnect. Bottlenecks: hot documents with hundreds of editors (batch and throttle broadcasts) and very large documents. Trade-off: OT needs a central authority but is compact; CRDTs decentralise at higher memory cost.

questions.title: Design a stock exchange matching engine
questions.prompt: Design the core of a stock exchange: order entry, the order book and matching engine, and market data publishing. Explain price-time priority, how you achieve microsecond latency and determinism, how you make the matching engine fault tolerant, and why it is usually single-threaded.

expectedConcepts.label: Microsecond latency, fairness, determinism, auditability
Order book: price levels with FIFO queues
Price-time priority matching; order types
Single-threaded engine per symbol, sequenced input
Kernel bypass, busy polling, preallocation, no GC
Replicated state machine: replay sequenced journal on standby
Market data multicast, gap recovery
Trade-offs: simplicity of single thread vs throughput; risk checks

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: accept, cancel and modify orders, match fairly by price then time, publish trades and book updates, with single-digit-microsecond engine latency, full audit and no lost orders. Flow: gateways handle client sessions (FIX or binary protocols), validate and run pre-trade risk checks, then send orders to a sequencer that stamps a global sequence number and writes them to a journal. The matching engine consumes the sequenced stream. The order book per symbol keeps bids and asks as price levels (sorted by price, often an array indexed by tick) each holding a FIFO queue of orders, plus a hash map from order id to node for O(1) cancels. A buy limit order matches against the best asks while prices cross, oldest first, and any remainder rests on the book. The engine is single-threaded per symbol partition: no locks, perfect determinism, and everything fits in cache. Latency techniques: kernel-bypass networking, busy-polling cores pinned to CPUs, preallocated object pools, lock-free ring buffers between stages (LMAX Disruptor style), no garbage collection on the hot path. Fault tolerance: because the engine is deterministic, a hot standby replays the same sequenced journal and produces identical state, so failover is just switching. Market data goes out over UDP multicast with sequence numbers; subscribers detect gaps and recover from a retransmission service. Trade-off: one thread per symbol caps per-symbol throughput but gives fairness and simplicity.
researchContext: The LMAX architecture processed millions of orders per second on a single thread.
Exchanges co-locate clients and equalise cable lengths for fairness.

questions.title: Consistent hashing
questions.prompt: Explain consistent hashing. Why does simple modulo hashing break when you add or remove servers, how does the hash ring work, why do we need virtual nodes, and where is it used in real systems? Mention alternatives such as rendezvous hashing or jump hash.

expectedConcepts.label: Modulo N remaps almost all keys when N changes
Hash ring: key goes to next server clockwise
Virtual nodes even out load and spread recovery
Only about K/N keys move on membership change
Replicas on the next distinct nodes
Uses: Dynamo, Cassandra, caches, load balancers
Alternatives: rendezvous, jump hash, hash slots
Hot keys still overload a node

questions.modelAnswer: With hash(key) mod N, changing N from 10 to 11 changes the owner of roughly 90% of keys - a cache would lose almost every entry at once and a database would have to move nearly all data. Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto the same circular hash space; a key belongs to the first server found moving clockwise from its position. Adding a server only takes keys from its successor, and removing one hands its keys to the next server, so only about K/N keys move. With few servers, random positions give very uneven arcs, so each physical server gets many virtual nodes (100-200 points) which smooths the load and spreads a failed server's keys across many others; weights can be expressed by giving bigger machines more vnodes. Replication: store a key on the next R distinct physical servers clockwise (Dynamo's preference list). Used in Amazon Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, Memcached clients, Envoy/Maglev load balancing and CDNs. Alternatives: rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing scores each server per key and needs no ring; jump consistent hash is tiny and perfectly balanced but only supports numbered buckets that grow or shrink at the end; Redis Cluster uses 16384 fixed hash slots moved explicitly. None of these fixes a single hot key.

questions.title: Implementing idempotency keys on the server
questions.prompt: POST /payments must be safe to retry. Design the server-side implementation of idempotency keys: where the key and stored response live, how you make the key check and the payment atomic, what happens when two identical requests arrive at the same moment, what to do when a key is reused with a different body, and when keys expire.

expectedConcepts.label: Same request repeated has the same effect as once
GET, PUT, DELETE idempotent; POST and PATCH not
Client-generated key stored with the result
Concurrent duplicates: lock or unique constraint, 409 while in progress
Expiry window, fingerprint body mismatch, storage cost

questions.modelAnswer: An operation is idempotent if performing it several times has the same effect on the server as performing it once. By HTTP semantics GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent and GET/HEAD are also safe; POST and PATCH are not. Networks fail ambiguously: if POST /payments times out, the client does not know whether the charge happened, and a blind retry could charge twice. The fix is an Idempotency-Key header with a client-generated UUID per logical operation. Server side: in one transaction insert (key, user, request fingerprint, status=in_progress) under a unique constraint; if the insert succeeds, process the request and store the final status code and body with the key; if the key already exists and is complete, return the stored response without re-executing; if it is still in progress, return 409 or wait. If the same key arrives with a different body, reject it with 422 because it indicates a client bug. Keys expire after a window such as 24 hours. Store the key in the same database transaction as the side effect, otherwise a crash between them breaks the guarantee. Stripe's API is the reference design.

questions.title: Pagination: offset versus cursor
questions.prompt: Explain how to paginate a large, frequently changing list in an API. Compare offset and limit pagination with cursor or keyset pagination, explain why offset gets slow and returns duplicates or skips, how you encode a cursor, and how you handle sorting and total counts.

expectedConcepts.label: Offset/limit: simple, random access, but O(offset) scans
Keyset/cursor: WHERE (sort_key, id) > last seen
Offset drifts when rows are inserted or deleted
Opaque base64 cursor with sort values and tie-breaker
No jumping to page N; total counts are expensive

questions.modelAnswer: Offset pagination (?limit=20&offset=10000) is easy and allows jumping to any page, but the database still has to walk and discard all the skipped rows, so deep pages get slower and slower. It is also unstable: if a row is inserted at the top while a user pages, every item shifts and they see a duplicate; a deletion makes them skip one. Cursor (keyset) pagination remembers where the last page ended and asks for the next rows after it: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. With an index on (created_at, id) every page is a fast index seek regardless of depth and results stay stable as data changes. The sort must be unique, so include the primary key as a tie-breaker. Return the cursor as an opaque, base64-encoded (ideally signed) token containing those values plus a next link, so clients cannot depend on its structure and you can change it later. Trade-offs: no jumping to page 57, the cursor is tied to one sort order, and total counts require a separate, often expensive COUNT - return an estimate or has_more instead.

questions.title: API versioning and backward compatibility
questions.prompt: How do you evolve a public API without breaking clients? Explain which changes are backward compatible and which are breaking, compare URL, header and date-based versioning, and describe how you deprecate and finally remove an old version.

expectedConcepts.label: Additive changes are safe; removing/renaming/retyping is breaking
Clients must ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader)
URL /v1, header/media type, date-based versions
Deprecation headers, sunset dates, usage tracking
Cost of maintaining many versions; translation layers

questions.modelAnswer: Backward-compatible changes: adding new endpoints, adding optional request fields, adding response fields, and relaxing validation - provided clients follow the tolerant-reader rule and ignore fields they do not know. Breaking changes: removing or renaming fields, changing types or formats, making optional fields required, changing default behaviour or error codes, and even adding a new enum value if clients switch over it exhaustively. Versioning schemes: a URL prefix (/v1/orders) is explicit and easy to route and cache but encourages big-bang versions; a header or media type (Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json) keeps URLs stable but is less visible; date-based versions pinned per account (Stripe-Version: 2024-06-20) let the server apply small dated changes and translate responses for older versions through a chain of adapters. Deprecation: announce early, add Deprecation and Sunset headers, track which clients still call the old version, contact them, provide a migration guide, use brownouts (temporary planned failures) close to the deadline, then remove. Each live version multiplies testing and maintenance, so prefer additive evolution and keep versions few.

questions.title: REST versus gRPC versus GraphQL
questions.prompt: Compare REST, gRPC and GraphQL for building APIs. For each, explain how it works on the wire, its strengths and weaknesses for performance, typing, caching, streaming and tooling, and say which you would choose for a public API, internal microservices and a mobile app.

expectedConcepts.label: REST: resources over HTTP, JSON, HTTP caching
gRPC: protobuf over HTTP/2, codegen, streaming
GraphQL: single endpoint, client selects fields, schema
Public: REST; internal: gRPC; aggregating UI data: GraphQL
Caching, browser support, N+1, query cost limits

questions.modelAnswer: REST models resources at URLs manipulated with HTTP methods, usually exchanging JSON. It is universal, human-readable and benefits from HTTP caching, CDNs and status codes, but clients often over-fetch or make many round trips, and typing depends on OpenAPI discipline. gRPC defines services in protobuf; it sends compact binary messages over HTTP/2 with generated, strongly typed clients in many languages, supports deadlines and bidirectional streaming, and is fast. Downsides: not natively callable from browsers (needs gRPC-Web or a proxy), harder to inspect with curl, and no HTTP-level caching. GraphQL exposes a typed schema at one endpoint; clients ask for exactly the fields they need, aggregating several backends in one round trip - great for varied mobile and web screens. Downsides: caching is harder because everything is POST to one URL, naive resolvers cause N+1 queries, and arbitrary queries need depth and cost limits. Choice: a public partner API - REST with OpenAPI; internal service-to-service calls - gRPC; a product UI that composes many entities for different clients - GraphQL, often as a gateway over gRPC services.

questions.title: GraphQL performance: N+1 queries and abuse
questions.prompt: A GraphQL API is slow when clients request a list of posts with each post's author and comments. Explain the N+1 problem in resolvers, how the DataLoader batching pattern fixes it, and how you protect a GraphQL server from expensive or malicious queries.

expectedConcepts.label: Per-item resolvers issue one query per parent: N+1
DataLoader batches keys per tick and caches per request
Depth limits, cost analysis, pagination limits, timeouts
Persisted queries / allowlists
Trade-offs: caching, introspection, rate limiting by cost

questions.modelAnswer: GraphQL resolves fields independently. Query posts(first: 50) { author { name } comments { text } } runs one query for the posts, then the author resolver runs once per post (50 queries) and comments once per post (50 more) - N+1 round trips that get worse with nesting. DataLoader fixes this: resolvers call authorLoader.load(id), the loader collects all ids requested in the same tick of the event loop, issues one batched query (WHERE id IN (...)), and distributes results back; it also memoises per request, so the same author is fetched once. Use one loader instance per request so caches do not leak between users. Protection: because clients choose the shape, one query can request millions of nodes. Enforce maximum depth, compute a cost per query from field weights and requested page sizes and reject or rate-limit by cost, cap list sizes, set execution timeouts, disable introspection in production if appropriate, and for first-party apps use persisted queries - the client sends a hash of a pre-registered query, so arbitrary queries are refused. Trade-off: GraphQL's flexibility shifts query-planning responsibility from the API designer to runtime safeguards.

questions.title: API authentication: OAuth 2.0, OIDC and JWTs
questions.prompt: Explain how a modern API authenticates and authorises clients. Cover API keys, OAuth 2.0 flows such as authorization code with PKCE and client credentials, what OpenID Connect adds, JWT access tokens versus opaque tokens, and how revocation and token theft are handled.

expectedConcepts.label: Authentication vs authorisation; API keys
Auth code + PKCE for users; client credentials for machines
OIDC adds ID token and user identity
JWT: signed claims, verified locally; scopes, expiry, audience
Revocation is hard for JWTs; short-lived tokens + refresh rotation; storage

questions.modelAnswer: Authentication proves who the caller is; authorisation decides what it may do. API keys identify an application and are fine for server-to-server use but grant broad access and are easy to leak. OAuth 2.0 issues scoped, expiring access tokens. For a user-facing app, the authorization code flow with PKCE redirects the user to the identity provider, gets their consent and returns a code that the app exchanges (with a one-time code verifier proving it started the flow) for tokens; for machine-to-machine calls the client credentials flow exchanges a client secret or signed assertion for a token. OAuth is about delegated access; OpenID Connect adds an ID token describing the user so it can be used for login. Access tokens are either opaque strings that the API checks via introspection, or JWTs: signed JSON claims (sub, scope, exp, aud, iss) that resource servers verify locally with the issuer's public keys - fast and stateless. Always validate signature, algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry. The catch: a JWT cannot be revoked before it expires without a denylist, so keep access tokens short-lived (5-15 minutes) and use refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection. Store tokens in httpOnly cookies or secure storage, use TLS everywhere, and consider sender-constrained tokens (DPoP, mTLS) against theft.

questions.title: Designing reliable webhooks
questions.prompt: Design a webhook system that notifies customers' servers when events happen in your platform. Explain delivery guarantees, retries with backoff, signing payloads, ordering, idempotent consumers, and what you do when a customer endpoint is down for days.

expectedConcepts.label: At-least-once delivery from a durable queue/outbox
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter; 2xx means success
HMAC signature with timestamp to prevent spoofing and replay
Event ids so consumers dedupe; no ordering guarantee
Dead letter, disabling endpoints, replay API, thin vs fat payloads

questions.modelAnswer: When an event happens, write it in the same transaction as the business change (transactional outbox) so it is never lost, then a dispatcher delivers it as an HTTPS POST to each subscribed endpoint. Delivery is at-least-once: any non-2xx response or timeout (keep it short, around 10 s, and ask customers to respond quickly and process asynchronously) triggers retries with exponential backoff and jitter over a period such as three days. Every payload carries a unique event id, type and created timestamp; consumers must deduplicate by id because the same event can arrive more than once. Ordering is not guaranteed across retries, so consumers should treat events as hints and fetch the latest state of the object, or compare versions. Sign each request with an HMAC of the timestamp plus body using a per-endpoint secret; receivers verify it with a constant-time comparison and reject old timestamps to block replays. Support secret rotation. If an endpoint keeps failing, move events to a dead-letter store, alert the customer, eventually disable the endpoint, and offer a dashboard or API to replay missed events. Thin payloads (just ids) reduce data exposure and staleness; fat payloads save a call.

questions.title: Designing API errors and status codes
questions.prompt: How should an HTTP API report errors? Explain choosing status codes (400 versus 422, 401 versus 403, 404, 409, 429, 500 versus 503), a consistent machine-readable error body such as RFC 9457 problem details, and what must never appear in an error response.

expectedConcepts.label: Correct status code families and common codes
Structured body: type, code, message, field errors, request id
Retryable signals: 429/503 with Retry-After
Never leak stack traces or secrets; 404 vs 403 to hide existence

questions.modelAnswer: Status codes tell generic clients and proxies what happened: 4xx means the client should change the request, 5xx means the server failed and the request may succeed later. 400 for malformed syntax, 422 for well-formed but semantically invalid input (validation failures), 401 when credentials are missing or invalid (the client should authenticate), 403 when the caller is known but not allowed, 404 when the resource does not exist, 409 for conflicts such as a version mismatch or duplicate, 412 for failed preconditions, 429 when rate limited, 500 for unexpected bugs and 503 when temporarily unavailable. Include Retry-After on 429 and 503 so clients back off correctly. The body should be consistent and machine-readable - RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) with type, title, status and detail, plus a stable application error code clients can switch on, per-field validation errors, and a request or trace id for support. Messages are for humans and may change; codes are the contract. Never include stack traces, SQL, internal hostnames or secrets; and for resources the caller should not know exist, return 404 rather than 403.

questions.title: Long-running operations in APIs
questions.prompt: An API endpoint starts a video export that takes ten minutes. Explain how to design it: returning 202 Accepted with an operation resource, polling with backoff, webhooks or server-sent events for completion, cancellation, progress, failure reporting and idempotency.

expectedConcepts.label: 202 Accepted plus an operation/job resource
Polling the status endpoint with Retry-After
Completion via webhook, SSE or WebSocket
States, progress, result link, error details, cancellation
Idempotent creation, result expiry, polling cost vs push complexity

questions.modelAnswer: Do not hold an HTTP request open for ten minutes - proxies time out and a dropped connection loses the result. Instead POST /exports validates input, enqueues the work and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing at an operation resource such as /operations/abc. That resource exposes status (pending, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled), percent progress, timestamps, and on success a link to the result (e.g. a pre-signed download URL), or on failure a structured error. Clients poll it, honouring a Retry-After header and backing off; to save polling, also offer a webhook callback or a server-sent-events stream for completion. Support cancellation via POST /operations/abc:cancel or DELETE, which is best-effort. The creation request takes an idempotency key so a retried POST does not start a second export. Results and operation records expire after a retention period. Workers update status durably and are retried on crash. Google's AIP-151 long-running operations pattern and Azure's async guidelines are good references. Trade-off: polling is simple and firewall-friendly but wastes requests; push is efficient but needs reachable endpoints or persistent connections.

questions.title: Rate limiting from the API consumer side
questions.prompt: Explain how a public API should communicate and enforce rate limits and quotas. Cover per-key versus per-user limits, token bucket semantics, the 429 status and rate limit headers, how well-behaved clients should back off, and how limits differ for burst and sustained traffic.

expectedConcepts.label: Limit by API key, user, IP, endpoint cost
Token bucket allows bursts up to capacity
429 with Retry-After and RateLimit headers
Clients back off exponentially with jitter, respect headers
Quotas vs rate limits; fairness; distributed counters

questions.modelAnswer: Rate limits protect the service and give tenants fair shares. Scope them by API key or account for authenticated traffic, by IP for anonymous traffic, and weight expensive endpoints (a search might cost 10 units, a read 1). A token bucket per key refills at the sustained rate (say 100 requests per second) and holds a capacity (say 500) to allow short bursts; sliding-window counters are an alternative. Separate longer-term quotas (requests per day or month) usually map to billing tiers. When a client exceeds a limit, respond with 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After, and on every response send headers such as RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset (the IETF RateLimit headers draft) so clients can pace themselves before hitting the wall. Well-behaved clients respect Retry-After, back off exponentially with jitter, and avoid synchronised retries. Do not treat 429 as an error to alert on blindly. Enforcement across many gateway instances uses a shared store such as Redis or approximate local counters; slight over-admission is usually acceptable. Document limits clearly and let customers request higher ones.

questions.title: Optimistic concurrency with ETags
questions.prompt: Two users edit the same resource through your API and one silently overwrites the other. Explain the lost update problem and how ETags with If-Match, or version fields, implement optimistic concurrency control. Also explain how ETags and If-None-Match enable conditional GETs and caching.

expectedConcepts.label: Lost update: read-modify-write races
ETag is a version identifier for a representation
If-Match on PUT/PATCH; 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch
If-None-Match on GET gives 304 Not Modified
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking; retries; requiring preconditions (428)

questions.modelAnswer: Lost update: Alice and Bob both GET document v7, Alice PUTs her changes, then Bob PUTs his, silently erasing Alice's - last write wins. Optimistic concurrency control detects this instead of locking. The server returns an ETag header with every representation - a version number or content hash. Clients send it back on writes: PUT /doc/1 with If-Match: "7". The server performs a conditional update (UPDATE ... SET ..., version = 8 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7); if no row matches, someone else changed it, and the API returns 412 Precondition Failed. The client then re-fetches, merges or asks the user, and retries. Servers can require preconditions on writes and reply 428 Precondition Required when they are missing. The same mechanism saves bandwidth on reads: GET with If-None-Match: "7" returns 304 Not Modified with no body if the version is unchanged. Strong ETags mean byte-identical; weak ETags (W/"7") mean semantically equivalent, fine for caching but not for range requests. Trade-off: optimistic control has no locks and scales well when conflicts are rare; under heavy contention many writers fail and retry, where pessimistic locks or a single serialising owner may be better.

questions.title: Schema evolution with Protocol Buffers
questions.prompt: Explain how Protocol Buffers support backward and forward compatibility. Why are field numbers what matter on the wire, which changes are safe and unsafe, what happens to unknown fields, how reserved works, and how proto3 optional and default values can cause bugs.

expectedConcepts.label: Wire format uses field numbers and wire types, not names
Backward and forward compatibility definitions
Safe: add fields, rename; unsafe: reuse numbers, change types
reserved numbers and names after deletion
proto3 defaults hide presence; required removed; enums zero value

questions.modelAnswer: Protobuf encodes each field as a tag (field number plus wire type) followed by the value; names exist only in generated code. So renaming a field is wire-safe, but changing its number or reusing a deleted field's number for something else is catastrophic - old data will be decoded into the wrong field. Backward compatibility means new code can read old data; forward compatibility means old code can read new data. Adding a new field with a new number is safe both ways: old readers skip it (and modern runtimes preserve it as unknown fields when re-serialising), new readers see the default when it is missing. Unsafe: changing a field's type to an incompatible wire type, changing numbers, moving fields into or out of a oneof carelessly, and changing semantics. When deleting a field, mark its number and name reserved so nobody reuses them. proto2 required fields were removed in proto3 because they made evolution impossible. In proto3, scalar fields without optional have no presence - 0, false and empty string are indistinguishable from "not set" - so use optional or wrapper types when the difference matters. Enums need a zero value like STATUS_UNSPECIFIED, and old readers seeing an unknown enum value must handle it. Tools like buf breaking catch these in CI.

questions.title: Real-time APIs: polling, SSE and WebSockets
questions.prompt: Compare short polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets for pushing real-time updates to clients. Explain how each works over HTTP, their trade-offs for latency, scalability, proxies and reconnection, and which you would choose for a live sports score page and a multiplayer game.

expectedConcepts.label: Short polling: repeated requests, wasteful
Long polling: server holds request until data
SSE: one-way text stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect, Last-Event-ID
WebSockets: upgraded full-duplex connection
Connection state, load balancing, proxies, fan-out via pub/sub

questions.modelAnswer: Short polling asks "anything new?" every few seconds - trivial to build and cache, but wasteful and adds up to an interval of latency. Long polling sends a request that the server holds open until there is data or a timeout, then the client immediately reconnects; latency is low but each message costs a new request. Server-sent events open one HTTP response with Content-Type text/event-stream and the server writes events down it; it is one-way (server to client), text-only, works through most proxies, and browsers reconnect automatically, resending Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. WebSockets upgrade an HTTP connection into a persistent full-duplex channel for binary or text frames in both directions with minimal overhead - best for interactive, high-frequency traffic. All persistent approaches make servers stateful: you need heartbeats to detect dead connections, load balancers that support long-lived connections, careful draining during deploys, and a pub/sub backbone (Redis, Kafka, NATS) to fan messages out to whichever server holds each client. Sports scores are one-way and read-heavy, so SSE (or even cached polling) is ideal; a multiplayer game needs low-latency bidirectional messages, so WebSockets (or WebRTC/UDP for the most latency-sensitive state).

questions.title: Binary search on the answer
questions.prompt: Explain the "binary search on the answer" technique using the problem of shipping packages within D days: find the minimum ship capacity. Why is the feasibility check monotonic, how do you choose the bounds, and what is the overall complexity?

expectedConcepts.label: Feasibility is monotonic: if capacity C works, any larger works
Bounds: max weight to total weight
Greedy check simulates days in O(n)
Time complexity
Space complexity
Off-by-one: find first true, lo < hi loop, overflow in mid
Other uses: Koko bananas, split array largest sum, square root

questions.modelAnswer: Instead of searching an array, search the range of possible answers. For shipping packages in order within D days, define feasible(C): greedily load packages in order, starting a new day whenever the next one would exceed C, and check the day count is at most D - O(n). Feasibility is monotonic: if capacity C works, every larger capacity also works, so the answers form false...false true...true and we want the first true. The lowest possible capacity is the heaviest package (it must fit) and the highest is the total weight (one day). Binary search with lo = max, hi = sum: while lo < hi, mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if feasible(mid) then hi = mid else lo = mid + 1; return lo. Complexity O(n log(sum)), O(1) extra space. Edge cases: using lo + (hi - lo) / 2 to avoid overflow, getting the loop invariant right so you return the first feasible value, and D larger than n. The same pattern solves "minimise the maximum" or "maximise the minimum" problems: Koko eating bananas, split array largest sum, aggressive cows, and integer square root. A linear scan over capacities would be O(n * sum).

questions.title: Search in a rotated sorted array
questions.prompt: A sorted array has been rotated at an unknown pivot, for example [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. Explain how to find a target in O(log n). How do you decide which half is sorted at each step, what changes when there are duplicates, and how would you find the rotation point itself?

expectedConcepts.label: One half is always sorted; compare with its endpoints
Check whether the target lies within the sorted half
Time complexity
Space complexity
Duplicates break the decision: worst case O(n)
Find the minimum/pivot with binary search comparing to the right end

questions.modelAnswer: At any mid point at least one side of a rotated sorted array is fully sorted. Compute mid; if nums[mid] equals the target, return it. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half [lo, mid] is sorted: if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], search left (hi = mid - 1), else search right. Otherwise the right half [mid, hi] is sorted: if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi], search right, else left. Each step discards half, so time is O(log n) with O(1) space. Edge cases: a single element, no rotation at all, and the target missing. With duplicates such as [2,2,2,3,2], nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] gives no information about which side is sorted; you shrink both ends by one, so the worst case degrades to O(n). An alternative approach first finds the rotation point - the minimum - by binary search comparing nums[mid] with nums[hi] (if greater, the minimum is to the right), then runs an ordinary binary search on the correct segment; that is two O(log n) passes.

questions.title: Subarray sum equals k with prefix sums
questions.prompt: Count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k, where the array can contain negative numbers. Explain why sliding window fails here, how prefix sums with a hash map solve it in linear time, and how the idea generalises to other subarray problems.

expectedConcepts.label: sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]
Count prior prefixes equal to current - k
Time complexity
Space complexity
Initialise map with {0: 1}; negatives; overflow
Sliding window fails with negatives; brute force O(n^2); variants

questions.modelAnswer: Let prefix[j] be the sum of the first j elements. The sum of a subarray (i, j] equals prefix[j] - prefix[i], so a subarray ending at j sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals prefix[j] - k. Scan once keeping a running sum and a hash map from prefix value to how many times it has occurred; at each element add count[sum - k] to the answer, then increment count[sum]. Initialise the map with {0: 1} so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted. Time O(n), space O(n). A sliding window does not work because with negative numbers extending the window can decrease the sum, so there is no monotonic rule for when to shrink. Brute force over all pairs is O(n^2). Edge cases: k = 0, all zeros (many overlapping answers), and integer overflow in other languages. The same trick solves "longest subarray with sum k" (store the first index of each prefix instead of a count), "subarray sum divisible by k" (store prefix mod k), and equal numbers of 0s and 1s (map 0 to -1).

questions.title: Maximum subarray and Kadane's algorithm
questions.prompt: Explain Kadane's algorithm for the maximum subarray sum. Why is it correct, what is its complexity, how do you handle an all-negative array and recover the indices, and how does it extend to maximum product subarray or a circular array?

expectedConcepts.label: Best sum ending here = max(x, best ending before + x)
A negative running prefix never helps
Time complexity
Space complexity
All negative: return the largest element; track start/end indices
Variants: max product (track min too), circular (total minus min subarray), divide and conquer

questions.modelAnswer: Kadane's algorithm is a one-dimensional DP. Let cur be the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index: cur = max(x, cur + x), i.e. either extend the previous best subarray or start fresh at x. Track best = max(best, cur). It is correct because if the best subarray ending at the previous index has a negative sum, adding it can only make any extension worse, so restarting is optimal. Time O(n), space O(1). If you initialise cur and best to the first element (not 0), an all-negative array correctly returns its largest element rather than 0 or an empty subarray. To return indices, remember a tentative start whenever you restart and record start/end whenever best improves. Variants: maximum product subarray must track both the maximum and minimum product ending here because a negative number swaps them; for a circular array the answer is max(normal Kadane, total sum - minimum subarray sum), except when all numbers are negative. A divide-and-conquer solution is O(n log n) and is a classic teaching contrast.

questions.title: Floyd's cycle detection (tortoise and hare)
questions.prompt: Explain Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm for detecting a cycle in a linked list. Prove why the pointers meet, how you find the start of the cycle, the complexity, and how the same idea finds a duplicate number in an array without modifying it.

expectedConcepts.label: Fast moves 2, slow moves 1; they meet inside the cycle
Reset one pointer to head; move both by 1 to find the entry
Time complexity
Space complexity
Null/one node, fast.next null checks
Hash set uses O(n) space; find duplicate number as linked list

questions.modelAnswer: Move slow one step and fast two steps per iteration. If there is no cycle, fast reaches null (check fast and fast.next). If there is a cycle, once both are inside it the gap between them shrinks by one each step, so fast must land on slow within one lap - they meet in O(n). To find where the cycle starts: let the distance from head to the cycle entry be a, and the meeting point be b steps past the entry, with cycle length c. Slow travelled a + b, fast travelled 2(a + b), and the difference a + b is a multiple of c, so a = kc - b: walking a steps from the meeting point lands on the entry. So reset one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the entry. Time O(n), space O(1), versus O(n) memory for a visited hash set. Edge cases: empty list, single node, self-loop. The same algorithm finds the duplicate in an array of n+1 numbers in range 1..n without modifying it: treat each value as a pointer to the index i -> nums[i]; the duplicate value is the cycle entry. Brent's algorithm is a faster variant.

questions.title: Core linked list techniques
questions.prompt: Explain the essential linked list techniques used in interviews: the dummy head node, reversing a list iteratively and recursively, fast and slow pointers to find the middle, and merging two sorted lists. Give the complexity and the edge cases that most often cause bugs.

expectedConcepts.label: Dummy node simplifies head insertion/deletion
Reverse with prev/curr/next pointers
Fast/slow pointers find the middle
Time complexity
Space complexity
Empty list, single node, losing the next pointer, even length
Arrays vs linked lists: cache locality, random access

questions.modelAnswer: A dummy (sentinel) node placed before the head means operations that might change the head - deleting the first element, merging, partitioning - need no special cases; return dummy.next at the end. Reversing iteratively uses three pointers: save next = curr.next, point curr.next at prev, then advance prev = curr and curr = next; when curr is null, prev is the new head. That is O(n) time and O(1) space; the recursive version is shorter but uses O(n) stack. Fast and slow pointers find the middle: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle (decide which middle you want for even lengths). Merging two sorted lists walks both with a tail pointer from a dummy node, attaching the smaller node each time, O(n + m). Together these solve palindrome lists (find middle, reverse second half, compare), reorder list and reverse in groups of k. Bugs usually come from null checks on empty or single-node lists and from overwriting next before saving it. In practice arrays beat linked lists for most workloads due to cache locality and random access.

questions.title: Binary search trees and why balancing matters
questions.prompt: Explain binary search tree insert, search and delete, including deleting a node with two children. Why can an unbalanced BST degrade to O(n), and how do self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees keep operations O(log n)? Where are they used in practice?

expectedConcepts.label: Search/insert by comparing and descending left or right
Delete with two children: replace by in-order successor
Time complexity
Space complexity
Sorted insertion degrades to a linked list; duplicates
AVL vs red-black; rotations; std::map, TreeMap; B-trees for disk

questions.modelAnswer: A BST keeps every left-subtree key smaller and every right-subtree key larger than the node. Search and insert start at the root and descend left or right by comparison; cost is proportional to the height h. Delete has three cases: a leaf is removed, a node with one child is replaced by that child, and a node with two children copies its in-order successor (the leftmost node of its right subtree), then deletes that successor, which has at most one child. An in-order traversal yields keys in sorted order. If keys arrive sorted, each goes to the right of the previous, so the tree becomes a linked list with height n and O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees bound the height to O(log n) using rotations after inserts and deletes: AVL trees keep subtree heights within one (stricter, faster lookups), red-black trees enforce colouring rules that keep the longest path at most twice the shortest (fewer rotations, cheaper updates). Red-black trees back std::map and Java TreeMap and Linux schedulers; databases use B-trees, which are wide and shallow to minimise disk reads. Space is O(n), and recursive implementations use O(h) stack.

questions.title: Tree traversals: recursive, iterative and Morris
questions.prompt: Explain preorder, inorder, postorder and level-order traversal of a binary tree. How do you implement inorder traversal iteratively with a stack, what are typical uses of each order, and how does Morris traversal achieve O(1) extra space?

expectedConcepts.label: Pre (node, left, right), in (left, node, right), post (left, right, node)
Iterative inorder: push left spine, pop, go right
Time complexity
Space complexity
Uses: copy/serialise (pre), sorted BST (in), delete/evaluate (post), BFS by levels
Morris traversal threads predecessors for O(1) space

questions.modelAnswer: Depth-first orders differ in when the node is visited: preorder visits node, left, right (good for copying or serialising a tree), inorder visits left, node, right (sorted order in a BST), and postorder visits left, right, node (deleting a tree or evaluating an expression tree, since children are processed first). Level order is breadth-first with a queue, visiting level by level (shortest depth, right-side view). All visit each node once, O(n) time. Recursive versions use O(h) stack, where h can be n for a skewed tree, risking stack overflow. Iterative inorder: starting at the root, push nodes while going left; pop a node, visit it, then move to its right child and repeat. Iterative postorder can use two stacks or track the last visited node. Morris traversal achieves O(1) extra space: for each node with a left child, find its inorder predecessor and temporarily set the predecessor's right pointer back to the node (a thread), go left, and when you return via the thread, remove it and visit the node. It modifies the tree temporarily, so it is unsafe with concurrent readers, but restores it fully.

questions.title: Lowest common ancestor
questions.prompt: Explain how to find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree, in a binary search tree, and when you must answer many LCA queries on a large static tree. Give complexities for each, and discuss edge cases like a node being its own ancestor or a missing node.

expectedConcepts.label: Binary tree: recurse; the node where p and q split is the LCA
BST: walk from root using ordering
Time complexity
Space complexity
Node is ancestor of itself; missing node; parent pointers
Many queries: binary lifting or Euler tour + RMQ

questions.modelAnswer: Binary tree: recursively search both subtrees. If the current node is null or equals p or q, return it. Otherwise recurse left and right; if both return non-null, p and q are on different sides, so this node is the LCA; else return whichever side is non-null. Each node is visited once: O(n) time, O(h) stack. This assumes both nodes exist - if one may be missing, track whether each was actually found. A node counts as its own ancestor, so if p is above q, p is the answer.
