Write conflicts: home region per user, CRDTs, LWW
Strong consistency needs consensus across regions: latency cost
Failover drills, capacity headroom, avoid split brain
Data residency and per-region capacity
Trade-offs: cost and complexity vs availability and latency

questions.modelAnswer: Start with targets: RTO (how fast you recover) and RPO (how much data you may lose), plus latency goals per geography. Active-passive runs everything in one primary region and replicates data to a standby region that takes over on failure; it is simpler, but failover is slow and risky if rarely exercised, and remote users get higher latency. Active-active serves traffic from every region simultaneously: users are routed to the nearest healthy region via geo-DNS or anycast with health checks. The hard part is data. Cross-region replication is usually asynchronous (a write in Mumbai reaches Virginia 100-200 ms later), so a region loss can drop recent writes (RPO > 0), and concurrent writes to the same record in two regions conflict. Avoid conflicts by giving each user or tenant a home region that owns their writes, use CRDTs or last-write-wins only where acceptable, and keep truly global invariants (unique usernames, balances) in a strongly consistent store using consensus across regions such as Spanner or CockroachDB - accepting cross-region round trips on those writes. Each region needs headroom to absorb a failed region's traffic; rehearse failovers regularly and guard against split brain with fencing. Data residency laws may pin data to regions. Trade-off: roughly double cost and much more complexity for higher availability and lower latency.

questions.title: Design an online code judge like LeetCode
questions.prompt: Design a system where users submit code in many languages and get results against hidden test cases within seconds. Focus on secure sandboxing of untrusted code, resource limits, the submission queue and worker fleet, handling contest traffic spikes, and returning results to the user.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Submissions queued; workers pull jobs
Sandbox: containers with seccomp/gVisor/Firecracker, no network
CPU time, memory, process and output limits
Results via polling or WebSocket; store verdicts
Autoscale workers on queue depth; prewarmed sandboxes
Deterministic, fair timing; retries for infra failures
Trade-offs: isolation strength vs startup latency

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: support a dozen languages, return a verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time or memory limit exceeded, runtime or compile error) within a few seconds normally, handle 10-50x spikes at contest start, and above all never let user code escape or harm other users. Flow: the API stores the submission and enqueues a job; the client polls or holds a WebSocket for the verdict. A worker fleet pulls jobs, compiles and runs the code against test cases inside a sandbox: a fresh container or microVM per submission with no network, a read-only filesystem except a scratch dir, seccomp syscall filtering (or gVisor/Firecracker for stronger isolation), a non-root user, and cgroup limits on CPU time, wall time, memory, process count (fork bombs) and output size. Test data is mounted read-only and never shown to users. Timing fairness: pin each run to a dedicated core and avoid noisy neighbours so the same code gets consistent times; rerun borderline cases. Scaling: autoscale workers on queue depth and keep a warm pool of sandboxes before scheduled contests; during spikes prioritise contest submissions. Infrastructure failures (worker died) are retried; user-code failures are not. Trade-off: microVMs isolate better than containers but start slower and cost more, so pooling and snapshots matter.

questions.title: Design route planning and ETA for a maps app
questions.prompt: Design the routing component of a maps application: given two points, return the fastest driving route and an ETA in under 200 milliseconds, considering live traffic. Explain the road graph, why plain Dijkstra is too slow on a continental graph, preprocessing techniques like contraction hierarchies, and how live traffic updates edge weights.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Road network as weighted directed graph
Dijkstra on 100M+ nodes is too slow per query
Preprocessing: contraction hierarchies, A* with landmarks, partitioning
Live traffic from GPS probes updates weights; customisable routing
ETA from historical + live speeds; ML correction
Replicated routing servers holding graph in memory
Trade-offs: preprocessing time vs query speed and update flexibility

questions.modelAnswer: Model the road network as a directed graph: intersections are nodes, road segments are edges weighted by travel time, with turn restrictions and one-way streets. A continent has hundreds of millions of nodes; Dijkstra explores everything within the route's radius, taking seconds per long query, far too slow for thousands of requests per second. Speed-up techniques preprocess the graph. Contraction hierarchies rank nodes by importance and add shortcut edges that bypass less important nodes; a query runs bidirectional Dijkstra that only moves "upward" in importance, settling a few hundred nodes instead of millions - sub-millisecond queries. A* with landmarks (ALT) uses precomputed distances to landmarks as a heuristic. Live traffic is the challenge for heavy preprocessing, so modern systems use customisable route planning: partition the graph into cells, preprocess topology once, and quickly recompute cell-level costs when weights change. Weights come from historical speeds by time of day blended with live speeds aggregated from anonymised GPS probes (streamed and map-matched to segments). ETA = route cost adjusted by ML models trained on actual trip times. Routing servers keep the graph in memory, are stateless per query and replicated per region. Trade-off: more preprocessing gives faster queries but slower adaptation to changes.

questions.title: Design a recommendation system
questions.prompt: Design the recommendation system for a video or e-commerce platform. Explain the two-stage architecture of candidate generation and ranking, collaborative filtering and embeddings, the offline training and online serving split, feature stores, cold start, feedback loops and how you evaluate it.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Candidate generation then ranking then re-ranking
Collaborative filtering / embeddings with ANN search
Offline training, online serving, feature store
Cold start: content features, popularity, exploration
Evaluation: offline metrics and A/B tests
Feedback loops, diversity, filter bubbles
Trade-offs: freshness vs cost, engagement vs user value

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: personalised recommendations from a catalogue of millions of items in under 100 ms, reflecting recent behaviour. You cannot score every item per request, so use a funnel. Candidate generation retrieves a few hundred to a few thousand items cheaply from several sources: collaborative filtering (users who watched X also watched Y), a two-tower model that embeds users and items into the same vector space with approximate nearest-neighbour search (FAISS, ScaNN), items similar to recent interactions, and trending items. Ranking scores those candidates with a heavier model (gradient-boosted trees or a deep network) using rich features - user history, item metadata, context like time and device - predicting objectives such as click or watch time. Re-ranking applies business rules: diversity, freshness, removing already-seen items. Models train offline on logged interactions; embeddings and indexes are rebuilt periodically; a feature store serves the same feature definitions offline and online to avoid training-serving skew, with streaming updates for recent activity. Cold start: use content features and popularity for new items and users, plus exploration (bandits). Evaluate offline (recall, NDCG) but decide with A/B tests on real engagement and long-term retention. Watch feedback loops that only recommend what was already recommended.

questions.title: Design live comments for a streaming event
questions.prompt: Design a live comment and reaction feature for a live-streamed event with 10 million concurrent viewers, like a cricket final. Explain connection management, fan-out of messages to millions of clients, why you cannot send every comment to everyone, sampling and aggregation, ordering and moderation.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Persistent connections to an edge/gateway fleet
Pub/sub fan-out tree: event -> gateways -> clients
Sampling: each viewer sees a subset; aggregate reactions
Moderation and rate limiting before fan-out
Loose ordering is acceptable; no persistence for most
Connection spikes at match start; reconnect storms
Graceful degradation: shed load, drop comments
Trade-offs: completeness vs scale and readability

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 10M concurrent viewers, perhaps 50k comments per second at peaks, under 2 s latency, reactions (emoji) counted in real time. Viewers hold persistent WebSocket or SSE connections to a large gateway fleet at the edge, each gateway holding hundreds of thousands of connections. Fan-out: comments are posted to an ingest service that rate-limits users, runs moderation (spam, abuse filters) and publishes to a pub/sub channel for the event. Each gateway subscribes once and forwards to its local connections, so the fan-out is a tree (1 publish -> thousands of gateways -> millions of clients) rather than a central server writing to 10M sockets. Sending every one of 50k comments per second to every viewer would be 500 billion messages per second and unreadable anyway, so each viewer gets a sampled stream - a few comments per second, prioritising friends and verified or highly-liked comments - while reactions are aggregated into counts per second and broadcast as totals. Ordering is best-effort and comments are mostly ephemeral, persisted only for replay or moderation. Spikes at key moments and reconnect storms after deploys need jittered reconnects and pre-scaled gateways. Under overload, shed load by lowering the sample rate. Trade-off: users never see everything, but the experience stays fast.

questions.title: Design authentication and session management at scale
questions.prompt: Design login and session management for a large consumer app with web and mobile clients. Compare server-side sessions and stateless tokens, explain password storage, refresh token rotation, logout and revocation, multi-factor authentication, and how you protect the login endpoint from credential stuffing.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Password hashing with Argon2/bcrypt, salts
Server-side session store vs JWT access tokens
Short access tokens, rotating refresh tokens
Logout and revocation: session deletion / denylist
MFA: TOTP, WebAuthn/passkeys
Credential stuffing: rate limits, breached-password checks, bot detection
Trade-offs: stateless scalability vs revocation

questions.modelAnswer: Store passwords only as slow, salted hashes (Argon2id or bcrypt) so a database leak does not reveal them; better still, support passkeys (WebAuthn) and offer TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor. Sessions: for web, a random session id in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie pointing at a server-side session store (Redis) is simple and instantly revocable, and a lookup per request is cheap. For mobile and APIs, issue a short-lived access token (often a JWT, 5-15 minutes) that services verify locally without a lookup, plus a long-lived refresh token stored securely and tracked server-side. Refresh tokens rotate on every use; if an old one is reused, assume theft and revoke the whole token family. Logout deletes the session or refresh token; access tokens die quickly by expiry, or a small denylist covers emergencies. "Log out all devices" and password changes revoke all of a user's sessions. The login endpoint is the main attack surface: rate-limit by IP and account with exponential delays (not hard lockouts that enable denial of service), check passwords against breached-password lists, use bot detection and step-up challenges for risky logins, and alert users about new devices. Trade-off: stateless tokens scale without lookups but are hard to revoke; sessions are revocable but need a fast shared store. The requirements frame the design: web and mobile clients, millions of users, login traffic that spikes at peak hours, and instant revocation when an account is compromised.

questions.title: Design a distributed lock service
questions.prompt: Several instances of a service must ensure only one of them processes a given job at a time. Explain how you would build a distributed lock with a lease, why a lock in Redis alone can be unsafe, what fencing tokens are, and when you should use ZooKeeper or etcd instead, or avoid locks entirely.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Locks need leases/TTLs so crashed holders release
GC pauses/clock issues: holder may act after expiry
Fencing tokens checked by the protected resource
ZooKeeper/etcd: consensus-backed locks with sessions
Redis SET NX PX for efficiency locks; Redlock debate
Avoid locks: idempotency, partitioning by key, DB constraints
Lock contention and lock service as a dependency
Trade-offs: efficiency locks vs correctness locks

questions.modelAnswer: Ask first whether the lock is for efficiency (avoid doing work twice; occasional duplicates are fine) or correctness (duplicates corrupt data). A distributed lock must expire, otherwise a crashed holder blocks everyone forever, so locks are leases with a TTL that the holder renews. That creates the core danger: a holder can pause (a long GC, VM migration, network delay) past its lease, another client acquires the lock, and the first one wakes up and writes anyway. Timeouts alone cannot fix this. Fencing tokens do: every acquisition returns a monotonically increasing number, the client passes it with each write, and the storage system rejects writes carrying a token lower than one it has already seen. For efficiency locks, Redis SET key value NX PX 30000 with a random value (deleted only if it still matches) is simple and fast; Redlock across several Redis nodes is debated because it relies on timing assumptions and provides no fencing. For correctness, use a consensus-backed system - ZooKeeper (ephemeral sequential nodes, zxid as a fencing token) or etcd (leases plus revision numbers) - which stays consistent under partitions. Better still, design locks away: partition work so each key has a single owner, make operations idempotent, or use conditional writes and unique constraints in the database. The lock service also becomes a dependency on the critical path, and heavy contention for one lock serialises work, so keep locks rare and short.

questions.title: Read replicas and replication lag
questions.prompt: Your primary database is overloaded by reads, so you add read replicas. Explain how leader-follower replication works, what replication lag is and the bugs it causes such as reading your own writes and non-monotonic reads, how to route queries, and how failover to a replica works and can lose data.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Primary streams WAL/binlog to replicas
Async replication lag
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads anomalies; fixes
Routing reads vs writes; proxies
Failover: promote replica; async means possible data loss
Writes still bottleneck on primary; long queries delay replay
Trade-offs: sync vs async replication

questions.modelAnswer: In leader-follower replication all writes go to the primary, which records them in its write-ahead log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog) and streams that log to replicas that replay it. Replicas serve reads, so read capacity scales by adding replicas; writes do not scale this way. Replication is usually asynchronous: the primary acknowledges a commit before replicas apply it, so replicas lag by milliseconds normally and by seconds or minutes under load or long-running queries. Lag causes anomalies. Read-your-writes: a user updates their profile, the next page reads a replica and shows the old value - fix by reading from the primary for a short time after a user writes, or by waiting until the replica has applied the write's log position (LSN/GTID). Monotonic reads: successive requests hit different replicas and data appears to go back in time - pin a user to one replica. Routing happens in the application or a proxy that sends writes and consistency-sensitive reads to the primary. Failover promotes the most up-to-date replica; with async replication, writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet replicated are lost, and a returning old primary must be fenced to avoid split brain. Synchronous or semi-synchronous replication avoids loss at the cost of write latency and availability.

questions.title: Counting likes and views at massive scale
questions.prompt: Design how a platform counts likes and views on posts, where a viral post can receive a million likes per minute. Explain why incrementing one database row fails, and compare sharded counters, in-memory aggregation with periodic flushes, stream aggregation and approximate counting with HyperLogLog for unique views.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Single-row counter becomes a lock hot spot
Sharded counters: N rows summed on read
Buffer increments in memory/stream and flush periodically
Likes are per-user facts; idempotent toggles
HyperLogLog for approximate unique counts
Losing buffered increments on crash; replay from log
Trade-offs: exactness and freshness vs throughput

questions.modelAnswer: UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = ? serialises every like on a single row lock; at thousands per second on a viral post, requests queue and time out. Separate the fact from the count: a like is a per-user fact (user_id, post_id) stored idempotently with a unique key, so double taps or retries do not double count and unlikes work; the displayed count is derived. Options for the count: sharded counters split it across N rows or keys (post:123:shard:7) incremented at random and summed on read, spreading contention; or buffer increments in memory or in a stream (Kafka) and have an aggregator flush the summed delta every few seconds - one write instead of thousands. Redis INCR handles very high rates for a single key in memory, with periodic persistence. Buffered approaches can lose a few seconds of increments if a node crashes, so either accept that for views or rebuild from the durable event log. For unique viewers, storing every viewer id per post is huge; HyperLogLog estimates cardinality with about 1% error in 12 KB per counter, and sketches can be merged across shards and time windows. Trade-off: counts become approximate or lag by seconds, which users accept for likes and views but not for money.

questions.title: Design matchmaking for an online multiplayer game
questions.prompt: Design the matchmaking service for an online game that groups players of similar skill into 5-versus-5 matches within a minute, across several regions. Explain the skill rating, the queueing and matching algorithm, widening search windows over time, latency-based region selection, and handling players who leave the queue.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Skill rating: Elo / Glicko / TrueSkill
Queues per region/mode; bucketed by rating
Widen the acceptable skill range as wait grows
Region by ping; game server allocation
Handling cancels, accept/decline and backfill
Matchmaker shards; in-memory state rebuilt from client requeue
Low population at off-hours or high ranks
Trade-offs: match quality vs wait time

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: form balanced 5v5 matches quickly (target under 60 s), keep ping low, support parties, and scale to peak hours across regions. Each player has a skill rating such as Elo, Glicko-2 or TrueSkill (which models uncertainty, helpful for new players), updated after each match. Players enter a queue for a game mode in their best region, chosen by measuring ping to each region. The matchmaker keeps queued tickets in memory, bucketed by rating. Every second or so it scans tickets ordered by wait time, tries to build matches from players within an acceptable rating window, and balances teams by total rating (parties stay together). If no match is found, the window widens gradually with wait time, trading quality for speed; after a long wait it may also allow neighbouring regions. Once a match forms, players must accept within a few seconds; anyone who declines returns the rest to the front of the queue. Then a game server is allocated in the region (Agones on Kubernetes or a fleet manager) and connection details are sent. Matchmaker state is ephemeral: shard by region and mode, and if a node dies, clients detect it and requeue. Low population (3 a.m., top ranks) forces wider windows. The fundamental trade-off is match quality versus wait time.

questions.title: Design trending hashtags
questions.prompt: Design a system that shows the top trending hashtags globally and per country, updated every minute, from a stream of 500,000 posts per second. Explain why trending is not the same as most popular, sliding windows, the heavy-hitters algorithms you would use, distributed aggregation and spam resistance.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Trending = growth versus baseline, not raw count
Sliding/hopping windows with time buckets
Heavy hitters: Count-Min Sketch + heap, Space-Saving
Local partial aggregation then merge
Spam and manipulation filtering; unique users
Approximate results acceptable; recover from checkpoints
Skewed keys: one hashtag dominates a partition
Trade-offs: accuracy vs memory, responsiveness vs stability

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 500k posts/s, top 10-50 trends globally and per country, refreshed every minute, robust to manipulation. Trending means unusual growth: a hashtag used a million times every day (#goodmorning) is popular, not trending, so compare the current rate with a baseline - for example the ratio or z-score of the last 15 minutes against the same hour over past weeks, with a minimum volume. Pipeline: posts flow through Kafka; extractors parse hashtags and attach country and user id. Counting exact counts for every hashtag in every window is expensive, so each stream worker does partial aggregation over one-minute buckets using a heavy-hitters structure - Space-Saving or a Count-Min Sketch with a min-heap of candidates - and emits its local top few thousand. An aggregator merges partials by country and globally, maintains sliding windows by summing recent buckets (or exponential decay), computes trend scores against stored baselines, and writes the ranked lists to a cache read by the API. Hot keys are pre-aggregated locally before shuffling. Spam resistance: count distinct users rather than posts (HyperLogLog per hashtag), down-weight new or bot-like accounts, and detect coordinated bursts; editorial blocklists remove abusive tags. Results are approximate and that is fine. Trade-off: shorter windows react faster but are noisier.

questions.title: HTTP method semantics: safe, idempotent, cacheable
questions.prompt: Explain the semantics of the main HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. Which are safe, which are idempotent and which are cacheable, what is the difference between PUT and PATCH, and what goes wrong when an API ignores these semantics?

expectedConcepts.label: Safe methods do not change state (GET, HEAD)
Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE; not POST
PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH applies partial changes
GET responses cacheable; proxies and retries rely on semantics
Pitfalls: GET that deletes, POST for everything

questions.modelAnswer: Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) promise not to change server state, so browsers, crawlers and prefetchers may call them freely. Idempotent methods produce the same server state whether sent once or many times: GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not (two POSTs create two orders) and PATCH is not guaranteed to be. GET responses are cacheable by default when headers allow; POST responses rarely are. PUT sends a complete representation that replaces the resource at that URL (and can create it at a client-chosen URL), so missing fields are cleared; PATCH sends a partial change, such as a JSON Merge Patch with only the fields to update. Infrastructure relies on these semantics: proxies and clients automatically retry idempotent requests after a network error, caches store GETs, and crawlers follow links. A GET /deleteUser?id=5 link can be triggered by a crawler or link preview and delete data; using POST for every operation loses caching and safe retries and hides intent. Use the right method, and make POST safe to retry with idempotency keys.

questions.title: Modelling resources and URLs in a REST API
questions.prompt: How do you model resources and URLs for a REST API of an online course platform with courses, lessons, enrolments and payments? Discuss nouns versus verbs, collection and item URLs, nesting depth, representing actions such as "publish" or "refund", and relationships between resources.

expectedConcepts.label: Resources are nouns; methods are the verbs
Shallow nesting: /courses/{id}/lessons but not deeper
Actions as state changes, sub-resources or custom methods
Relationships as links or ids; enrolment as its own resource
Trade-offs: purity vs pragmatism, consistency across the API

questions.modelAnswer: Model the domain as resources (nouns) and let HTTP methods supply the verbs: GET /courses lists, POST /courses creates, GET /courses/{courseId} reads, PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Use plural collection names and stable opaque ids. Nest only when the child has no meaning without its parent and keep it shallow: /courses/{id}/lessons for listing a course's lessons, but address an individual lesson as /lessons/{lessonId} rather than /courses/1/modules/2/lessons/3, which breaks when things move. Many-to-many relationships often deserve their own resource: an enrolment links a user and a course and has its own data (enrolled_at, progress), so POST /enrollments creates one. Actions that do not map cleanly to CRUD can be modelled as state changes (PATCH /courses/{id} {"status": "published"}), as resources (POST /payments/{id}/refunds creates a refund, which can then be listed and queried), or as explicit custom methods (POST /courses/{id}:publish, as in Google's API guidelines) - pick one convention. Return links or ids for related resources. Consistency across the whole API matters more than theoretical purity, so write a style guide.

questions.title: Filtering, sorting and field selection in list APIs
questions.prompt: Design query parameters for a list endpoint that needs filtering by several fields, ranges and dates, sorting by multiple keys, and selecting which fields to return. How do you keep it consistent, safe and fast, and when does a dedicated search endpoint make more sense?

expectedConcepts.label: Filter params: field=value, ranges, operators
Sort param with direction and stable tie-breaker
Sparse fieldsets / field masks
Allowlist filterable/sortable fields, indexed; validate inputs
Search endpoint for complex queries; cursor pagination interaction

questions.modelAnswer: Keep a consistent grammar across endpoints: equality filters as ?status=active&country=IN, ranges with explicit operators such as ?created_after=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z or ?price[gte]=100, and lists as ?status=active,pending. Sorting: ?sort=-created_at,name where a minus means descending; always append a unique tie-breaker such as id so ordering is stable and cursor pagination works. Field selection: ?fields=id,name,price (sparse fieldsets, or field masks in gRPC) reduces payload size for mobile clients. Safety and performance: only allow filtering and sorting on an explicit allowlist of fields that are backed by database indexes, otherwise one query can force a full table scan; validate types and reject unknown parameters with 400 rather than ignoring them silently; never build SQL by string concatenation. Cursor tokens must encode the sort order they were created with. When queries need boolean logic, full-text matching or many nested conditions, URLs get unwieldy and hit length limits; a POST /orders:search with a JSON body, or a search service, is cleaner - accepting that POST responses are not cached.

questions.title: Batch and bulk operations with partial failure
questions.prompt: Clients need to create or update thousands of records at once through your API. Compare one-request-per-item, a batch endpoint, and an asynchronous bulk job. How do you report partial failures, keep operations idempotent, enforce limits, and decide between all-or-nothing and per-item results?

expectedConcepts.label: Per-item requests cost round trips and rate limits
Batch endpoint with per-item results (207 / results array)
All-or-nothing vs partial success semantics
Large bulk: async job with status and error report
Limits, idempotency per item, timeouts, ordering

questions.modelAnswer: Sending thousands of individual requests multiplies round trips, connection overhead and rate-limit consumption. A batch endpoint (POST /contacts:batchCreate with an array) amortises that, but you must define failure semantics. All-or-nothing runs the batch in one transaction: simple for clients, but one bad item rejects everything and big transactions hold locks. Partial success processes each item independently and returns a result per item in the same order - status, created id or error code - with an overall 200 or 207 Multi-Status; clients must inspect every result. Make items idempotent: each carries a client-generated id or the batch has an idempotency key, so a retried batch does not duplicate successes. Enforce limits (for example 100 items or 1 MB per request) and a server timeout. For very large imports (a CSV of a million rows), switch to an asynchronous bulk job: upload the file, get 202 with a job id, poll status and progress, and download a report listing failed rows. Ordering and dependencies between items within a batch should be documented or forbidden. Trade-off: batch APIs are efficient but more complex for clients and servers than single-item calls.

questions.title: HTTP caching for APIs
questions.prompt: Explain how HTTP caching works for API responses. Cover Cache-Control directives such as max-age, no-cache, no-store, private and public, validators with ETag and Last-Modified, the Vary header, CDN caching of API responses, and the mistakes that leak private data or serve stale data.

expectedConcepts.label: Cache-Control: max-age, s-maxage, no-store, no-cache
private (browser only) vs public (shared caches)
Revalidation with ETag/If-None-Match and 304
Vary by headers like Authorization, Accept-Encoding
Pitfalls: caching personalised responses publicly, missing headers, stale data

questions.modelAnswer: Cache-Control tells browsers and shared caches (CDNs, proxies) what they may do. max-age=60 lets a response be reused for 60 seconds; s-maxage applies only to shared caches; no-cache means "store it but revalidate before each reuse"; no-store means never store it at all - right for sensitive data like account details. public allows shared caches to store responses even for authenticated requests, while private restricts caching to the end user's browser. Validators make revalidation cheap: the server sends an ETag (or Last-Modified); the client later sends If-None-Match, and if unchanged the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body. stale-while-revalidate lets caches serve slightly stale content while refreshing in the background. Vary lists request headers that change the response (Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language) so caches key on them. Public, non-personalised API responses - product catalogues, exchange rates - can be cached at a CDN for seconds to minutes, dramatically reducing load. Mistakes: marking a personalised response public so a CDN serves one user's data to another, omitting Cache-Control so caches apply heuristics, and long max-age on data that must update quickly without a versioning or purge strategy.

questions.title: CORS and preflight requests
questions.prompt: Explain Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. Why does the browser block some cross-origin requests by default, what triggers a preflight OPTIONS request, which response headers grant access, how credentials such as cookies change the rules, and what security mistakes teams make when "fixing" CORS errors?

expectedConcepts.label: Same-origin policy restricts reading cross-origin responses
Preflight for non-simple methods/headers/content types
Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers, Max-Age
Credentials require explicit origin, not *
Mistakes: reflecting any origin with credentials; CORS is not auth; CSRF

questions.modelAnswer: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a page from https://app.example.com may send requests elsewhere, but script cannot read responses from a different origin (scheme, host and port) unless that server opts in with CORS headers. CORS protects users' data, not servers - curl or a backend ignores it entirely. Simple requests (GET, HEAD or POST with form-like content types and no custom headers) are sent directly and the browser checks Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the response. Anything else - PUT/DELETE, Content-Type: application/json, an Authorization header - triggers a preflight OPTIONS request asking permission; the server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods and -Headers, and Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache the answer. To send cookies, the client sets credentials: "include" and the server must reply with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and an explicit origin, never *. The common dangerous "fix" is reflecting whatever Origin arrives together with Allow-Credentials, which lets any website read users' private data using their cookies; use an allowlist. CORS does not stop requests from being sent, so state-changing endpoints still need CSRF defences such as SameSite cookies or tokens.

questions.title: API security: broken object level authorisation and friends
questions.prompt: Walk through the most common API security flaws from the OWASP API Security Top 10: broken object level authorisation, broken authentication, excessive data exposure, mass assignment, lack of rate limiting and server-side request forgery. Give a concrete example of each and how to prevent it.

expectedConcepts.label: BOLA/IDOR: changing an id in the URL accesses others' data
Mass assignment: client sets fields like role or price
Excessive data exposure: returning full objects and filtering in the client
SSRF: server fetches attacker-supplied URLs (cloud metadata)
Prevention: authorise every object access, explicit DTOs, rate limits, egress allowlists

questions.modelAnswer: Broken object level authorisation (IDOR) is the most common: GET /invoices/1043 returns the invoice after checking only that the caller is logged in, so changing the id to 1044 reads another customer's invoice. Fix by checking ownership or permissions for every object on every request, centrally (policy layer, row-level security), and test it with two users; random ids are not a fix. Broken authentication: weak token validation, no expiry, accepting unsigned JWTs (alg none), or credential stuffing with no throttling. Excessive data exposure: the API serialises whole database objects (including password hashes, internal flags, other users' emails) and relies on the frontend to hide fields; define explicit response schemas. Mass assignment: PATCH /users/me binds the JSON body directly onto the model, so a client adds "role": "admin" or "price": 0; bind only an allowlist of writable fields. Lack of rate limiting enables brute force, scraping and cost attacks. SSRF: an endpoint that fetches a user-supplied URL (webhooks, image import) can be pointed at internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254 to steal credentials; validate and resolve URLs, block private ranges, and use an egress proxy. Also: log security events, keep an inventory of all API versions, and validate inputs strictly.

questions.title: API gateways and the backend-for-frontend pattern
questions.prompt: Explain what an API gateway does in a microservices architecture and when to add a backend-for-frontend layer for web and mobile clients. What belongs in the gateway, what must stay out of it, and what are the risks of a gateway becoming a bottleneck or a distributed monolith?

expectedConcepts.label: Gateway: single entry, routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS
BFF: per-client backend aggregating services for a UI
Keep business logic out of the gateway
Aggregation reduces round trips for mobile
Risks: bottleneck, single point of failure, team coupling

questions.modelAnswer: An API gateway is the single entry point for external clients: it terminates TLS, routes requests to backend services, authenticates tokens, applies rate limits and quotas, enforces request size limits, adds request ids and collects metrics - cross-cutting concerns implemented once instead of in every service. It lets internal services change and move without clients noticing. Business logic does not belong there; once teams start writing domain rules in gateway configuration, every change needs the gateway team and it turns into a distributed monolith. A backend-for-frontend is a thin service owned by a client team that shapes data for one UI: the mobile BFF aggregates calls to users, orders and recommendations into one response tailored to a screen, reducing round trips on slow networks and keeping the core services generic, while the web BFF may return different shapes. GraphQL is often used for the same goal. Risks: the gateway is a critical dependency and potential bottleneck, so run it highly available and horizontally scaled; each hop adds latency; and BFFs can duplicate logic across clients, so push shared rules down into services.

questions.title: Contract-first APIs with OpenAPI
questions.prompt: Explain contract-first API development using an OpenAPI specification. How does writing the spec before code help teams, what can you generate from it, how do contract tests and schema linting catch breaking changes in CI, and what are the drawbacks compared with code-first approaches?

expectedConcepts.label: OpenAPI describes paths, schemas, errors, auth
Contract first enables parallel work and review
Generate clients, server stubs, docs, validators
Breaking-change detection and contract tests in CI
Drawbacks: spec drift, verbose specs, generated code quality

questions.modelAnswer: In contract-first development the team writes the OpenAPI document - paths, methods, request and response schemas, error formats, auth schemes, examples - and reviews it like code before implementing anything. Frontend, mobile and partner teams can then build against a mock server generated from the spec while the backend implements it, and design problems are caught when they are cheap to fix. From the spec you can generate typed client SDKs in many languages, server stubs or request validators, and interactive documentation. In CI, a linter (Spectral) enforces the style guide - naming, pagination, error shape - and an OpenAPI diff tool flags breaking changes such as removed fields or newly required parameters before they ship. Contract tests verify that the running service actually matches the spec, and consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) verify that changes do not break specific consumers. Drawbacks: if the spec is not enforced by validation or generation, it drifts from reality; large specs are verbose YAML; generated code can be awkward. Code-first (generating the spec from annotations) avoids drift but encourages designing the API around implementation details, so many teams combine generated specs with review and breaking-change checks.

questions.title: gRPC in production: deadlines, streaming and errors
questions.prompt: Explain how to use gRPC well in production. Cover the four streaming modes, deadlines and their propagation across services, status codes and rich error details, retries and hedging, load balancing of long-lived HTTP/2 connections, and backward-compatible proto changes.

expectedConcepts.label: Unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional
Deadlines set by caller and propagated
Status codes (UNAVAILABLE, INVALID_ARGUMENT...) and error details
HTTP/2 connections need L7 or client-side load balancing
Retries only on retryable codes; hedging; proto compatibility

questions.modelAnswer: gRPC supports four call types: unary (request-response), server streaming (one request, many responses - e.g. a price feed), client streaming (upload many messages, one response) and bidirectional streaming (chat, real-time sync). Every call should carry a deadline set by the original caller; servers read the remaining time from the context and pass it to downstream calls, so a request that the user abandoned or that cannot finish in time stops consuming resources across the whole call chain - a missing deadline means a stuck call can hang forever. Errors use canonical status codes: INVALID_ARGUMENT and NOT_FOUND are the caller's fault and not retryable; UNAVAILABLE is transient and retryable; DEADLINE_EXCEEDED and RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED need care. Rich error details (google.rpc.Status with BadRequest or RetryInfo) give structured information. Configure retry policies only for idempotent methods and retryable codes, with backoff and retry budgets; hedging sends a second request after a delay to cut tail latency. Because gRPC multiplexes many calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, an L4 load balancer pins all traffic from a client to one backend; use L7 proxies (Envoy) or client-side load balancing with service discovery, and cap connection age. Evolve protos additively and never reuse field numbers.

questions.title: Designing a GraphQL schema
questions.prompt: Explain the principles of good GraphQL schema design: modelling a graph rather than mirroring database tables, nullability choices, cursor-based connections for pagination, mutation design with input and payload types, error handling with typed results, and evolving the schema without versions.

expectedConcepts.label: Model the domain graph, not tables or REST endpoints
Nullability: non-null is a strong promise; nulls propagate
Relay connections: edges, nodes, pageInfo, cursors
Mutations with specific names, input and payload types, typed errors
Evolve by adding fields and @deprecated; no versions

questions.modelAnswer: Design the schema around how clients think about the domain, not around database tables or existing REST endpoints: types like Product, Order and Customer connected by fields, so a screen can fetch exactly the graph it needs. Nullability is a contract: marking a field non-null promises it is always present, and if resolving it fails the null propagates up to the nearest nullable parent, possibly wiping out a large part of the response; many teams make fields that depend on other services nullable so partial data survives. Lists that can grow should be connections following the Relay convention - edges with nodes and cursors plus pageInfo { hasNextPage, endCursor } - with required limits. Mutations should be specific and intention-revealing (cancelOrder, not updateOrder with a status), take a single input object, and return a payload type containing the changed objects plus typed user errors, often modelled as a union (CancelOrderResult = Order | OrderNotCancellable) so clients handle expected failures explicitly instead of parsing the top-level errors array, which is better reserved for unexpected failures. GraphQL schemas evolve without versions: add fields freely, mark old ones @deprecated with a reason, monitor field usage, and remove them only when no clients query them.

questions.title: Designing client SDKs for an API
questions.prompt: Your company offers a public API and wants official client libraries. Explain what a good SDK does beyond wrapping HTTP calls: authentication, retries with backoff and idempotency keys, pagination helpers, typed errors, timeouts, versioning and telemetry. What are the trade-offs of generated versus hand-written SDKs?

expectedConcepts.label: Handles auth and token refresh
Safe retries with backoff, jitter and idempotency keys
Auto-pagination iterators; typed models and errors
Sensible timeouts, configurable; telemetry headers
Generated vs hand-written; semantic versioning; idiomatic per language

questions.modelAnswer: A good SDK makes the right thing the easy thing. It handles authentication (API keys, OAuth token refresh) so users never hand-craft headers. It sets sensible default timeouts and retries transient failures - network errors, 429 and 503 - with exponential backoff, jitter and Retry-After, automatically attaching idempotency keys to POSTs so retries cannot double-charge. It turns paginated endpoints into iterators (for invoice in client.invoices.list()) that fetch pages lazily. It exposes typed request and response models and maps API errors to typed exceptions with the error code, message and request id, which users quote to support. It identifies itself in a User-Agent header with SDK and API versions so you can measure adoption and deprecate safely, and lets users plug in logging, proxies and custom HTTP clients. Versioning: follow semantic versioning and pin to an API version. Generated SDKs (from OpenAPI or protobuf) stay complete and consistent across many languages, but can feel unidiomatic; hand-written SDKs feel natural but lag behind the API and cost more to maintain. Many companies generate the core and hand-write ergonomic layers on top.

questions.title: Multi-tenant API design and tenant isolation
questions.prompt: You are building a B2B SaaS API used by thousands of companies. Explain how tenant identity flows through requests, how to guarantee one tenant can never read another tenant's data, the database isolation models from shared tables to separate databases, and how you handle noisy neighbours and per-tenant limits.

expectedConcepts.label: Tenant derived from the authenticated token, not a client parameter
Every query scoped by tenant; row-level security
Shared tables, schema per tenant, database per tenant
Noisy neighbours: per-tenant rate limits and quotas, sharding big tenants
Trade-offs: cost and operations vs isolation and compliance

questions.modelAnswer: Tenant identity should come from the authenticated principal - a claim in the access token or the API key's owner - never from a client-supplied header or URL segment alone, which can be changed. Middleware puts the tenant id into the request context, and the data access layer automatically scopes every query (WHERE tenant_id = ?); database row-level security policies add defence in depth so even a forgotten filter cannot leak data. Caches, search indexes, file storage paths and background jobs must also carry the tenant id, since leaks often happen there. Isolation models: shared tables with a tenant_id column (cheapest, easiest to operate, weakest isolation), a schema per tenant, or a database or deployment per tenant (strongest isolation, per-tenant encryption keys and data residency, much higher cost and operational effort). Many SaaS products pool small tenants and give large or regulated ones dedicated cells. Noisy neighbours: apply per-tenant rate limits, quotas and concurrency limits, put heavy jobs in per-tenant fair queues, and move very large tenants to their own shards. Test isolation explicitly with automated cross-tenant access tests. Trade-off: stronger isolation costs more money and makes migrations across many databases harder.

questions.title: Designing file upload APIs
questions.prompt: Design an API for uploading files from a few kilobytes up to several gigabytes from browsers and mobile apps. Compare multipart form uploads through your servers, pre-signed URLs direct to object storage, and resumable chunked uploads. Cover validation, virus scanning, and how the application learns that an upload finished.

expectedConcepts.label: Multipart through app servers: simple but ties up servers
Pre-signed URLs upload directly to object storage
Resumable/multipart uploads in chunks for large files
Completion: client confirms or storage event triggers processing
Validation, size limits, content-type sniffing, scanning, quarantine

questions.modelAnswer: For small files, a multipart/form-data POST to your API is simplest, but large uploads tie up app server connections and memory for minutes and multiply bandwidth costs. The standard design for anything big: the client asks the API for an upload (POST /uploads with name, size and type); the API checks permissions and quota, creates a pending record, and returns a short-lived pre-signed URL that lets the client PUT the bytes directly to object storage. For multi-gigabyte files on flaky mobile networks, use resumable uploads - object storage multipart uploads with pre-signed URLs per part, or the tus protocol - so a dropped connection resumes from the last completed chunk, and parts can upload in parallel. The application learns about completion either by the client calling POST /uploads/{id}/complete (the server verifies the object exists and its size and checksum) or from the storage service's event notification; both should be idempotent. Then a pipeline validates the real content type (do not trust the extension or the client's header), enforces size limits, scans for malware, and keeps files quarantined and inaccessible until checks pass. Serve downloads through signed URLs or a CDN, never from a public bucket by default.

questions.title: Event-driven APIs and event contracts
questions.prompt: Many systems expose events as well as request-response APIs. Explain the difference between commands, events and queries, how you design event payloads and schemas, versioning with a schema registry, ordering and delivery guarantees consumers can rely on, and how AsyncAPI documents event-driven interfaces.

expectedConcepts.label: Commands request action; events state facts; queries read
Event envelope: id, type, time, source, subject, data; thin vs fat
Schema registry with compatibility checks
At-least-once, ordering per key, idempotent consumers
AsyncAPI docs; coupling through events; replay and retention

questions.modelAnswer: A command asks a specific service to do something (ChargeCard) and may be rejected; an event announces a fact that already happened (PaymentCaptured), named in the past tense, owned by the producer, and consumed by any number of subscribers who decide what to do; a query reads state. Events decouple producers from consumers in time and knowledge, but they are still an API contract. Use a consistent envelope - unique event id, type, version, occurred-at time, source, subject id (CloudEvents standardises this) - and decide between thin events (ids only; consumers call back for details, always fresh but chatty) and fat events (full state; self-contained but larger and may leak data). Register schemas (Avro, Protobuf, JSON Schema) in a schema registry that enforces compatibility rules so producers cannot publish breaking changes; evolve by adding optional fields and introduce a new event type for incompatible changes. Document guarantees honestly: usually at-least-once delivery and ordering only per partition key, so consumers must deduplicate by event id and tolerate out-of-order events using versions. AsyncAPI describes channels, messages and schemas the way OpenAPI does for HTTP. Retention and replay let new consumers rebuild state, which makes event schemas long-lived.

questions.title: Making APIs observable
questions.prompt: How do you make an API observable in production? Explain request ids and W3C trace context propagation, structured access logs, the RED metrics of rate, errors and duration per endpoint, SLOs on latency percentiles, and what you should never log. How does this help when a customer reports a failed request?

expectedConcepts.label: Request id returned to clients; traceparent propagation
Structured access logs per request
RED metrics per endpoint; percentiles
SLOs and alerting on burn rate
Never log secrets, tokens, full bodies with PII

questions.modelAnswer: Give every request an id - generated at the edge if the client did not send one - and return it in a response header such as X-Request-Id, so when a customer reports a failure they can quote it and you can find exactly that request. Propagate W3C trace context (traceparent header) to every downstream call so distributed tracing shows where time went across services. Emit one structured access log line per request with method, route template (not the raw URL with ids), status, latency, response size, client or tenant id, API version and the trace id. Record RED metrics per endpoint: request rate, error rate (split 4xx and 5xx, since 4xx usually means client mistakes) and duration as histograms, so you can chart p50, p95 and p99 latency - averages hide the slow tail. Define SLOs such as 99.9% of requests succeeding and p99 below 300 ms over 30 days, and alert on error-budget burn rate rather than single spikes. Never log passwords, tokens, API keys, full request bodies or personal data; redact at the logging library. With this in place, a customer's request id leads to the trace, which leads to the failing dependency in minutes.

questions.title: Representing dates, money and identifiers in APIs
questions.prompt: Explain best practices for representing timestamps, dates, time zones, money amounts and identifiers in JSON APIs. Why are floating-point prices and local times without offsets dangerous, why should large integer ids be strings, and how do you design these fields so clients in every language handle them correctly?

expectedConcepts.label: Timestamps in RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 UTC with offset
Calendar dates vs instants; IANA zone names for scheduling
Money as integer minor units or decimal string plus currency
Floats cannot represent 0.1 exactly
Large ids as strings: JavaScript loses precision above 2^53

questions.modelAnswer: Timestamps should be instants in RFC 3339 / ISO 8601 with an explicit offset, normally UTC: "2026-10-19T14:05:00Z". A local time without an offset is ambiguous - the client cannot know which zone was meant, and daylight-saving transitions make some local times occur twice or never. Distinguish instants from calendar dates: a birthday or invoice date is "2026-10-19" with no time zone, and converting it to midnight UTC shifts it a day for users in the Americas. For future events tied to a place (a meeting at 9:00 in Mumbai), store the local time plus an IANA zone name like Asia/Kolkata, because offsets and rules change. Money must never be a binary float: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, and rounding errors accumulate. Represent amounts as integer minor units ({"amount": 129900, "currency": "INR"} for 1299.00 rupees) or as a decimal string, always with an ISO 4217 currency code, and note that some currencies have zero or three decimal places. Identifiers: JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53, so 64-bit ids such as Snowflake ids must be sent as strings; treating all ids as opaque strings also lets you change id schemes later.

questions.title: Partial updates: PATCH, merge patch and field masks
questions.prompt: Explain how to design partial updates in an API. Compare JSON Merge Patch, JSON Patch and field masks as used by Google APIs and gRPC. How do you distinguish "set this field to null" from "do not change this field", handle arrays, validate the resulting object, and avoid lost updates?

expectedConcepts.label: JSON Merge Patch: send changed fields; null deletes
JSON Patch: list of operations (add, remove, replace, test)
Field masks: explicit list of paths to update
Absent vs null distinction; arrays replaced wholesale in merge patch
Validate the merged result; ETags against lost updates

questions.modelAnswer: With PUT the client sends the whole resource, which is wasteful and risks overwriting fields it did not know about. PATCH sends only changes, and there are three common formats. JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, application/merge-patch+json) is a partial document: fields present are set, fields absent are untouched, and null means delete. It is intuitive, but it cannot set a field to a literal null, and arrays are replaced wholesale, so you cannot append one item. JSON Patch (RFC 6902) is an ordered list of operations - add, remove, replace, move, copy, test - addressed by JSON Pointer paths; it can edit array elements and the test operation gives a conditional check, but it is verbose and tied to document structure. Field masks (Google AIP-134, gRPC FieldMask) send the new resource plus an explicit list of paths to update ("update_mask": "display_name,address.city"), which removes ambiguity: a listed field with an empty value is cleared, an unlisted field is ignored. Whatever the format, apply the patch to the current state, then validate the complete resulting object against business rules, and reject patches touching read-only fields. Combine with ETags and If-Match so two clients patching concurrently cannot silently overwrite each other.

questions.title: API naming and consistency conventions
questions.prompt: Why does consistency matter so much in API design? Describe the conventions a team should agree on: naming and casing of fields, plural resource names, boolean and date field names, response envelopes, error format, pagination style and units. How do you enforce them across many teams?

expectedConcepts.label: Consistency reduces surprises and client code
Casing, plurals, clear names, booleans like is_active
Shared error format, pagination and envelopes
Units and formats in names or standards (duration_ms, ISO dates)
Style guide, linting in CI, design reviews

questions.modelAnswer: Developers learn an API by pattern: if one endpoint uses created_at, pages with cursors and returns errors in a certain shape, they expect every endpoint to do the same. Inconsistency forces special cases in every client and causes bugs. A team style guide should fix: one casing for JSON fields (snake_case or camelCase, never both); plural nouns for collections; clear, unabbreviated names; booleans phrased as is_/has_ (is_active), timestamps with a suffix like _at in RFC 3339 UTC, and units in names where not obvious (timeout_ms, size_bytes); one error format (for example RFC 9457 problem details with stable error codes); one pagination style (cursor with next_cursor and has_more); consistent enums (UPPER_SNAKE strings, an UNSPECIFIED default); whether responses are wrapped in an envelope; and id formats. Enforce it automatically - lint OpenAPI or protobuf definitions in CI (Spectral, buf lint) - and with lightweight design reviews for new public endpoints. Published guides such as Google's AIPs, Microsoft's REST guidelines and Zalando's guidelines are good starting points. Consistency beats local optimisation: a slightly worse but consistent convention is better than a perfect one used in only one place.

questions.title: Request signing, HMAC and mutual TLS
questions.prompt: Bearer tokens can be stolen and replayed. Explain stronger ways to authenticate API clients: HMAC request signing like AWS Signature Version 4, mutual TLS with client certificates, and sender-constrained tokens. How does each prevent tampering and replay, and what are the operational costs?

expectedConcepts.label: Bearer tokens work for whoever holds them
HMAC signs a canonical request with a secret; timestamp and nonce
mTLS: client proves possession of a private key
Sender-constrained tokens: DPoP, certificate-bound tokens
Operational costs: key rotation, clock skew, certificate management

questions.modelAnswer: A bearer token or API key grants access to whoever presents it, so a token leaked through logs, a proxy or a compromised client can be replayed until it expires. HMAC request signing never sends the secret: the client builds a canonical string from the method, path, sorted query, selected headers, a timestamp and a hash of the body, computes HMAC-SHA256 with its secret, and sends the signature with a key id. The server recomputes and compares in constant time. Because the body and headers are covered, tampering is detected, and rejecting timestamps older than a few minutes (plus optional nonces) limits replay - this is how AWS Signature V4 and most webhook signatures work. Mutual TLS makes the client present a certificate during the TLS handshake and prove possession of its private key, authenticating the connection itself; it is common for service-to-service and banking APIs. Sender-constrained OAuth tokens bind an access token to a key: with mTLS-bound tokens or DPoP, the client must also prove possession of the private key on each request, so a stolen token alone is useless. Costs: distributing and rotating secrets or certificates, handling clock skew, canonicalisation bugs, revocation infrastructure and harder debugging.

questions.title: Isolation levels and the anomalies they allow
questions.prompt: Explain SQL transaction isolation levels - read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, snapshot and serializable - in terms of the anomalies they prevent: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates and write skew. Give a concrete write-skew example and how to prevent it.

expectedConcepts.label: Levels from read uncommitted to serializable
Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update
Write skew: two transactions read the same data and write different rows
Fixes: SERIALIZABLE/SSI, SELECT FOR UPDATE, constraints
Stronger isolation costs throughput and causes retries; defaults differ

questions.modelAnswer: Isolation defines what concurrent transactions can see of each other. Read uncommitted allows dirty reads of uncommitted data. Read committed (PostgreSQL's default) only shows committed data but each statement sees a new snapshot, so reading a row twice can return different values (non-repeatable read). Repeatable read / snapshot isolation (MySQL InnoDB's default is repeatable read) gives the whole transaction one snapshot, preventing non-repeatable reads and, in most engines, phantoms (new rows matching a predicate). Lost updates - two read-modify-write cycles where one overwrites the other - are prevented by atomic updates (SET x = x + 1), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or detection under snapshot isolation in some engines. Write skew survives snapshot isolation: a hospital requires at least one doctor on call; Alice and Bob each check that two doctors are on call, both see 2, and each takes themselves off - different rows, no conflict detected - leaving zero. Prevent it with SERIALIZABLE (PostgreSQL uses serializable snapshot isolation, aborting one transaction), by locking the rows read with FOR UPDATE, or by materialising the conflict into a row both must update. Higher isolation reduces concurrency and causes serialization failures that applications must retry.

questions.title: Multi-version concurrency control
questions.prompt: Explain multi-version concurrency control as implemented in PostgreSQL or MySQL InnoDB. How do readers avoid blocking writers, what is a snapshot, how are row versions stored and made visible, and what operational problems does MVCC create, such as bloat and long-running transactions?

expectedConcepts.label: Updates create new row versions instead of overwriting
Snapshot decides visibility by transaction ids
Readers do not block writers and vice versa
Postgres: versions in table + VACUUM; InnoDB: undo logs
Bloat and long transactions holding back cleanup; write conflicts

questions.modelAnswer: With MVCC, a write does not overwrite data in place; it creates a new version of the row tagged with the creating transaction's id, while older versions remain for transactions that still need them. Each transaction (or statement, under read committed) takes a snapshot: the set of transactions that had committed when it started. A row version is visible if it was created by a transaction in the snapshot and not deleted by one. So readers see a consistent state without taking read locks, and writers do not wait for readers; only two writers on the same row conflict. PostgreSQL stores all versions in the table heap (xmin/xmax fields) and relies on VACUUM to remove dead tuples once no snapshot can see them; InnoDB updates rows in place and keeps old versions in undo logs that consistent reads follow backwards, purged later. Problems: heavy update workloads create bloat - dead versions waste space and slow scans - if vacuum or purge cannot keep up; a long-running transaction (or an idle-in-transaction session, or a stale replication slot) pins an old snapshot so nothing newer than it can be cleaned up; PostgreSQL must also freeze old transaction ids to avoid wraparound. Monitor transaction age and dead-tuple counts.

questions.title: Reading query plans with EXPLAIN
questions.prompt: A query that used to take 10 ms now takes 4 seconds. Explain how you would use EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to understand it: sequential versus index scans, join algorithms, row estimates versus actual rows, and what typically causes the planner to choose a bad plan and how to fix it.

expectedConcepts.label: EXPLAIN shows the plan; ANALYZE runs it with actual timings
Seq scan vs index scan vs index-only scan, bitmap
Compare estimated vs actual rows; stale statistics
Causes: missing index, function on column, type mismatch, skew, parameter sniffing
Fixes: indexes, rewrite, update stats; avoid hints; test on real data volumes

questions.modelAnswer: EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimiser chose - a tree of operations with estimated costs and row counts; EXPLAIN ANALYZE (with BUFFERS in PostgreSQL) actually runs the query and adds real timings, row counts and pages read per node. Read from the innermost nodes outward, looking for the node where time jumps. Scans: a sequential scan reads the whole table (fine for small tables or when most rows are needed), an index scan follows the index then fetches rows, an index-only scan answers from the index alone, and a bitmap scan collects many matches then reads pages in order. Joins: nested loop (great when the outer side is tiny and the inner side is indexed), hash join (large unsorted inputs), merge join (inputs already sorted). The key diagnostic is estimated versus actual rows: if the planner expected 10 rows and got 2 million, it chose a nested loop that is now catastrophic. Causes: stale statistics after a bulk load (run ANALYZE), correlated columns (extended statistics), skewed values, wrapping an indexed column in a function or comparing with a mismatched type so the index cannot be used, a missing or wrong-order composite index, or a cached generic plan for a parameterised query. Fix the root cause rather than forcing plans with hints, and test on production-sized data.

questions.title: Composite and covering indexes
questions.prompt: Explain how a composite index on several columns works and why column order matters. What is the leftmost-prefix rule, how should equality and range conditions be ordered, what is a covering index, and what does every extra index cost on writes?

expectedConcepts.label: Composite B-tree sorted by first column, then second...
Leftmost prefix rule
Equality columns first, then range/sort column
Covering index / INCLUDE avoids table lookups
Each index slows writes, uses memory; unused indexes

questions.modelAnswer: A composite B-tree index on (customer_id, status, created_at) stores entries sorted by customer_id, then by status within each customer, then by created_at - like a phone book sorted by last name then first name. It can therefore serve queries that constrain a leftmost prefix: customer_id alone; customer_id and status; or all three. It cannot efficiently serve a query on status alone, because matching entries are scattered across every customer (some engines offer limited skip scans). Ordering rule of thumb: put columns used with equality first and the range or sort column last. For WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20, the index above finds the exact slice and reads 20 entries already in order with no sort. If the range column came first, the following columns could not narrow the search. A covering index contains every column the query needs (via extra key columns or INCLUDE in PostgreSQL/SQL Server), so the database answers from the index without visiting the table - an index-only scan. Costs: every index must be updated on each insert, update of indexed columns and delete, adding write latency, write amplification and memory pressure, so remove unused or redundant indexes (one on (a) is redundant with (a, b)).

questions.title: Normalisation and denormalisation
questions.prompt: Explain database normalisation through third normal form with an example of the update, insert and delete anomalies it prevents. Then explain when and how you would deliberately denormalise for read performance, and how you keep denormalised data consistent.

expectedConcepts.label: 1NF atomic values, 2NF full key dependency, 3NF no transitive dependency
Update, insert and delete anomalies from duplicated facts
Denormalise: precomputed counts, copied fields, read models
Keep in sync with transactions, triggers, events, or rebuilds
Trade-offs: join cost vs write complexity and inconsistency risk

questions.modelAnswer: Normalisation organises data so each fact is stored once. Suppose an orders table stores customer_name and customer_city on every order row: changing a customer's city requires updating many rows (update anomaly) and missing one leaves contradictions; you cannot record a customer who has not ordered yet (insert anomaly); deleting their last order loses the customer (delete anomaly). First normal form requires atomic values (no comma-separated lists in a column); second normal form requires non-key columns to depend on the whole key, not part of a composite key; third normal form removes transitive dependencies - city depends on the customer, not the order - so customers move to their own table referenced by customer_id. Normalised schemas make writes simple and correct but reads need joins. Denormalisation deliberately duplicates data for read speed: storing comment_count on posts, copying the product name onto order lines (which is also correct historically), materialised views, or a separate read model in a cache or search index. Keep copies consistent by updating them in the same transaction, with triggers, or asynchronously via events, and keep the normalised data as the source of truth so copies can be rebuilt. Denormalise only for measured read hotspots.

questions.title: LSM trees versus B-trees
questions.prompt: Compare log-structured merge trees, used by RocksDB and Cassandra, with B-trees, used by PostgreSQL and InnoDB. Explain how writes and reads work in each, compaction, Bloom filters, and the trade-off between read, write and space amplification. Which workloads suit each?

expectedConcepts.label: LSM: memtable + WAL, flushed to immutable sorted SSTables
B-tree: in-place page updates, one location per key
Compaction merges files; leveled vs tiered
LSM reads check several levels; Bloom filters help
Write vs read vs space amplification; workload fit

questions.modelAnswer: A B-tree keeps each key in exactly one page: an update finds the page and rewrites it in place (after logging to the WAL). Reads are predictable - a few page reads down the tree - but random writes cause random I/O and page splits, and rewriting a whole 8-16 KB page for a small change is write amplification. An LSM tree buffers writes in an in-memory sorted memtable (plus a sequential WAL for durability); when full it is flushed as an immutable sorted file (SSTable). Writes are therefore sequential and very fast. Reads must check the memtable and potentially several SSTables, newest first; per-file Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain the key, and block indexes locate data within a file. Background compaction merges SSTables, discarding overwritten values and tombstones. Leveled compaction keeps read and space amplification low at the cost of rewriting data many times; size-tiered compaction writes less but temporarily uses more space and has more files to read. So LSM trees favour write-heavy workloads (event ingestion, time series, messaging) and compress well, while B-trees give steadier read latency and are better for read-heavy, update-in-place OLTP with range queries. Compaction can cause latency spikes if it falls behind.

questions.title: Write-ahead logging, fsync and durability
questions.prompt: Explain how a database guarantees that a committed transaction survives a crash. Describe the write-ahead log, why the log must be flushed with fsync before commit returns, checkpoints, crash recovery by redo and undo, group commit, and what settings trade durability for speed.

expectedConcepts.label: Log changes before data pages; sequential append
Commit waits for fsync of the log to stable storage
Recovery replays the log from the last checkpoint
Group commit batches fsyncs
synchronous_commit off / innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit; lying disks

questions.modelAnswer: Writing modified data pages to disk at every commit would mean many random writes. Instead the database first appends a description of each change to the write-ahead log, a sequential file, and only later writes the data pages lazily from its buffer pool. The rule is that a log record must be durable before the corresponding data page is written, and before COMMIT returns the log up to the commit record must be flushed with fsync (or O_DSYNC) so it is on stable storage, not just in the OS page cache. After a crash, recovery starts from the last checkpoint - a point where all dirty pages up to some log position were written - and replays (redoes) log records after it, then rolls back transactions that never committed (undo, or simply ignoring them in PostgreSQL's design). fsync takes around a millisecond even on SSDs, so group commit lets many concurrent transactions share one flush. You can trade durability for speed: PostgreSQL synchronous_commit = off or MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 return before the flush, risking loss of the last fraction of a second of commits on a crash (but not corruption). Durability also depends on hardware honouring flushes: disks with volatile write caches that lie about fsync can lose data.

questions.title: Row locks, gap locks and database deadlocks
questions.prompt: Explain how relational databases lock rows during updates, what shared and exclusive locks are, how InnoDB gap and next-key locks prevent phantoms, how deadlocks between transactions arise and are detected, and how application code should avoid and handle them.

expectedConcepts.label: Shared vs exclusive row locks held until commit
Gap/next-key locks lock ranges to prevent phantom inserts
Deadlock: cycle of waits; detector aborts a victim
Avoid: consistent lock order, short transactions, indexes
Handle by retrying the whole transaction; lock timeouts

questions.modelAnswer: When a transaction updates or deletes a row, it takes an exclusive lock on it, held until commit or rollback, so concurrent writers to the same row wait; SELECT ... FOR SHARE takes shared locks that allow other readers but block writers, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes exclusive locks. Under MVCC plain reads take no locks. To prevent phantoms at REPEATABLE READ, InnoDB locks not just matching index records but the gaps between them (gap locks and next-key locks), so another transaction cannot insert a new row into a range you scanned; this also means a range update on an unindexed column can lock far more than expected. A deadlock occurs when transaction A holds a lock B needs while B holds one A needs - for example two transfers updating accounts 1 and 2 in opposite orders. Databases detect cycles in the wait-for graph and abort one transaction (the victim) with a deadlock error, or rely on lock timeouts. Avoid them by acquiring locks in a consistent order (sort ids before updating), keeping transactions short with no user or network waits inside, and indexing the columns in WHERE clauses so fewer rows are locked. Since deadlocks cannot be fully eliminated, application code must catch the error and retry the whole transaction.

questions.title: The N+1 query problem with ORMs
questions.prompt: Explain the N+1 query problem that object-relational mappers make easy to create. Show how it happens with lazy loading, how to detect it, and how eager loading with joins or batched IN queries fixes it. What other ORM performance traps should engineers know?

expectedConcepts.label: One query for the list plus one per item via lazy loading
Detect with query logs/counts, APM, tests asserting query counts
Eager loading: join or batched WHERE id IN
Other traps: SELECT *, loading whole tables, implicit transactions
Joins can duplicate rows; ORM abstractions vs raw SQL

questions.modelAnswer: Code like posts = Post.all(); for post in posts: print(post.author.name) looks innocent, but with lazy loading the ORM runs one query to load 100 posts and then one more query per post to load its author: 101 round trips. Each query is fast, so the problem hides in development with ten rows and explodes in production with thousands, often multiplied by network latency to the database. Detect it by logging SQL in development, using APM traces that show hundreds of identical queries in one request, or tests that assert the number of queries per endpoint. Fix it with eager loading: the ORM either joins the related table in the same query (select_related, JOIN FETCH, include) or runs a second batched query WHERE author_id IN (...) and stitches results in memory (prefetch_related); GraphQL resolvers use DataLoader for the same purpose. Other traps: loading full objects with SELECT * when you need two columns, loading unbounded collections into memory, eager-joining several one-to-many relations at once (which multiplies rows into a cartesian product), and transactions accidentally held open across a request. ORMs are productive, but engineers must still read the generated SQL for hot paths.

questions.title: Zero-downtime schema migrations
questions.prompt: You need to rename a column and change its type on a 500-million-row table without downtime while the application keeps running. Explain the expand-and-contract pattern, which DDL operations lock tables, how to backfill safely, and how you coordinate application deploys with migrations.

expectedConcepts.label: Expand and contract: add new, dual-write, backfill, switch, remove old
Some DDL takes long locks or rewrites tables
Backfill in small batches, throttled
Online schema change tools; concurrent index builds
Deploy ordering, backward-compatible code, rollback; time cost

questions.modelAnswer: Never rename or retype a column in place while old application versions are running - during a rolling deploy, old and new code run simultaneously and one of them will break.
