Use expand and contract: (1) expand - add the new column (nullable, no default that forces a rewrite) in a migration that old code ignores; (2) deploy code that writes to both columns and still reads the old one; (3) backfill existing rows in small batches (say 1,000-10,000 rows per transaction), throttled by monitoring replication lag and load, idempotently so it can restart; (4) deploy code that reads from the new column; (5) stop writing the old column; (6) contract - drop it in a later release. Each step is backward compatible, so any deploy can be rolled back. Know which DDL is dangerous: adding a column with a volatile default, changing a type, or adding a non-validated constraint may rewrite the table or hold an exclusive lock, and even a quick ALTER can queue behind a long-running query and block all traffic, so set a short lock_timeout and retry. Create indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL) or online DDL, and use tools like gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change for MySQL table rebuilds. It takes several deploys - that is the price of zero downtime.

questions.title: Table partitioning
questions.prompt: Explain table partitioning inside a single database: range, list and hash partitioning, partition pruning, and how partitioning helps with time-series data retention. How is it different from sharding across servers, and what problems does a bad partition key cause?

expectedConcepts.label: Range, list and hash partitioning
Partition pruning skips irrelevant partitions
Drop old partitions instead of mass DELETE
Partitioning is within one server; sharding spans servers
Bad keys: queries without the key hit all partitions; too many partitions

questions.modelAnswer: Partitioning splits one logical table into several physical tables inside the same database, chosen by a partition key. Range partitioning by time (one partition per month) is the most common; list partitioning groups discrete values such as region; hash partitioning spreads rows evenly by hashing a key. The planner applies partition pruning: a query with WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01' scans only the relevant partitions, and each partition's indexes are smaller and more likely to fit in memory. Retention becomes cheap: instead of DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < ... (which generates huge WAL, bloat and lock pressure), you detach and drop an entire old partition instantly. Maintenance such as vacuuming and reindexing also works per partition. This differs from sharding, which spreads data across multiple servers to scale writes and storage beyond one machine and requires routing in the application or a proxy. Pitfalls: queries that do not filter on the partition key must touch every partition; thousands of tiny partitions add planning overhead; unique constraints usually have to include the partition key; and a hot current partition still receives all writes. Pick the key that matches your most important filters and lifecycle.

questions.title: OLTP versus OLAP and columnar storage
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads, why analytical databases such as BigQuery, Snowflake or ClickHouse store data by column, how compression and vectorised execution make them fast, and why you should not run heavy analytics on your production transactional database.

expectedConcepts.label: OLTP: many small reads/writes by key; OLAP: scans and aggregates
Columnar storage reads only needed columns
Compression and vectorised execution
Separate warehouse fed by ETL/CDC
Columnar is bad at single-row updates; freshness lag

questions.modelAnswer: OLTP (online transaction processing) serves the application: many concurrent, short transactions that read or write a few rows by key - place an order, update a profile - needing low latency and strong consistency. OLAP (online analytical processing) answers questions over history: revenue by region per month across billions of rows - few queries, each scanning huge amounts of data and aggregating. Row stores keep each row's columns together, perfect for fetching one order but wasteful for summing one column across a billion rows. Columnar databases store each column separately, so a query touching 3 of 100 columns reads 3% of the data; values in a column are similar, so they compress extremely well with dictionary, run-length and delta encoding, and the engine processes batches of values with vectorised, SIMD-friendly loops, often operating directly on compressed data. Running heavy analytics on the production OLTP database competes for CPU, memory and I/O, evicts the cache and can hold locks or long snapshots that slow the application. Instead feed a warehouse via ETL or CDC (or at least use a replica). Trade-offs: columnar stores handle single-row updates and point lookups poorly, and the warehouse lags the source by minutes to hours.

questions.title: Redis: data structures, persistence and pitfalls
questions.prompt: Explain what Redis is good for beyond a simple cache. Describe its single-threaded execution model, key data structures and their use cases, persistence with RDB snapshots and AOF, replication and Redis Cluster, and the operational pitfalls such as large keys, KEYS commands and memory eviction.

expectedConcepts.label: Single-threaded command execution: atomic commands, no locks
Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams
RDB snapshots vs AOF; durability trade-off
Replication and Redis Cluster hash slots
Pitfalls: big keys, KEYS/O(n) commands block, eviction policy, memory

questions.modelAnswer: Redis is an in-memory data structure server. Commands execute one at a time on a single main thread (I/O threads help with networking), so each command is atomic without locks, and MULTI/EXEC or Lua scripts group several atomically. Its data structures map directly to common needs: strings with INCR for counters and rate limits, SET NX with expiry for simple locks and idempotency keys, hashes for objects, lists for queues, sets for unique membership, sorted sets for leaderboards and time-ordered indexes, HyperLogLog for unique counts, streams for consumer-group messaging, and pub/sub. Persistence is optional: RDB writes periodic point-in-time snapshots (fast restarts, but loses changes since the last one); AOF logs every write and can fsync every second (losing about a second on a crash). Replicas copy the primary asynchronously; Sentinel automates failover; Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 hash slots, and multi-key operations must use keys in the same slot (hash tags). Pitfalls: because it is single-threaded, one slow command - KEYS *, SMEMBERS on a million-element set, deleting a huge key - blocks everyone, so use SCAN and UNLINK; memory is the limit, so set maxmemory and an eviction policy; and asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged writes on failover.

questions.title: Document databases versus relational databases
questions.prompt: When would you choose a document database such as MongoDB over a relational database such as PostgreSQL? Explain embedding versus referencing, schema flexibility, how joins and transactions differ, and the data modelling mistakes teams make when they pick a document store for the wrong reasons.

expectedConcepts.label: Documents store nested JSON-like records
Embed data accessed together; reference shared/unbounded data
Relational joins and constraints vs application-side joins
Transactions: single-document atomic; multi-document costlier
Mistakes: relational data in documents, schema-less meaning no schema; JSONB alternative

questions.modelAnswer: Document databases store each record as a nested JSON-like document, so an aggregate that is read and written together - a product with its variants and attributes, a user profile with settings - lives in one place and is fetched in one read, and different documents can have different shapes, which suits evolving or heterogeneous data. Modelling guidance: embed data that is owned by the parent, accessed together and bounded in size; reference data that is shared across many parents, updated independently or grows without bound (embedding every comment in a post eventually hits document size limits). Relational databases normalise data into tables linked by foreign keys, enforce constraints, and join flexibly at query time, which makes them strong for many-to-many relationships and ad-hoc queries you did not foresee. In a document store, cross-document relationships become application-side joins or $lookup, and while single-document writes are atomic, multi-document transactions exist but are more expensive. Common mistakes: choosing a document store because "schemaless is flexible" and ending up with inconsistent documents (schema-less really means schema-in-the-application, so validate it), duplicating relational data into documents and then struggling to keep copies in sync. PostgreSQL with JSONB columns often gives both: relational integrity plus flexible attributes.

questions.title: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking
questions.prompt: Two users edit the same inventory record at the same time. Compare pessimistic locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE and optimistic locking with a version column. Explain how each works, what happens under high contention, and how optimistic locking maps to HTTP ETags in APIs.

expectedConcepts.label: Pessimistic: lock the row before reading/modifying
Optimistic: version check in UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?
Optimistic conflicts require retry or user merge
HTTP ETag / If-Match is optimistic locking
Low contention: optimistic; high contention or long holds: pessimistic

questions.modelAnswer: Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely: inside a transaction, SELECT ... FROM inventory WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE locks the row, so any other transaction trying to lock or update it waits until commit. It guarantees no conflicting change, but holding locks reduces concurrency, can deadlock, and is unsuitable when a user takes minutes to edit a form - you cannot hold a database lock across HTTP requests. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: each row has a version number (or timestamp). Read the row and its version; when saving, run UPDATE inventory SET qty = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 5. If another writer got there first, zero rows are affected, and the application reloads and retries the operation or asks the user to merge. No locks are held between read and write, so it scales well and works across requests: an HTTP API exposes the version as an ETag, and clients send If-Match, receiving 412 Precondition Failed on conflict. Under heavy contention on the same rows (a hot counter, flash-sale stock), optimistic writers keep failing and retrying, wasting work, so pessimistic locks or atomic updates (SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0) are better there.

questions.title: PostgreSQL vacuum, bloat and transaction ID wraparound
questions.prompt: Explain why PostgreSQL needs VACUUM. What are dead tuples and table bloat, what does autovacuum do and how do you tune it for a heavily updated table, what is transaction ID wraparound and why can it force a shutdown, and what blocks vacuum from making progress?

expectedConcepts.label: Updates/deletes leave dead tuples (MVCC)
VACUUM marks space reusable; VACUUM FULL rewrites with lock
Autovacuum thresholds and scale factor per table
32-bit transaction ids: freezing to avoid wraparound
Blockers: long transactions, replication slots, prepared transactions

questions.modelAnswer: PostgreSQL implements MVCC by writing a new row version on every UPDATE and marking the old one dead; DELETE also just marks rows. Dead tuples keep occupying space and are scanned by queries until VACUUM finds those no snapshot can still see and marks their space reusable (it also updates the visibility map, enabling index-only scans). Space is reused rather than returned to the OS, so a table that was bloated stays large; VACUUM FULL or pg_repack rewrites it compactly, VACUUM FULL under an exclusive lock. Autovacuum runs vacuum when dead tuples exceed threshold + scale_factor * rows - the default 20% is far too lax for a 500-million-row table, so set per-table scale factors around 0.01 or fixed thresholds, and raise the cost limit so it keeps up. Transaction ids are 32-bit; to compare ages safely, rows older than about 2 billion transactions must be frozen. If freezing falls behind, PostgreSQL issues warnings and eventually refuses new writes to prevent wraparound corruption - an outage that requires a long vacuum. Vacuum cannot remove tuples newer than the oldest snapshot still needed, so long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions, abandoned replication slots, forgotten prepared transactions and hot_standby_feedback from lagging replicas all cause runaway bloat. Monitor dead tuples and transaction age.

questions.title: Backups and point-in-time recovery
questions.prompt: Design a backup strategy for a production database. Explain logical versus physical backups, continuous WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery, recovery point and recovery time objectives, why replicas are not backups, and why untested backups should be assumed broken.

expectedConcepts.label: Logical dumps vs physical/base backups and snapshots
Point-in-time recovery: base backup + archived WAL
RPO and RTO drive frequency and method
Replicas copy mistakes instantly; not backups
Test restores, off-site/immutable copies, encryption, retention cost

questions.modelAnswer: Logical backups (pg_dump, mysqldump) export SQL or data; they are portable across versions and allow restoring single tables, but are slow for large databases and capture only one moment. Physical backups copy the database files or take storage snapshots - fast to restore at scale but tied to the engine version. For point-in-time recovery, take periodic base backups and continuously archive the write-ahead log (WAL or binlog) to durable storage; to recover, restore the latest base backup before the target time and replay logs up to just before the mistake, such as 14:02:59, one second before someone ran DELETE without a WHERE clause. Choose methods from targets: RPO (how much data you can lose - continuous archiving gives seconds) and RTO (how long recovery may take - which drives snapshot frequency and restore speed). Replicas are not backups: they faithfully replicate a dropped table or corrupted data within milliseconds (a delayed replica helps a little). Keep copies off-site in another region and account, make them immutable or versioned against ransomware and accidental deletion, encrypt them, and define retention. Most importantly, regularly restore backups into a test environment and measure the time; a backup that has never been restored should be assumed not to work.

questions.title: Choosing primary keys: auto-increment, UUIDv4, UUIDv7
questions.prompt: Compare auto-increment integers, random UUIDv4 and time-ordered identifiers such as UUIDv7, ULID or Snowflake ids as primary keys. Explain their effect on B-tree index locality and write performance, storage size, exposure of business information, and generation in distributed systems.

expectedConcepts.label: Auto-increment: compact, sequential, but central and guessable
UUIDv4 random: no coordination but scattered index inserts
UUIDv7/ULID/Snowflake: time-ordered, good locality
16 bytes vs 8 bytes; secondary indexes repeat the key
Exposure of creation time/volume; client-side generation

questions.modelAnswer: Auto-increment integers (8 bytes as BIGINT) are compact and always insert at the right edge of the B-tree, so inserts touch the same hot pages that stay cached, keeping indexes dense. Downsides: a single database must issue them, which complicates sharding and offline or client-side creation, and sequential ids leak business volume and invite enumeration (/orders/1001, /orders/1002), so they should not be exposed as the only protection. Random UUIDv4s can be generated anywhere with no coordination, but each insert lands at a random place in the index: pages split, fill factor drops, the working set becomes the whole index, and write throughput falls sharply once the index exceeds memory. In clustered-index engines like InnoDB, the primary key orders the table itself and every secondary index stores the 16-byte primary key, magnifying the cost. Time-ordered identifiers - UUIDv7 (RFC 9562), ULID, or 64-bit Snowflake ids - put a timestamp in the high bits, so new keys are roughly increasing and keep index locality, while still being generated without coordination. They reveal creation time, which is usually acceptable. A common design: internal BIGINT or UUIDv7 primary keys plus an opaque public identifier where enumeration matters.

questions.title: How databases execute joins
questions.prompt: Explain the three main join algorithms a database uses - nested loop join, hash join and sort-merge join. Describe how each works, its cost, the memory it needs, and when the optimiser picks each one. How do indexes and join order affect performance in multi-table queries?

expectedConcepts.label: Nested loop: for each outer row probe the inner (with an index)
Hash join: build hash table on smaller input, probe with larger
Merge join: both inputs sorted on the key
Optimiser chooses by estimated sizes, indexes, memory; join order
Bad estimates lead to nested loops over huge inputs; equality-only hash

questions.modelAnswer: Nested loop join iterates over each row of the outer input and finds matching inner rows; with an index on the inner join column, each probe is a quick index lookup, so it is excellent when the outer side is small (fetch 20 orders and their customers) and it starts returning rows immediately. Without an index it degenerates to O(n * m). Hash join builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller input keyed by the join column, then scans the larger input and probes it: roughly O(n + m), great for large unsorted inputs, but it only supports equality joins and spills to disk in batches if the build side exceeds working memory (work_mem). Sort-merge join sorts both inputs on the key (or uses inputs already ordered by an index) and walks them in step; it handles large inputs and range-friendly ordering, and is attractive when sorted data is available anyway. The cost-based optimiser chooses algorithms and the join order from estimated row counts, available indexes and memory settings; with many tables the number of possible orders explodes, so it uses heuristics. Most disasters come from bad cardinality estimates: the planner expects 10 rows, picks a nested loop, and gets 10 million. Keep statistics fresh, index foreign keys used in joins, and filter early.

questions.title: Vector databases and approximate nearest neighbour search
questions.prompt: Explain how vector databases store embeddings and answer similarity queries. Why is exact nearest-neighbour search too slow at scale, how do approximate indexes such as HNSW and IVF work, what do recall and the speed trade-off mean, and how do you combine vector search with metadata filters?

expectedConcepts.label: Embeddings compared with cosine/dot product/L2
Exact search is O(n * d) per query
HNSW: layered proximity graph, greedy search
IVF clusters with centroids; product quantisation compresses
Recall vs latency/memory; filtering pre vs post; pgvector vs dedicated

questions.modelAnswer: Embedding models turn text, images or users into vectors of a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions, where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness measured by cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance. Exact k-nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every stored vector - O(n * d) - which for 100 million 1,536-dimensional vectors is far too slow per query. Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes trade a little accuracy for orders-of-magnitude speed. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph: upper layers are sparse long-range links, lower layers dense local links; a query starts at the top and greedily moves to closer neighbours, descending layers, exploring a candidate list of size ef. It gives high recall and low latency but uses a lot of memory and is slower to build. IVF clusters vectors around k-means centroids and searches only the nprobe nearest clusters; product quantisation compresses vectors into short codes so billions fit in memory, at some accuracy cost. Recall@k measures how many true neighbours are returned; parameters like ef and nprobe tune recall against latency. Metadata filters (tenant, date, language) are tricky: post-filtering can return too few results, so engines integrate filtering into the search. pgvector adds this to PostgreSQL; dedicated engines scale further.

questions.title: Change data capture
questions.prompt: Explain change data capture. How do tools like Debezium read a database's transaction log to stream row changes, why is this better than dual writes or polling for updated rows, and what is it used for, such as keeping search indexes, caches and warehouses in sync? What are the pitfalls?

expectedConcepts.label: Reads the WAL/binlog via replication slot
Emits ordered insert/update/delete events to Kafka
Avoids dual-write inconsistency and polling gaps
Uses: search indexes, caches, warehouses, outbox relay
Pitfalls: schema changes, slot retention bloat, exposing internal schema, ordering

questions.modelAnswer: Every relational database already records each committed change in its transaction log for durability and replication. CDC tools such as Debezium attach as a replication client (a PostgreSQL logical replication slot or the MySQL binlog), decode the log, and publish an ordered stream of row-level change events - inserts, updates with before and after values, deletes - usually to Kafka, starting with an initial snapshot of existing data. The alternatives are worse. Dual writes (the application writes to the database and then to Elasticsearch) diverge whenever one write fails or concurrent writes interleave differently. Polling for rows with updated_at greater than the last check misses deletes, misses updates within the same timestamp, and adds load. CDC captures exactly what committed, in commit order, without changing application code. Uses: keeping search indexes, caches and read models in sync, loading data warehouses in near real time, relaying a transactional outbox to a message broker, and migrating databases. Pitfalls: a stalled connector makes the database retain WAL until the disk fills; schema changes must be handled downstream; publishing raw table changes couples consumers to your internal schema, so prefer outbox events for public contracts; and consumers must be idempotent.

questions.title: SQL window functions
questions.prompt: Explain SQL window functions and how they differ from GROUP BY. Using examples such as ranking each customer's orders, running totals, comparing with the previous row, and top-N per group, describe PARTITION BY, ORDER BY and frame clauses, and common performance considerations.

expectedConcepts.label: Windows keep each row; GROUP BY collapses rows
OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG/LEAD, SUM over
Frame clause ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN
Performance: sorting per partition; indexes; filtering with CTE

questions.modelAnswer: An aggregate with GROUP BY collapses many rows into one per group; a window function computes a value across related rows while keeping every row. The syntax is function() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame). Ranking: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) numbers each customer's orders newest first; RANK leaves gaps after ties and DENSE_RANK does not. Top-N per group: compute that row number in a subquery or CTE and keep rows where it is at most 3 (window functions cannot appear directly in WHERE; some engines offer QUALIFY). Comparing with the previous row: LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at) gives the prior order's amount, and LEAD the next, useful for differences and gaps. Running totals: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW); a 7-day moving average uses a frame of 6 PRECEDING. Be explicit about the frame - the default with ORDER BY is RANGE, which treats ties as peers and can surprise you. Performance: each distinct window needs its input sorted by the partition and order keys, so an index matching (customer_id, created_at) avoids big sorts, and filtering rows before windowing reduces work.

questions.title: NULL and three-valued logic in SQL
questions.prompt: Explain how NULL works in SQL. Why does WHERE column = NULL never match, what is three-valued logic, how do NULLs behave in aggregates, NOT IN, joins, unique constraints and sorting, and how should you design columns to avoid NULL-related bugs?

expectedConcepts.label: NULL means unknown; comparisons yield UNKNOWN
Use IS NULL / IS DISTINCT FROM / COALESCE
Aggregates ignore NULLs; COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)
NOT IN with a NULL returns no rows
Design: NOT NULL by default, defaults; unique allows many NULLs

questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents a missing or unknown value, not zero or an empty string. Any comparison with NULL - including NULL = NULL - yields UNKNOWN rather than true or false, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so WHERE email = NULL matches nothing; use IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, or IS DISTINCT FROM for null-safe comparison. This is three-valued logic: TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE, and NOT UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN. Aggregates such as SUM and AVG skip NULLs, so AVG(rating) averages only rated rows, and COUNT(column) counts non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows. A classic bug: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) returns no rows at all if any manager_id is NULL, because id <> NULL is unknown; use NOT EXISTS instead. Outer joins produce NULLs for missing matches, so filters on the outer table in WHERE can turn a LEFT JOIN into an inner join. Unique constraints typically allow multiple NULLs (PostgreSQL 15 added NULLS NOT DISTINCT), and NULLs sort first or last depending on the engine. Design columns NOT NULL by default with sensible defaults, allow NULL only when "unknown" is a real state, and use COALESCE when presenting values.

questions.title: Context switches and their cost
questions.prompt: Explain what happens during a context switch between threads and between processes. What state is saved and restored, why switching processes costs more than switching threads, what indirect costs such as cache and TLB pollution mean, and how you would detect excessive context switching.

expectedConcepts.label: Save registers, PC, stack pointer; scheduler picks next
Process switch also changes address space (page tables, TLB)
Indirect costs: cold caches, TLB misses
Detect with vmstat cs, pidstat -w, perf; voluntary vs involuntary
Reduce: fewer threads, async I/O, batching, pinning

questions.modelAnswer: A context switch happens when the kernel stops running one thread and starts another - because the thread blocked (voluntary), its time slice expired or a higher-priority thread became runnable (involuntary), or an interrupt occurred. The kernel saves the current thread's CPU registers, program counter and stack pointer (and FPU/SIMD state when used) into its kernel structure, runs the scheduler to choose the next thread, and restores that thread's registers. Switching between threads of the same process keeps the same address space. Switching between processes also loads a different page table root, which invalidates TLB entries unless the CPU tags them with address-space ids (PCID). The direct cost is a few microseconds; the larger indirect cost is that the new thread finds caches and TLB full of the previous thread's data and runs slowly for a while. Excessive switching shows up as a high cs column in vmstat, pidstat -w per-thread voluntary and involuntary counts, or perf sched. Common causes: far more runnable threads than cores, lock contention causing threads to sleep and wake, and tiny blocking I/O operations. Fixes: right-size thread pools, use async I/O or event loops, batch work, and pin latency-critical threads to dedicated cores.

questions.title: CPU scheduling in Linux
questions.prompt: Explain how an operating system decides which thread runs next. Cover preemptive scheduling, time slices, priorities and nice values, how Linux CFS and its successor EEVDF approximate fairness, real-time scheduling classes, and how scheduling affects latency-sensitive applications.

expectedConcepts.label: Preemptive multitasking with time slices
CFS: virtual runtime in a red-black tree; EEVDF deadlines
Nice values weight CPU share
Real-time classes SCHED_FIFO/RR
Latency: wakeup latency, isolcpus, starvation risk with RT

questions.modelAnswer: Modern kernels use preemptive scheduling: a timer interrupt lets the kernel take the CPU away from a running thread so no thread can monopolise it, and threads also give up the CPU when they block on I/O or locks. Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler tracked each runnable thread's virtual runtime - CPU time used, scaled by its weight - in a red-black tree per CPU and always ran the thread with the smallest vruntime, so all threads converge to a fair share. Since kernel 6.6 the EEVDF scheduler replaces it, adding virtual deadlines so latency-sensitive tasks with short requests get the CPU sooner while staying fair. Nice values from -20 to 19 change a thread's weight: each step is roughly a 10% difference in CPU share. Real-time classes (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR, SCHED_DEADLINE) always run before normal threads; a SCHED_FIFO thread runs until it blocks or yields, so a busy loop at real-time priority can starve the system. Schedulers also balance load across cores and consider cache affinity. For latency-sensitive work, the main issues are wakeup latency and interference: isolate cores with isolcpus or cpusets, pin threads, avoid oversubscription, and use real-time priorities carefully.

questions.title: System calls and the user-kernel boundary
questions.prompt: Explain what a system call is and what happens when a program calls read() or write(). Why are user mode and kernel mode separated, what does crossing the boundary cost, how do vDSO calls like clock_gettime avoid it, and how does this shape the design of high-performance I/O?

expectedConcepts.label: User vs kernel mode; protection rings
syscall instruction traps into the kernel; arguments in registers
Cost: mode switch, mitigations, cache effects
vDSO maps some calls into user space
Batching (readv, io_uring), buffering, kernel bypass

questions.modelAnswer: Applications run in user mode, where the CPU forbids direct access to hardware and other processes' memory; the kernel runs in kernel mode with full privileges. This separation provides isolation and security. To do anything privileged - read a file, send on a socket, allocate memory from the OS - a program makes a system call: the C library puts the syscall number and arguments in registers and executes the syscall instruction, which switches to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's entry point. The kernel validates arguments, copies data between user and kernel memory as needed (for read, from the page cache into the user buffer), and returns a result or an error code (errno). The round trip costs from roughly a hundred nanoseconds to a few microseconds, more since Spectre and Meltdown mitigations added page-table switching, plus cache and TLB disruption. The vDSO is a small kernel-provided library mapped into every process so frequently used, read-only calls like clock_gettime and gettimeofday run without entering the kernel. High-performance I/O therefore minimises syscalls: buffered I/O (fewer, larger reads), vectored calls (readv/writev), sendfile and splice for zero-copy, io_uring's shared submission and completion rings to batch many operations, and kernel-bypass networking for the extreme case.

questions.title: Page faults, the TLB and huge pages
questions.prompt: Explain what happens on a page fault. Distinguish minor and major faults, explain the translation lookaside buffer and the cost of TLB misses on large memory workloads, and describe how huge pages and transparent huge pages help and what problems transparent huge pages can cause.

expectedConcepts.label: Page fault: MMU finds no valid mapping; kernel handles it
Minor (page in memory) vs major (disk read)
TLB caches translations; misses walk page tables
Huge pages (2 MB/1 GB) increase TLB reach
THP: compaction stalls, memory bloat, latency spikes

questions.modelAnswer: Virtual addresses are translated to physical ones by the MMU using page tables. If a page is not mapped or the access violates permissions, the CPU raises a page fault and the kernel decides what to do. A minor fault needs no disk I/O: the page is already in memory (in the page cache or shared library) or is a fresh anonymous page that just needs zeroing and mapping, as on first touch of malloc'd memory - microseconds. A major fault must read from disk - a file-backed page or swap - costing milliseconds on SSD or more. An invalid access becomes SIGSEGV. Translation itself is cached in the TLB; a miss forces a multi-level page-table walk. With 4 KB pages and a TLB of around 1,500 entries, only a few MB of memory is covered, so random access over tens of GB (databases, JVM heaps, hash tables) suffers constant TLB misses. Huge pages (2 MB or 1 GB) cover much more memory per entry. Explicit huge pages (hugetlbfs) must be reserved in advance. Transparent huge pages are automatic, but the kernel may stall allocations to compact memory, khugepaged collapses pages in the background, and partially used huge pages waste memory - causing latency spikes, which is why databases like Redis and many low-latency systems recommend THP set to madvise or never.

questions.title: How malloc works and memory fragmentation
questions.prompt: Explain how a user-space memory allocator such as glibc malloc, jemalloc or tcmalloc gets memory from the kernel and manages it. Cover brk and mmap, size classes, free lists, per-thread caches, internal and external fragmentation, and why a process can use far more memory than its live data.

expectedConcepts.label: Gets memory via brk/sbrk and mmap
Size classes and free lists; large allocations mmap directly
Per-thread caches/arenas reduce lock contention
Internal vs external fragmentation
RSS stays high: memory not returned; switching allocators; tuning

questions.modelAnswer: malloc is a user-space library that requests big regions from the kernel and carves them up. Small allocations come from the heap, grown with brk/sbrk, or from mmap'd regions; large allocations (glibc's default threshold is 128 KB) are mmap'd individually and returned with munmap on free. To serve requests quickly, allocators round sizes up to size classes and keep free lists (bins) of freed chunks per class; jemalloc and tcmalloc organise memory into runs or spans of same-sized objects, similar to slab allocation. Contention on a global lock would kill multithreaded performance, so allocators keep per-thread caches (glibc tcache, tcmalloc thread caches) and multiple arenas. Internal fragmentation is waste inside a block from rounding up a 33-byte request to 48 bytes; external fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small or scattered to satisfy requests or to give back to the OS - a single live object can pin an entire page or span. Consequently a process's resident memory (RSS) can stay far above its live data after a spike: freed memory remains cached in arenas or fragmented. glibc with many threads can create many arenas and bloat; services often switch to jemalloc or tcmalloc, cap arenas (MALLOC_ARENA_MAX), or call malloc_trim, and use pools for hot fixed-size objects.

questions.title: Memory-mapped files
questions.prompt: Explain memory-mapped files with mmap. How does mapping a file into the address space work with the page cache, how does it compare with read and write calls, when is it a good idea, and what are the pitfalls such as page-fault latency, SIGBUS and databases relying on mmap?

expectedConcepts.label: mmap maps file pages into virtual memory; loaded lazily via page faults
Shares the page cache; no copy into user buffer
MAP_SHARED writes back; MAP_PRIVATE copy-on-write; msync
Good for random reads of large files, shared read-only data
Pitfalls: unpredictable fault latency, SIGBUS on truncation, I/O errors, DB control

questions.modelAnswer: mmap creates a mapping between a range of virtual addresses and a file. No data is read immediately; the first access to each page triggers a page fault, and the kernel fills the page from the page cache (reading from disk if needed) and maps it. Reads then become plain memory accesses with no system call and no copy from a kernel buffer into a user buffer, and several processes mapping the same file share the same physical pages. With MAP_SHARED, writes modify the page cache and are written back to the file eventually (msync forces it); MAP_PRIVATE gives copy-on-write private changes. mmap shines for random access to large, mostly read-only files, for loading executables and shared libraries, and for sharing data between processes. Pitfalls: you cannot control when I/O happens - any memory access may block for a disk read, which is unacceptable on latency-critical threads; I/O errors and a file truncated by another process surface as SIGBUS signals instead of error codes; the kernel decides eviction, not your application; and 32-bit address spaces limit mapping size. Database researchers have argued that DBMSs using mmap instead of their own buffer pool (to avoid copying) suffer from these problems at scale, which is why most databases manage their own caches with explicit I/O.

questions.title: I/O models: blocking, non-blocking, epoll and io_uring
questions.prompt: Explain the I/O models a server can use: blocking I/O with a thread per connection, non-blocking I/O with select, poll and epoll, and asynchronous I/O with io_uring. Why does epoll scale to hundreds of thousands of connections, what are edge-triggered and level-triggered modes, and what does io_uring add?

expectedConcepts.label: Blocking I/O: thread per connection, memory/switch cost
Non-blocking sockets with readiness notification
epoll: register once, O(ready) wakeups vs select/poll O(n)
Level- vs edge-triggered; drain until EAGAIN
io_uring: completion-based, shared rings, batched syscalls, works for files

questions.modelAnswer: With blocking I/O, read() on a socket sleeps until data arrives, so a server needs a thread per connection; at tens of thousands of connections, stack memory and context switches become the bottleneck (the C10K problem). Non-blocking sockets return EAGAIN instead of sleeping, and an event loop asks the kernel which sockets are ready. select and poll pass the whole list of descriptors on every call, so each call costs O(n) even if one socket is ready. epoll keeps an interest list inside the kernel (epoll_ctl registers a descriptor once) and epoll_wait returns only the ready ones, so cost scales with activity, not with total connections - the basis of nginx, Node.js, Redis and Go's netpoller. Level-triggered mode (default) reports a descriptor as long as it is readable; edge-triggered reports only on transitions, which is more efficient but requires reading until EAGAIN or you may never be notified again. epoll is a readiness model and does not work for regular files, which are always "ready" but may block on disk. io_uring is a completion model: the application places requests in a submission ring shared with the kernel and reaps results from a completion ring, batching many operations per syscall (or none with polling mode), and it supports files, sockets and more - at the cost of complexity and a history of security issues leading some platforms to restrict it.

questions.title: The page cache, write-back and fsync
questions.prompt: Explain the operating system page cache. What happens when a program calls write() on a file - is the data on disk when write returns? Describe dirty pages and write-back, fsync and fdatasync, O_DIRECT, and the classic bugs where applications believe data is durable when it is not.

expectedConcepts.label: Page cache keeps file data in RAM for reads and writes
write() returns after copying to cache; dirty pages flushed later
fsync forces data and metadata to stable storage
O_DIRECT bypasses the cache (databases)
Pitfalls: missing fsync of directory, rename without fsync, fsync error handling

questions.modelAnswer: Linux keeps recently used file data in the page cache, using otherwise free RAM, so repeated reads are served from memory - which is why free memory looks low on a healthy server. write() normally just copies data into the page cache, marks those pages dirty and returns; the kernel writes dirty pages to disk later (after about 30 seconds or under memory pressure). If the machine loses power before that, the data is gone even though write succeeded. fsync(fd) blocks until the file's data and metadata reach stable storage; fdatasync skips non-essential metadata such as modification time. Databases use O_DIRECT to bypass the page cache and manage their own buffer pool, avoiding double caching. Classic bugs: writing a new file and renaming it over the old one for atomic replacement, but not fsyncing the new file before the rename (a crash can leave an empty file) and not fsyncing the containing directory afterwards (the rename itself may not be durable); assuming close() flushes data; and ignoring fsync errors - after a failed fsync Linux may drop the dirty pages, so retrying fsync can falsely succeed, as PostgreSQL discovered in 2018, after which it chose to crash and recover from its WAL instead.

questions.title: Mutexes, semaphores, spinlocks and futexes
questions.prompt: Explain the main synchronisation primitives an operating system provides: mutexes, semaphores, spinlocks, condition variables and read-write locks. How are they implemented using atomic instructions and futexes, when is spinning better than sleeping, and what does each cost?

expectedConcepts.label: Mutex: mutual exclusion with ownership
Semaphore: counter for N resources; signalling
Spinlock busy-waits; good for very short critical sections
Futex: uncontended path in user space via atomics; kernel only on contention
Costs and choices: spinning wastes CPU; adaptive mutexes; RW lock writer starvation

questions.modelAnswer: A mutex gives one thread at a time exclusive access to a critical section and has an owner who must unlock it. A semaphore holds a counter: wait decrements it and blocks at zero, post increments it - useful to limit concurrent access to N resources (a connection pool) or to signal between threads, and it has no owner. Condition variables let threads sleep until a predicate becomes true, always used with a mutex. Read-write locks allow many readers or one writer. All are built on atomic CPU instructions such as compare-and-swap and atomic exchange. A spinlock loops on an atomic flag until it becomes free; it never sleeps, so it suits very short critical sections and kernel code that cannot sleep (interrupt handlers), but spinning while the holder is descheduled wastes whole time slices. Linux user-space mutexes use futexes: locking and unlocking an uncontended mutex is a single atomic operation entirely in user space; only when there is contention does the thread call futex_wait to sleep in the kernel, and the unlocker calls futex_wake. Many implementations are adaptive: spin briefly, then sleep. Costs: an uncontended lock is tens of nanoseconds; contended locks cost context switches and cache-line bouncing; read-write locks have higher overhead and can starve writers.

questions.title: Priority inversion
questions.prompt: Explain priority inversion with a concrete example, including the famous Mars Pathfinder incident. Why can a high-priority task end up waiting behind a medium-priority one, and how do priority inheritance and priority ceiling protocols fix it? Where does this matter outside real-time systems?

expectedConcepts.label: High waits on lock held by low; medium preempts low
Mars Pathfinder watchdog resets
Priority inheritance boosts the lock holder
Priority ceiling protocol
Beyond RTOS: PI mutexes on Linux, nice values, thread pools; avoid shared locks

questions.modelAnswer: Priority inversion happens when a high-priority task needs a lock held by a low-priority task. The high-priority task blocks, which is expected for a short time. But if a medium-priority task becomes runnable, it preempts the low-priority holder - it does not need the lock - so the low task cannot run to release it, and the high task effectively waits on the medium one for an unbounded time. On Mars Pathfinder in 1997, a low-priority meteorological task held a mutex protecting a shared information bus; a high-priority bus management task waited for it while medium-priority communication tasks kept running, so the high task missed its deadline and a watchdog repeatedly reset the spacecraft. Engineers fixed it remotely by enabling priority inheritance on that mutex in VxWorks. Priority inheritance temporarily raises the lock holder to the priority of the highest task waiting on it, so it finishes and releases quickly. The priority ceiling protocol assigns each lock the priority of the highest task that may ever use it and raises any holder to that ceiling immediately, which also prevents some deadlocks. Outside real-time systems the same pattern appears with low-priority background threads holding locks needed by latency-critical threads; Linux offers priority-inheritance pthread mutexes, but the simplest fix is to avoid sharing locks across priority levels.

questions.title: Unix signals
questions.prompt: Explain Unix signals. What are SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGSEGV, SIGCHLD and SIGPIPE used for, how does a process install a signal handler, why can only async-signal-safe functions be called inside a handler, and how should a server handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown?

expectedConcepts.label: Signals are asynchronous notifications to a process
Common signals and default actions; SIGKILL cannot be caught
Handlers via sigaction; async-signal-safe only
Set a flag or use a self-pipe / signalfd and handle in main loop
Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM; SIGPIPE on closed sockets

questions.modelAnswer: Signals are small asynchronous notifications the kernel delivers to a process. SIGINT is sent by Ctrl+C; SIGTERM is the polite request to terminate used by kill and by Kubernetes on shutdown; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored, so they always kill or stop the process; SIGSEGV reports an invalid memory access; SIGCHLD tells a parent a child exited; SIGPIPE is raised when writing to a pipe or socket whose reader has closed, and its default action kills the process - servers usually ignore it and handle the EPIPE error instead. Each signal has a default action (terminate, core dump, ignore, stop), which a process can change with sigaction to install a handler. A handler can interrupt the program at almost any instruction, even inside malloc or printf, so it may only call async-signal-safe functions; calling non-reentrant functions can deadlock or corrupt state. The robust pattern is to do almost nothing in the handler - set a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or write a byte to a self-pipe - and handle the event in the main loop, or use signalfd. For SIGTERM a server should stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests within a deadline, flush and close resources, then exit, before the orchestrator escalates to SIGKILL.

questions.title: fork, exec and copy-on-write
questions.prompt: Explain how Unix creates processes with fork and exec. What does fork copy, how does copy-on-write make it cheap, why do shells call exec right after fork, and what are the pitfalls of forking a large or multithreaded process? Mention vfork and posix_spawn.

expectedConcepts.label: fork duplicates the process; returns twice
Copy-on-write shares pages until written
exec replaces the program image
Forking multithreaded processes: only one thread, locks held
Large processes: page-table copy, memory spikes (Redis BGSAVE); vfork/posix_spawn

questions.modelAnswer: fork creates a new process that is a near-identical copy of the caller: same memory contents, open file descriptors, and program position. It returns twice - 0 in the child and the child's pid in the parent. Copying all memory eagerly would be slow, so the kernel uses copy-on-write: parent and child share the same physical pages marked read-only, and only when either writes to a page does a page fault trigger copying that single page. fork still copies page tables, which for a process with tens of GB of memory takes noticeable time. exec replaces the current process image with a new program, keeping the pid and (unless marked close-on-exec) open descriptors; shells fork, adjust file descriptors for redirection in the child, then exec the command. Pitfalls: forking a multithreaded process copies only the calling thread, so locks held by other threads at that moment stay locked forever in the child - only async-signal-safe calls are safe before exec. Redis uses fork for background snapshots: a write-heavy workload during the snapshot copies many pages and can double memory use, which is why memory overcommit settings matter. vfork and posix_spawn avoid copying page tables when you just want to run another program, and are preferred for spawning from large processes.

questions.title: Zombie and orphan processes
questions.prompt: Explain what zombie and orphan processes are in Unix. Why does a terminated child remain in the process table, how does wait or waitpid reap it, what happens when a parent dies first, and why does PID 1 inside a container need to reap zombies?

expectedConcepts.label: Zombie: exited child whose status was not collected
Parent reaps with wait/waitpid; SIGCHLD
Orphans are re-parented to init/subreaper
Container PID 1 must reap; use tini or --init
Too many zombies exhaust PIDs; zombies use no memory

questions.modelAnswer: When a process exits, the kernel frees its memory and resources but keeps a small entry in the process table containing its exit status, so the parent can find out how it finished. Until the parent collects it with wait or waitpid, the child is a zombie (shown as <defunct> in ps). Zombies use no memory or CPU and cannot be killed - they are already dead - but each holds a PID, so a buggy parent that never reaps can exhaust the PID space and prevent new processes from starting. The fix is in the parent: call waitpid when SIGCHLD arrives, or set SIGCHLD to SIG_IGN to have children reaped automatically; killing the parent also works because its zombies are then inherited and reaped. An orphan is a running process whose parent died; the kernel re-parents it to PID 1 (or a designated subreaper), which is expected to reap it when it exits. In containers, your application often runs as PID 1, which has special duties: it must reap orphaned grandchildren and has no default signal handlers, so SIGTERM may be ignored. Using a tiny init such as tini (docker run --init) forwards signals and reaps zombies.

questions.title: Inter-process communication mechanisms
questions.prompt: Compare the ways processes on the same machine can communicate: pipes, named pipes, Unix domain sockets, shared memory, message queues, signals and memory-mapped files. Discuss their performance, synchronisation needs and typical uses, including how low-latency systems use shared memory.

expectedConcepts.label: Pipes/FIFOs: byte streams between related processes
Unix domain sockets: bidirectional, pass file descriptors
Shared memory: fastest, no copies, needs synchronisation
Message queues, signals for notifications
Trade-offs: kernel copies and syscalls vs complexity; ring buffers in shared memory

questions.modelAnswer: Pipes are one-way byte streams through a kernel buffer, typically between a parent and child (shell pipelines); named pipes (FIFOs) give them a filesystem name for unrelated processes. Unix domain sockets look like network sockets but stay inside the kernel: bidirectional, stream or datagram, with filesystem permissions, and they can pass file descriptors and credentials between processes - used by Docker, PostgreSQL local connections and systemd. All of these copy data from the sender into the kernel and out to the receiver, costing two copies and syscalls per message - fine for most applications, a few microseconds each. POSIX message queues preserve message boundaries and priorities. Signals carry almost no data and are for notification only. Shared memory (shm_open plus mmap, or a memory-mapped file) maps the same physical pages into several processes: once set up, communication is plain memory access with no syscalls and no copies, the fastest option. But the processes must synchronise themselves, using atomics, process-shared mutexes or lock-free ring buffers, and a crashing process can leave shared state inconsistent. Low-latency trading systems connect processes through single-producer single-consumer ring buffers in shared memory with busy-polling consumers, reaching sub-microsecond latencies.

questions.title: How containers work: namespaces and cgroups
questions.prompt: Explain what a Linux container actually is at the kernel level. Describe namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits, the union or overlay filesystem, capabilities and seccomp for security, and why containers provide weaker isolation than virtual machines.

expectedConcepts.label: Namespaces isolate PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user views
cgroups limit and account CPU, memory, I/O, PIDs
Overlay filesystem of image layers
Capabilities, seccomp, LSMs reduce privileges
Shared kernel: weaker isolation than VMs; gVisor, Kata, Firecracker

questions.modelAnswer: A container is just an ordinary Linux process configured with kernel features; there is no "container" object in the kernel. Namespaces give the process its own view of system resources: a PID namespace where it sees itself as PID 1, a network namespace with its own interfaces and routing, a mount namespace with its own filesystem tree, plus UTS (hostname), IPC and user namespaces (mapping container root to an unprivileged host user). Control groups (cgroups v2) limit and account resources: CPU quotas and weights (exceeding a quota causes throttling, a common latency problem), memory limits enforced by the OOM killer, I/O bandwidth and maximum process count. The filesystem comes from an image made of read-only layers stacked with an overlay filesystem, with a thin writable copy-on-write layer on top. Security hardening drops Linux capabilities, filters system calls with seccomp profiles, applies AppArmor or SELinux policies and can run rootless. Because every container shares the host kernel, a kernel vulnerability or a misconfiguration (privileged containers, mounted Docker socket) can let a process escape to the host, so containers isolate less strongly than virtual machines, which run separate kernels on a hypervisor. Sandboxes like gVisor (user-space kernel) and microVMs like Firecracker or Kata Containers close that gap for untrusted code.

questions.title: Memory overcommit and the OOM killer
questions.prompt: Explain why Linux lets processes allocate more memory than the machine has, how overcommit modes work, what happens when memory actually runs out, how the OOM killer chooses its victim, and how cgroup memory limits change this in containers. How do you protect critical processes?

expectedConcepts.label: Overcommit: allocations reserve address space; pages backed on first touch
vm.overcommit_memory modes 0, 1, 2
OOM killer picks a victim by oom_score
cgroup memory limits trigger container-level OOM kills
Protection: oom_score_adj, requests/limits, swap, earlyoom, page cache counts

questions.modelAnswer: When a program calls malloc or mmap, Linux normally only reserves virtual address space; physical pages are allocated when first touched. Many programs reserve more than they use (thread stacks, sparse arrays, fork with copy-on-write), so the kernel overcommits: it allows total reservations to exceed RAM plus swap. vm.overcommit_memory = 0 (default) uses a heuristic that refuses only obviously absurd requests, 1 always allows, and 2 enforces a strict commit limit so allocations fail up front instead. The catch: if processes actually touch more memory than exists and reclaim (dropping page cache, swapping) cannot free enough, the kernel invokes the OOM killer. It computes an oom_score for each process, mainly proportional to its memory use, adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to 1000), and kills the highest-scoring one with SIGKILL - often the biggest, most important service. In containers, the cgroup memory limit applies first: exceeding it triggers an OOM kill inside that cgroup, which Kubernetes reports as OOMKilled with exit code 137, and page cache counts toward the limit. Protect critical processes with negative oom_score_adj, size container limits from measured peak usage with headroom, cap runtime heaps (GOMEMLIMIT, JVM -Xmx), and consider tools like earlyoom or systemd-oomd that act before the system thrashes.

questions.title: NUMA and memory locality
questions.prompt: Explain non-uniform memory access on multi-socket servers. Why is accessing memory attached to another socket slower, how does Linux decide where to allocate memory, what problems arise for databases and JVMs, and how do you use numactl, CPU pinning and NUMA-aware design to fix them?

expectedConcepts.label: Each socket has local memory; remote access crosses interconnect
Remote access higher latency and lower bandwidth
First-touch allocation policy; interleave; automatic balancing
numactl, taskset, pinning threads and memory together
Issues: one node exhausted, swapping with free memory elsewhere, cross-node locks

questions.modelAnswer: Multi-socket servers attach each bank of RAM to one CPU socket (a NUMA node). A core can access any memory, but local memory is faster: remote accesses traverse the socket interconnect, adding roughly 50-100% latency and sharing limited bandwidth. Linux allocates physical memory on first touch: a page is placed on the node of the CPU that first writes it. So if one thread initialises a large buffer and many threads on other sockets use it, most of their accesses are remote; if the scheduler migrates a thread to another socket, its memory stays behind. Automatic NUMA balancing migrates pages toward the threads using them, at some overhead. Problems in practice: databases and JVMs with huge heaps can fill one node while the other has free memory, and with zone reclaim settings the kernel may swap or reclaim cache on the full node despite plenty of free RAM elsewhere (historically a MySQL "swap insanity" issue) - interleaving memory across nodes (numactl --interleave=all) spreads it evenly. For latency-critical systems, do the opposite: pin each thread and its memory to the same node (numactl --cpunodebind --membind, taskset, cpusets), keep the NIC's interrupts and the processing threads on the NIC's node, and avoid sharing hot data or locks across sockets. Tools: numactl --hardware, numastat, perf.

questions.title: File systems: inodes, directories and journaling
questions.prompt: Explain how a Unix file system organises data. What is an inode and what does it store, how do directories, hard links and symbolic links work, what happens when you delete a file that is still open, and how does journaling keep the file system consistent after a crash?

expectedConcepts.label: Inode stores metadata and block pointers, not the name
Directory maps names to inode numbers
Hard links share an inode; symlinks store a path
Deleted-but-open files keep space until closed
Journaling: metadata (or data) logged before applying

questions.modelAnswer: A file's content and metadata live in an inode: owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count, and pointers (or extents) to the disk blocks holding the data. The inode does not contain the file name. A directory is a special file mapping names to inode numbers, so a path lookup walks directory entries from the root. A hard link is simply another directory entry pointing to the same inode, increasing its link count; both names are equal and the data is freed only when the link count reaches zero and no process has it open. A symbolic link is a separate small file containing a path, which can dangle if the target moves and can cross file systems. Deleting a file calls unlink, removing a name; if a process still has it open, the inode and blocks remain until the last descriptor is closed - the classic "disk is full but du finds nothing" problem caused by a deleted log file still held open (lsof +L1 finds it). Updating a file touches several structures (inode, bitmap, data blocks, directory); a crash in the middle used to require a long fsck. Journaling file systems (ext4, XFS) first write intended metadata changes to a journal and then apply them, so recovery just replays or discards the journal; ext4's default ordered mode writes data blocks before committing metadata. Btrfs and ZFS use copy-on-write instead.

questions.title: Interrupts, DMA and how network packets reach your program
questions.prompt: Trace a network packet from the wire to a read() call in your application. Explain interrupts, DMA, ring buffers, NAPI polling, softirqs, receive-side scaling, and copying into the socket buffer. Where does latency come from, and what do interrupt coalescing and busy polling change?

expectedConcepts.label: NIC writes packets to RX ring via DMA
Interrupt, then NAPI polling in softirq context
Protocol processing and socket receive buffer; wake the reader
RSS spreads queues across cores; IRQ affinity
Coalescing trades latency for throughput; busy polling; kernel bypass

questions.modelAnswer: The NIC receives a frame and, using DMA, writes it directly into a pre-allocated buffer referenced by a descriptor in its receive ring in main memory, without involving the CPU. It then raises a hardware interrupt. The interrupt handler does minimal work: it disables further interrupts for that queue and schedules NAPI polling in softirq context. The poll loop then processes a batch of packets from the ring, building socket buffers (sk_buff) and running them through the IP and TCP layers - checksums (often offloaded to the NIC), reassembly with GRO, connection lookup - and appends the data to the socket's receive queue, waking any thread blocked in read() or epoll_wait. When the application calls read(), the kernel copies data from the socket buffer into the user buffer. With receive-side scaling, the NIC hashes flows into several queues, each with its own interrupt pinned to a core, spreading load and keeping a flow on one core. Latency comes from interrupt moderation, softirq scheduling, wakeup and context switch, and copies. Interrupt coalescing waits for several packets or microseconds before interrupting - better throughput, worse latency. Busy polling (SO_BUSY_POLL) lets the application spin on the queue instead of sleeping; kernel-bypass frameworks such as DPDK or Onload map the NIC rings into user space entirely, reaching single-digit microsecond latencies used in trading.

questions.title: CPU caches and cache coherence
questions.prompt: Explain how multi-core CPUs keep their caches coherent. Describe the cache hierarchy and its latencies, cache lines, the MESI protocol states, what happens when two cores write to the same line, and how this explains the cost of atomic operations, contended locks and false sharing.

expectedConcepts.label: L1/L2 per core, shared L3; latencies from ~1 ns to ~100 ns DRAM
64-byte cache lines are the unit of coherence
MESI: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid
Writes require exclusive ownership; other copies invalidated
Consequences: contended atomics, lock bouncing, false sharing

questions.modelAnswer: Each core has small private L1 (about 32-48 KB, ~1 ns) and L2 caches (~1-2 MB, ~4 ns), while cores share a larger L3 (tens of MB, ~10-20 ns); main memory costs around 80-100 ns. Data moves in 64-byte cache lines. Because several cores may cache the same line, the hardware runs a coherence protocol so all cores observe a single consistent value per address. In MESI, each line in a cache is Modified (only copy, dirty), Exclusive (only copy, clean), Shared (clean, possibly in other caches) or Invalid. Reading a line others hold makes it Shared. To write, a core must own the line exclusively, so it broadcasts or sends via a directory a request that invalidates all other copies; their next access misses and must fetch the new value from the owner. Modern CPUs extend this with states like Owned or Forward and use directories or snoop filters to scale. Consequences: a contended atomic counter or lock word bounces between cores, each operation costing tens to hundreds of nanoseconds instead of one; false sharing does the same for unrelated variables that happen to share a line; and read-mostly data scales well because it stays Shared everywhere. Performance-sensitive code keeps per-core data separate, pads hot variables to their own lines, and batches updates to shared state.

questions.title: Diagnosing a slow Linux server
questions.prompt: A Linux server is slow and its load average is 40 on a 16-core machine. Explain what load average actually measures on Linux, how you would use top, vmstat, iostat, free and the USE method to determine whether the problem is CPU, memory, disk I/O or something else, and what iowait and steal time mean.

expectedConcepts.label: Load average counts runnable plus uninterruptible (D state) tasks
USE method: utilisation, saturation, errors per resource
top, vmstat, iostat, free, pidstat, dmesg
iowait and steal time meaning
Memory pressure: swapping, page cache; check per-process

questions.modelAnswer: On Linux, load average is the exponentially averaged number of tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep (state D, usually waiting on disk or NFS) over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. So 40 on 16 cores could mean CPU saturation or many threads stuck on I/O - it does not say which. Work through each resource with the USE method: utilisation, saturation and errors. Start with uptime and dmesg (OOM kills, disk errors), then vmstat 1: the r column shows runnable tasks versus cores (CPU saturation), b shows blocked tasks, si/so show swapping, us/sy/id/wa/st show where CPU time goes. mpstat -P ALL reveals one hot core; pidstat and top identify the processes. High wa (iowait) means CPUs are idle while tasks wait for I/O, so check iostat -xz 1 for device utilisation, queue size and await latency. High st (steal) means the hypervisor is giving your vCPUs' time to other tenants - a noisy neighbour or a throttled cloud instance. free -m: look at available rather than free, because page cache uses spare memory; swapping and kernel reclaim indicate genuine memory pressure. Also check network (sar -n DEV, ss) and file descriptor limits. Then drill into the culprit with perf, strace or application profilers.

questions.title: Linux tracing tools: strace, perf and eBPF
questions.prompt: Explain when and how to use strace, ltrace, perf and eBPF-based tools such as bpftrace or BCC to debug performance and behaviour of a running process. What can each see, what overhead does each impose, and why has eBPF become so important for production observability?

expectedConcepts.label: strace shows system calls; high overhead via ptrace
perf samples CPU stacks and hardware counters; flame graphs
eBPF runs verified programs in the kernel at hook points
Use cases: latency histograms, off-CPU time, file/network tracing
Overhead and safety; symbols and frame pointers needed

questions.modelAnswer: strace attaches with ptrace and prints every system call a process makes with arguments, return values and timing (strace -f -tt -T -p PID), revealing what a stuck process is waiting on, which files it opens, or errors like EACCES and ENOENT; but ptrace stops the process on every syscall, slowing it massively, so use it briefly in production. ltrace does the same for library calls. perf uses kernel and CPU sampling: perf top and perf record -g sample stack traces at a fixed frequency with low overhead, producing CPU flame graphs that show exactly which functions burn time; perf stat reads hardware counters such as cycles, instructions, cache and branch misses. It needs symbols and frame pointers or DWARF/LBR for good stacks. eBPF lets you load small programs into the kernel, checked by a verifier for safety, attached to kprobes, tracepoints, uprobes and network hooks, aggregating data in kernel maps so only summaries reach user space. Tools like bpftrace one-liners and the BCC suite (biolatency, opensnoop, execsnoop, tcpretrans, offcputime) give latency histograms, off-CPU analysis and per-event tracing at production-safe overhead without restarting anything. eBPF also powers modern networking and security tools (Cilium, Falco) and continuous profilers.

questions.title: Kernel threads, green threads and M:N scheduling
questions.prompt: Compare 1:1 kernel threads, N:1 user-level green threads and M:N scheduling as used by Go goroutines, Java virtual threads and Erlang processes. Explain the trade-offs in creation cost, blocking system calls, preemption, multicore use and debugging.

expectedConcepts.label: 1:1: each user thread is a kernel thread
N:1 green threads: cheap but no parallelism; blocking stalls all
M:N: runtime multiplexes many tasks on a few kernel threads
Handling blocking syscalls and preemption in M:N
Trade-offs: memory per task, scheduler complexity, debugging, FFI

questions.modelAnswer: In the 1:1 model (pthreads, classic Java threads) each application thread is a kernel thread scheduled by the OS: true parallelism and simple semantics - a blocking system call blocks only that thread - but each costs kernel structures, a large stack reservation and a syscall to create, and switches go through the kernel, so tens of thousands become expensive. N:1 green threads run many user-level threads on a single kernel thread: very cheap to create and switch, but no multicore parallelism, and one blocking syscall freezes all of them (early Java and Ruby). M:N scheduling multiplexes many lightweight tasks onto a pool of kernel threads, roughly one per core: Go's goroutines, Java 21 virtual threads, Erlang processes and Tokio tasks. Creation costs a few hundred bytes to a few KB and switches happen in user space. The runtime must handle the hard parts: it uses non-blocking I/O behind blocking-looking APIs, detaches a carrier thread that enters a blocking syscall and starts another (Go hands off its P), and preempts long-running tasks (Go uses signals; Java virtual threads only yield at blocking points and get pinned inside synchronized blocks or native calls in some versions). Costs: a complex runtime scheduler, harder debugging and profiling, and surprises when calling native code.

questions.title: TCP connection setup and teardown
questions.prompt: Walk through how a TCP connection is established with the three-way handshake and closed with FIN exchanges. Why are sequence numbers randomised, what is the TIME_WAIT state for and how long does it last, and what problems do SYN floods and lingering TIME_WAIT sockets cause?

expectedConcepts.label: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; exchange initial sequence numbers
FIN/ACK in each direction; half-close; RST
TIME_WAIT 2*MSL protects against delayed segments
SYN floods and SYN cookies
TIME_WAIT exhaustion on clients; connection reuse instead

questions.modelAnswer: To open a connection, the client sends SYN with a randomly chosen initial sequence number; the server replies SYN-ACK with its own ISN and acknowledges the client's; the client ACKs, and data can flow (one round trip before the first byte, which is why connection reuse matters). Randomised ISNs make it hard for attackers to inject spoofed segments and prevent confusion with old connections. Closing is independent per direction: one side sends FIN and the other ACKs it; that side may keep sending (half-close) until it sends its own FIN, which is ACKed. RST aborts a connection immediately. The side that closes first enters TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime (60 seconds on Linux), so delayed duplicate packets from the old connection cannot be mistaken for a new connection with the same four-tuple, and so its final ACK can be retransmitted if lost. A SYN flood sends many SYNs without completing handshakes, filling the half-open queue; SYN cookies encode the state in the sequence number so the server keeps none until the ACK arrives. Clients that open and close many short connections to the same server accumulate TIME_WAIT sockets and can exhaust ephemeral ports; the fix is connection pooling and keep-alive rather than kernel hacks.

questions.title: TCP flow control and congestion control
questions.prompt: Explain how TCP avoids overwhelming the receiver and the network. Distinguish flow control with the receive window from congestion control with the congestion window, and explain slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and how CUBIC and BBR differ in deciding how fast to send.

expectedConcepts.label: Flow control: receiver advertises rwnd
Congestion window limits in-flight data; min(rwnd, cwnd)
Slow start doubles per RTT; AIMD in congestion avoidance
Fast retransmit on 3 duplicate ACKs; timeouts
CUBIC is loss-based; BBR models bandwidth and RTT; bufferbloat

questions.modelAnswer: Flow control protects the receiver: each ACK advertises a receive window - how much buffer space is left - and the sender never has more unacknowledged data in flight than that. Congestion control protects the network: the sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd), its estimate of what the path can carry, and the effective limit is min(rwnd, cwnd). A new connection starts in slow start with a small cwnd (typically 10 segments) and roughly doubles it every round trip until it detects loss or crosses a threshold - which is why a fresh connection cannot use full bandwidth for short transfers. Then congestion avoidance grows cwnd by about one segment per RTT and cuts it multiplicatively on loss (AIMD), which converges to fair sharing. Three duplicate ACKs signal a single lost segment, triggering fast retransmit and recovery without a full timeout; a retransmission timeout resets cwnd much further. Linux's default CUBIC is loss-based: it grows cwnd as a cubic function of time since the last loss, filling buffers until packets drop, which causes bufferbloat - high latency from full router queues. Google's BBR instead estimates bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT and paces sending to match, achieving higher throughput on lossy long-distance links with lower queueing delay, though fairness against CUBIC flows has been debated.

questions.title: HTTP/1.1 versus HTTP/2 versus HTTP/3
questions.prompt: Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Explain persistent connections and the limits of HTTP/1.1, how HTTP/2 multiplexes streams with binary framing and header compression, why HTTP/2 still suffers from TCP head-of-line blocking, and how HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes it.

expectedConcepts.label: HTTP/1.1: keep-alive, one request at a time per connection; 6 connections
HTTP/2: binary frames, multiplexed streams, HPACK
TCP head-of-line blocking affects all HTTP/2 streams
HTTP/3 over QUIC/UDP: independent streams, faster handshakes
Trade-offs: middleboxes, CPU cost, server push abandoned

questions.modelAnswer: HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent (keep-alive) connections, but a connection carries one request-response at a time; pipelining existed but was broken by head-of-line issues and was never adopted. Browsers therefore open about six connections per host, and sites resorted to domain sharding, sprites and bundling. HTTP/2 keeps the same semantics (methods, headers, status codes) but encodes messages as binary frames on independent streams multiplexed over a single TCP connection, so many requests are in flight at once; HPACK compresses repetitive headers; streams have priorities. However, TCP delivers a single ordered byte stream: if one packet is lost, all streams wait for its retransmission - TCP head-of-line blocking, which on lossy mobile networks can make HTTP/2 worse than several HTTP/1.1 connections. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport built on UDP that implements reliable, independently ordered streams, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream. QUIC also merges the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes (one round trip, or zero with resumption) and supports connection migration when the client's IP changes. Trade-offs: some networks block or throttle UDP, so clients fall back to HTTP/2; QUIC runs in user space and costs more CPU; HTTP/2 server push was largely abandoned.

questions.title: QUIC in depth
questions.prompt: Explain the QUIC transport protocol. Why was it built on UDP and implemented in user space, how does it combine the transport and cryptographic handshakes, how do connection IDs enable migration between networks, how does it handle loss and congestion, and what are its operational challenges?

expectedConcepts.label: Built on UDP to deploy through middleboxes and evolve in user space
Integrated TLS 1.3: 1-RTT and 0-RTT handshakes; encrypted headers
Independent streams avoid head-of-line blocking
Connection IDs allow migration across IP changes
Challenges: CPU cost, UDP blocking, load balancer routing, 0-RTT replay

questions.modelAnswer: TCP is implemented in operating system kernels and inspected by countless middleboxes, so changing it takes a decade - protocol ossification. QUIC runs over UDP, which middleboxes pass through, and is implemented in user-space libraries shipped with browsers and servers, so it can evolve quickly. Nearly everything, including most header fields, is encrypted, which also prevents ossification. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into its handshake: a new connection is ready after one round trip, and resumption allows 0-RTT data sent with the very first packet - though 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker, so it must only carry idempotent requests. QUIC provides multiple streams with independent ordering, so loss on one stream does not stall others, and its loss recovery uses packet numbers that are never reused, making RTT measurement and retransmission unambiguous; congestion control is pluggable (CUBIC, BBR). Connections are identified by connection IDs rather than the IP and port four-tuple, so a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular keeps its connection. Challenges: higher CPU cost than kernel TCP (mitigated by UDP GSO/GRO offloads), networks that block or rate-limit UDP requiring TCP fallback, load balancers that must route by connection ID, and less visibility for operators because headers are encrypted.

questions.title: How TLS works
questions.prompt: Explain what happens in a TLS 1.3 handshake when a browser connects to https://example.com. Cover key exchange with ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, certificates and the chain of trust, server name indication, forward secrecy, session resumption, and common certificate errors in production.

expectedConcepts.label: Ephemeral (EC)DHE key exchange gives shared secret and forward secrecy
Certificate proves identity; chain to trusted root CA
TLS 1.3: one round trip; ClientHello with key share
SNI, ALPN, session resumption/0-RTT
