Defence in depth: give the model and its tools least privilege; require human confirmation for consequential actions; separate or quarantine untrusted content (a model that reads it but cannot act); restrict outbound channels and block rendering of arbitrary URLs; validate and treat model outputs as untrusted input to downstream systems; and log and monitor tool use.

questions.title: Evaluating LLM applications
questions.prompt: How do you know whether a change to an LLM application - a new prompt, model or retrieval setting - made it better? Explain building evaluation datasets, reference-based and reference-free metrics, LLM-as-judge and its biases, evaluating RAG retrieval and faithfulness separately, regression testing in CI, and online monitoring.

expectedConcepts.label: Curated eval set from real queries, edge cases, failures
Exact match, assertions, rubric scoring; task-specific checks
LLM-as-judge and its biases; calibrate with humans
RAG: retrieval recall/precision vs answer faithfulness and relevance
CI regression gates, online feedback, A/B tests, cost and latency

questions.modelAnswer: Vibes-based checking of a few examples misses regressions, so build an evaluation set: a few hundred inputs drawn from real user queries, known hard cases, past failures and adversarial inputs, each with an expected answer, required facts or a grading rubric, versioned like code. Use the cheapest reliable grader for each property: deterministic checks wherever possible - exact match for classification or extraction, JSON schema validation, regex, executing generated code against tests, checking that cited sources exist. For open-ended answers, use rubric-based grading by humans or an LLM-as-judge prompted with specific criteria; judges are scalable but biased toward longer answers, toward the first option in pairwise comparisons and toward their own model family, so randomise order, use clear rubrics, and measure agreement with human labels before trusting them. For RAG, evaluate the stages separately: retrieval (did the top-k contain the needed passages - recall and precision against labelled relevant chunks) and generation (is the answer faithful to the retrieved context, relevant and complete), otherwise you cannot tell which part to fix. Run the eval suite in CI on every prompt, model or pipeline change and block regressions, tracking cost and latency too. In production, collect user feedback, sample conversations for review, monitor refusal and error rates, and A/B test meaningful changes.

questions.title: Improving retrieval quality in RAG
questions.prompt: Your retrieval-augmented chatbot often answers from the wrong documents. Walk through how you would improve retrieval: chunking strategy, embedding model choice, hybrid search with BM25, metadata filtering, query rewriting, re-ranking with a cross-encoder, and how you measure each change.

expectedConcepts.label: Chunk size and overlap; structure-aware chunking
Hybrid dense + BM25 keyword search
Cross-encoder re-ranking of top candidates
Query rewriting, expansion, metadata filters
Measure recall@k on labelled queries; inspect failures

questions.modelAnswer: First measure: label a set of real questions with the passages that answer them and compute recall@k and MRR, so every change is judged by numbers and failures can be inspected. Chunking: chunks that are too large dilute the embedding with unrelated content; too small loses context. Split along document structure (headings, sections, code blocks), use moderate sizes with some overlap, and prepend context such as the document title and section path to each chunk. Embeddings: choose a model that performs well on your domain and language - benchmark a few on your labelled set - and embed queries and documents with the right instructions or prefixes. Dense embeddings miss exact identifiers, error codes, product names and rare terms, so add BM25 keyword search and merge the two result lists with reciprocal rank fusion (hybrid search). Use metadata filters for product, version, language and access permissions. Query processing: rewrite conversational follow-ups into standalone questions using chat history, expand or split complex queries into sub-queries, or generate a hypothetical answer and embed it (HyDE). Re-ranking: retrieve generously (say the top 50) and re-score candidates with a cross-encoder that reads the query and passage together - far more accurate than bi-encoder similarity - then pass only the best few to the model. Each stage adds latency and cost, so keep only what the metrics justify.

questions.title: LLM agents and tool use
questions.prompt: Explain how LLM agents work. Describe tool or function calling, the reason-act loop, planning, memory, and multi-step tasks such as researching a question or fixing a bug in a codebase. Why are agents unreliable, and what design practices make them safer and more effective?

expectedConcepts.label: Tool calling: model emits structured calls, app executes, result fed back
Agent loop: think, act, observe until done
Context management and memory; planning and sub-agents
Errors compound over steps; loops; prompt injection
Practices: good tool design, limits, checkpoints, human approval, evals

questions.modelAnswer: An agent is an LLM placed in a loop with tools. The application describes available tools - search, read file, run tests, query a database, send a message - with names, descriptions and JSON schemas. Given a task, the model either answers or emits a structured tool call; the application executes it and appends the result to the conversation; the model observes it, reasons about the next step and continues until it decides the task is done. This reason-act-observe loop lets the model gather information it lacks and take actions: to fix a bug it might search the codebase, read relevant files, edit one, run the tests, read the failure and iterate. Longer tasks need context management - summarising old steps, storing notes or using sub-agents with fresh contexts - and sometimes an explicit plan. Agents are unreliable because errors compound: a 95%-reliable step repeated 20 times succeeds only about a third of the time; models can loop, give up early, hallucinate tool arguments, or be hijacked by injected instructions in tool results. Practices that help: few, well-designed tools with clear descriptions and helpful error messages; step and cost limits; sandboxed execution; verification steps such as running tests; checkpoints and human approval for irreversible actions; least-privilege credentials; and an evaluation suite of realistic tasks to measure success rates before and after changes.

questions.title: Structured outputs and function calling
questions.prompt: Your application needs an LLM to return data that code can parse reliably, such as extracted invoice fields. Compare asking for JSON in the prompt, JSON mode, schema-constrained decoding and function calling. How does constrained decoding work, and what validation and error handling do you still need?

expectedConcepts.label: Prompt-only JSON is unreliable: extra text, invalid syntax
Constrained decoding masks tokens to follow a grammar/schema
Function calling returns arguments matching a tool schema
Still validate semantically; retry with error feedback
Valid syntax is not correct content; schema design; refusals

questions.modelAnswer: Asking for JSON in the prompt works most of the time, but models sometimes add explanations, wrap output in markdown fences, truncate, or produce invalid syntax, which breaks parsers at scale. JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON but not your schema. Schema-constrained decoding (structured outputs) guarantees that output matches a JSON schema or grammar: at each step, the decoder computes which tokens could continue a valid document from the current state and masks out all others before sampling, so the model physically cannot emit a missing bracket or a wrong field name. Function or tool calling is the same idea framed as invoking a function: the model returns a function name and arguments matching the declared parameter schema. Even with guaranteed structure, the content can be wrong: the model can hallucinate an invoice number, put a date in the wrong field or invent a value instead of admitting it is absent. So design schemas that allow null or "not found" for missing data, include enums and descriptions, and keep schemas reasonably flat. Validate semantically with a library like Zod or Pydantic - types, ranges, cross-field rules, values present in the source text - and on failure retry with the validation error included, or route to human review. Also handle refusals and truncation explicitly, and evaluate extraction accuracy on a labelled set.

questions.title: Quantising large language models
questions.prompt: Explain model quantisation for LLMs. Why does reducing weights from 16-bit to 8 or 4 bits speed up inference and cut memory, what is the difference between weight-only and weight-and-activation quantisation, how do methods like GPTQ and AWQ preserve accuracy, and what are the quality trade-offs?

expectedConcepts.label: Represent weights with fewer bits using scales/zero points
Less memory and bandwidth; decode is memory-bound
Weight-only vs weights+activations; PTQ vs QAT; group-wise scales
GPTQ, AWQ handle outliers and salient weights; FP8
Quality loss grows below 4 bits; evaluate on your tasks

questions.modelAnswer: Model weights are normally stored in 16-bit floating point (FP16 or BF16). Quantisation stores them with fewer bits - 8-bit or 4-bit integers, or FP8 - by mapping ranges of values onto a small set of levels with a scale (and sometimes a zero point) per tensor, per channel or per small group of weights. A 70-billion-parameter model needs about 140 GB in 16-bit but roughly 35-40 GB in 4-bit, so it fits on far fewer GPUs or even a laptop. Speed improves too because token-by-token decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: reading half or a quarter of the bytes per weight makes each step faster, even though values are dequantised for computation. Weight-only quantisation (common for 4-bit) keeps activations in 16-bit; weight-and-activation quantisation (W8A8, FP8) also speeds up the matrix multiplications on hardware that supports low-precision math, which helps the compute-bound prefill phase. Post-training quantisation needs no retraining, but naive rounding hurts accuracy because LLMs have outlier features and some weights matter much more than others. GPTQ quantises layer by layer while compensating for rounding error using second-order information; AWQ protects salient weight channels identified from activation magnitudes; SmoothQuant shifts activation outliers into weights. Quantisation-aware training gives the best low-bit quality. 8-bit is usually near-lossless, 4-bit costs a little, and below 4 bits quality drops noticeably, so evaluate on your own tasks.

questions.title: Serving LLMs efficiently: batching and throughput
questions.prompt: You must serve an open-weights LLM to thousands of users. Explain the latency metrics that matter (time to first token, inter-token latency), why static batching wastes GPU capacity, how continuous batching and paged attention in servers like vLLM work, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, and how you trade throughput against latency.

expectedConcepts.label: TTFT, inter-token latency/TPOT, throughput tokens/s
Batching amortises weight reads; static batching waits for longest
Continuous batching adds/removes requests every step
Paged attention, chunked prefill, prefix caching
Throughput vs latency, tensor parallelism, autoscaling, speculative decoding

questions.modelAnswer: Users feel two latencies: time to first token (dominated by queueing and the prefill of their prompt) and inter-token latency or time per output token (the decode speed, which determines whether text streams smoothly). Operators care about throughput - total tokens per second per GPU - and therefore cost. A decode step for one sequence reads all the model weights to produce a single token, so the GPU is mostly waiting on memory; batching many sequences together reuses each weight read for many tokens, raising throughput dramatically. Static batching groups requests and waits until the longest one finishes, leaving slots idle and forcing new requests to wait. Continuous (iteration-level) batching, introduced by Orca and used in vLLM, TGI and TensorRT-LLM, inserts new requests and removes finished ones at every decode step. The KV cache limits how many sequences fit, so paged attention allocates it in blocks to avoid fragmentation and enable sharing, and prefix caching reuses common prompts. Chunked prefill splits long prompts so they do not stall everyone's decoding. Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, cutting latency without changing outputs. Larger batches raise throughput but slow each user's tokens, so set limits per SLO, use tensor parallelism across GPUs for big models, and autoscale on queue depth.

questions.title: Mixture-of-experts models
questions.prompt: Explain mixture-of-experts transformer architectures. How does a router send each token to a few expert feed-forward networks, why does this give a model many parameters but low compute per token, what are the challenges of load balancing and training stability, and what does MoE mean for memory and serving?

expectedConcepts.label: Many expert FFNs per layer; router picks top-k per token
Sparse activation: total vs active parameters
Load balancing losses, capacity factor, token dropping
All experts must be in memory; expert parallelism; communication
Better quality per FLOP vs memory, routing instability, batching complexity

questions.modelAnswer: In a standard dense transformer every token passes through every parameter. A mixture-of-experts layer replaces the single feed-forward block in some or all layers with many expert feed-forward networks - say 8 to over 100 - plus a small router network. For each token, the router scores the experts and sends the token to the top one or two (or a few of many fine-grained experts), combining their outputs weighted by the router probabilities; attention layers usually stay dense. The model therefore has a huge total parameter count, giving more capacity to store knowledge, while each token uses only a small fraction - its active parameters - so training and inference compute per token resemble a much smaller dense model. Mixtral, for example, has about 47 billion total parameters but roughly 13 billion active per token. Challenges: routers tend to collapse onto a few favourite experts, so training adds auxiliary load-balancing losses or bias adjustments, and experts have capacity limits beyond which tokens may be dropped or rerouted; routing can make training unstable and fine-tuning trickier. For serving, all experts must be held in memory even though few are used per token, so memory needs match the total size; large deployments shard experts across GPUs (expert parallelism), which requires all-to-all communication, and efficiency depends on batching enough tokens to keep every expert busy.

questions.title: Multimodal models: vision-language
questions.prompt: Explain how multimodal models that understand images and text work. Describe how images are turned into tokens with a vision encoder, how those are connected to a language model, contrastive pretraining like CLIP, typical capabilities and failure modes such as counting, fine text and spatial reasoning, and practical uses.

expectedConcepts.label: Vision encoder (ViT) turns image patches into embeddings
Projection/adapter maps image features into the LLM token space
CLIP: contrastive image-text pretraining aligns embeddings
Failures: counting, small text, spatial relations, hallucinated details
Uses: document understanding, charts, UI agents, accessibility

questions.modelAnswer: A typical vision-language model has three parts. A vision encoder, usually a vision transformer, splits an image into patches (for example 14x14 pixels) and turns each into an embedding, producing a sequence of image features. A connector - a linear projection, small MLP or cross-attention module - maps those features into the language model's embedding space so they can be treated like tokens and interleaved with text. The language model then reads the combined sequence and generates text. Vision encoders are often initialised from contrastive pretraining such as CLIP, which trains an image encoder and a text encoder on hundreds of millions of image-caption pairs so matching pairs have similar embeddings and mismatched pairs do not; this alone enables zero-shot classification and image search. The combined model is then trained on captioning, visual question answering and instruction data, and some models are trained natively multimodal from the start. High-resolution images are tiled into crops, which costs many tokens. Capabilities: describing images, reading documents and charts, answering questions about screenshots, and operating user interfaces. Failure modes: counting many objects, reading tiny or dense text, precise spatial relationships and measurements, and confidently describing details that are not there. Uses include document processing, accessibility descriptions, visual QA in support, and computer-use agents.

questions.title: How diffusion models generate images
questions.prompt: Explain how diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion generate images. Describe the forward noising process, training a network to predict noise, the reverse denoising process, latent diffusion with an autoencoder, how text conditioning and classifier-free guidance work, and how the number of sampling steps affects speed and quality.

expectedConcepts.label: Forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise
Network (U-Net/transformer) learns to predict the noise
Sampling iteratively denoises from random noise
Latent diffusion in a compressed space via a VAE
Text conditioning via cross-attention; classifier-free guidance; fewer steps trade-off

questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual corruption process. In the forward process, Gaussian noise is added to a training image over many small steps until it becomes pure noise; this needs no learning, and any intermediate noise level can be sampled directly. A neural network - historically a U-Net, increasingly a transformer - is trained to take a noisy image and the noise level and predict the noise that was added (or equivalently the clean image), using a simple mean squared error loss. Generation runs in reverse: start from random noise and repeatedly apply the network to remove a little predicted noise, step by step, until a clean image emerges. Stable Diffusion is a latent diffusion model: an autoencoder first compresses images into a much smaller latent representation, diffusion runs in that latent space, and the decoder turns the final latent into pixels, cutting compute enormously. Text conditioning feeds embeddings from a text encoder (such as CLIP's) into the network through cross-attention. Classifier-free guidance trains the model both with and without the prompt and at sampling time extrapolates from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one; a higher guidance scale follows the prompt more closely at the cost of diversity and naturalness. Early models needed hundreds of steps; better samplers and distillation (consistency models, few-step variants) now produce good images in a handful of steps, trading some quality for speed.

questions.title: Reducing the cost and latency of LLM applications
questions.prompt: Your LLM-powered feature is too slow and too expensive. Explain the levers you have: choosing smaller models and routing between models, prompt and context trimming, prompt caching, response caching, batching, streaming, parallelising calls, and distillation. How do you make sure quality does not regress?

expectedConcepts.label: Cost and latency scale with input and output tokens
Smaller models and routing/cascades
Prompt (prefix) caching and response caching
Streaming, parallel calls, batch APIs for offline work
Guard quality with evals; distillation/fine-tuning a small model

questions.modelAnswer: Cost and latency are roughly proportional to tokens processed and generated, and to model size; output tokens are slower and usually pricier than input tokens. Levers: use the smallest model that meets the quality bar for each step - many classification, extraction or routing steps do not need a frontier model - and build a cascade where a cheap model handles easy requests and escalates hard or low-confidence ones. Trim the context: shorter system prompts, fewer and better-chosen retrieved chunks, summarising long histories. Ask for concise outputs and set sensible max tokens. Prompt caching (offered by major APIs and serving engines) reuses the processed prefix of long, repeated prompts such as system instructions or documents, cutting both cost and time to first token - so put stable content first. Cache full responses for repeated questions, and consider semantic caching carefully because near-duplicate questions may need different answers. Improve perceived latency by streaming tokens and running independent calls in parallel rather than sequentially; move non-interactive work to discounted batch APIs. For high volume, distil or fine-tune a small model on outputs from a large one. Every change needs an evaluation suite run before shipping, plus monitoring of quality, cost per request and p95 latency in production, because savings that silently reduce answer quality are false economies.

questions.title: Guardrails and safety for LLM applications
questions.prompt: Explain how you would add guardrails to a customer-facing LLM chatbot. Cover input filtering, output moderation, keeping the bot on topic, protecting personal data, preventing harmful or legally risky answers, handling uncertainty honestly, and the trade-off between safety and helpfulness.

expectedConcepts.label: Input checks: abuse, injection attempts, PII, off-topic
Output moderation and policy checks before showing users
Grounding and honest uncertainty; escalation to humans
Scope limits, tool permissions, rate limits, logging
Over-blocking vs harm; measure both; red teaming

questions.modelAnswer: Guardrails are layered checks around the model, not a single prompt. On input: detect abusive content, obvious jailbreak or prompt-injection attempts, and personal data that should be masked before it is sent to a third-party model or logged; classify intent so off-topic requests (a banking bot asked for medical advice) get a polite redirect. In the system prompt and tool design: narrow the bot's scope, give it only the tools and data it needs, and define what it must never do, such as promising refunds or giving legal advice. Ground answers in retrieved, approved content and instruct the model to say it does not know and offer escalation to a human when information is missing, rather than guessing. On output: run moderation for harmful content, check policy rules (no account numbers, no competitor pricing, required disclaimers), verify that cited sources exist, and block or rewrite violations before the user sees them. Operationally: rate limits against abuse, audit logs with privacy controls, monitoring of flagged conversations, and regular red-teaming. Guardrails have their own false positives: over-blocking frustrates users and makes the product useless, so evaluate both harmful-content leakage and wrongful refusals on test sets and tune thresholds deliberately.

questions.title: Chain-of-thought and reasoning models
questions.prompt: Explain chain-of-thought prompting and why asking a model to reason step by step improves performance on maths and logic problems. How do modern reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning extend this with longer thinking, what are test-time compute trade-offs, and what are the limitations of visible reasoning?

expectedConcepts.label: Chain-of-thought: intermediate steps before the answer
More tokens = more computation; decomposes problems
Reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable rewards
Test-time compute: longer thinking, self-consistency, more cost/latency
Limits: unfaithful reasoning, overthinking, cost; not needed for simple tasks

questions.modelAnswer: A transformer does a fixed amount of computation per generated token, so a model answering a multi-step problem in one token has little room to work it out. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write intermediate steps first; each written step becomes context for the next, effectively giving the model more serial computation and a scratchpad, and decomposing the problem into easier pieces. This substantially improves maths, logic and multi-step planning. Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and takes the majority answer, trading more compute for accuracy. Reasoning models take this further: they are trained with reinforcement learning on problems with verifiable answers (maths, code with tests) to generate long internal reasoning before answering - exploring approaches, checking work, backtracking. Performance then scales with test-time compute: allowing more thinking tokens improves results on hard problems, at the cost of latency and token spend, and many APIs expose a reasoning-effort or budget setting. Limitations: the visible reasoning is not guaranteed to be a faithful account of how the model reached its answer; models can overthink simple questions, wasting time and sometimes talking themselves into errors; and for simple lookups, extraction or classification, a non-reasoning model is faster and cheaper. Use reasoning where problems genuinely require multi-step work.

questions.title: Knowledge distillation for language models
questions.prompt: Explain knowledge distillation: training a small student model to imitate a large teacher. Compare matching soft probability distributions with training on teacher-generated outputs, why soft targets carry more information than labels, how distillation is used to create small capable LLMs, and its limits and legal considerations.

expectedConcepts.label: Student learns to mimic teacher outputs
Soft targets with temperature carry dark knowledge
Sequence-level distillation via synthetic data from the teacher
Uses: small fast models, task-specific students, reasoning traces
Limits: student capacity, inherits teacher errors, terms of service

questions.modelAnswer: Distillation trains a small student model to reproduce the behaviour of a larger, more capable teacher, so you get much of the teacher's quality at a fraction of the inference cost. In classic distillation (Hinton et al.), the student is trained to match the teacher's full output probability distribution, softened with a temperature, usually alongside the true labels. These soft targets contain "dark knowledge": a teacher that says an image is 80% dog, 15% wolf and 0.01% car teaches similarity structure that a one-hot label cannot, giving the student a richer signal per example. For LLMs, logit-level distillation minimises the KL divergence between teacher and student next-token distributions, which requires access to the teacher's logits and compatible tokenizers. The more common approach is sequence-level distillation: use the teacher to generate large amounts of high-quality responses, explanations or reasoning traces for many prompts, and fine-tune the student on that synthetic data. Many small open models and task-specific production models are built this way, and reasoning abilities can be partly transferred by training on teacher reasoning traces. Limits: a student with far fewer parameters cannot absorb everything, especially broad factual knowledge; it inherits the teacher's biases and mistakes; and generating training data from a proprietary model may violate its terms of service, so check licences.

questions.title: Speculative decoding
questions.prompt: Explain speculative decoding for faster LLM inference. How does a small draft model propose several tokens that the large target model verifies in a single forward pass, why the output distribution stays exactly the same as the target model's, what determines the speed-up, and variants such as Medusa heads and n-gram or prompt-lookup drafting.

expectedConcepts.label: Draft model proposes k tokens cheaply
Target verifies all k in one parallel pass
Rejection sampling keeps output distribution identical
Speed-up depends on acceptance rate and draft cost; decode is memory-bound
Medusa heads, EAGLE, prompt lookup / n-gram drafting

questions.modelAnswer: Decoding is slow because each token requires a full forward pass of the large model, and that pass is memory-bandwidth bound - the GPU spends most of its time reading weights, with spare compute. Verifying several tokens costs about the same as generating one, because a forward pass over k positions processes them in parallel. Speculative decoding exploits this: a small, fast draft model proposes the next k tokens (say 4-8); the large target model runs once over the context plus those k tokens, producing its own probability distribution at each position. Draft tokens are accepted left to right using a rejection-sampling rule - accept token t with probability min(1, p_target / p_draft) - and at the first rejection the target samples a replacement from a corrected distribution, so the final output follows exactly the target model's distribution: it is lossless, not an approximation. Each verification pass yields at least one token and up to k + 1. The speed-up depends on how often the target agrees with the draft (high for predictable text like code or boilerplate) and on how cheap the draft is; 2-3x is typical. Variants avoid a separate draft model: Medusa and EAGLE add lightweight extra heads to predict several future tokens, self-speculative methods skip layers, and prompt-lookup or n-gram drafting copies spans from the prompt, which works very well for editing and summarisation where output repeats input.

questions.title: Hypermedia, HATEOAS and the REST maturity model
questions.prompt: Explain the Richardson maturity model for REST APIs and what HATEOAS - hypermedia as the engine of application state - means. Show what links in a response look like, what benefits they promise, and why most real-world APIs stop short of full hypermedia.

expectedConcepts.label: Richardson levels 0-3: RPC, resources, HTTP verbs, hypermedia
Responses include links to available actions
Benefits: discoverability, server-controlled workflows, evolvable URLs
Formats: HAL, JSON:API, Siren; pagination links
Why rare: clients hard-code anyway, verbosity, tooling; partial use

questions.modelAnswer: Leonard Richardson described levels of REST adoption. Level 0 tunnels everything through one endpoint, like RPC over HTTP POST. Level 1 introduces resources with their own URLs. Level 2 uses HTTP methods and status codes properly - where most "REST" APIs live. Level 3 adds hypermedia controls: HATEOAS, the idea that responses tell the client what it can do next through links, just as web pages contain links and forms. An order response might include "_links": {"self": {"href": "/orders/42"}, "cancel": {"href": "/orders/42/cancellation", "method": "POST"}, "payment": {"href": "/orders/42/payment"}}, and the cancel link appears only while cancellation is allowed. The promised benefits: clients discover capabilities instead of hard-coding URL patterns and business rules, the server can change URLs and workflows without breaking clients, and the available links describe the resource's state machine. Formats such as HAL, JSON:API and Siren standardise links. In practice most APIs adopt only pieces - self links and next/prev pagination links are common - because client developers still hard-code flows against documentation, generic hypermedia clients never became widespread, responses get more verbose, and OpenAPI-based tooling and code generation assume fixed URL templates.

questions.title: IPv6: why and how
questions.prompt: Explain why IPv6 was created and how it differs from IPv4. Describe the 128-bit address format and notation, how devices get addresses with SLAAC or DHCPv6, why NAT is not needed, how the header and features differ, and why the transition has taken decades, including dual-stack networks.

expectedConcepts.label: IPv4 exhaustion of ~4.3 billion addresses
128-bit addresses in hexadecimal groups; :: shortening
SLAAC and DHCPv6; link-local addresses
End-to-end addressing without NAT; firewalls still needed
Transition: dual stack, tunnels, NAT64; slow adoption; India high adoption

questions.modelAnswer: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, about 4.3 billion in total - far too few for every phone, laptop and sensor - and the regional registries effectively ran out in the 2010s, kept going only by NAT and address trading. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, with leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups shortened to "::" - for example 2001:db8::1. The space is so large that every device can have globally unique addresses; a typical home gets a /56 or /64 prefix. Devices can configure themselves using stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) from router advertisements, or use DHCPv6, and every interface also has a link-local address for the local network. Because addresses are plentiful, NAT is unnecessary and end-to-end connectivity returns, which simplifies peer-to-peer and VoIP - but a stateful firewall is still needed for security. The header is simpler and fixed-size, routers no longer fragment packets, ARP is replaced by neighbour discovery, and broadcast is replaced by multicast. Adoption took decades because IPv4 and IPv6 are not directly compatible: networks run dual stack, translation such as NAT64 bridges them, and every device, application and ISP must support it. Mobile networks drove adoption; India is among the countries with the highest IPv6 usage.

questions.title: Partial failures, gray failures and network partitions in practice
questions.prompt: Real distributed systems rarely fail cleanly. Explain partial and gray failures - a node that answers health checks but serves requests slowly, an asymmetric network partition, or a disk that is slowly failing. Why do these defeat simple failure detection, how do they cause cascading outages, and what designs and observability help?

expectedConcepts.label: Gray failure: component appears healthy to some observers but not others
Examples: slow disk, packet loss, asymmetric partition, overloaded dependency
Simple heartbeats miss them; use request-level signals and outlier detection
Cascades via retries, timeouts, thread pool exhaustion
Designs: deep health checks, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fail fast

questions.modelAnswer: Textbook failures are clean: a node crashes and stops responding. Production failures are often partial. In a gray failure a component looks healthy to one observer and broken to another: a server answers the load balancer's lightweight health check but times out on real requests because its disk is degrading, a dependency is overloaded, or one network link drops 5% of packets. Partitions can be asymmetric - A can reach B but not the reverse - or partial, where some nodes see each other and others do not. These defeat simple heartbeat-based detection because the heartbeat path is fine; the cluster keeps routing traffic to the sick node, and consensus or leader election may behave strangely when nodes disagree about who is alive. Gray failures often trigger cascades: callers block on slow responses, thread or connection pools fill up, retries multiply load, and the slowness spreads upstream until a whole service is down. Defences: health checks that exercise real dependencies (carefully, so one bad dependency does not mark everything unhealthy), outlier detection that ejects instances with elevated error rates or latency as measured by their callers, strict timeouts and deadlines, circuit breakers and bulkheads that isolate pools per dependency, failing fast instead of queueing, and observability from the client's perspective - per-instance latency percentiles and error rates - because the system's own view of itself is exactly what gray failures fool.

questions.title: Compile-time versus runtime errors
questions.prompt: How do compile-time and runtime errors differ, and how should a developer debug each?

expectedConcepts.label: Compile-time errors are caught before running
Runtime errors happen while executing
Debugging: read compiler message vs reproduce and inspect state

questions.modelAnswer: Compile-time errors are found by the compiler or type checker before the program runs: syntax mistakes, type mismatches, missing symbols. You fix them by reading the error message, which points to a file and line. Runtime errors only appear while the program executes with real inputs: null dereferences, out-of-bounds access, division by zero, failed I/O. To debug them, reproduce the failure, read the stack trace, add logging or use a debugger to inspect state. Stronger static typing moves more bugs from runtime to compile time.

questions.title: Interpreters, compilers and virtual machines
questions.prompt: What is the difference between an interpreter, a compiler, and a virtual machine?

expectedConcepts.label: Compiler translates ahead of time to machine code
Interpreter executes source or bytecode directly
Virtual machine runs bytecode, often with a JIT

questions.modelAnswer: A compiler translates source code ahead of time into another form, usually native machine code, producing a binary that runs without the compiler. An interpreter executes the program directly, reading source or an intermediate form and performing each operation, which starts fast but runs slower. A virtual machine is a runtime that executes a portable bytecode, such as the JVM or the CPython VM; many VMs include a just-in-time compiler that turns hot bytecode into machine code while running. Real languages mix these: Java compiles to bytecode, then the JVM interprets and JIT-compiles it.

questions.title: Static typing and type inference
questions.prompt: How do static typing and type inference work together in a modern language?

expectedConcepts.label: Static typing checks types before running
Type inference deduces types from context
Inference limits: explicit types at boundaries, unreadable errors

questions.modelAnswer: Static typing means every expression has a type that is checked before the program runs. Type inference lets the compiler work out many of those types from context, so you write let x = 5 or auto x = f() and the compiler still knows the exact type. You keep the safety and tooling of static types without repetitive annotations. Most languages still ask for explicit types at boundaries such as function signatures and public APIs, because they document intent and keep error messages local. Overusing inference can hide what a value is, so readability decides where to annotate.

questions.title: Ergonomic APIs for developers
questions.prompt: What makes an API ergonomic for the developer who consumes it?

expectedConcepts.label: Easy to use correctly, hard to misuse
Consistent naming, sensible defaults, clear errors
Small surface area and good documentation with examples

questions.modelAnswer: An ergonomic API makes the common task easy and the wrong thing hard. Names are consistent and predictable, so once you learn one function you can guess the others. It has sensible defaults, so simple uses need few parameters, while advanced options remain available. Types and parameter order prevent mistakes, for example a typed duration instead of a bare integer. Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it. It keeps the surface area small, documents behaviour with short examples, and avoids surprising side effects. The test is how quickly a new developer succeeds without reading the source.

questions.title: Immutability and safety
questions.prompt: Explain immutability and describe when it makes software safer.

expectedConcepts.label: Immutable values cannot change after creation
Safer sharing across threads and simpler reasoning
Cost: copying and allocation; persistent data structures

questions.modelAnswer: An immutable value cannot change after it is created; to "modify" it you create a new value. That makes code easier to reason about, because a function cannot surprise you by changing data you passed in, and it makes concurrency safer, because immutable data can be shared between threads without locks or races. It also helps caching, hashing and undo history. The cost is copying and extra allocation, which persistent data structures reduce by sharing unchanged parts. Use immutability for shared state, configuration, keys and messages; use controlled mutation in hot, local code where performance matters.

questions.title: Values versus references
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a value and a reference?

expectedConcepts.label: Value semantics copy the data
Reference points to shared data
Pitfall: unexpected shared mutation

questions.modelAnswer: With value semantics, assigning or passing a variable copies the data, so each variable has its own independent copy and changing one does not affect the other. With reference semantics, the variable holds a reference or pointer to an object, so several variables can refer to the same object and a change through one is visible through all of them. References avoid expensive copies of large objects, but they create aliasing: a function can unexpectedly modify data its caller still uses. Knowing which semantics a language uses for each type, such as structs versus classes, prevents those surprises.

questions.title: Exceptions versus explicit error values
questions.prompt: How do exceptions compare with explicit error values?

expectedConcepts.label: Exceptions unwind the stack to a handler
Error values are returned and checked explicitly
Trade-off: visibility versus boilerplate

questions.modelAnswer: Exceptions separate the error path from normal code: a failure throws, the stack unwinds, and a handler further up catches it. Code stays short, but the control flow is hidden, so it is easy to forget which calls can fail. Explicit error values, like Go errors or Rust Result, are returned and must be checked, so every failure point is visible and the type system can force handling, at the cost of more boilerplate. Exceptions suit truly exceptional, rare failures; error values suit expected failures such as "not found" or invalid input. Either way, never swallow errors silently.

questions.title: Pure functions and testing
questions.prompt: What is a pure function, and why is it useful for testing?

expectedConcepts.label: Same input gives same output, no side effects
Easy to test without mocks or setup
Push side effects to the edges

questions.modelAnswer: A pure function always returns the same output for the same inputs and has no side effects: it does not read or change global state, files, the network or the clock. That makes it trivial to test: call it with inputs and assert on the output, with no mocks, setup or cleanup, and the test is deterministic. Pure functions are also easy to reason about, reuse, cache and run in parallel. Real programs need side effects, so a good design keeps a pure core of business logic and pushes I/O to the edges, where fewer tests need mocks.

questions.title: Cohesion and coupling
questions.prompt: Explain cohesion and coupling with a practical software example.

expectedConcepts.label: Cohesion: a module focuses on one responsibility
Coupling: how much modules depend on each other
Aim for high cohesion and low coupling

questions.modelAnswer: Cohesion measures how closely the parts of one module belong together; coupling measures how much modules depend on each other. You want high cohesion and low coupling. For example, a billing module that calculates invoices, applies taxes and formats invoice PDFs is cohesive because everything relates to invoicing. If the billing code reaches directly into the user module's database tables, the two are tightly coupled: changing the user schema breaks billing. Exposing a small interface such as getCustomerAddress reduces coupling, so each module can change independently and be tested in isolation.

questions.title: Useful abstractions
questions.prompt: What makes an abstraction useful rather than merely hiding complexity?

expectedConcepts.label: Good abstraction gives a simpler, correct model
Stable interface that matches real use cases
Leaky or premature abstractions add cost

questions.modelAnswer: A useful abstraction gives callers a simpler mental model that is still correct for what they need, so they can solve their problem without knowing the details underneath. A file API that hides disk sectors is useful because the model "a named stream of bytes" is enough for most work. A bad abstraction just adds a layer: it mirrors the implementation, forces callers to understand both layers, or leaks details at the worst times, such as errors that only make sense internally. Build abstractions from real repeated use cases rather than guesses, and keep their interface small and stable.

questions.title: Packages, modules and libraries
questions.prompt: How do packages, modules, and libraries differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Module: a unit of code organisation and namespace
Package groups modules; library is reusable code
Package managers distribute versioned libraries

questions.modelAnswer: Exact meanings vary by language, but broadly a module is a unit of code organisation that defines a namespace, often a single file, with its own exported and private names. A package groups related modules together, and in many ecosystems it is also the unit you install and version. A library is reusable code meant to be called by other programs, delivered as one or more packages. Package managers such as npm, pip or Go modules download versioned libraries and their dependencies. In Go, for example, a package is a directory, and a module is a versioned collection of packages.

questions.title: Explaining technical debt
questions.prompt: How would you explain technical debt to a non-technical stakeholder?

expectedConcepts.label: Shortcuts that make future changes slower
Interest: every new feature costs more
Sometimes worth taking, but must be repaid

questions.modelAnswer: I would compare it to financial debt. To ship faster, the team sometimes takes shortcuts: a quick fix instead of a clean design, or skipped tests. That is like borrowing money, and it can be a smart decision when speed matters. But the debt charges interest: every later feature in that area takes longer, bugs appear more often, and onboarding gets harder. If we never repay it by refactoring, the interest eventually consumes most of the team's time. So the question is not whether to have any debt, but which debt is worth taking and when to pay it down.

questions.title: Dependency injection
questions.prompt: What is dependency injection, and what problem does it solve?

expectedConcepts.label: Dependencies are passed in rather than created inside
Enables testing with fakes and swapping implementations
Overuse: complex frameworks and hidden wiring

questions.modelAnswer: Dependency injection means a component receives the things it depends on, such as a database client, clock or logger, from outside, usually through its constructor or function parameters, instead of creating them itself. That decouples the component from specific implementations: in production you pass the real database, in tests you pass an in-memory fake, and you can swap a payment provider without changing business logic. Simple constructor injection needs no framework. Heavy DI frameworks with automatic wiring can make it hard to see where an object comes from, so many teams prefer explicit wiring in main.

questions.title: Synchronous versus asynchronous execution
questions.prompt: How do synchronous and asynchronous execution differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Synchronous call blocks until the result is ready
Asynchronous starts work and continues; result arrives later
Async improves throughput for I/O but adds complexity

questions.modelAnswer: In synchronous execution a call blocks: the caller waits until the operation finishes and then continues, which is simple to read and debug. In asynchronous execution the caller starts the operation and keeps doing other work; the result arrives later through a callback, promise, future or await. Asynchrony shines for I/O-bound work, because one thread can keep thousands of network requests in flight instead of sitting idle. The cost is complexity: error handling, cancellation, ordering and debugging stack traces become harder, and CPU-heavy work does not get faster just by being async.

questions.title: Concurrency versus parallelism
questions.prompt: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

expectedConcepts.label: Concurrency: dealing with many tasks at once, interleaved
Parallelism: executing at the same instant on multiple cores
Concurrency is about structure, parallelism about speed

questions.modelAnswer: Concurrency is about structuring a program to deal with many tasks that are in progress at the same time, which can be interleaved even on a single core: a web server handling many connections by switching between them while each waits for I/O. Parallelism is about executing multiple computations at literally the same instant on multiple cores to finish faster, such as splitting an image across eight cores. A concurrent program may or may not run in parallel. As Rob Pike put it, concurrency is about dealing with lots of things at once; parallelism is about doing lots of things at once.

questions.title: Deterministic versus nondeterministic behaviour
questions.prompt: Explain deterministic versus nondeterministic program behavior.

expectedConcepts.label: Deterministic: same input always gives same result
Sources of nondeterminism: threads, time, randomness, I/O
Nondeterminism causes flaky tests and hard-to-reproduce bugs

questions.modelAnswer: A deterministic program produces the same output every time for the same input, which makes it reproducible and easy to test. Nondeterminism enters through thread scheduling, the current time, random numbers, hash map iteration order, network timing and external services. It is not always a bug, since randomness and concurrency are often intended, but it causes flaky tests and bugs that appear only occasionally, such as race conditions. To control it, inject the clock and random seed, avoid relying on iteration order, synchronise shared state, and record inputs so failures can be replayed.

questions.title: Serialisation between services
questions.prompt: What is serialization, and what risks arise when exchanging data between services?

expectedConcepts.label: Serialisation converts objects to bytes or text
Schema compatibility between versions
Risks: precision loss, unsafe deserialisation, size

questions.modelAnswer: Serialisation converts in-memory objects into a format such as JSON, Protocol Buffers or Avro so they can be stored or sent over the network, and deserialisation turns them back. Between services the main risks are compatibility, when one side changes the schema and the other cannot read it, so you evolve schemas additively and ignore unknown fields; precision and type loss, such as large integers in JSON or time zones; and security, because deserialising untrusted data with formats that can instantiate arbitrary types has led to remote code execution. Also enforce size limits and validate the decoded data.

questions.title: Configuration across environments
questions.prompt: How should a program handle configuration across development, testing, and production?

expectedConcepts.label: Separate config from code, same build everywhere
Validate config at startup with clear errors
Secrets must not live in code or repos

questions.modelAnswer: Keep configuration out of the code so the same build artifact runs in every environment, with only the configuration changing, for example through environment variables or config files. Load it once at startup into a typed structure, validate it and fail fast with a clear message if something is missing or invalid, rather than crashing later. Provide safe defaults for development, but make production values explicit. Secrets such as passwords and API keys belong in a secret manager or the platform's secret store, never in the repository. Keep the number of environment-specific differences small to avoid "works in staging" surprises.

questions.title: Defensive programming
questions.prompt: What is defensive programming, and when can it become counterproductive?

expectedConcepts.label: Validate inputs and assumptions, handle unexpected cases
Most valuable at trust boundaries
Counterproductive: hiding bugs and redundant checks everywhere

questions.modelAnswer: Defensive programming means not trusting that everything will go right: validating inputs, checking assumptions with assertions, handling error cases and using safe defaults. It is most valuable at trust boundaries, such as user input, network data and public APIs. It becomes counterproductive when it hides bugs instead of exposing them, for example catching every exception and continuing, or replacing an impossible null with a default so the real defect surfaces far away. Redundant checks in every internal function also clutter code. A better rule is to validate at the boundary, then fail fast and loudly on broken internal invariants.

questions.title: A safe deployment pipeline
questions.prompt: Walk through a safe deployment pipeline from commit to production.

expectedConcepts.label: Build once, test, then promote the same artifact
Stages: CI tests, staging, gradual rollout
Automated rollback and monitoring gates

questions.modelAnswer: A commit triggers CI, which builds the artifact once, for example a container image tagged with the commit, and runs linting, unit and integration tests and security scans. The same immutable artifact is deployed to a staging environment for end-to-end checks. Production rollout is gradual: a canary or a small percentage of traffic first, while dashboards compare error rate and latency with the old version. If health checks or metrics regress, the pipeline rolls back automatically; otherwise it widens the rollout. Database migrations are backward compatible, and every step is logged so you know exactly what is running.

questions.title: What CI should check before merging
questions.prompt: What should a CI pipeline check before allowing a merge?

expectedConcepts.label: Build and automated tests must pass
Static checks: lint, types, formatting, security scans
Keep it fast and reliable or people bypass it

questions.modelAnswer: At minimum the code must build and the automated tests must pass: unit tests and the integration tests that cover critical paths. Add static checks that catch problems cheaply: formatting, linting, type checking, and dependency and secret scanning. For services, check that migrations apply and that API contracts or generated clients still match. Many teams also require a code review and an up-to-date branch. The pipeline has to be fast, ideally a few minutes, and reliable: flaky tests and half-hour builds teach people to rerun until green or bypass the checks, which defeats the purpose.

questions.title: Infrastructure as code
questions.prompt: Your staging and production environments were built by hand in the cloud console, no longer match, and nobody could recreate production after a disaster. How does infrastructure as code solve this, and what new risks does it bring?

expectedConcepts.label: Infrastructure defined in version-controlled files
Reproducible environments and reviewable changes
Risks: state management and blast radius of a bad apply

questions.modelAnswer: Without infrastructure as code, servers, networks and permissions are created by clicking in a console, so nobody knows exactly how production is configured, environments drift apart and disasters are hard to rebuild. With tools such as Terraform, Pulumi or CloudFormation, infrastructure is declared in files kept in version control. Changes go through code review, a plan shows exactly what will change before applying, and the same definitions recreate identical environments. The costs are managing the state file safely, handling drift when someone changes things manually, and the large blast radius of a mistaken apply, so changes deserve the same care as application code.

questions.title: Rollback strategy for a failed deployment
questions.prompt: How would you design a rollback strategy for a failed deployment?

expectedConcepts.label: Keep the previous version ready and redeploy it quickly
Detect failure automatically with health and error metrics
Data and schema changes must be backward compatible

questions.modelAnswer: Rollback must be fast and boring. Deploy immutable, versioned artifacts so the previous version can be redeployed with one command or automatically. Detect failure early with health checks, error rates and latency compared against the previous version, ideally during a canary, so a bad release reaches few users. The hard part is data: code can roll back, but a destructive schema migration cannot, so use expand-and-contract migrations that keep the old version working. Feature flags let you switch off a feature without redeploying. Sometimes rolling forward with a fix is safer, but the default should be a tested, practised rollback.

questions.title: Blue-green versus canary deployment
questions.prompt: What is the difference between blue-green and canary deployment?

expectedConcepts.label: Blue-green switches all traffic between two environments
Canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first
Blue-green needs double capacity; canary limits blast radius

questions.modelAnswer: In blue-green deployment you run two full environments: blue serves production while green gets the new version. After testing green, you switch all traffic to it at once, and rolling back is just switching back. It is simple and fast to revert but needs double capacity, and every user hits the new version at the same moment. A canary deployment sends a small share of real traffic, say 1 to 5 percent, to the new version, compares its error rate and latency with the old one, and gradually increases the share. It limits the blast radius of bugs but takes longer and needs good metrics.

questions.title: Injecting secrets into services
questions.prompt: How should secrets be injected into a running service?

expectedConcepts.label: Use a secret manager, not code or images
Inject at runtime via mounted files or env, with identity-based access
Rotation, auditing and avoiding leaks in logs

questions.modelAnswer: Secrets should never be baked into code, container images or config committed to Git. Store them in a secret manager such as Vault or a cloud secret service, and grant each service access through its workload identity rather than another static password. At runtime the platform injects them, typically as files mounted into the container or environment variables, or the service fetches them at startup. Files are often preferred because environment variables leak more easily into crash dumps and child processes. Support rotation without redeploying, audit who read which secret, give each service only the secrets it needs, and make sure they never appear in logs.

questions.title: Readiness, liveness and startup probes
questions.prompt: Your pods restart in a loop whenever the database is briefly slow, and new pods get traffic before they finish warming up. How should readiness, liveness and startup probes be set up to fix both problems?

expectedConcepts.label: Liveness restarts a stuck container
Readiness controls whether traffic is sent
Startup probe protects slow-starting apps; avoid dependency checks in liveness
Aggressive probes cause restart storms; lenient ones delay recovery

questions.modelAnswer: In Kubernetes, a liveness probe asks "is this process healthy, or should it be restarted?" If it fails repeatedly, the kubelet restarts the container, which recovers from deadlocks or hung processes. A readiness probe asks "should this pod receive traffic right now?" If it fails, the pod is removed from the service endpoints but not restarted, useful during warm-up, overload or shutdown. A startup probe holds off the other probes until a slow-starting application has initialised. A common mistake is checking external dependencies such as the database in liveness: when the database blips, every pod restarts at once and makes the outage worse. Probe timing is a trade-off too: aggressive thresholds restart pods that are merely slow, while lenient ones leave broken pods serving for longer.

questions.title: Horizontal versus vertical scaling
questions.prompt: How do horizontal and vertical scaling differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Vertical: bigger machine; horizontal: more machines
Horizontal needs stateless design and load balancing
Vertical has hard limits; horizontal adds distributed complexity

questions.modelAnswer: Vertical scaling means giving one machine more resources: more CPU, memory or faster disks. It needs no code changes and keeps things simple, but it hits a hardware ceiling, gets expensive at the top end and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines and spreading load across them with a load balancer or sharding. It scales much further and improves availability, but requires the application to be stateless or to partition its state, and brings distributed-systems problems such as consistency and coordination. Databases often scale vertically first, while stateless web tiers scale horizontally.

questions.title: Autoscaling signals
questions.prompt: Your service autoscales on CPU, yet latency still spikes when traffic surges and queue workers fall behind. Which autoscaling signals would work better, and what are the pitfalls of autoscaling?

expectedConcepts.label: Automatically adds or removes capacity with demand
Signals: CPU, request rate, queue depth, latency, custom metrics
Lag, cooldowns, limits and cost spikes

questions.modelAnswer: Autoscaling automatically adds capacity when demand rises and removes it when demand falls, so you pay for what you need while keeping latency acceptable. Common signals are CPU utilisation, request rate per instance, queue depth for workers, latency, or custom business metrics, and scheduled scaling for predictable peaks. The best signal reflects the real bottleneck: queue length often beats CPU for consumers. Autoscaling reacts with a delay, since new instances take time to start, so keep headroom and tune cooldowns to avoid flapping. Always set maximum limits, because a bug or attack can otherwise scale costs without bound.

questions.title: Investigating a restarting container
questions.prompt: How would you investigate a container that repeatedly restarts?

expectedConcepts.label: Read status, exit code and previous logs
Common causes: OOM kill, failing probe, crash on config
Reproduce locally and check resource limits

questions.modelAnswer: First look at what the platform says: kubectl describe pod shows the last state, the exit code and events, and kubectl logs --previous shows the output of the crashed instance. Exit code 137 with reason OOMKilled means the memory limit was exceeded; a failing liveness probe means the platform is killing it; an immediate non-zero exit usually means a crash at startup, often missing configuration, a bad secret or an unreachable dependency. Check recent changes to the image, config or limits. Then reproduce with the same image and environment locally, and fix the root cause rather than just raising limits or loosening probes.

questions.title: Managed services versus self-hosting
questions.prompt: What are the trade-offs between managed services and self-hosting?

expectedConcepts.label: Managed: provider runs operations, you pay more per unit
Self-hosting gives control at the cost of staff time
Lock-in, cost at scale, compliance

questions.modelAnswer: A managed service, such as a hosted database or queue, means the provider handles provisioning, patching, backups, failover and scaling. You ship faster and need less specialist operations knowledge, but pay a premium per unit, accept the provider's limits and versions, and risk lock-in. Self-hosting gives full control over configuration, versions and cost at large scale, and may be needed for compliance or unusual requirements, but your team now owns upgrades, on-call and disaster recovery. For most teams, managed services are cheaper once engineer time is counted; self-hosting pays off when scale is huge or requirements are special.

questions.title: Object, block and file storage
questions.prompt: Explain object storage, block storage, and file storage.

expectedConcepts.label: Block storage: raw volumes attached to one machine
File storage: shared hierarchical filesystem
Object storage: HTTP API for whole objects, huge scale
Block is fastest, file shares, object scales cheapest

questions.modelAnswer: Block storage provides raw volumes, like a virtual hard disk, attached to one machine; the operating system formats it with a filesystem, and it gives low latency for databases and boot disks. File storage provides a shared hierarchical filesystem, such as NFS, that many machines can mount and use with normal file operations, useful for shared content or legacy apps. Object storage, such as S3, stores whole objects with metadata in a flat namespace accessed over an HTTP API; you cannot edit part of an object in place, but it is cheap, extremely durable and scales almost without limit, ideal for media, backups and data lakes. The trade-off is latency and semantics versus scale and price: block is fastest but tied to one machine, file adds sharing with locking overhead, and object is cheapest at scale but has no in-place edits.

questions.title: IAM roles versus long-lived access keys
questions.prompt: How do IAM roles differ from long-lived access keys?

expectedConcepts.label: Roles give temporary credentials to an identity
Long-lived keys are static secrets that leak
Roles enable rotation and least privilege automatically

questions.modelAnswer: A long-lived access key is a static secret, an ID and key pair, that stays valid until someone revokes it. It gets copied into config files, laptops and CI variables, and when it leaks, an attacker can use it indefinitely. An IAM role is an identity that workloads or people assume; the platform issues short-lived temporary credentials that rotate automatically and expire within hours. A server, container or CI job gets its role through its instance or workload identity, so there is no secret to store. Roles also make least privilege and auditing easier, so they should be the default.

questions.title: Logs, metrics, traces and profiles
questions.prompt: How do logs, metrics, traces, and profiles complement each other?

expectedConcepts.label: Metrics: cheap numbers over time for alerting
Logs: detailed events; traces: request path across services
Profiles show where CPU and memory go in code
Volume makes them expensive: sample traces, limit labels

questions.modelAnswer: They answer different questions. Metrics are cheap aggregated numbers over time, such as request rate, error rate and latency percentiles; they power dashboards and alerts and tell you that something is wrong. Traces follow a single request across services as a tree of timed spans and tell you where in the system the time or error occurred. Logs record detailed events with context and tell you what exactly happened for a particular request. Profiles sample CPU, memory or lock usage and tell you which functions in the code are responsible. A good workflow moves from a metric alert to traces to logs and profiles, linked by request or trace IDs. Each signal has a price at volume: teams sample traces, limit log levels and avoid high-cardinality metric labels to keep them affordable.

questions.title: Disaster recovery with RPO and RTO
questions.prompt: What should a disaster-recovery plan measure with RPO and RTO?

expectedConcepts.label: RPO: how much data loss is acceptable
RTO: how long until service is restored
Targets drive design and cost; test with drills

questions.modelAnswer: RPO, the recovery point objective, is the maximum amount of data you can afford to lose, measured in time: an RPO of five minutes means after a disaster you may lose at most the last five minutes of writes. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long the service may be down before it is restored. The targets drive the design and cost: nightly backups give an RPO of a day, continuous replication gives seconds; a cold standby gives an RTO of hours, a warm multi-region setup gives minutes. Set them per system with the business, then test with regular restore and failover drills.

questions.title: Cloud cost drivers for a backend
questions.prompt: Your cloud bill doubled in three months while traffic grew only 20 percent. Where would you look first, and how would you bring the costs under control?

expectedConcepts.label: Compute and over-provisioned capacity
Storage, managed databases and data transfer
Measure with tags and cost allocation; right-size
Savings trade off flexibility and reliability

questions.modelAnswer: The usual big items are compute, especially instances sized for peak and idle most of the day; managed databases, which are often the single largest line; storage, including forgotten snapshots and logs; and network data transfer, particularly egress to the internet and traffic between zones or regions, which surprises many teams. Observability can also cost a lot through log ingestion and high-cardinality metrics. To control costs, tag resources by team and service so spending is visible, right-size and autoscale, use reserved or spot capacity where appropriate, set retention policies, and keep chatty services in the same zone. Each saving has a price: reservations lock you in, spot capacity can be reclaimed at short notice, and cutting headroom risks latency at peak.

questions.title: Responding to a secret committed to Git
questions.prompt: How would you detect and respond to a secret accidentally committed to Git?

expectedConcepts.label: Detect with secret scanning in CI and pre-commit
Revoke and rotate the secret immediately
Rewriting history is not enough; audit usage

questions.modelAnswer: Detection comes from secret-scanning tools in pre-commit hooks and CI, and from the hosting platform's push protection. The first response is to revoke and rotate the secret immediately, because once it was pushed you must assume it is compromised, especially in a public repository where bots scan for keys within minutes. Removing it from the latest commit is not enough, since it remains in history and in clones; rewriting history helps hygiene but does not undo exposure. Then check the provider's audit logs for misuse, move the secret into a secret manager, and add scanning so it does not happen again.

questions.title: GitOps
questions.prompt: Production keeps drifting from your deployment scripts because engineers run kubectl by hand during incidents. How would GitOps address this, and how does it change the workflow?

expectedConcepts.label: Git is the source of truth for desired state
An agent reconciles the cluster to match Git
Benefits: audit and rollback via Git; risks: secrets and drift

questions.modelAnswer: GitOps means the desired state of your infrastructure and deployments is declared in a Git repository, and an agent running in the environment, such as Argo CD or Flux, continuously reconciles the live system to match it. Instead of running kubectl or deploy scripts by hand, you open a pull request; once merged, the agent applies it. This solves configuration drift and "who changed production?" problems: every change is reviewed, audited and reversible with a git revert, and the agent corrects manual changes. Secrets need special handling because they must not sit in plain text in the repository.

questions.title: Building a minimal container image
questions.prompt: How would you build a minimal container image safely?

expectedConcepts.label: Multi-stage build: compile in one stage, copy artefact to a slim base
Minimal or distroless base, non-root user, pinned versions
Fewer packages means fewer vulnerabilities; scan and rebuild

questions.modelAnswer: Use a multi-stage build: one stage has the compilers and build tools and produces the binary or bundle, and the final stage copies only that artefact onto a small base image, such as distroless, Alpine or even scratch for static binaries. Pin the base image by version or digest so builds are reproducible. Run as a non-root user, add no shells or package managers you do not need, and keep secrets out of build layers. Fewer packages means a smaller attack surface, faster pulls and fewer vulnerability findings. Scan the image in CI and rebuild regularly to pick up base-image security patches.

questions.title: Environment configuration versus feature flags
questions.prompt: How do environment-specific configuration and feature flags differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Config: how the app connects in each environment
Feature flags: whether behaviour is enabled, changed at runtime
Flags enable gradual rollout but add debt; config changes need deploys

questions.modelAnswer: Environment configuration describes how the application runs in a given environment: database URLs, service endpoints, pool sizes, log levels. It usually changes rarely and is set at deploy or startup time. Feature flags control what the application does: whether a feature is on, for which users or what percentage, and they can change at runtime without a deploy. Flags let you separate deployment from release, roll out gradually and switch off a broken feature instantly. The cost is complexity and technical debt: every flag doubles code paths, so remove flags once a feature is fully rolled out.

questions.title: Managing dependency and base-image vulnerabilities
questions.prompt: How should teams manage dependency and base-image vulnerabilities?

expectedConcepts.label: Inventory and scan dependencies and images continuously
Automated update PRs and regular rebuilds
Prioritise by exploitability and reachability, not raw counts

questions.modelAnswer: Start with an inventory: lockfiles and a software bill of materials for each service and image. Scan them continuously in CI and in the registry against vulnerability databases. Use automated tools such as Dependabot or Renovate to open small, frequent update pull requests, backed by good tests so updates are safe to merge, and rebuild images regularly so base-image patches land. Do not chase raw counts: prioritise by severity, whether the vulnerable code is actually reachable, whether it is exploitable or internet-facing, and known active exploitation. Define fix-time targets per severity and track exceptions explicitly.

questions.title: Least privilege for a service
questions.prompt: What is the principle of least privilege, and how would you apply it to a service?

expectedConcepts.label: Grant only the permissions needed for the job
Apply via scoped IAM roles, DB users and network rules
Limits blast radius when compromised; needs upkeep

questions.modelAnswer: Least privilege means every user, service and process gets only the permissions it needs to do its job, and nothing more. For a service, that means its own identity rather than a shared admin key; an IAM role allowing only the specific buckets and queues it uses; a database user that can only touch its own tables, read-only where possible; network rules that only allow the connections it needs; and running as a non-root user. If the service is compromised, the attacker is limited to that small set of permissions, which shrinks the blast radius. Review and trim permissions regularly, because they tend to grow over time.

questions.title: Password hashing versus encryption
questions.prompt: How does password hashing differ from encryption?

expectedConcepts.label: Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible with a key
Verify a password by hashing the attempt and comparing
Use slow password hashes, never encryption or fast hashes

questions.modelAnswer: Encryption is reversible: anyone with the key can decrypt the data back to the original, which is right for data you need to read later. Hashing is one-way: you cannot recover the input from the hash. Passwords should be hashed, not encrypted, because the system never needs to know the original password; to log someone in, it hashes the password they typed and compares it with the stored hash. If passwords were encrypted, stealing the key would expose all of them. And plain fast hashes like SHA-256 are also wrong for passwords; use slow, salted password-hashing functions such as Argon2id or bcrypt.

questions.title: Salts and work factors
questions.prompt: An attacker has stolen your user table, including the password hashes. How do per-user salts and a slow work factor limit what they can do with it?

expectedConcepts.label: Salt: unique random value per password
Salt defeats rainbow tables and identical-hash detection
Work factor makes each guess slow; tune over time

questions.modelAnswer: A salt is a random value generated for each password and stored alongside its hash. Because every user has a different salt, two users with the same password get different hashes, and attackers cannot use precomputed rainbow tables; they have to attack each hash separately. A work factor, also called cost or iterations, makes the hash function deliberately slow and, for Argon2 and scrypt, memory-hungry. Hashing once takes a fraction of a second for a legitimate login, but makes brute-forcing billions of guesses on GPUs very expensive. Increase the work factor as hardware gets faster, and rehash passwords on login.

questions.title: Server-side request forgery
questions.prompt: Your app lets users import an image from a URL, and the server fetches it. How could an attacker abuse this to reach internal services or cloud metadata, and how do you reduce that exposure?

expectedConcepts.label: Attacker makes the server fetch a URL of their choice
Targets internal services and cloud metadata endpoints
Defences: allowlists, block private ranges, egress proxy

questions.modelAnswer: Server-side request forgery happens when a backend fetches a URL supplied by a user, for example to import an image or call a webhook, and an attacker points it at something only the server can reach: internal admin services, localhost, or the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254 that can leak credentials. Reduce exposure by allowlisting destinations where possible, resolving the hostname and blocking private, loopback and link-local addresses, re-checking after redirects and DNS changes, sending outbound requests through an egress proxy with strict rules, and requiring session tokens for the metadata service, as with AWS IMDSv2.

questions.title: Threat modelling a small API
questions.prompt: What is a threat model, and how would you create one for a small API?
