expectedConcepts.label: A structured look at what can go wrong and who attacks
Map data flows and trust boundaries, then list threats (STRIDE)
Prioritise and mitigate the top risks; revisit on changes

questions.modelAnswer: A threat model is a structured way to ask what we are protecting, who might attack it, how, and what we will do about it. For a small API, I would sketch the data flow: clients, the API, its database and third-party services, marking trust boundaries such as the internet edge and the database connection. Then I would list threats at each boundary, using STRIDE as a checklist: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege, for example broken object-level authorisation or a stolen API key. Finally I would rank them by likelihood and impact and pick concrete mitigations.

questions.title: Storing and rotating secrets
questions.prompt: How should an application store and rotate secrets?

expectedConcepts.label: Keep secrets in a secret manager, not code or config files
Rotation without downtime: overlap old and new credentials
Short-lived credentials and audit reduce exposure

questions.modelAnswer: Secrets such as database passwords, API keys and signing keys belong in a dedicated secret manager, encrypted at rest, with access granted per service identity and every read audited, never in source code, images or plain config files. Rotation should be routine and automated. The usual pattern is to support two valid credentials at once: create the new secret, roll it out to all instances, confirm nothing still uses the old one, then revoke it, so rotation causes no downtime. Better still, use short-lived dynamic credentials issued on demand, so a leaked secret expires on its own.

questions.title: Encryption in transit versus at rest
questions.prompt: What is the difference between encryption in transit and encryption at rest?

expectedConcepts.label: In transit: protects data moving over networks (TLS)
At rest: protects stored data on disks and backups
Neither protects against a compromised application

questions.modelAnswer: Encryption in transit protects data while it moves between systems, for example between a browser and a server or between two services, usually with TLS. It stops anyone on the network path from reading or modifying the traffic. Encryption at rest protects data stored on disks, databases, backups and object storage, so a stolen disk or a misplaced backup cannot be read without the key. You need both, and key management matters as much as the algorithm. Neither protects you if the application itself is compromised or an authorised user misuses access, because the application sees decrypted data.

questions.title: Software supply-chain attacks
questions.prompt: A package your service depends on publishes a malicious release. How do supply-chain attacks like this work, and which practices would have limited the damage?

expectedConcepts.label: Attack via dependencies, build tools or distribution
Examples: malicious packages, typosquatting, compromised build
Defences: pin and verify, review updates, signed artefacts, SBOM

questions.modelAnswer: A supply-chain attack compromises your software through something you trust instead of attacking you directly: an open-source dependency, a package registry, a build tool, a CI pipeline or a vendor update. Examples include malicious packages with names close to popular ones, maintainers' accounts being hijacked to publish backdoored versions, and compromised build systems like the SolarWinds incident, where signed updates carried malware. Defences include pinning dependencies with lockfiles and checksums, reviewing and delaying updates, minimising dependencies, signing build artefacts and verifying provenance, keeping a software bill of materials, and locking down CI credentials.

questions.title: Lockfiles and safer builds
questions.prompt: How do dependency lockfiles help reproducible and safer builds?

expectedConcepts.label: Lockfile records exact versions of every dependency
Same install everywhere; integrity hashes
Updates become deliberate, reviewable changes

questions.modelAnswer: A manifest like package.json usually allows version ranges, so two installs on different days can pull different versions of transitive dependencies. A lockfile records the exact resolved version of every dependency, including transitive ones, often with an integrity hash. Committing it means every developer machine and CI build installs exactly the same code, so builds are reproducible and "works on my machine" problems shrink. It is also safer: a newly published malicious version cannot slip in silently, the checksum detects tampering, and updates arrive as explicit lockfile diffs you can review. Use the install mode that respects the lockfile in CI, such as npm ci.

questions.title: Race conditions in authorisation logic
questions.prompt: Two simultaneous requests manage to redeem the same gift card twice. What kind of race condition in authorisation logic is this, and how do you fix it?

expectedConcepts.label: Check and use happen separately (time-of-check to time-of-use)
Example: double spend or revoked permission still used
Fix with atomic operations, locks or constraints

questions.modelAnswer: It happens when the code checks whether an action is allowed and then performs it as a separate step, so concurrent requests can slip between the check and the use, known as time-of-check to time-of-use. For example, a gift card worth 100 is redeemed by two simultaneous requests: both check the balance, both see 100, both spend it. Or a coupon limited to one use per user is applied twice. Attackers trigger these deliberately with parallel requests. The fix is to make check and action atomic: a conditional update such as UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount, a database transaction with appropriate locking, or a unique constraint.

questions.title: Responding to a suspected data breach
questions.prompt: How would you respond to a suspected data breach?

expectedConcepts.label: Contain first: isolate systems and revoke credentials
Preserve evidence and investigate scope
Communicate: legal, regulators and affected users

questions.modelAnswer: Follow the incident response plan and assemble the right people: engineering, security, legal and communications. First contain the breach: isolate affected systems, revoke and rotate exposed credentials, block the attacker's access, without destroying evidence. Preserve logs and snapshots so you can work out what was accessed, when and how. Determine the scope: which data, how many users, whether it is ongoing. Eradicate the cause and recover systems from a known-good state. Then notify as required: many laws, such as GDPR's 72-hour rule and India's data protection law, impose deadlines for informing regulators and affected users. Finish with a blameless postmortem.

questions.title: What security headers mitigate
questions.prompt: A security scan reports that your site sends no Content-Security-Policy, HSTS or frame-protection headers. What does each header protect against, and what can headers not fix?

expectedConcepts.label: Headers tell the browser to enforce protections
CSP limits scripts (XSS); HSTS forces HTTPS
Frame options stop clickjacking; nosniff stops MIME confusion

questions.modelAnswer: Security headers are HTTP response headers that instruct the browser to enforce extra protections. Content-Security-Policy restricts where scripts, styles and other resources may load from, which limits the damage of cross-site scripting. Strict-Transport-Security tells the browser to always use HTTPS for the site, defeating downgrade attacks. X-Frame-Options or the CSP frame-ancestors directive prevents other sites from embedding yours in a frame, stopping clickjacking. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops MIME-type confusion, Referrer-Policy limits URL leakage, and Permissions-Policy disables features like the camera. They are defence in depth, not a substitute for fixing vulnerabilities.

questions.title: Audit logs versus application logs
questions.prompt: How do audit logs differ from ordinary application logs?

expectedConcepts.label: Audit logs record who did what, when, for accountability
Tamper-resistant, append-only, retained long term
App logs are for debugging, sampled and short-lived

questions.modelAnswer: Application logs exist to help engineers debug and operate the system: they are verbose, can be sampled or rotated after days, and their format changes freely. Audit logs exist for accountability and compliance: they record security-relevant actions, such as who logged in, who changed a permission, who exported customer data, with the actor, action, target, time and outcome. They must be complete, consistently structured, tamper-resistant, typically append-only or written to separate storage the actors cannot modify, and kept for a defined retention period. Access to audit logs is itself restricted and audited.

questions.title: What rate limiting can and cannot prevent
questions.prompt: What is rate limiting's role in abuse prevention, and what can it not prevent?

expectedConcepts.label: Caps requests per client to stop floods and brute force
Keys: IP, account, API key; returns 429
Cannot stop distributed attacks, logic flaws or low-and-slow abuse

questions.modelAnswer: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, keyed by IP, account or API key. It blunts brute-force login attempts, credential stuffing from a single source, scraping, and accidental floods from buggy clients, and protects capacity and costs, returning 429 when exceeded. But it cannot stop attacks spread across thousands of IPs and accounts, such as a botnet, which stay under per-key limits; it does not fix authorisation bugs, injection or business-logic abuse that needs only a few requests; and low-and-slow attacks evade it. Combine it with authentication, bot detection, anomaly detection and secure design.

questions.title: Minimising personal data in logs
questions.prompt: How should personally identifiable information be minimized in logs?

expectedConcepts.label: Log only what is needed; avoid raw personal data
Redact, mask or hash at the logging layer
Retention limits and access control for logs

questions.modelAnswer: Start from the principle of logging only what you need to operate and debug the system. Prefer stable internal identifiers, such as a user ID or request ID, over names, emails, phone numbers, addresses or full request bodies. Enforce this in the logging library rather than relying on every developer: structured logging with an allowlist of fields, automatic redaction or masking of known sensitive fields and patterns, and hashing where you need to correlate without storing the raw value. Never log passwords, tokens or payment details. Then limit who can read logs and how long they are kept, since logs are often copied to many systems.

questions.title: Reviewing a third-party OAuth integration
questions.prompt: How would you review a third-party OAuth integration for common risks?

expectedConcepts.label: Use authorization code flow with PKCE and validate state
Strict redirect URIs and token validation
Minimal scopes and secure token storage

questions.modelAnswer: I would check the flow first: use the authorization code flow with PKCE, never the deprecated implicit flow, and verify the state parameter on the callback to prevent CSRF login attacks. Redirect URIs must be registered exactly, with no wildcards, so codes cannot be sent to an attacker's site. Tokens must be validated properly: signature, issuer, audience and expiry for ID tokens. Request the minimal scopes the feature needs. Store access and refresh tokens server-side or in httpOnly cookies, encrypted, and support revocation when users disconnect. Finally, handle the provider being down, and do not trust unverified email claims for account linking.

questions.title: Bounded contexts
questions.prompt: In your company 'customer' means a lead to sales, an account to billing and a delivery address to shipping, and one shared Customer model keeps breaking. How do bounded contexts help?

expectedConcepts.label: A boundary inside which a model and its terms have one meaning
Same word, different models per context, e.g. customer
Guides team and service boundaries; integration between contexts

questions.modelAnswer: A bounded context, from domain-driven design, is a boundary inside which a particular domain model and its vocabulary have one consistent meaning. Large businesses use the same word differently: a "customer" in sales is a lead with a pipeline stage, in billing it is an account with invoices and tax details, in support it is someone with tickets. Forcing one shared model makes it bloated and full of conditionals. Instead each context owns its own model, and contexts integrate through explicit contracts and translations. Bounded contexts are a natural guide for module boundaries, team ownership and, when needed, service boundaries.

questions.title: Domain logic versus infrastructure concerns
questions.prompt: How do domain logic and infrastructure concerns differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Domain logic: business rules independent of technology
Infrastructure: databases, HTTP, queues, frameworks
Separating them eases testing and technology changes

questions.modelAnswer: Domain logic is the business knowledge of the system: rules like "an order cannot be shipped before payment" or "discounts cannot exceed 30 percent", the calculations and invariants that would exist even if the software were written in a different language. Infrastructure concerns are how the system talks to the outside world: SQL queries, HTTP handlers, message queues, file storage, frameworks and third-party SDKs. Mixing them, for example business rules inside controller code or SQL, makes the rules hard to find, test and change. Keeping domain logic in plain code that depends on small interfaces lets you unit-test rules without a database and swap infrastructure later.

questions.title: Costs of an event-driven architecture
questions.prompt: What are the costs of introducing an event-driven architecture?

expectedConcepts.label: Asynchrony brings eventual consistency
Harder debugging: implicit flows across many consumers
Operational load: brokers, schemas, retries, duplicates, ordering

questions.modelAnswer: Events decouple producers from consumers, but the costs are real. Data becomes eventually consistent: after a write, other services see the change later, so UIs and business rules must tolerate stale views. The flow of a business process is no longer visible in one place; it emerges from many consumers reacting to events, which makes it hard to understand, debug and change without distributed tracing and good documentation. You must handle at-least-once delivery, duplicates, out-of-order events, poison messages and replays, and version event schemas carefully because consumers depend on them. Finally you operate a broker. For simple request-response flows, synchronous calls are often better.

questions.title: When a plugin architecture fits
questions.prompt: When is a plugin architecture a good fit?

expectedConcepts.label: Core defines extension points; plugins add behaviour
Fits when third parties or teams extend independently
Costs: stable API commitments, isolation and security

questions.modelAnswer: A plugin architecture has a small core that defines extension points, interfaces that plugins implement to add behaviour, and a mechanism to discover and load them. It fits when you expect many optional or customer-specific features, when third parties should extend the product without changing the core, as with IDEs, browsers, build tools and CMSs, or when features evolve at different speeds. The costs are significant: the plugin API becomes a public contract you must keep compatible for years, plugins can crash or slow the host, so you need isolation and versioning, and untrusted plugins raise security concerns. For a handful of internal variations, plain modules are simpler.

questions.title: Synchronous calls, events and coupling
questions.prompt: How do synchronous calls and asynchronous events affect service coupling?

expectedConcepts.label: Synchronous calls create runtime coupling: caller needs callee up
Events decouple in time; producer does not know consumers
Events still couple through schemas; harder to follow flow

questions.modelAnswer: A synchronous call, such as HTTP or gRPC, couples services at runtime: the caller blocks until the callee answers, so the callee's latency and availability become the caller's, and outages cascade along call chains. The caller also knows exactly whom it calls. Asynchronous events decouple in time and knowledge: the producer publishes "order placed" and moves on, and consumers process it later, even if they were down. But coupling does not disappear: every consumer depends on the event schema and semantics, so changing it needs care, and the overall flow becomes harder to see. Use calls when you need an immediate answer, events for reactions that can happen later.

questions.title: Anti-corruption layer
questions.prompt: Your new service must integrate with a legacy ERP whose data model is awkward and inconsistent. How would an anti-corruption layer keep that model out of your code, and when is it worth building?

expectedConcepts.label: A translation layer between your model and an external or legacy model
Converts concepts so foreign terms do not leak in
Useful for legacy migrations and third-party APIs; extra code to maintain

questions.modelAnswer: An anti-corruption layer is a translation boundary between your system's domain model and another model you do not control, such as a legacy system or a third-party API. Without it, the other system's awkward names, data shapes and assumptions leak into your code, and your model slowly "corrupts" to match theirs. The layer, often a set of adapters and translators, converts their concepts into yours and back, so the rest of your code only sees clean domain objects. You need one when integrating with a legacy system during a migration, when a vendor's API changes often, or when two bounded contexts model the same thing very differently.

questions.title: Splitting a legacy application without a rewrite
questions.prompt: How would you split a legacy application without a risky rewrite?

expectedConcepts.label: Incremental strangler approach rather than big-bang rewrite
Route one capability at a time to new code behind a facade
Add tests and seams first; measure and retire old code

questions.modelAnswer: Big-bang rewrites usually take longer than planned and lose behaviour nobody documented, so I would use the strangler-fig approach. First put a facade, often a proxy or routing layer, in front of the legacy system so traffic can be redirected without clients noticing. Add characterisation tests around the behaviour you will move, and introduce seams inside the codebase. Then pick one well-bounded capability, build it in the new code, route its traffic there, ideally gradually with comparison against the old path, and delete the old implementation. Repeat capability by capability, tracking how much traffic and code remains in the legacy system until it can be switched off.

questions.title: Evolvable systems
questions.prompt: Every feature request in your codebase now needs changes across many modules and a coordinated release. What makes a system evolvable, and which properties would you work towards?

expectedConcepts.label: Can change safely and cheaply as requirements change
Enablers: modularity, tests, clear interfaces, automation
Avoid over-engineering for imagined futures

questions.modelAnswer: An evolvable system is one you can keep changing safely and at reasonable cost as requirements, scale and technology change, without each change requiring a rewrite. The enablers are well-defined module boundaries with small interfaces, so changes stay local; good automated tests that catch regressions; fast build and deployment pipelines; observability, so you see the effect of changes; and decisions that are reversible, such as feature flags and backward-compatible APIs. Evolvability is not about predicting every future need and building for it; speculative abstractions often make change harder. Keep things simple and easy to modify.

questions.title: Architectural decision records
questions.prompt: How do architectural decision records improve engineering work?

expectedConcepts.label: Short documents recording a decision, context and consequences
Stored with the code, numbered, immutable once accepted
Preserve the why for future engineers; avoid relitigating

questions.modelAnswer: An architectural decision record is a short document that captures one significant decision: the context and constraints at the time, the options considered, the decision made and its consequences. ADRs are usually stored in the repository next to the code, numbered and given a status such as proposed, accepted or superseded, and are not rewritten later; a new ADR supersedes an old one. Their value is preserving the "why". Months later, new engineers can understand why the system uses a queue or a particular database instead of guessing, teams stop relitigating settled questions, and when the context changes, everyone can see which assumptions no longer hold.

questions.title: Library boundary versus service boundary
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a library and a service boundary?

expectedConcepts.label: Library: in-process call, deployed with the caller
Service: network call, deployed and scaled independently
Services add latency, failures and versioning cost

questions.modelAnswer: A library boundary is crossed by an in-process function call: the code is compiled or loaded into the caller, shares its memory, deploys with it and fails with it, and calls are fast and reliable. A service boundary is crossed over the network: the service runs as a separate process, owns its data, and is deployed, scaled and versioned independently, possibly by another team. That independence costs network latency, partial failures, retries and timeouts, serialisation, API versioning and more operational work. A good rule is to start with a library or module and only make it a service when you need independent deployment, scaling, ownership or isolation.

questions.title: Deciding what belongs in a shared platform
questions.prompt: How would you decide whether a capability belongs in a shared platform?

expectedConcepts.label: Many teams need it in the same way
Stable, well-understood problem with clear interface
Platform costs: ownership, roadmap coupling, one size fits none

questions.modelAnswer: A capability belongs in a shared platform when several teams need it in roughly the same way, they are currently duplicating effort or making inconsistent choices, and the problem is well understood and stable enough to offer through a clear, self-service interface: examples are authentication, deployment pipelines, logging and feature flags. It should not go into the platform when only one team needs it, when requirements are still changing quickly, or when each team needs something genuinely different. A platform also needs an owning team, documentation, support and a roadmap, and it can become a bottleneck, so the saving must outweigh that cost.

questions.title: A shared database across services
questions.prompt: What are the trade-offs of a shared database across services?

expectedConcepts.label: Easy joins and transactions across data
Tight coupling through schema; services cannot change independently
Contention and blast radius; prefer data ownership with APIs

questions.modelAnswer: Letting several services read and write the same database is attractive at first: joins across domains are easy, transactions keep everything consistent, and there is no data duplication. The cost is coupling through the schema: any service may depend on any table, so renaming a column or changing a table can break services owned by other teams, and nobody clearly owns the data or its invariants. Load from one service can slow all of them, and migrations need cross-team coordination. The usual alternative is that each service owns its data and others access it via APIs or events, accepting eventual consistency, often starting with separate schemas in one database.

questions.title: Preventing circular dependencies between modules
questions.prompt: How can you prevent circular dependencies between modules?

expectedConcepts.label: Cycle: A depends on B and B on A
Break with interfaces, dependency inversion or extracting shared code
Enforce layering with tooling in CI

questions.modelAnswer: A circular dependency means module A depends on B, and B depends back on A, directly or through others. It makes modules impossible to understand, test or reuse separately, and some languages, like Go, forbid it at compile time. To break a cycle, extract the shared piece both need into a third, lower-level module; or apply dependency inversion, where the lower-level module defines an interface and the higher-level one implements it, so the dependency points one way; or use events or callbacks instead of direct calls. Prevent cycles by defining a layering rule, for example domain must not import infrastructure, and enforcing it automatically in CI.

questions.title: Graceful degradation when a dependency is down
questions.prompt: How would you design graceful degradation when a dependency is unavailable?

expectedConcepts.label: Keep core functionality working with reduced features
Timeouts, circuit breakers, cached or default responses
Decide per dependency what is critical and tell users

questions.modelAnswer: Start by classifying each dependency as critical or optional for each feature. For optional ones, design a fallback: if the recommendation service is down, show popular items; if the reviews service times out, render the product page without reviews; if personalisation fails, show defaults; serve slightly stale cached data rather than nothing. Protect the core with short timeouts, so a slow dependency cannot hold threads, and circuit breakers that stop calling a failing service and use the fallback immediately. Queue non-urgent work for later. Make degraded states visible in metrics and, where relevant, to users, and test them in chaos experiments.

questions.title: Architecture for fast local feedback
questions.prompt: How can architecture support local development and fast feedback?

expectedConcepts.label: Run and test most code locally without the whole system
Interfaces and fakes for external services; modular code
Fast builds and dev environments, few services to start

questions.modelAnswer: Fast feedback means a developer can change code and see the result in seconds, not after deploying to a shared environment. Architecture helps when business logic sits behind interfaces, so tests can use in-memory fakes instead of real databases, queues and third-party services; when the system is modular, so you can build and test one module alone; and when the number of services needed to run a feature locally is small, ideally one process plus a database started from a single command or dev container. Reproducible local configuration, seed data, and contract tests for external APIs keep local results trustworthy. Many microservices with no local story slow teams down badly.

questions.title: What belongs in each kind of test
questions.prompt: What belongs in unit, integration, contract, and end-to-end tests?

expectedConcepts.label: Unit tests check one unit of logic in isolation
Integration tests check real components together
Contract tests check service agreements; end-to-end tests check user journeys
Higher-level tests add confidence but are slow and brittle

questions.modelAnswer: Unit tests check a small piece of logic, such as a function or class, in isolation; they run in milliseconds and should cover most business rules and edge cases. Integration tests check that your code works with real components such as the database, a message broker or the file system, catching wrong SQL or serialisation. Contract tests check that two services agree on an API, for example that a provider still returns what its consumers expect, without starting both. End-to-end tests drive the whole system like a user, covering a few critical journeys such as sign-up and checkout; they are slow and brittle, so keep them few.

questions.title: Deciding which behaviour deserves a test
questions.prompt: How do you decide which behavior deserves a test?

expectedConcepts.label: Test behaviour that matters to users and is risky
Edge cases, past bugs and complex logic
Skip trivial code; test behaviour, not implementation

questions.modelAnswer: I prioritise by risk and value. Behaviour that users or the business depend on, such as payments, permissions and data integrity, gets tests first, as does complex logic with branches and calculations, edge cases like empty inputs and boundaries, and every bug that reached production, as a regression test. Trivial code such as simple getters, generated code or thin wiring rarely needs its own test. Tests should assert observable behaviour through public interfaces rather than internal implementation details, so refactoring does not break them. A useful question is: if this broke, how bad would it be and how quickly would we notice?

questions.title: Diagnosing flaky tests
questions.prompt: What makes a test flaky, and how would you diagnose it?

expectedConcepts.label: Flaky: passes and fails without code changes
Causes: timing, order dependence, shared state, external services
Diagnose by rerunning, randomising order, logging; quarantine and fix

questions.modelAnswer: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Common causes are timing assumptions, such as fixed sleeps instead of waiting for a condition; dependence on test order or shared state left by another test; real clocks, time zones and randomness; concurrency races; and calls to real networks or services. To diagnose, rerun it many times, ideally in isolation and in random order, capture logs and seeds on failure, and compare CI and local environments. Fix the root cause by waiting on explicit conditions, isolating state, injecting clocks and seeds, and faking external dependencies. Quarantine it briefly, but do not leave it ignored.

questions.title: Property-based testing
questions.prompt: How can property-based testing find bugs example-based tests miss?

expectedConcepts.label: State properties that hold for all inputs
Framework generates many random inputs and shrinks failures
Finds edge cases humans do not think of; properties can be hard to write

questions.modelAnswer: In example-based tests you pick specific inputs and expected outputs, so you only test cases you thought of. In property-based testing you state a property that should hold for all inputs, for example that sorting returns a list of the same length in non-decreasing order, or that decoding an encoded value gives back the original, and a framework such as QuickCheck or Hypothesis generates hundreds of random inputs. When one fails, it shrinks the input to a minimal counterexample. This finds edge cases people rarely write by hand: empty collections, huge numbers, Unicode, duplicates. The hard part is choosing meaningful properties.

questions.title: Mutation testing
questions.prompt: Your test suite has 95 percent line coverage, yet bugs keep slipping through. How could mutation testing show whether the tests actually check behaviour?

expectedConcepts.label: Tool introduces small code changes (mutants)
Tests should fail; surviving mutants reveal weak tests
Better signal than coverage but slow

questions.modelAnswer: Mutation testing deliberately introduces small bugs, called mutants, into your code: flipping a comparison from < to <=, removing a line, changing a constant. It then runs the test suite against each mutant. If a test fails, the mutant is "killed"; if all tests still pass, it "survived", which means the tests execute that code without actually checking its behaviour. The mutation score, the percentage killed, is a much better measure of test quality than line coverage, since coverage only shows code was run. The downsides are long run times and some equivalent mutants that cannot be killed, so it is often run on critical modules only.

questions.title: Mocks, fakes and stubs
questions.prompt: How do mocks differ from fakes and stubs?

expectedConcepts.label: Stub returns canned answers
Fake is a working lightweight implementation
Mock verifies interactions were made as expected
Interaction tests couple to implementation details

questions.modelAnswer: All three are test doubles that replace a real dependency. A stub just returns canned answers, for example a payment gateway stub that always says "approved", so the code under test can proceed. A fake is a working but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository instead of a real database; it has real behaviour and is reusable across many tests. A mock is programmed with expectations and verifies interactions: that the email service was called exactly once with this address. Stubs and fakes support state-based testing, checking outcomes, while mocks support interaction-based testing, which couples tests more tightly to implementation.

questions.title: When mocking misleads
questions.prompt: When can excessive mocking make a test suite misleading?

expectedConcepts.label: Mocks encode assumptions that may be wrong
Tests pass while the integration is broken
Tests tied to implementation break on refactors; prefer fakes and integration tests

questions.modelAnswer: Every mock encodes your assumption of how the real dependency behaves. If that assumption is wrong, for example the real database returns rows in a different order, the API returns an error format you never mocked, or a library throws instead of returning null, the tests stay green while production fails. Heavy mocking also couples tests to implementation: they verify which methods were called rather than outcomes, so harmless refactors break dozens of tests and real bugs slip through. Mock only at boundaries you own, such as an interface around a third-party client, prefer fakes and real in-memory components, and keep integration tests against real dependencies.

questions.title: Contract testing between services
questions.prompt: A provider team renamed a field in their API and broke your service in production, although both teams' test suites passed. How would contract testing have caught it?

expectedConcepts.label: Verify provider and consumer agree on the API
Consumer-driven contracts (Pact) recorded and verified in CI
Faster than end-to-end, catches breaking changes before deploy

questions.modelAnswer: When services deploy independently, a provider can change its API and break consumers that are not tested together. Contract testing checks the agreement between them without running the whole system. In consumer-driven contract testing, using tools like Pact, each consumer writes tests describing the requests it makes and the responses it relies on; these generate a contract file, which is published to a broker. The provider's CI then replays those expectations against the real provider and fails if any contract is broken. It catches breaking changes before deployment, runs much faster than end-to-end tests, and tells you which consumer would break.

questions.title: Testing retry logic without waiting
questions.prompt: How would you test retry logic without waiting for real timeouts?

expectedConcepts.label: Inject a fake clock or sleeper
Use a fake dependency that fails N times then succeeds
Assert attempts, backoff schedule and give-up behaviour

questions.modelAnswer: Make time and the dependency controllable. Instead of calling the real sleep or clock, the retry code takes an injected clock or sleeper, and in tests a fake records requested delays and returns immediately or advances virtual time. The dependency is replaced by a fake that fails a chosen number of times, with timeouts or retryable errors, then succeeds. Then assert the observable behaviour: how many attempts were made, that delays follow the expected exponential backoff with jitter bounds, that non-retryable errors are not retried, and that the code gives up and reports the error after the maximum attempts or deadline. Such tests run in milliseconds and are deterministic.

questions.title: Golden and snapshot tests
questions.prompt: Your snapshot tests fail on almost every change, and developers now update them without reading the diff. When are golden tests useful, and when do snapshots become risky?

expectedConcepts.label: Golden test compares output to a stored approved file
Good for large structured outputs like rendered HTML or compiler output
Risk: blind updates, noisy diffs, brittle details

questions.modelAnswer: A golden or snapshot test runs the code, captures its output, such as rendered HTML, a generated report, JSON or compiler output, and compares it with a previously approved file; any difference fails the test. It is efficient for large, structured outputs that would be tedious to assert piece by piece, and diffs show exactly what changed. The risks: when snapshots are large, people update them without reading the diff, so bugs get approved; snapshots that include timestamps, IDs or ordering are flaky; and snapshots capture incidental details, so harmless changes break many tests. Keep snapshots small, deterministic and reviewed.

questions.title: Testing time zones and daylight saving
questions.prompt: How should tests cover time zones and daylight-saving transitions?

expectedConcepts.label: Inject the clock and time zone rather than using system time
Test DST gaps and overlaps and day boundaries
Store UTC, convert at the edges, cover several zones

questions.modelAnswer: Never let tests depend on the machine's real clock or time zone: inject a fixed clock and an explicit time zone so tests are deterministic on any CI runner. Then deliberately cover the tricky cases: the spring-forward gap, where a local time like 2:30 does not exist; the fall-back overlap, where an hour happens twice; scheduling across midnight and month or year ends; leap years and February 29; and zones with unusual offsets, such as India's +05:30. Run the suite under a couple of different time zones. In the code itself, store and compute in UTC and convert to local time only at the edges.

questions.title: Testing nondeterministic concurrency bugs
questions.prompt: How do you test concurrency bugs that occur nondeterministically?

expectedConcepts.label: Race detectors and sanitizers find data races
Stress tests with many iterations and injected delays
Deterministic simulation or model checking for hard cases

questions.modelAnswer: Concurrency bugs depend on thread interleavings, so a single run rarely shows them. First use tools that detect races regardless of timing: ThreadSanitizer, Go's race detector, Java's jcstress for memory-model issues. Then run stress tests: the same scenario thousands of times with many goroutines or threads, on many cores, sometimes with injected random delays or yields to shake out different interleavings. For critical logic, deterministic testing tools control scheduling and explore interleavings systematically, such as Rust's loom, or deterministic simulation like FoundationDB uses. Also design to reduce the problem: immutable data, message passing and simpler locking.

questions.title: Meaningful coverage targets
questions.prompt: How should a team choose meaningful coverage targets?

expectedConcepts.label: Coverage shows what ran, not what was verified
Use coverage to find untested risky areas
Hard high targets encourage useless tests

questions.modelAnswer: Code coverage only tells you which lines or branches ran during tests, not whether anything was checked, so a test with no assertions can reach 100 percent. A rigid target like 90 percent across the codebase encourages tests that touch code without verifying behaviour and wastes effort on trivial code. More useful practices are to look at coverage reports to find critical code with no tests, to require coverage on changed lines in pull requests, to set higher expectations for core business logic than for glue code, and to complement coverage with mutation testing or reviewing assertions. Treat coverage as a flashlight for finding gaps, not a score.

questions.title: Regression tests for production incidents
questions.prompt: What makes a good regression test for a production incident?

expectedConcepts.label: Reproduces the exact failure first (fails before the fix)
Tests the root cause at the right level
Fast, deterministic and clearly named for future readers

questions.modelAnswer: A good regression test reproduces the actual failure: you write it before the fix and confirm it fails for the same reason the incident did, then passes after the fix. It targets the root cause at the lowest level that can show it, often a unit or integration test rather than an end-to-end test, so it stays fast and reliable. It is deterministic, without depending on timing or real external services, and clearly named or commented with the incident reference, so future engineers understand why it exists. Where the incident revealed a class of bugs, add tests for the neighbouring cases too.

questions.title: Testing a migration on a large database
questions.prompt: How would you test a migration against a large database safely?

expectedConcepts.label: Rehearse on a production-sized copy or snapshot
Measure duration, locks and replication lag
Verify data and rollback plan; anonymise data

questions.modelAnswer: Never test only on a tiny development database, because a migration that takes milliseconds there may lock a billion-row table for an hour in production. Restore a recent production snapshot, anonymised if it contains personal data, into an isolated environment with similar hardware, and run the migration there. Measure how long it takes, what locks it holds, how much write-ahead log and replication lag it creates, and whether queries still use their indexes. Verify the result with row counts and spot checks, test the application against the new schema, and rehearse the rollback. Then run it in production during low traffic with monitoring.

questions.title: Fuzz testing
questions.prompt: You maintain a parser for a file format that users upload. How would fuzz testing find crashes that your unit tests miss?

expectedConcepts.label: Feeds large volumes of random or mutated input
Coverage-guided fuzzers evolve inputs that reach new code
Best for parsers and untrusted input; pair with sanitizers

questions.modelAnswer: Fuzz testing automatically feeds a program huge numbers of random, malformed or mutated inputs and watches for crashes, hangs, assertion failures or memory errors. Modern coverage-guided fuzzers, such as libFuzzer, AFL and Go's built-in fuzzing, keep a corpus of inputs and mutate those that reach new code paths, so they explore deep logic surprisingly well. Fuzzing is especially valuable for code that parses untrusted input: file formats, network protocols, decoders, compilers and serialisers, where security bugs hide. Combined with sanitizers like AddressSanitizer, it finds memory-safety bugs that normal tests rarely trigger. Saved crashing inputs become regression tests.

questions.title: Smoke tests versus canary analysis
questions.prompt: How do smoke tests differ from canary analysis?

expectedConcepts.label: Smoke tests: quick scripted checks that basics work
Canary analysis compares real traffic metrics of new versus old
Smoke catches obvious breakage; canary catches subtle regressions

questions.modelAnswer: Smoke tests are a small set of fast, scripted checks run right after a deployment: can the service start, does the health endpoint respond, can a user log in and load the main page. They catch obvious breakage quickly but only cover the paths you scripted. Canary analysis sends a small share of real production traffic to the new version and statistically compares its metrics, such as error rate, latency and business KPIs, with the old version serving the rest. It catches subtle regressions that only appear with real users and data, at the cost of needing good metrics and time. Most pipelines use both.

questions.title: Test data without production personal data
questions.prompt: How should test data be created without exposing production personal data?

expectedConcepts.label: Do not copy raw production personal data into test environments
Use synthetic data, factories and anonymisation
Anonymisation must resist re-identification; keep realistic distributions

questions.modelAnswer: Raw production data in test or developer environments is a privacy and compliance risk, because those environments are less protected and more people can see them. Prefer synthetic data: factories and builders in tests that create exactly the records each test needs, and generators that produce realistic volumes and distributions for performance testing. When production-like data is genuinely needed, for example to test a migration, use an anonymisation pipeline that masks or replaces names, emails, phone numbers and addresses, preserves formats and relationships, and is reviewed for re-identification risk, since combinations of fields can identify people. Restrict access and delete it when done.

questions.title: Verification versus validation
questions.prompt: What is the difference between verification and validation?

expectedConcepts.label: Verification: are we building the product right (meets spec)
Validation: are we building the right product (meets user needs)
Verification via tests and reviews; validation via users and feedback
Passing verification does not prove value; validate early

questions.modelAnswer: Verification asks "are we building the product right?" It checks that the software meets its specification and requirements, through code reviews, static analysis, unit and integration tests and inspections. Validation asks "are we building the right product?" It checks that the software actually solves the user's problem and fits its intended use, through user testing, acceptance testing, beta programmes, prototypes and analytics. A system can pass every verification check and still fail validation if the specification itself was wrong, which is why teams validate early with real users before investing heavily in verification.

questions.title: CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work
questions.prompt: How do you distinguish CPU-bound work from I/O-bound work?

expectedConcepts.label: CPU-bound: limited by computation; I/O-bound: by waiting
Diagnose with CPU utilisation and profiles
Different fixes: algorithms and parallelism versus concurrency and caching

questions.modelAnswer: CPU-bound work spends its time computing: compressing data, image processing, parsing, encryption. A CPU-bound process runs near 100 percent of a core, and it gets faster with better algorithms, optimisation or more cores. I/O-bound work spends its time waiting for disks, databases or networks; CPU usage stays low while latency is high. Profiles help: a CPU profile shows hot functions, while off-CPU or wall-clock profiles and traces show time spent waiting. The fixes differ: for I/O-bound work use concurrency, async I/O, batching, caching and fewer round trips; adding threads to CPU-bound work beyond the core count does not help.

questions.title: Amdahl's law
questions.prompt: You moved a batch job from 16 to 64 cores and it got only slightly faster. How does Amdahl's law explain this, and what should you fix first?

expectedConcepts.label: Speed-up limited by the serial fraction
Speedup = 1 / (s + p/n): 10% serial caps at 10x
Optimise the serial part; coordination overhead also matters

questions.modelAnswer: Amdahl's law says the speed-up from parallelising a task is limited by the part that must stay serial. If a fraction s of the work is serial and the rest is spread over n processors, the speed-up is 1 / (s + (1 - s) / n). So if 10 percent of a job is serial, even infinite cores give at most a 10 times speed-up, and going from 16 to 64 cores adds little. The lessons are to measure and reduce the serial part, such as a single lock, a coordinator or sequential I/O, before adding cores, and to remember that real parallel code also pays for coordination and contention, so actual gains are often lower.

questions.title: Batching: throughput versus latency
questions.prompt: How can batching improve throughput while harming latency?

expectedConcepts.label: Batching amortises fixed per-operation costs
Items wait for the batch to fill or a timer
Tune batch size and max wait for the latency budget

questions.modelAnswer: Many operations have a fixed cost per call: a network round trip, a disk flush, a system call, a database transaction. Batching groups many items into one operation, so the fixed cost is paid once for the whole batch, which can raise throughput dramatically, for example inserting 1,000 rows in one statement or sending many messages in one Kafka request. The price is latency: the first item in a batch waits until the batch is full or a timer fires before anything happens. Systems therefore cap both batch size and maximum wait time, such as Kafka's linger setting, tuned so throughput improves without breaking the latency budget.

questions.title: Reading a flame graph
questions.prompt: A teammate shares a CPU flame graph of a slow service. How do you read it to find where the time goes, and what are the common misreadings?

expectedConcepts.label: Visualises sampled stack traces
Width is time spent; y-axis is stack depth; colour is arbitrary
Look for wide frames, not the tallest; check sampling type

questions.modelAnswer: A flame graph visualises many sampled stack traces from a profiler. Each box is a function; boxes stacked on top of one another show the call stack, with callers below and callees above. The width of a box is the share of samples in which that function was on the stack, so wide boxes are where time goes; the left-to-right order is usually alphabetical, not chronological, and colour is mostly decoration. To read it, look for wide plateaus near the top, functions that themselves consume a lot of time, and wide frames you did not expect. Also check whether it is a CPU profile or an off-CPU profile, since waiting time only appears in the latter.

questions.title: p50, p95 and p99 latency
questions.prompt: How do p50, p95, and p99 latency tell different stories?

expectedConcepts.label: Percentiles: p50 is the median, p99 is the slowest 1%
Averages hide the tail; p99 shows outliers many users hit
Different causes: GC, queuing, cold caches; cannot average percentiles

questions.modelAnswer: p50, the median, is the latency half of requests beat: the typical experience. p95 and p99 show the tail: 5 percent and 1 percent of requests are slower than those values. The tail matters because heavy users and pages that make many requests hit it often, and at scale 1 percent is a lot of people. A stable p50 with a rising p99 points to intermittent causes such as garbage collection pauses, lock contention, queueing during bursts, cold caches or one slow dependency, while a rising p50 suggests everything got slower. Averages hide all this, and percentiles cannot be averaged across servers; aggregate histograms instead.

questions.title: Allocation rate, GC and latency
questions.prompt: How do memory allocation rate and garbage collection affect latency?

expectedConcepts.label: Higher allocation rate triggers more frequent GC
GC costs CPU and may pause or slow threads
Reduce allocations: reuse, pooling, avoid boxing; tune heap

questions.modelAnswer: In garbage-collected languages, every allocation adds to the heap, and the collector must eventually find and reclaim unreachable objects. The more you allocate per request, the more often collections run. Collections consume CPU that would otherwise serve requests, and depending on the collector they introduce stop-the-world pauses or slow application threads with write barriers and assist work, which shows up as spikes in tail latency. To reduce the impact, measure allocations with a profiler, cut needless ones by reusing buffers, preallocating collections, avoiding boxing and temporary strings in hot paths, and tune the heap size or collector settings to trade memory for less frequent collection.

questions.title: Benchmarking without fooling yourself
questions.prompt: How would you benchmark a service without misleading yourself?

expectedConcepts.label: Production-like environment, data and workload
Warm up, run long enough, repeat and report distributions
Avoid coordinated omission and noisy neighbours; change one thing

questions.modelAnswer: Benchmark in an environment that resembles production: similar hardware, configuration, data volume and realistic request mix, because a tiny dataset fits in cache and lies. Warm up first so JIT compilation, caches and connection pools settle. Run long enough and repeat several times, reporting latency percentiles and variance rather than one average. Use an open-model load generator that sends requests at a fixed rate, avoiding coordinated omission, and make sure the load generator itself is not the bottleneck. Change one variable at a time against a fixed baseline, watch for noisy neighbours on shared machines, and confirm results with profiles that explain why something got faster.

questions.title: Warm-up effects in measurements
questions.prompt: The first run of your benchmark is three times slower than the next ten. What warm-up effects explain this, and how do you measure fairly?

expectedConcepts.label: Early runs are slower than steady state
Causes: JIT compilation, cold caches, lazy initialisation, connection setup
Discard warm-up or measure cold start separately

questions.modelAnswer: The first requests or iterations of a program are often much slower than later ones. The JIT compiler has not yet optimised hot code, CPU caches, the page cache and application caches are empty, objects and connection pools are initialised lazily, and TLS or database connections must be established. If you include this period in a benchmark, results look worse and vary a lot; if you measure only a few iterations, you mostly measure warm-up. Good benchmarks run warm-up iterations first and discard them, as JMH and Go's benchmark tooling encourage. Cold-start performance matters too, for serverless and autoscaling, so measure it separately.

questions.title: Lock contention and throughput
questions.prompt: How can lock contention limit throughput?

expectedConcepts.label: Threads wait for a lock instead of doing work
Critical section becomes the serial bottleneck; cache lines bounce
Fixes: shorter critical sections, sharding, lock-free or per-thread data

questions.modelAnswer: When many threads need the same lock, only one can hold it, so the code inside the critical section runs serially no matter how many cores you have. Throughput stops scaling and can even drop as threads are added, because waiting threads spin or sleep, cause context switches, and the lock's cache line bounces between cores. Profilers show this as time blocked on mutexes and low CPU use despite high load. Fixes include doing less work while holding the lock, such as no I/O; splitting one lock into many by sharding the data; using read-write locks for read-heavy data; and atomic operations, copy-on-write or per-thread state merged later.

questions.title: Throughput, latency and capacity
questions.prompt: What is the difference between throughput, latency, and capacity?

expectedConcepts.label: Latency: time for one request; throughput: requests per second
Capacity: maximum sustainable throughput within latency goals
Latency rises sharply near capacity due to queueing
Run with headroom below capacity to protect latency

questions.modelAnswer: Latency is how long one operation takes from the requester's point of view, for example 80 milliseconds per request. Throughput is how many operations the system completes per unit of time, such as 2,000 requests per second. Capacity is the maximum throughput the system can sustain while still meeting its latency and error targets. They are linked by queueing: as load approaches capacity, utilisation nears 100 percent, queues build, and latency rises sharply rather than linearly. That is why services are run with headroom, often at 50 to 70 percent of measured capacity, and why capacity is defined with a latency target.

questions.title: Setting a performance budget for an API
questions.prompt: How would you set a performance budget for an API?

expectedConcepts.label: Start from user-facing goals and SLOs
Split the budget across dependencies and steps
Enforce with load tests and alerts in CI and production

questions.modelAnswer: Start from what users need: for example, the checkout page must render in under one second at p95, which gives the checkout API perhaps 300 milliseconds at p99. Then divide that budget across the work the request does: network and TLS, authentication, database queries, calls to other services, serialisation, leaving headroom for variance. Each dependency gets its own latency target and timeout derived from the budget, and fan-out calls are made in parallel. Also budget resources such as payload size and queries per request. Enforce the budget with load tests in CI that fail on regressions, dashboards and SLO alerts in production.

questions.title: Why a bigger thread pool can be slower
questions.prompt: Why can increasing a thread pool make a service slower?

expectedConcepts.label: More threads than cores or downstream capacity adds contention
Context switching, memory and lock contention increase
Overloads the database or dependency; size from measurements

questions.modelAnswer: More threads only help if they have something useful to do. For CPU-bound work, threads beyond the number of cores just take turns, adding context switches, cache misses and memory for stacks. For I/O-bound work, more threads send more concurrent requests to the database or downstream service, which may itself be saturated, so everything queues there, latency rises and timeouts start. Bigger pools also increase lock contention inside the process. Size thread pools from measurements, using Little's law and the limits of downstream resources, such as the database connection pool, and prefer bounded queues with backpressure.

questions.title: Coordinated omission
questions.prompt: Your load test reports a p99 of 50 milliseconds, but users see multi-second stalls. How can coordinated omission make the load tool hide them?

expectedConcepts.label: Load generator waits for slow responses and sends fewer requests
Missed requests during stalls are never measured, hiding the tail
Use open-model, constant-rate generators or correct for it

questions.modelAnswer: Many load generators send a request, wait for the response, then send the next one. If the server stalls for two seconds, the tool simply stops sending during the stall, so it records one slow request instead of the hundreds that real users, who keep arriving at their own rate, would have experienced. The slow periods are under-sampled, so reported p99 and p99.9 latencies look far better than reality. This is coordinated omission, a term popularised by Gil Tene. Avoid it with open-model generators that send at a constant rate regardless of responses, such as wrk2, or tools that correct for it, and record latency in HDR histograms.

questions.title: Load, stress, spike and soak tests
questions.prompt: How do load, stress, spike, and soak tests differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Load test: expected traffic levels
Stress test: beyond capacity to find the breaking point
Spike: sudden surges; soak: sustained load for hours
Results hold only for the traffic you simulated

questions.modelAnswer: A load test runs the system at its expected traffic, including normal peaks, to confirm it meets latency and error targets. A stress test pushes beyond expected capacity to find the breaking point and see how the system fails: does it degrade gracefully and recover, or collapse? A spike test applies a sudden surge, such as a ticket sale opening or a push notification, to check autoscaling, queues and rate limits react fast enough. A soak or endurance test holds a realistic load for many hours or days to expose slow problems like memory leaks, connection exhaustion, log growth and gradual degradation. Every test is only as good as its realism: production-like data and traffic shapes are hard to reproduce, and long soak runs tie up environments, so results hold only for what you simulated.

questions.title: Finding a memory leak in a long-running process
questions.prompt: How would you find a memory leak in a long-running process?

expectedConcepts.label: Confirm growth trend under steady load
Compare heap snapshots or profiles over time
Common culprits: caches, listeners, goroutines or threads, unclosed resources

questions.modelAnswer: First confirm it is a leak: memory keeps growing under steady load and never levels off after garbage collection, rather than a cache warming up or the runtime holding freed memory. Then take heap snapshots or heap profiles at intervals and compare them: the object types or allocation sites whose retained size keeps growing point to the culprit, and retention paths show what is holding them alive. Typical causes are unbounded caches or maps, event listeners and callbacks never removed, blocked threads or goroutines, unclosed connections and file handles, and global registries. In native code, use tools such as AddressSanitizer's leak checker, Valgrind or heaptrack.

questions.title: Evidence for a performance optimisation
questions.prompt: What evidence should justify a performance optimization?

expectedConcepts.label: A measured problem that matters to users or cost
Profile showing where time goes; benchmark before and after
Gain must outweigh complexity and maintenance

questions.modelAnswer: An optimisation should start from a real problem: a missed latency target, user complaints, a cost that matters, or a capacity limit, not a hunch that something "looks slow". Then a profile or trace should show that the code you want to change actually accounts for a meaningful share of the time or resources, since optimising something that takes 2 percent cannot give more than 2 percent. You need a reproducible benchmark or load test with a baseline, and results after the change showing a significant improvement beyond noise, ideally confirmed in production metrics. Finally, the gain must justify any added complexity and maintenance cost.

questions.title: ETL versus ELT
questions.prompt: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?

expectedConcepts.label: ETL transforms before loading into the warehouse
ELT loads raw data then transforms inside the warehouse
ELT uses cheap scalable warehouse compute but stores raw data

questions.modelAnswer: Both move data from source systems into an analytics store. In ETL, extract-transform-load, data is cleaned, joined and reshaped in a separate processing step before it is loaded, so the warehouse only receives finished tables. In ELT, extract-load-transform, raw data is loaded first and transformations run inside the warehouse itself, often as SQL models managed with tools like dbt. ELT became popular because cloud warehouses provide cheap, elastic compute, and keeping raw data lets you re-run or change transformations later. ETL still fits when data must be filtered or masked before it lands, or the target cannot do heavy transformations.

questions.title: Data lineage during incidents
questions.prompt: A finance dashboard shows wrong revenue this morning. How does data lineage help you find the broken upstream job and everything else it affected?

expectedConcepts.label: Lineage maps where data comes from and where it flows
Captured from pipeline definitions and query logs
Speeds root cause and impact analysis

questions.modelAnswer: Data lineage is a map of how data moves: which source tables and jobs feed each dataset, column or dashboard, and what depends on it downstream. It is usually captured automatically from pipeline definitions, orchestration metadata and query logs into a data catalog. During an incident, for example a revenue dashboard suddenly showing half the usual value, lineage lets you walk upstream to find which job or source broke, and walk downstream to see every report, model and export affected so you can warn their owners. It also helps plan schema changes and answer compliance questions about where personal data goes.

questions.title: Warehouse, lake and lakehouse
questions.prompt: What is a data warehouse versus a data lake versus a lakehouse?

expectedConcepts.label: Warehouse: structured, schema-enforced, SQL analytics
Lake: raw files of any format in cheap object storage
Lakehouse: table formats add transactions and schema on the lake
Lakes are flexible but risk becoming a swamp

questions.modelAnswer: A data warehouse stores cleaned, structured data with an enforced schema, optimised for fast SQL analytics and BI, such as Snowflake or BigQuery. A data lake stores raw data of any format, such as logs, JSON, images and Parquet files, cheaply in object storage, which is flexible and good for data science, but without governance it becomes a "data swamp" with weak consistency guarantees. A lakehouse adds warehouse-like features on top of lake storage using open table formats such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake or Hudi: ACID transactions, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel and efficient queries, so one copy of the data serves both BI and machine learning.

questions.title: Schema-on-write versus schema-on-read
questions.prompt: How do schema-on-write and schema-on-read differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Schema-on-write validates structure when data is stored
Schema-on-read applies structure when data is queried
Write: reliable and fast queries; read: flexible but errors surface late

questions.modelAnswer: With schema-on-write, the structure is defined up front and enforced when data is stored, as in a relational database or warehouse: bad records are rejected at load time, and queries are fast and reliable because the data is already well-formed. With schema-on-read, data is stored raw, for example JSON files in a data lake, and a schema is applied only when someone queries it. That makes ingestion easy and lets different users interpret the same data differently, but problems such as missing fields or type changes are discovered late, at query time, and every reader must handle messy data. Most platforms combine both: raw landing zones, then curated tables.

questions.title: Slowly changing dimensions
questions.prompt: A customer moved city, and last year's sales report now shows all their old orders under the new city. How do slowly changing dimension types handle this?

expectedConcepts.label: Dimension attributes that change over time, like a customer address
Type 1 overwrites; type 2 adds versioned rows with validity dates
Type 2 preserves history for correct reports but adds complexity

questions.modelAnswer: In a star schema, dimension tables describe entities such as customers, products or stores, and their attributes change slowly: a customer moves city, a product changes category. Type 1 handling simply overwrites the old value, which is simple but rewrites history, so last year's sales by city now use today's address. Type 2 keeps history: each change inserts a new row with a new surrogate key and valid-from and valid-to dates or a current flag, and facts point to the version that was valid when they happened, so historical reports stay correct. Other types store a previous value column. Type 2 is the most common for analytics, at the cost of more complex joins.

questions.title: Partitioning and clustering for analytics
questions.prompt: How do partitioning and clustering affect analytical query performance?

expectedConcepts.label: Partitioning splits a table so queries skip irrelevant partitions
Clustering sorts data within partitions to skip blocks
Choose keys from filter patterns; too many small partitions hurt

questions.modelAnswer: Analytical queries usually scan large tables, so the goal is to read less data. Partitioning splits a table into separate chunks by a column, most often the event date, so a query filtering on last week reads only seven partitions instead of years of data; this is partition pruning. Clustering, or sorting, orders data within each partition by other frequently filtered columns, such as customer or country, and storage keeps min and max statistics per block, so the engine can skip blocks that cannot match. Choose keys from real filter patterns. Over-partitioning on a high-cardinality column creates many tiny files and slows everything down, and in pay-per-scan warehouses good partitioning directly cuts cost.

questions.title: Dead-letter queues in data pipelines
questions.prompt: One malformed record keeps failing a nightly pipeline, so either the whole job stops or the record is silently dropped. How does a dead-letter queue give you a better option?

expectedConcepts.label: Holds messages that repeatedly fail processing
Keeps the main pipeline flowing while bad records are isolated
Must be monitored, inspected and replayed

questions.modelAnswer: A dead-letter queue is a separate queue or table where a pipeline puts records it cannot process after a limited number of retries: malformed JSON, a schema violation, or a value that crashes the transformation. Without it, one poison record either blocks the whole partition, as the consumer retries it forever, or gets silently dropped. With a DLQ, the main pipeline keeps flowing while bad records are isolated with error details and metadata. A DLQ is not a trash can: it needs alerts on its size, a process to inspect the failures and fix the bug or the data, and tooling to replay records back into the pipeline.

questions.title: Making a data pipeline idempotent
questions.prompt: How do you make a data pipeline idempotent?

expectedConcepts.label: Rerunning produces the same result, no duplicates
Overwrite partitions or upsert by key instead of appending
Deterministic inputs and unique keys; dedupe events

questions.modelAnswer: An idempotent pipeline can be run again for the same input, after a failure or for a backfill, and produce exactly the same output without duplicates. Common techniques: process data in well-defined units such as a date partition, and have each run overwrite its whole output partition instead of appending; write with upserts or MERGE statements keyed on a natural or event ID rather than plain inserts; deduplicate incoming events by unique ID; and keep transformations deterministic, avoiding the current time or random values unless they are pinned to the run. Then retries and reruns are safe, which makes failures cheap to recover from.

questions.title: Event time versus processing time
questions.prompt: Mobile clients upload events hours late after being offline, and your hourly counts keep changing. How do event time and processing time differ, and which should the counts use?

expectedConcepts.label: Event time: when the event happened at the source
Processing time: when the system handles it
Event time gives correct results despite delays but needs late-data handling

questions.modelAnswer: Event time is when something actually happened, the timestamp recorded by the device or service that produced the event. Processing time is when the pipeline happens to handle it. They differ because events are delayed by networks, offline mobile devices, retries and backlogs, and arrive out of order. If you count "orders per hour" by processing time, a backlog after an outage piles hours of orders into the wrong window. Event-time processing assigns each event to windows by its own timestamp, so results are correct regardless of delays, but the system must decide how long to wait for late events, using watermarks.

questions.title: Watermarks and late data
questions.prompt: How do watermarks help stream processors handle late data?

expectedConcepts.label: Watermark: estimate that events before time T have arrived
Windows close and emit when the watermark passes their end
Trade latency for completeness; allowed lateness and updates

questions.modelAnswer: In event-time stream processing, the system never knows for sure that all events for a window have arrived. A watermark is its running estimate of progress: a statement that "events with timestamps before T have probably all arrived", often computed as the latest event time seen minus a bounded delay. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the processor closes it and emits the result. Events that arrive after that are late; they can be dropped, sent to a side output, or, with allowed lateness, used to emit a corrected result. A conservative watermark gives more complete results but higher latency; an aggressive one is faster but misses more late data.

questions.title: Automating data quality checks
questions.prompt: A broken upstream job loaded half the usual rows, and nobody noticed for a week. Which data quality checks would you automate to catch this kind of problem?

expectedConcepts.label: Continuously checking data is complete, valid and fresh
Checks: row counts, nulls, uniqueness, ranges, schema changes
Alert and stop bad data before it reaches consumers

questions.modelAnswer: Data quality monitoring continuously checks that datasets are trustworthy before people and models use them. Checks I would automate: freshness, meaning the table was updated on schedule; volume, meaning row counts within the expected range compared with history; completeness, such as null rates on key columns; validity, such as values in allowed ranges and formats; uniqueness of primary keys; referential integrity between tables; schema changes, such as new, missing or retyped columns; and distribution drift in important metrics. Tools like Great Expectations, dbt tests or Soda make this declarative. Failures should alert the owner and, for critical data, stop the pipeline rather than publish bad numbers.

questions.title: Masking sensitive fields in analytics
questions.prompt: How should personally sensitive fields be masked in analytics data?

expectedConcepts.label: Minimise: do not copy sensitive fields unless needed
Masking, tokenisation, hashing with salt, aggregation
Access controls and re-identification risk

questions.modelAnswer: First, do not bring sensitive fields into the analytics environment unless an analysis genuinely needs them. When joins across datasets need an identifier, replace it with a pseudonymous token or a keyed hash, so analysts can count and join users without seeing emails or phone numbers; keep the mapping key separately and tightly controlled. Mask or truncate fields, for example only the city instead of the full address or the birth year instead of the date, and aggregate before sharing. Apply column-level access controls and dynamic masking so only approved roles see raw values. Remember that combinations of quasi-identifiers can re-identify people, so review datasets before wider sharing.

questions.title: The small-files problem
questions.prompt: A streaming job writes a new file every few seconds, and queries on the table have become very slow. What is the small-files problem, and how do you fix it?

expectedConcepts.label: Huge numbers of tiny files slow distributed storage and queries
Per-file metadata and open costs dominate; poor compression
Fix with compaction and better batching or partitioning

questions.modelAnswer: Distributed storage and query engines are designed for fewer, larger files, typically a hundred megabytes to a gigabyte each. When streaming jobs or over-partitioned tables write millions of tiny files, every file adds metadata overhead, such as NameNode memory in HDFS or listing calls in object storage, and every query must open and read many files, so planning and I/O time dominate instead of actual scanning. Small files also compress poorly and keep columnar formats from using their statistics. The fixes are compaction jobs that periodically merge small files into larger ones, which table formats like Iceberg and Delta support, writing in bigger batches, and avoiding partitioning on high-cardinality columns.

questions.title: Parquet versus CSV for analytics
questions.prompt: How do Parquet and CSV differ for analytical workloads?

expectedConcepts.label: Parquet is columnar, binary and typed; CSV is row text
Column pruning, compression and statistics speed scans
CSV is human-readable and universal but slow and ambiguous

questions.modelAnswer: CSV is a plain-text, row-oriented format: human-readable and supported everywhere, but every value is text, types and escaping are ambiguous, and a query must read and parse entire rows even if it needs two columns. Parquet is a binary, columnar format with an embedded schema: values of each column are stored together, so a query reads only the columns it needs; similar values compress very well; and per-block min and max statistics let engines skip data that cannot match a filter. For analytics, Parquet is usually many times smaller and faster. CSV remains useful for small exports and data exchange with people and spreadsheets.

questions.title: Reconciling counts between source and warehouse
questions.prompt: How do you reconcile counts between a source database and a warehouse?

expectedConcepts.label: Compare counts and aggregates for the same slice of data
Align definitions: time zones, deletes, late updates, filters
Automate reconciliation and investigate drift by drilling down

questions.modelAnswer: Pick a well-defined slice, for example orders created on a given day, and compute the same measures on both sides: row counts, sums of key amounts, and ideally checksums of IDs. Differences usually come from definitions rather than lost data: different time zones for the day boundary, soft-deleted or cancelled rows filtered on one side only, late updates that the warehouse has not received yet, or duplicates from replays. When totals differ, drill down by hour or by ID range to find the missing or extra records. Automate these checks after each load with a tolerance, alert on drift, and document the definition of each metric.

questions.title: Backfilling a year of data safely
questions.prompt: How would you backfill a year of data without overwhelming production?

expectedConcepts.label: Process in small idempotent chunks, such as per day
Read from replicas or exports, not the primary database
Throttle, schedule off-peak, monitor and resume

questions.modelAnswer: Never run one giant query over a year of data against the production primary. Instead, split the backfill into small units, such as one day or one partition at a time, and make each unit idempotent so failures can simply be retried. Read from a replica, a snapshot or an existing export rather than the live primary, and write into partitions that overwrite cleanly.
