Throttle concurrency and rate, schedule heavy work off-peak, and watch database load, replication lag and pipeline latency, pausing automatically if they cross thresholds. Record progress with checkpoints so the job can resume, and validate each chunk's counts as you go.

questions.title: Static analysis versus compilation
questions.prompt: How do static analysis and compilation differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Compilation translates code to an executable form
Static analysis inspects code for bugs without running it
Analysers trade false positives for deeper checks

questions.modelAnswer: Compilation transforms source code into something executable, such as machine code or bytecode, rejecting only programs that violate the language rules. Static analysis examines source code, without running it, to find likely bugs, security issues and style problems that are still legal programs: null dereferences, resource leaks, unused results, injection risks, data races. Compilers perform some analysis, warnings are a form of it, but dedicated analysers like clang-tidy, ESLint, go vet, SonarQube or CodeQL go deeper. Because perfect analysis of program behaviour is undecidable, analysers trade precision for coverage and can produce false positives, so teams tune rule sets.

questions.title: Common compiler optimisations
questions.prompt: Your hot loop runs ten times faster at -O2 than at -O0, but a small refactor made it slow again. Which compiler optimisations explain this, and what can block them?

expectedConcepts.label: Inlining, constant folding, dead code elimination, loop optimisations
Vectorisation and register allocation exploit hardware
Results depend on code shape, aliasing and flags; measure

questions.modelAnswer: Compilers apply many transformations that keep a program's meaning but make it faster: inlining small functions to remove call overhead and unlock further optimisation; constant folding and propagation; eliminating dead code and redundant computations; hoisting loop-invariant work; loop unrolling; auto-vectorisation using SIMD instructions; and good register allocation. Whether they kick in depends on code shape and on what the compiler can prove: possible pointer aliasing, virtual calls or code across separate files can block optimisations, while optimisation levels, link-time optimisation and profile-guided optimisation unlock more. Small code changes can therefore cause large performance swings, so measure rather than assume.

questions.title: Static versus dynamic linking
questions.prompt: What is the difference between static and dynamic linking?

expectedConcepts.label: Static linking copies library code into the executable
Dynamic linking loads shared libraries at runtime
Static: portable but larger and must rebuild for patches; dynamic: shared updates, version issues

questions.modelAnswer: With static linking, the linker copies the needed library code into the executable, producing one self-contained binary that runs without those libraries installed, which simplifies deployment, as Go and many container images rely on. The downsides are larger binaries, duplicated code in memory, and having to rebuild and redeploy every program to pick up a library security fix. With dynamic linking, the executable references shared libraries, .so or .dll files, that the loader maps at runtime; many programs share one copy, and patching the library fixes them all. The cost is dependency and version management, sometimes called DLL hell, and slightly slower startup.

questions.title: Incremental compilation
questions.prompt: Changing one header in your project triggers a twenty-minute full rebuild. How does incremental compilation decide what to rebuild, and why might it be rebuilding too much?

expectedConcepts.label: Only recompile what changed and what depends on it
Track dependencies and content hashes of inputs
Wrong dependency tracking gives stale or slow builds

questions.modelAnswer: Incremental compilation means rebuilding only the parts of a program affected by a change instead of everything. The build system tracks, for every output, which inputs it was built from, such as source files, headers, flags and tool versions, using timestamps or better content hashes. When you edit a file, it rebuilds that unit and everything that depends on it, and reuses the rest. Fine-grained modules, small headers or stable interfaces mean fewer dependents and faster rebuilds. The risk is incorrect dependency information: a missed dependency gives stale, wrong builds, while overly broad dependencies make every change rebuild too much.

questions.title: Dependency graphs in build tools
questions.prompt: How do dependency graphs help a build tool schedule work?

expectedConcepts.label: Targets and their inputs form a directed acyclic graph
Topological order; independent nodes build in parallel
Graph enables caching and minimal rebuilds; cycles are errors

questions.modelAnswer: A build tool models the project as a directed acyclic graph: each node is a target such as a library, object file or test, and edges point to what it depends on. From this graph it can compute a valid order, building dependencies before dependents, which is a topological sort, and run independent targets in parallel across all cores or remote workers. When something changes, it walks the graph to find exactly the affected targets, skipping or caching the rest, which also lets CI run only the tests affected by a change. A cycle in the graph is an error, because no valid order exists.

questions.title: Reproducible builds
questions.prompt: What makes a build reproducible?

expectedConcepts.label: Same source and inputs produce bit-for-bit identical output
Pin toolchains and dependencies; remove timestamps and paths
Enables verifying binaries and reliable caching

questions.modelAnswer: A build is reproducible when the same source code, built with the same declared inputs, produces bit-for-bit identical output, no matter who builds it, when or on which machine. That requires pinning everything that affects the output: compiler and toolchain versions, dependency versions via lockfiles, and build flags, usually inside a fixed container or hermetic build environment. It also requires removing nondeterminism such as embedded timestamps, absolute file paths, random IDs and unordered file listings. Reproducibility lets independent parties verify that a published binary really came from the published source, which defends against supply-chain attacks, and it makes build caches trustworthy.

questions.title: Generated source files and dependency tracking
questions.prompt: How do generated source files complicate dependency tracking?

expectedConcepts.label: Generated files depend on generators and their inputs
Build must declare generator as a step with explicit inputs and outputs
Missed edges cause stale code or ordering failures

questions.modelAnswer: Code generators, such as protobuf compilers, parser generators or ORM tools, produce source files that the compiler then consumes. The build must know that the generated file depends on the schema or grammar and on the generator version, and that everything compiling the generated file must wait for it. If the build system does not model these edges, you get stale generated code after a schema change, races in parallel builds where compilation starts before generation finishes, or headers that do not exist yet. Solutions include declaring generation as explicit build rules with inputs and outputs, as Bazel requires, or committing generated code and checking in CI that it is up to date.

questions.title: Link-time optimisation
questions.prompt: A small function defined in another source file is called in your hot loop but never inlined. How can link-time optimisation help, and what does it cost?

expectedConcepts.label: Optimises across translation units at link time
Compiler emits intermediate representation; linker optimises it
Faster code and smaller binaries versus longer builds

questions.modelAnswer: Normally a compiler optimises each source file, or translation unit, separately, so it cannot inline a function defined in another file or see that a function is never called. With link-time optimisation, the compiler emits an intermediate representation instead of final machine code, and at link time the toolchain optimises the whole program together: inlining across files, removing unused code, and propagating constants across module boundaries. This often gives noticeably faster and smaller binaries. The cost is longer and more memory-hungry link steps, which ThinLTO mitigates by parallelising, and debugging can become harder.

questions.title: Builds that pass locally but fail in CI
questions.prompt: How would you diagnose a build that succeeds locally but fails in CI?

expectedConcepts.label: Environment differences: tool versions, OS, env variables
Uncommitted or ignored files and caches locally
Reproduce CI exactly with the same container; make builds hermetic

questions.modelAnswer: A local-only success means something differs between the environments. Compare tool versions, such as compiler, Node or Go, and the operating system and architecture; environment variables and secrets; and file system case-sensitivity. Check for files that exist locally but are not committed: generated code, ignored config, or dependencies cached in your home directory. Also consider ordering and parallelism differences that reveal missing dependency declarations, network access, time-zone and locale differences, and resource limits. The quickest diagnosis is reproducing CI exactly: a clean checkout in the same container image with the same commands. Then fix the root cause by pinning versions and making the build hermetic.

questions.title: Cross-compilation pitfalls
questions.prompt: Your ARM64 binary, built on an x86 laptop, fails on the device with missing-library errors. What are the common cross-compilation pitfalls behind problems like this?

expectedConcepts.label: Building on one platform for another target
Needs the target toolchain, headers and libraries (sysroot)
Pitfalls: native dependencies, host-specific assumptions, testing on target

questions.modelAnswer: Cross-compilation means building on one platform, the host, binaries for another, the target, for example building ARM64 Linux binaries on an x86 laptop, or firmware for a microcontroller. It needs a toolchain that generates code for the target and the target's headers and libraries, usually in a sysroot. Pitfalls include native dependencies, such as C libraries in a Go or Python project, that must also be built for the target; build scripts that run host tools or detect features by probing the host; assumptions about pointer size, endianness or alignment; and dynamic linking against libraries the target does not have. Always test on the real target or under emulation such as QEMU.

questions.title: A package manager's role in a toolchain
questions.prompt: Two of your dependencies need different versions of the same library. How does a package manager resolve this, and what else is it responsible for?

expectedConcepts.label: Finds, downloads and installs dependencies with versions
Resolves version constraints and writes a lockfile
Also handles publishing, security and reproducibility

questions.modelAnswer: A package manager, such as npm, pip, Cargo, Maven or Go modules, finds the libraries a project depends on in a registry, downloads them and makes them available to the compiler or runtime. Its hardest job is resolution: reading the version constraints of every direct and transitive dependency and choosing a compatible set, then recording the exact result in a lockfile so builds are reproducible. It also verifies integrity with checksums, caches downloads, handles publishing packages, runs install scripts, and increasingly reports known vulnerabilities. Because it decides what third-party code ends up in your program, it is also a key part of supply-chain security.

questions.title: When a build cache becomes incorrect or unsafe
questions.prompt: How can a build cache become incorrect or unsafe?

expectedConcepts.label: Cache key misses an input, so stale outputs are reused
Nondeterministic outputs and environment leaks
Shared remote caches can be poisoned; restrict writes

questions.modelAnswer: A build cache reuses an output when the hash of its inputs matches a previous build. It becomes incorrect when the cache key misses an input that actually affects the output: an undeclared header, an environment variable, a tool version or a file read implicitly. Then a change does not invalidate the entry and you silently get stale output. Nondeterministic builds also reduce hits and can mix outputs inconsistently. Shared remote caches add a security risk: if untrusted builds, such as pull requests from forks, can write to the cache, an attacker can poison it with malicious artefacts used by release builds. Keep builds hermetic and restrict cache writes to trusted CI.

questions.title: Debug symbols versus optimisation settings
questions.prompt: A production crash report shows only raw addresses, and the release build uses -O2. How do debug symbols and optimisation settings differ, and can you have both?

expectedConcepts.label: Debug symbols map machine code back to source
Optimisation level changes generated code
They are independent; release builds can keep separate symbols

questions.modelAnswer: They are independent settings that people often confuse. Debug symbols, enabled with flags like -g, are metadata such as DWARF that map machine code back to source files, line numbers, functions and variables, so debuggers and profilers can show readable stack traces. Optimisation level, like -O0 or -O2, controls how aggressively the compiler transforms the code. You can have an optimised build with symbols: it runs fast and still produces useful stack traces, though some variables may be "optimised out". Production builds commonly keep symbols in separate files, stripped from the shipped binary, and use them to symbolise crash reports.

questions.title: Reducing compile times in a large C++ codebase
questions.prompt: How would you reduce compile times in a large C++ repository?

expectedConcepts.label: Reduce what each file includes and parses
Precompiled headers, modules, pimpl, fewer templates in headers
Build infrastructure: caching, distributed builds, faster linkers

questions.modelAnswer: Most C++ build time goes into parsing the same headers thousands of times, so first measure which headers and translation units are most expensive, for example with Clang's -ftime-trace. Then reduce includes: forward-declare instead of including, follow include-what-you-use, split large headers, and move implementation and heavy template code out of headers, using the pimpl idiom to hide private members. Precompiled headers and C++20 modules avoid reparsing common code. Extern templates cut repeated instantiation. On the infrastructure side, use compiler caches like ccache, distributed or remote builds, unity builds where suitable, and faster linkers such as lld or mold.

questions.title: Investigating a crash with a debugger
questions.prompt: How would you use a debugger to investigate a crash without guessing?

expectedConcepts.label: Reproduce the crash under the debugger or load a core dump
Read the stack trace, inspect variables, set breakpoints
Form and test one hypothesis at a time from evidence

questions.modelAnswer: First make the crash observable: reproduce it while running under the debugger, or open the core dump or crash report it produced. Read the stack trace from the top to see which function failed and how the program got there. Move up the frames and inspect the actual values of variables and arguments, looking for the one that is wrong, such as a null pointer, an out-of-range index or a freed object. Then work backwards: set breakpoints or conditional breakpoints earlier, or a watchpoint on the variable, and step through to find where the bad value first appeared. Each step tests a specific hypothesis using evidence, not guesses.

questions.title: Debuggers, profilers and tracers
questions.prompt: What is the difference between a debugger, profiler, and tracer?

expectedConcepts.label: Debugger: pause and inspect program state step by step
Profiler: measures where time or memory goes in aggregate
Tracer: records a timeline of events across calls or services
Debuggers change timing; each tool fits a different problem

questions.modelAnswer: A debugger lets you stop a program at chosen points with breakpoints, step through it and inspect variables and memory, which is ideal for understanding why a specific execution is wrong, but it changes timing and is rarely used in production. A profiler measures where resources go in aggregate, usually by sampling stacks many times per second, answering which functions consume the CPU time or allocate the memory. A tracer records a timeline of individual events, such as system calls, function entries or spans across services, showing order, duration and causality of specific requests. Choose the debugger for correctness bugs, the profiler for hotspots, and the tracer for latency and interaction problems.

questions.title: Useful code review comments
questions.prompt: What makes a useful code review comment?

expectedConcepts.label: Specific and actionable, pointing to the exact issue
Explains why: the risk or principle behind it
Kind tone and clear priority, blocking versus nit

questions.modelAnswer: A useful comment is specific and actionable: it points to the exact line and says what could go wrong, ideally with a suggested change or example, instead of "this looks off". It explains why, for example "this query runs inside the loop, so a page of 100 items makes 100 database calls", so the author learns the principle rather than just obeying. It signals priority clearly, separating blocking issues such as bugs or security problems from optional nits and personal preferences. It is phrased about the code, not the person, and often as a question when the reviewer may be missing context. Style issues that a linter can catch should be automated instead.

questions.title: Commit messages and small commits
questions.prompt: How should a team structure commit messages and small commits?

expectedConcepts.label: Each commit is one logical change that builds and passes tests
Message: short imperative summary plus why in the body
Easier review, bisect and revert

questions.modelAnswer: Each commit should contain one logical change, such as a refactor, a bug fix or a feature step, and leave the code building and the tests passing, rather than mixing a rename, a fix and formatting in one commit. The message should have a short summary line in the imperative mood, like "Add retry limit to email worker", followed by a body explaining why the change was needed and any important consequences, since the diff already shows what changed. Link the issue or ticket. Small, well-described commits make reviews faster, make git bisect useful for finding regressions, and let you revert a single change safely. Conventions such as Conventional Commits can also drive changelogs.

questions.title: Pre-commit hooks
questions.prompt: What are pre-commit hooks good for, and what should not go into them?

expectedConcepts.label: Fast local checks before a commit is created
Good for formatting, linting and secret scanning
Keep slow tests out; CI must still enforce checks

questions.modelAnswer: A pre-commit hook runs automatically when a developer creates a commit and can block it if a check fails. Good uses are fast, local checks that catch common mistakes early: formatting, linting changed files, detecting committed secrets or large files, and validating config syntax. Keep them to a few seconds, otherwise people bypass them with --no-verify. Do not put the full test suite, network calls, or slow builds in hooks, and never rely on hooks as the only gate, because they run on developer machines and can be skipped. CI must enforce the same checks on every pull request.

questions.title: Language servers
questions.prompt: Your editor offers go-to-definition and rename for a dozen languages without building each one in. How does a language server make that possible?

expectedConcepts.label: A separate process that understands a language for editors
Language Server Protocol: editor sends edits, server returns diagnostics and completions
One server works in many editors; large projects can be slow

questions.modelAnswer: A language server is a separate process that understands a programming language: it parses and type-checks the project and keeps an index of symbols. Editors talk to it using the Language Server Protocol, a JSON-RPC protocol: the editor sends file open and change events, and the server answers requests for completions, hover information, go to definition, find references, rename, formatting and diagnostics such as errors and warnings. Before LSP, every editor needed its own plugin for every language; now one server, such as rust-analyzer, gopls, clangd or the TypeScript server, works in VS Code, Neovim and others. The trade-off is that indexing huge projects can use a lot of memory and CPU.

questions.title: A minimal reproducible bug report
questions.prompt: How would you create a minimal reproducible bug report?

expectedConcepts.label: Exact steps, expected versus actual result
Strip the example down to the smallest code that still fails
Include versions and environment, logs and evidence

questions.modelAnswer: A good bug report lets someone else see the bug in minutes. State the exact steps to reproduce, the expected result and the actual result, including the full error message or a screenshot. Then make it minimal: start from the failing case and remove code, data and configuration piece by piece, keeping only what is needed for the failure to still occur, ideally a short script or a small repository. This process often reveals the real cause. Include environment details such as versions of the library, language, operating system and browser, and whether it happens every time or intermittently. Leave out secrets and personal data.

questions.title: Bisecting a regression with Git
questions.prompt: A test started failing somewhere in the last 400 commits, and nobody knows why. How would you use git bisect to find the commit that broke it?

expectedConcepts.label: Binary search over commit history to find the breaking commit
git bisect marks good and bad commits and checks out midpoints
Automate with a test script; needs buildable small commits

questions.modelAnswer: Bisecting finds the commit that introduced a regression by binary search over history. You tell git bisect one commit where the behaviour was good and one where it is bad; Git checks out the commit halfway between them, you test it and mark it good or bad, and Git halves the range again. Even across a thousand commits that takes only about ten steps. With git bisect run you can give it a script that exits successfully or not, and it finds the culprit automatically. It works best when every commit builds and is small and focused, so the guilty commit clearly shows the cause.

questions.title: Software bill of materials
questions.prompt: A critical vulnerability is announced in a logging library, and you must know within an hour which of your services ship it. How does a software bill of materials help?

expectedConcepts.label: An inventory of all components and dependencies in software
Machine-readable formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX generated at build
Used for vulnerability response, licensing and compliance

questions.modelAnswer: A software bill of materials, or SBOM, is a machine-readable inventory of everything inside a piece of software: every library and package, including transitive dependencies, with versions, suppliers and licences. It is usually generated automatically during the build in standard formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX. Security teams use it to answer within minutes "are we affected?" when a new vulnerability like Log4Shell is announced. Legal teams use it for licence compliance. Customers and regulators increasingly require it from vendors, for example in government procurement. An SBOM is only useful if it is accurate, kept up to date and actually queried.

questions.title: Safer command-line workflows
questions.prompt: How can command-line tools make a developer workflow safer?

expectedConcepts.label: Dry runs and confirmations before destructive actions
Scripts encode repeatable steps instead of manual typing
Safe defaults, environment indicators and guardrails

questions.modelAnswer: Command-line tooling reduces human error by turning risky manual steps into repeatable scripts: a single make deploy or migration command does the same thing every time instead of someone typing ten commands from memory. Good tools have safe defaults, offer a dry-run mode that shows what would change, require explicit confirmation or flags for destructive operations, and refuse to act on production unless the environment is named. Shell prompts that display the current Kubernetes context or cloud account prevent running commands against the wrong target. Using set -euo pipefail in scripts makes failures stop the script instead of continuing silently.

questions.title: What an incident runbook contains
questions.prompt: What should an incident runbook contain?

expectedConcepts.label: When to use it: symptoms and the alert it belongs to
Step-by-step diagnosis and mitigation commands
Escalation, rollback, verification and ownership

questions.modelAnswer: A runbook is written for a stressed on-call engineer at three in the morning, so it should be short and concrete. It states which alert or symptoms it covers and what the impact on users is. It lists diagnosis steps with exact commands, dashboards and queries, and the likely causes. It gives mitigation actions, such as restarting, scaling, failing over or rolling back, with their risks, and how to verify that the system has recovered. It says when and whom to escalate to and how to communicate status. It has an owner and a last-reviewed date, and should be updated after each incident that used it.

questions.title: Separating deployment from release with feature flags
questions.prompt: How do feature flags help separate deployment from release?

expectedConcepts.label: Code is deployed dark and turned on later
Flags gate code paths for percentages, users or regions
Fast kill switch, but flag debt and testing combinations

questions.modelAnswer: Deployment means putting new code onto production servers; release means letting users experience the change. Feature flags separate the two: the new code ships behind a flag that is off, so it can be deployed at any time, even unfinished, as part of trunk-based development. The team then releases by turning the flag on, first for employees, then for one percent of users, a region or specific customers, watching metrics as they go. If something breaks, they flip the flag off in seconds instead of rolling back a deployment. The costs are extra code paths to test and old flags piling up, so every flag needs an owner and a removal date.

questions.title: Evaluating whether a tool saves time
questions.prompt: How would you evaluate whether an engineering tool saves time?

expectedConcepts.label: Define the problem and baseline metric before adopting
Pilot with a small team and compare outcomes
Count total cost: learning, maintenance and lock-in

questions.modelAnswer: Start from the problem, not the tool: what slows the team down, and how would we notice it improving? Measure a baseline first, for example build time, time from pull request to merge, number of flaky failures, or hours spent on a manual task. Then run a time-boxed pilot with a small group on real work and compare the same metrics, plus their honest feedback. Count the total cost, not just the licence: migration effort, learning curve, maintenance, integration with existing systems, and the risk of lock-in. A tool is worth adopting only if the measured savings clearly outweigh those costs.

questions.title: Risks of automated code fixes at scale
questions.prompt: What are the risks of automatically applying code fixes at scale?

expectedConcepts.label: A wrong fix is multiplied across many places at once
Semantic changes slip through syntactic transforms and weak tests
Mitigate with small batches, review, owners and easy rollback

questions.modelAnswer: Automated fixes, such as codemods, linter auto-fixes, dependency bumps or AI-generated patches, are powerful because one change applies to thousands of files, but so is a mistake. A transform that is syntactically correct can still change behaviour in edge cases, and if test coverage is weak nobody notices until production. Huge diffs are hard to review, so people approve them blindly, and they cause merge conflicts and blur ownership. Mitigations: roll out in small batches starting with low-risk code, require tests to pass and code owners to review, keep each change mechanical and explainable, and make it easy to revert.

questions.title: Development containers and environment drift
questions.prompt: How can local development containers reduce environment drift?

expectedConcepts.label: Drift: machines differ in tools and versions over time
A container definition pins the toolchain for everyone
Faster onboarding, but performance and resource costs

questions.modelAnswer: Environment drift is when each developer machine slowly ends up with different compiler, runtime, database and tool versions, causing "works on my machine" bugs. A development container defines the whole toolchain in a versioned file, such as a Dockerfile or devcontainer.json, stored in the repository, so every developer and CI job runs the same image. Onboarding becomes opening the project rather than following a long setup document, and upgrading a tool is a reviewed change. Trade-offs: file-system performance can be slower, especially on macOS and Windows, containers use memory and disk, and GUI tools or hardware access can be awkward.

questions.title: Documenting a complex command-line interface
questions.prompt: How would you document a complex command-line interface?

expectedConcepts.label: Built-in help for every command and flag
Task-oriented examples for common workflows
Generate reference docs from code so they stay accurate

questions.modelAnswer: Layer the documentation. Every command and subcommand should have built-in help with a one-line description, usage syntax, flags with defaults, and a couple of examples, because that is what users see first. Then write task-oriented guides showing complete examples for the most common workflows that people can copy and adapt, since few users read reference pages end to end. Generate the full reference, such as man pages or a website, from the same code that defines the flags so it never drifts. Document exit codes, environment variables, config files and error messages with what to do next.

questions.title: Avoiding alert fatigue
questions.prompt: How can an engineering team avoid alert fatigue from tooling?

expectedConcepts.label: Too many noisy alerts make people ignore real ones
Alert on user-facing symptoms and SLOs, not every cause
Route by severity, tune or delete alerts, review regularly

questions.modelAnswer: Alert fatigue happens when people receive so many alerts, most of them false or not actionable, that they start ignoring them, and then miss the one that matters. Every alert that pages a human should be urgent, actionable and tied to user impact: alert on symptoms such as error rate or latency against an SLO, or on burning the error budget, rather than every CPU spike or single failed job. Send lower-severity signals to tickets or dashboards instead of pages, group related alerts, and give each alert a runbook. Review alerts regularly, and delete or fix any that fired without anyone needing to act.

questions.title: Validating input at a trust boundary
questions.prompt: How should a backend validate input at a trust boundary?

expectedConcepts.label: Never trust client input; validate on the server
Schema validation: types, lengths, ranges, allow-lists
Reject early with clear errors; encode output by context

questions.modelAnswer: A trust boundary is where data enters from something you do not control, such as a browser, a mobile app, a partner or even another team's service. Client-side checks are only for user experience; the server must validate everything again. Parse requests against an explicit schema: required fields, types, lengths, ranges, formats, and allow-lists of permitted values, rejecting unknown fields where that matters. Reject invalid input early with a clear 400 error that does not leak internals. Validation is not the whole defence: still use parameterised queries, encode output for its context, and check authorisation on every object the request touches.

questions.title: Request-scoped versus application-scoped dependencies
questions.prompt: How do request-scoped and application-scoped dependencies differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Application-scoped: created once and shared by all requests
Request-scoped: a new instance per request
Shared ones must be thread-safe; mixing lifetimes causes leaks

questions.modelAnswer: In a dependency-injection setup, every object has a lifetime. Application-scoped, or singleton, dependencies are created once at startup and shared by every request: database connection pools, HTTP clients, configuration and caches. They must be thread-safe and must not hold per-user state. Request-scoped dependencies are created for each request and discarded afterwards: the current user, the request's trace context, or a unit-of-work transaction. A classic bug is a captive dependency, where a singleton holds onto a request-scoped object, so one user's data or transaction leaks into other requests. Choose lifetimes deliberately.

questions.title: Connection pool exhaustion
questions.prompt: What causes a connection pool to become exhausted?

expectedConcepts.label: All connections are checked out and new requests wait or fail
Causes: slow queries, leaks, long transactions, traffic spikes
Fix the cause; tune size with database limits and timeouts

questions.modelAnswer: A connection pool has a fixed number of connections; it becomes exhausted when all of them are checked out and new requests wait until the acquire timeout, then fail. Common causes are connections that are never returned, for example a code path that forgets to close them on an error; slow queries or long-held transactions that keep connections busy; doing slow work, like calling another API, while holding a connection; and traffic spikes or a slow database making each connection busy for longer. Simply enlarging the pool often just moves the bottleneck to the database's own connection limit. Monitor in-use and waiting counts, set acquire timeouts, and fix leaks and slow queries.

questions.title: Bulkheads for failure isolation
questions.prompt: What is bulkheading, and how can it isolate failures?

expectedConcepts.label: Partition resources so one failure cannot consume everything
Separate thread pools, connection pools or instances per dependency or tenant
Limits blast radius but lowers utilisation and needs sizing

questions.modelAnswer: The name comes from ships, which are divided into watertight compartments so one leak does not sink the whole vessel. In software, bulkheading partitions limited resources so a failure in one area cannot exhaust them for everything else. For example, if all requests share one thread pool and a single downstream service becomes slow, its calls pile up and take every thread, so even unrelated endpoints stop responding. With separate pools or concurrency limits per dependency, or separate instances per critical customer or tenant, the slow dependency only fills its own compartment. The cost is lower overall utilisation, since idle capacity in one partition cannot help another, and each partition must be sized and tuned. It works best combined with timeouts and circuit breakers.

questions.title: Request handlers versus background jobs
questions.prompt: How do synchronous request handlers and background jobs differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Handlers do work while the client waits for a response
Background jobs go on a queue and run in workers later
Jobs need retries, status reporting and idempotency

questions.modelAnswer: A synchronous request handler does its work while the client waits, so it should do only what is needed to give a correct response quickly. Slow, unreliable or heavy work, such as sending emails, generating reports, resizing images or calling slow third-party APIs, is better placed on a queue as a background job that worker processes execute later. The handler returns quickly, perhaps with 202 Accepted and a job ID, and workers can scale independently and retry failures. The trade-offs are complexity: the user sees the result later, so you need status reporting or notifications, jobs must be idempotent because they may run twice, and the queue needs monitoring.

questions.title: API responses versus application logs
questions.prompt: What belongs in an API response versus an application log?

expectedConcepts.label: Responses give clients what they need to act, nothing internal
Logs hold internal diagnostic detail for operators
Link them with a request ID; keep secrets and personal data out of both

questions.modelAnswer: An API response is for the client: the result, or an error with a status code, a stable machine-readable error code and a human-readable message that tells them how to fix their request. It must not expose internals such as stack traces, SQL, file paths or the names of internal hosts, which help attackers. Logs are for operators and can hold diagnostic detail: the exception and stack trace, which dependency failed, timings and relevant IDs. Include the same request or correlation ID in both, so support can find the log entry for a customer's failed request. Neither should contain passwords, tokens or unnecessary personal data.

questions.title: Per-user and per-tenant quotas
questions.prompt: How should a backend enforce per-user and per-tenant quotas?

expectedConcepts.label: Quotas cap usage per user or tenant to protect fairness
Counters in shared fast storage checked atomically at the edge
Clear errors, headers and plan-based limits; handle bursts

questions.modelAnswer: Quotas protect the system and other customers from one heavy user, and often reflect pricing plans. Define what is counted and over which window: requests per second, jobs per day, storage or tokens per month, separately per user and per tenant. Enforce them centrally, at the gateway or a shared middleware, using counters in fast shared storage such as Redis, updated atomically with algorithms like token bucket or sliding window, so multiple servers agree. When the limit is reached, return a clear 429 response with headers that show the limit, remaining amount and reset time. Allow short bursts where reasonable, and alert customers before they hit hard limits.

questions.title: What a health endpoint should reveal
questions.prompt: What should a health endpoint reveal, and what should it hide?

expectedConcepts.label: Reveal a simple status that the orchestrator or load balancer can act on
Hide versions, internal hosts, secrets and stack traces publicly
Detailed dependency checks only on an internal or authenticated endpoint

questions.modelAnswer: A health endpoint exists so load balancers, orchestrators and monitors can decide whether to send traffic to an instance or restart it. Publicly, it should reveal very little: a status code such as 200 or 503 and perhaps "ok". It should not expose software versions, dependency hostnames, configuration, error messages or stack traces, because attackers use them to find vulnerable components. Detailed diagnostics, such as the status of each database and downstream service, belong on an internal or authenticated endpoint. Also keep the checks cheap, so frequent probes cannot overload the service or its database.

questions.title: Reloading configuration without a restart
questions.prompt: How would you design configuration reload without restarting a service?

expectedConcepts.label: Watch a source for changes: file, config service or signal
Validate the new config, then swap it atomically
Not every setting can change live; keep last good config and audit

questions.modelAnswer: The service learns about changes by watching a config file, subscribing to a config service, or handling a signal such as SIGHUP. It loads the new configuration, validates it fully, and only if it is valid swaps it in atomically, for example by replacing an immutable config object behind an atomic reference, so each request sees either the whole old or the whole new config, never a mix. If validation fails, it keeps running with the last known good config and alerts. Some settings, such as listening ports or pool sizes, cannot easily change live and should be documented as needing a restart. Log every change and who made it so incidents can be traced.

questions.title: Handling client disconnects and request cancellation
questions.prompt: How do you handle request cancellation after a client disconnects?

expectedConcepts.label: Detect the disconnect or deadline and stop wasted work
Propagate a cancellation signal to queries and downstream calls
Cancel safely; finish or compensate side effects

questions.modelAnswer: When a client gives up, through a timeout, closed tab or cancelled mobile request, the server may keep computing a response nobody will read, wasting database time and threads, which makes overloads worse. Most frameworks expose a cancellation signal, such as Go's context, .NET's CancellationToken or an AbortSignal in Node. The handler should pass it to every database query and downstream call so they stop early, and check it between expensive steps. Cancel carefully around side effects: an operation such as charging a card should either complete and be recorded or roll back, never be left half done, so wrap such steps in transactions or make them idempotent.

questions.title: Investigating rising 5xx errors after a release
questions.prompt: How would you investigate rising 5xx errors after a release?

expectedConcepts.label: Check correlation with the deploy; roll back first if impact is high
Break down errors by endpoint, instance, version and status
Read logs and traces of failing requests to find root cause

questions.modelAnswer: First confirm the timing: did the error rate rise exactly when the new version rolled out? If users are significantly affected, mitigate first by rolling back or turning off the feature flag, and investigate afterwards. Then narrow it down: break the errors down by endpoint, status code such as 500 versus 502 versus 503, instance, region and version, to see whether only new instances fail or only one route. Look at logs and traces of failing requests for the stack trace or the downstream dependency that is erroring or timing out. Compare the diff and configuration changes in the release. Finally, add a test or alert so the same failure is caught earlier next time.

questions.title: Keeping database transactions within request boundaries
questions.prompt: How do you avoid leaking database transactions across request boundaries?

expectedConcepts.label: Every transaction must commit or roll back before the request ends
Use scoped helpers or middleware that always close the transaction
Leaks hold locks and connections, causing exhaustion and deadlocks

questions.modelAnswer: A leaked transaction is one that is opened during a request but never committed or rolled back, for example because an exception skips the commit or the connection is returned to the pool still inside a transaction. It keeps holding locks and a connection, blocks other requests, prevents vacuum cleanup in PostgreSQL, and can even leak uncommitted state into the next request that reuses the connection. Prevent it structurally: open transactions in one place through a scoped helper, middleware or unit-of-work that always commits on success and rolls back in a finally or defer block. Keep transactions short, never span them over external calls, and monitor for sessions that stay idle in transaction.

questions.title: A reliable email-sending workflow
questions.prompt: How would you design a reliable email-sending workflow?

expectedConcepts.label: Record the email intent in the database with the business change
A worker sends via the provider with retries and an idempotency key
Handle bounces, rate limits, templates and unsubscribes

questions.modelAnswer: Do not send email directly inside the request that creates an order, because the provider may be slow or down, and a crash between the database commit and the send loses or duplicates the email. Instead, in the same database transaction as the business change, insert an email record with its status, then let a background worker pick it up and call the provider. The worker retries transient failures with exponential backoff, passes a unique message ID so retries do not send duplicates, respects provider rate limits, and marks the record sent or failed. Webhooks from the provider update the status for bounces and complaints, and unsubscribed or bounced addresses are suppressed.

questions.title: Retryable jobs with retry limits
questions.prompt: How do you make background jobs retryable without retrying forever?

expectedConcepts.label: Retry only transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter
Cap attempts or total time, then move to a dead-letter queue
Jobs must be idempotent; alert on failures and allow replay

questions.modelAnswer: Retries help when failures are temporary, such as a timeout or a 503, so classify errors first: permanent errors such as invalid input or a missing record should fail immediately, because retrying cannot help. For transient errors, retry with exponential backoff and random jitter, so a failing dependency is not hammered and jobs do not retry in lockstep. Set a maximum number of attempts or a maximum age, after which the job moves to a dead-letter queue with its error, and alert someone. Because a job can run more than once, make it idempotent. Provide tooling to inspect and replay dead-lettered jobs after the cause is fixed.

questions.title: How the browser renders a page
questions.prompt: How does the browser construct and render a page from HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?

expectedConcepts.label: Parse HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM
Render tree, then layout, paint and composite
Scripts and stylesheets can block rendering

questions.modelAnswer: The browser downloads the HTML and parses it into the DOM, a tree of elements. Stylesheets are parsed into the CSSOM. Combining the two produces the render tree of visible elements with their computed styles. Then layout calculates the exact size and position of each box, paint fills in pixels such as text, colours and images into layers, and compositing assembles the layers on the GPU into the final frame. JavaScript can modify the DOM and styles at any time, triggering layout and paint again. Ordinary script tags block HTML parsing and CSS blocks rendering, so pages defer scripts and inline critical CSS to show content sooner.

questions.title: Reducing layout shift
questions.prompt: What causes layout shift, and how can a team reduce it?

expectedConcepts.label: Visible content moves after it first appears
Causes: images without size, late ads and embeds, web fonts, injected banners
Reserve space, size media and avoid inserting above content

questions.modelAnswer: Layout shift is when visible content jumps after it first renders, for example a button moving just as you tap it; Cumulative Layout Shift is the Core Web Vitals metric for it. Common causes are images and videos without width and height, so the browser cannot reserve space until they load; ads, embeds and iframes that resize; web fonts that swap in with different metrics; and banners or content inserted above what the user is reading. Fixes: always set dimensions or a CSS aspect ratio for media, reserve space with placeholders or skeletons for late content, use font-display with fallback fonts of similar size, and insert new content below the viewport or in response to user actions.

questions.title: Controlled versus uncontrolled inputs
questions.prompt: How do controlled and uncontrolled form inputs differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Controlled: the value lives in component state
Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value; read it with a ref or on submit
Controlled enables live validation; uncontrolled is simpler and fewer re-renders

questions.modelAnswer: In React, a controlled input gets its value from component state and reports every change through an onChange handler, so state is the single source of truth. That makes live validation, formatting, conditional fields and resetting easy, at the cost of a re-render on every keystroke and more code. An uncontrolled input keeps its own value in the DOM, like plain HTML; you set an initial defaultValue and read the current value through a ref or from the form data on submit. That is simpler and faster for large forms, and form libraries often use it internally. Switching an input between the two modes is a common bug.

questions.title: Hydration in server-rendered React
questions.prompt: What is hydration in server-rendered React applications?

expectedConcepts.label: Server sends rendered HTML; client attaches React to it
Client re-runs components and must produce matching output
Fast first paint but delayed interactivity; partial or streaming hydration

questions.modelAnswer: With server-side rendering, the server runs React components and sends ready HTML, so users see content quickly. Hydration is the step where React loads in the browser, renders the same components again and attaches its state and event handlers to the existing HTML instead of recreating it, making the page interactive. The client render must produce the same markup as the server; using things like the current time, random values or browser-only APIs during render causes hydration mismatches and errors. The page can look ready before it is interactive, because all that JavaScript must still download and run, so frameworks use streaming, selective hydration and server components to reduce that cost.

questions.title: Stale closures in event handlers
questions.prompt: How can stale closures cause bugs in UI event handlers?

expectedConcepts.label: A function captures variables from the render it was created in
Long-lived callbacks such as timers or listeners keep reading old state
Fix with correct dependencies, functional updates or refs

questions.modelAnswer: In React, each render creates new functions that close over the props and state of that render. If a function is stored and called later, such as in a setInterval, an event listener registered once in an effect, or a memoised callback with missing dependencies, it keeps seeing the values from the render where it was created; that is a stale closure. Typical bug: a counter interval that always logs zero or increments from the same old value. Fixes include listing correct dependencies in useEffect and useCallback, which the exhaustive-deps lint rule checks, using functional updates like setCount(c => c + 1), or reading the latest value from a ref.

questions.title: Local, global or URL state
questions.prompt: When should state live locally, globally, or in the URL?

expectedConcepts.label: Local: used by one component, such as an open dropdown
Global: shared across distant parts, such as the current user
URL: anything that should survive reload or be shareable, such as filters
Too much global state couples code and re-renders

questions.modelAnswer: Start with the narrowest scope. Local component state suits things only one component cares about: whether a dropdown is open, the text being typed into an input. Lift it to a common parent when siblings need it. Global state, in context or a store, is for data many distant parts of the app need, such as the signed-in user, theme or a shopping cart; overusing it couples everything and causes extra re-renders. The URL should hold state that users expect to survive a reload, bookmark, share or navigate with the back button: the current page, search query, filters, sort order and selected tab. Server data is often best kept in a data-fetching cache rather than global state.

questions.title: Memoisation versus virtualisation
questions.prompt: How do memoization and virtualization solve different performance problems?

expectedConcepts.label: Memoisation skips recomputing or re-rendering unchanged work
Virtualisation renders only the visible part of a long list
Memo helps repeated work; virtualisation helps huge DOM size; both add complexity

questions.modelAnswer: They target different costs. Memoisation, such as React.memo, useMemo or useCallback, caches the result of a computation or render and reuses it when the inputs have not changed, which helps when the same expensive work repeats on every render. Virtualisation, or windowing, helps when there is simply too much to render: a list or table with ten thousand rows creates ten thousand DOM nodes, which is slow to build, lay out and scroll. A virtualised list renders only the rows in or near the viewport and swaps them as you scroll. Memoising a ten-thousand-row list does not fix its DOM size, and virtualising does not fix an expensive calculation. Both add complexity, so profile first.

questions.title: Accessibility semantics and native elements
questions.prompt: What is accessibility semantics, and why are native elements often preferable?

expectedConcepts.label: Semantics tell assistive tech what an element is and its state
Native elements bring keyboard, focus and roles for free
ARIA can fill gaps but is easy to get wrong

questions.modelAnswer: Screen readers and other assistive technologies do not see pixels; they read the accessibility tree, which describes each element's role, such as button, link or heading, its name and its state, such as expanded or checked. Native HTML elements provide these semantics and behaviours automatically: a real button is focusable, works with Enter and Space, and is announced as a button, while a div with a click handler is none of those. ARIA attributes can add semantics to custom widgets, but the first rule of ARIA is not to use it when a native element will do, because incorrect ARIA is worse than none and you must reimplement keyboard handling yourself.

questions.title: Handling API errors and retries in the frontend
questions.prompt: How should a frontend handle API errors and retryable requests?

expectedConcepts.label: Distinguish error types: network, 4xx and 5xx
Retry only safe, transient failures with backoff
Show clear, actionable messages and keep user input

questions.modelAnswer: First classify the failure. Network errors, timeouts and 5xx or 429 responses may be temporary, so idempotent requests such as GETs can be retried automatically a few times with exponential backoff, respecting a Retry-After header. Most 4xx errors, such as validation or permission problems, will fail again and should be shown to the user: highlight the invalid field or explain they need to sign in. Do not automatically retry non-idempotent actions like payments unless the API supports idempotency keys. Show clear, human messages with a retry button, never raw error dumps, keep what the user typed, and handle being offline gracefully.

questions.title: Optimistic UI updates and rollback
questions.prompt: What are optimistic UI updates, and how should rollback work?

expectedConcepts.label: Update the UI immediately, before the server confirms
Keep the previous state to restore if the request fails
Feels fast but must handle conflicts and tell the user

questions.modelAnswer: An optimistic update shows the result of an action, such as a like, a renamed item or a checked task, immediately, assuming the server will succeed, which makes the app feel instant. To roll back safely, save a snapshot of the affected state before changing it, send the request, and when the response arrives replace the optimistic data with the server's version, since it may include IDs or normalisation. If the request fails, restore the snapshot and tell the user clearly, perhaps with a retry option, instead of silently undoing their action. Use it for actions that usually succeed and are easy to reverse, not for payments or irreversible operations.

questions.title: Cookies, local storage and session storage
questions.prompt: How do cookies, local storage, and session storage differ in security and lifetime?

expectedConcepts.label: Cookies are sent with requests and can be HttpOnly and Secure
Local storage persists until cleared; session storage lasts for a tab
Script-readable storage is exposed to XSS; cookies need CSRF protection

questions.modelAnswer: Cookies are small values that the browser automatically sends with matching requests to the server. They can have an expiry, and the flags HttpOnly, which hides them from JavaScript, Secure, which sends them only over HTTPS, and SameSite, which limits cross-site sending and helps against CSRF. Local storage and session storage are larger key-value stores accessible only through JavaScript and never sent automatically; local storage persists until cleared, while session storage disappears when the tab closes. Because any script on the page can read web storage, an XSS bug can steal tokens kept there, which is why session tokens are often kept in HttpOnly cookies instead.

questions.title: Memory leaks in single-page applications
questions.prompt: What causes a memory leak in a single-page application?

expectedConcepts.label: Objects stay reachable after they are no longer needed
Forgotten listeners, timers, subscriptions and detached DOM nodes
Clean up on unmount and verify with heap snapshots

questions.modelAnswer: Single-page apps can run for hours without a page reload, so anything that stays reachable keeps using memory. Common causes are event listeners added to window or document and never removed; setInterval timers and WebSocket or store subscriptions that outlive the component that created them; caches and global arrays that only grow; closures holding large objects; and detached DOM nodes still referenced from JavaScript. In React, the fix is returning a cleanup function from effects to remove listeners, clear timers and unsubscribe. To confirm a leak, use the browser memory tools: take heap snapshots before and after repeating an action and look for objects whose count keeps rising.

questions.title: Code splitting and lazy loading
questions.prompt: How do code splitting and lazy loading affect user experience?

expectedConcepts.label: Split the bundle so each page loads only the code it needs
Lazy-load routes, heavy components and below-the-fold media
Faster first load but possible delays later; preload and show fallbacks

questions.modelAnswer: Without code splitting, users download the JavaScript for the whole application before seeing the first page. Splitting divides the bundle into chunks, usually per route and for heavy components such as editors or charts, loaded on demand with dynamic import. Images and iframes below the fold can also load lazily. This reduces the initial download and parse time, improving first load and interactivity, especially on slow phones. The trade-off is a delay when the user first reaches a lazily loaded part, so show a good loading fallback, prefetch likely next routes when the browser is idle, and avoid splitting so finely that requests chain into a waterfall.

questions.title: Preventing duplicate form submissions
questions.prompt: How would you prevent duplicate form submissions?

expectedConcepts.label: Users double-click or retry, sending the same request twice
Disable the button and track pending state in the UI
The server must also deduplicate with an idempotency key

questions.modelAnswer: Duplicates happen when users double-click, press Enter twice, refresh after submitting, or retry on a slow network. On the frontend, track the pending state: disable the submit button and show a spinner while the request is in flight, and ignore further submits until it completes. Use the post-redirect-get pattern so refreshing the result page does not resubmit. But the client cannot be trusted alone, because requests can be retried by the network or by scripts, so the server should also deduplicate: generate an idempotency key when the form loads and send it with the request, or rely on a unique constraint, so a repeated submission returns the original result.

questions.title: Browser caching versus service workers
questions.prompt: How do browser caching and service workers differ?

expectedConcepts.label: HTTP cache follows server cache headers automatically
Service workers are scripts that intercept requests programmatically
Service workers enable offline and custom strategies but risk stale versions

questions.modelAnswer: The browser's HTTP cache is automatic and controlled by the server through headers such as Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified: the browser stores responses and reuses or revalidates them according to those rules, with no application code. A service worker is a script that the site installs, which sits between the page and the network and intercepts every request. It can decide in code to serve from its own Cache Storage, go to the network, or combine them, as in cache-first, network-first or stale-while-revalidate, and it enables offline use, background sync and push notifications. That power brings risk: a buggy service worker can keep serving old versions, so versioning and update handling must be planned.

questions.title: Responsive layouts, narrow screens and zoom
questions.prompt: How should a responsive layout adapt to narrow screens and zoom?

expectedConcepts.label: Fluid layouts using flexible units, flexbox and grid
Media or container queries reflow content at breakpoints
Support 400 percent zoom without horizontal scrolling; never block zoom

questions.modelAnswer: Build layouts that are fluid by default, using flexbox and grid, relative units such as rem and percentages, and max-width instead of fixed pixel widths, so content naturally fits any width. Use media queries, or container queries for components, to reflow at breakpoints, for example turning a multi-column layout into a single column and collapsing navigation into a menu. Accessibility requires that content still works when users zoom to 400 percent, which is equivalent to a 320-pixel-wide screen, without horizontal scrolling or overlapping text. Never disable pinch zoom in the viewport meta tag, size text in rem so user font settings apply, and keep tap targets large.

questions.title: Debounce versus throttle
questions.prompt: What is the difference between debounce and throttle in UI interactions?

expectedConcepts.label: Debounce waits for a pause, then runs once
Throttle runs at most once per interval during continuous events
Debounce for search-as-you-type; throttle for scroll and resize

questions.modelAnswer: Both limit how often a function runs in response to rapid events. Debounce delays the call until the events stop for a set time: with a 300-millisecond debounce on a search box, the request fires only once the user pauses typing, not on every keystroke. Throttle guarantees the function runs at most once per interval while events keep firing: a scroll handler throttled to every 100 milliseconds still updates regularly during scrolling. So debounce suits actions that should happen after the user is done, such as search suggestions, autosave and validation, while throttle suits continuous feedback such as scroll position, resize handling and drag. For animation, requestAnimationFrame is often better than either.

questions.title: Testing keyboard navigation
questions.prompt: How would you test keyboard navigation for a complex component?

expectedConcepts.label: Every action must be reachable and usable with the keyboard alone
Check focus order, visible focus and expected keys like arrows and Escape
Automate interactions in tests and also test manually with screen readers

questions.modelAnswer: First test manually, without a mouse: can you reach every interactive part with Tab and Shift+Tab, in a logical order, and is the focus indicator always visible? Then check the component follows the expected pattern from the ARIA Authoring Practices: for a menu or listbox, arrow keys move between items, Enter or Space selects, Home and End jump, and Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger; modals trap focus while open. Then automate those behaviours with testing tools that simulate real key presses, such as Testing Library's user-event or Playwright, asserting where focus lands. Finally, try it with a screen reader to confirm names and states are announced.

questions.title: Loading, empty, error and success states
questions.prompt: How should a frontend represent loading, empty, error, and success states?

expectedConcepts.label: Every data view needs all four states designed
Skeletons for loading, guidance for empty, actions for errors
Avoid flicker and announce changes to assistive tech

questions.modelAnswer: Every screen that loads data can be in at least four states, and each should be designed rather than left to chance. Loading: show a skeleton or spinner, ideally after a short delay so fast responses do not flicker, and keep the layout stable. Empty: explain that there is nothing yet and offer a next step, such as "Create your first project", which is different from "no results for this filter". Error: say what went wrong in plain language and offer a retry or alternative, without losing user input. Success: show the data and confirm completed actions. Modelling these explicitly, for example as a status field, prevents impossible combinations, and screen readers should be told about changes.

questions.title: Web Workers for CPU-heavy work
questions.prompt: How do Web Workers help with CPU-intensive browser work?

expectedConcepts.label: Run JavaScript on a background thread so the main thread stays responsive
Communicate through postMessage; no direct DOM access
Copying overhead and complexity; good for parsing, image or data processing

questions.modelAnswer: Browser JavaScript runs your UI code on a single main thread, which also handles input and rendering, so a heavy computation, such as parsing a large file, processing an image or running a search over thousands of items, freezes the page. A Web Worker runs a script on a separate background thread. The main thread sends it data with postMessage and receives results the same way, so the UI stays responsive during the work. Workers cannot touch the DOM, and messages are copied using structured cloning unless you transfer ownership of buffers, so the overhead only pays off for substantial work. Libraries like Comlink make the messaging feel like normal function calls.

questions.title: Rendering user-generated rich text safely
questions.prompt: How would you safely render user-generated rich text?

expectedConcepts.label: Rich text HTML from users can carry scripts, causing XSS
Sanitise with an allow-list of tags and attributes
Prefer structured formats such as Markdown; add CSP as defence in depth

questions.modelAnswer: User-generated rich text, such as comments, posts or descriptions with formatting, is dangerous if you insert it as raw HTML, because it can contain script tags, event handler attributes like onerror, or javascript: links, giving an attacker cross-site scripting. Prefer storing a structured or restricted format, such as Markdown or an editor's JSON document, and rendering it with a trusted renderer. If you must accept HTML, sanitise it with a well-maintained allow-list sanitiser such as DOMPurify, keeping only safe tags and attributes and validating link protocols, ideally on the server and again before rendering. Add a strict Content Security Policy as defence in depth.

questions.title: Core Web Vitals and perceived performance
questions.prompt: How do Core Web Vitals relate to perceived performance?

expectedConcepts.label: LCP measures loading of the main content
INP measures responsiveness; CLS measures visual stability
Measured from real users at the 75th percentile; proxies for experience

questions.modelAnswer: Core Web Vitals are Google's metrics for how fast and stable a page feels to real users. Largest Contentful Paint measures when the main content, usually the hero image or headline, appears, with a target under 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness: how long the page takes to visibly respond to clicks, taps and key presses, ideally under 200 milliseconds. Cumulative Layout Shift measures how much content unexpectedly jumps around. They are judged on field data from real users at the 75th percentile, not just lab tests. They are good proxies for perceived performance, but not complete: a page can score well and still have a confusing loading experience.

questions.title: Partial indexes
questions.prompt: Only 1 percent of 200 million orders are pending, but most queries filter on pending orders. How can a partial index help, and when can the planner not use it?

expectedConcepts.label: An index over only the rows matching a condition
Queries must include the same condition to use it
Smaller and cheaper to maintain; great for skewed data

questions.modelAnswer: A partial index, supported by PostgreSQL and others, indexes only the rows that satisfy a WHERE condition, for example only orders with status pending, or only rows where deleted_at is null. If you mostly query that small subset, the index is far smaller than a full one, so it fits in memory, is faster to scan, and costs less to maintain because writes to other rows do not touch it. The planner can use it only when the query's filter implies the index condition. A useful trick is a partial unique index, for example enforcing that each user has only one active subscription while allowing many cancelled ones.

questions.title: Constraints and invariants under concurrency
questions.prompt: How do database constraints protect invariants under concurrency?

expectedConcepts.label: Constraints are enforced by the database for every write
Application check-then-insert races; the database check is atomic
Handle violation errors as normal outcomes; some invariants need locks or serializable

questions.modelAnswer: An invariant like "each email is registered once" is often coded as check-then-insert: query whether the email exists, and insert if not. Under concurrency, two requests can both check, both see nothing, and both insert, giving duplicates. Database constraints, such as unique, foreign key, check and not-null constraints, and in PostgreSQL exclusion constraints for non-overlapping bookings, are enforced atomically by the database for every write regardless of which code path or service wrote it, so one of the two inserts fails. The application should treat that error as a normal outcome, for example "email already taken". Invariants spanning multiple rows that constraints cannot express need explicit locking or serializable isolation.

questions.title: Advisory locks versus row locks
questions.prompt: How do advisory locks differ from row-level locks?

expectedConcepts.label: Row locks are taken automatically on rows being modified
Advisory locks are application-defined locks on arbitrary keys
Advisory locks coordinate jobs but only work if all code uses them

questions.modelAnswer: Row-level locks are taken by the database itself on specific rows when you update, delete or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE them, and they protect those rows until the transaction ends. Advisory locks, as in PostgreSQL's pg_advisory_lock, are locks on an arbitrary number or key that the application chooses; the database does not associate them with any data. They are useful for coordinating work that does not map to one row, for example ensuring only one instance runs a migration or processes a given customer's batch at a time. They are purely cooperative, since code that does not ask for the lock ignores it, and session-level advisory locks must be released explicitly or they leak until the connection closes.

questions.title: A query that slowed down as data grew
questions.prompt: How would you investigate a query that became slow after data growth?

expectedConcepts.label: Compare the current execution plan with the expected one
Look for full scans, plan changes from stale statistics, or bad estimates
Fix with indexes, query rewrites, partitioning or archiving

questions.modelAnswer: Start by capturing the slow query and running EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the actual plan, row counts and time spent in each step. Growth often exposes problems that were invisible on small tables: a sequential scan that used to be cheap, a sort that now spills to disk, or a nested-loop join over many more rows. Compare estimated and actual row counts; large differences point to stale or insufficient statistics, so the planner chose a plan that was right for old data. Fixes include running ANALYZE, adding or adjusting an index for the filter and sort, rewriting the query, paginating with keysets, or partitioning and archiving old data.

questions.title: Materialised views versus views
questions.prompt: How do materialized views differ from ordinary views?

expectedConcepts.label: A view is a stored query run each time it is used
A materialised view stores the query result physically
Fast reads but stale until refreshed; refresh cost

questions.modelAnswer: An ordinary view is just a named, saved query: each time you select from it, the database runs the underlying query against current data, so results are always fresh but it is no faster than writing the query yourself. A materialised view runs the query once and stores the result as a physical table, which can be indexed, so expensive aggregations and joins become fast reads. The cost is staleness: the data is only as current as the last refresh, and refreshing can be expensive and, unless done concurrently, can block readers. Materialised views suit dashboards and reports where slightly old data is acceptable.

questions.title: Redis eviction policies and correctness
questions.prompt: How do Redis eviction policies affect application correctness?

expectedConcepts.label: When memory is full, Redis evicts keys or rejects writes
Policies: noeviction, allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, LFU, TTL-based
Fine for caches; dangerous when Redis holds data you cannot lose

questions.modelAnswer: When Redis reaches its maxmemory limit, the eviction policy decides what happens. With noeviction, writes fail with errors. With allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu, any key may be removed, choosing the least recently or least frequently used. The volatile policies only evict keys that have an expiry, and if none qualify, writes fail. For a pure cache, evicting is fine because the application can reload from the database. But if the same Redis also holds sessions, rate-limit counters, distributed locks or job queues, an eviction silently deletes state: users get logged out, limits reset, or jobs disappear. Separate cache and durable data into different instances, or choose policies deliberately.

questions.title: Search engines alongside relational databases
questions.prompt: When should a search engine complement rather than replace a relational database?

expectedConcepts.label: Search engines excel at full-text relevance, fuzzy matching and facets
Keep the database as the source of truth and sync to the index
Search indexes are eventually consistent and weak at transactions

questions.modelAnswer: A search engine such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch is excellent at things relational databases do poorly: relevance-ranked full-text search, typo tolerance, stemming, synonyms, faceted filtering and fast aggregations over text. But it is not a good primary store: it lacks multi-row transactions and strong constraints, and it is eventually consistent. So it usually complements the database: the relational database remains the source of truth for writes and correctness, and changes are synchronised to the search index through change data capture, an outbox or a queue. The application must tolerate brief lag and be able to rebuild the index from the database. For modest needs, the database's built-in full-text search may be enough.

questions.title: Connection pinning with database proxies
questions.prompt: After putting PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of Postgres, the database still runs out of connections. How can connection pinning cause this?

expectedConcepts.label: A proxy multiplexes many client sessions over fewer database connections
Session state forces the proxy to pin a client to one connection
Pinning reduces multiplexing and can exhaust connections

questions.modelAnswer: Database proxies like PgBouncer in transaction mode or Amazon RDS Proxy let thousands of application connections share a small pool of real database connections, assigning a server connection only for the duration of each transaction. That only works if no state lives in the session between transactions. If a client sets a session variable, creates temporary tables, holds an advisory lock or uses certain prepared statements, the proxy must pin that client to one server connection for the rest of its session. Pinned connections are no longer shared, so heavy pinning quietly removes the benefit of the proxy and can exhaust database connections. Avoid session-level features or monitor pinning metrics.

questions.title: Handling serialisation failures
questions.prompt: How should an application handle transaction serialization failures?

expectedConcepts.label: Serializable and some repeatable-read transactions can abort on conflicts
Retry the whole transaction from the start
Limit retries with backoff; keep transactions short and side effects outside

questions.modelAnswer: Under serializable isolation, and repeatable read in some databases, the database prevents anomalies by aborting one of two conflicting transactions with a serialisation failure, SQLSTATE 40001 in PostgreSQL. This is expected behaviour, not a bug. The correct response is to retry the entire transaction from the beginning, re-reading the data, because the decisions it made were based on values that changed; retrying only the failed statement is wrong. Wrap transactions in a helper that retries a limited number of times with backoff and jitter. Keep transactions short to reduce conflicts, and never perform external side effects, such as sending email, inside a transaction that might be retried.

questions.title: Logical versus physical replication
questions.prompt: How do logical and physical replication differ?

expectedConcepts.label: Physical replication copies storage-level changes byte for byte
Logical replication sends row-level changes that are decoded
Physical: exact replica, same version; logical: selective, cross-version, but gaps like DDL

questions.modelAnswer: Physical replication ships the low-level write-ahead log, changes to disk blocks, to a replica that applies them byte for byte.
