The replica is an exact copy of the entire cluster, must run the same major version and architecture, and is read-only; it is simple, fast and ideal for failover and read replicas. Logical replication decodes those changes into row-level operations, such as insert this row into this table, and sends them to subscribers. That allows replicating only selected tables, replicating between different major versions, which enables near-zero-downtime upgrades, and feeding other systems through change data capture. Its costs are more overhead and gaps: schema changes and sequences are often not replicated automatically, and conflicts are possible on writable subscribers.

questions.title: Data retention policies and index design
questions.prompt: What is a data retention policy, and how can it affect index design?

expectedConcepts.label: A rule for how long each kind of data is kept before deletion
Deleting old rows needs efficient time-based access
Partition by time to drop whole partitions instead of mass deletes

questions.modelAnswer: A data retention policy states how long each kind of data is kept, for example logs for 30 days or invoices for seven years, based on legal requirements, privacy principles such as data minimisation, and cost. Enforcing it means regularly deleting or archiving old data, and that shapes the schema. Mass DELETE statements on a huge table are slow, cause lock contention and bloat, and churn every index, so you at least need an index on the timestamp used to find expiring rows and should delete in small batches. Better, partition large tables by time, such as by month, so expiring data means simply dropping an old partition, which is instant and leaves no bloat.

questions.title: Reverse proxies versus forward proxies
questions.prompt: How does a reverse proxy differ from a forward proxy?

expectedConcepts.label: Forward proxy acts for clients reaching the internet
Reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts for them
Reverse proxies do TLS, load balancing, caching and protection
An extra hop and a component that must be redundant

questions.modelAnswer: Both sit in the middle of a connection, but they represent different sides. A forward proxy acts on behalf of clients: browsers inside a company send their outbound requests through it, and it can filter content, cache, log, or hide the clients' addresses from websites. A reverse proxy acts on behalf of servers: clients on the internet connect to it thinking it is the website, and it forwards requests to backend servers they never see directly. Reverse proxies such as Nginx, Envoy or a CDN terminate TLS, balance load across backends, cache responses, compress, enforce rate limits and absorb attacks. The price is an extra hop and a critical component on the request path, so a reverse proxy must itself be redundant.

questions.title: TLS certificate validation failures
questions.prompt: What happens during a TLS certificate validation failure?

expectedConcepts.label: The client refuses the connection because it cannot trust the certificate
Causes: expired, wrong hostname, missing intermediate, unknown CA, clock wrong
Fix the certificate; never disable verification

questions.modelAnswer: During the TLS handshake, the server presents its certificate chain and the client checks that it chains up to a trusted root certificate authority, that it is within its validity dates, that the hostname matches, and that it has not been revoked. If any check fails, the client aborts the handshake: browsers show a warning page and programs throw an error. Common causes are an expired certificate, a hostname mismatch, a server that forgets to send the intermediate certificate, a private CA the client does not trust, or a client with a wrong system clock. Diagnose with openssl s_client or curl -v and fix the certificate; disabling verification exposes you to man-in-the-middle attacks.

questions.title: DNS TTLs, failover and caching
questions.prompt: How do DNS TTLs affect failover and caching?

expectedConcepts.label: TTL is how long resolvers may cache a record
Failover by changing records only takes effect as caches expire
Short TTLs speed changes but add query load; some clients ignore TTLs

questions.modelAnswer: Every DNS record has a time-to-live that tells resolvers and clients how long they may cache the answer. If you fail over by pointing a hostname at a new IP address, clients keep using the cached old address until their TTL expires, so a one-hour TTL can mean up to an hour of traffic still going to the dead server. Short TTLs, such as 30 to 60 seconds, allow faster failover and migrations, at the cost of more DNS queries and more dependence on DNS availability. A common practice is lowering the TTL a day before a planned migration. Beware that some clients, such as JVMs and long-lived connections, cache longer than the TTL.

questions.title: Connection pooling and keep-alive
questions.prompt: How do connection pooling and keep-alive reduce network overhead?

expectedConcepts.label: Each new connection costs handshakes and slow start
Keep-alive reuses one connection for many requests; pools share them
Mind idle timeouts, stale connections and pool sizing

questions.modelAnswer: Opening a new connection is expensive: a TCP handshake takes a round trip, TLS adds one or two more plus CPU for cryptography, and a fresh connection starts with a small congestion window, so early transfers are slow. HTTP keep-alive leaves the connection open after a response so later requests reuse it, and connection pools in HTTP and database clients keep several open connections ready to share across requests. That cuts latency and CPU significantly for chatty services. The pitfalls: idle connections may be closed by servers, load balancers or NAT devices, so clients must handle stale connections and set idle timeouts shorter than the other side's, and pools must be sized sensibly.

questions.title: Sockets and accepting connections
questions.prompt: What is a socket, and how does a server accept client connections?

expectedConcepts.label: A socket is an endpoint for network communication, an IP address plus port
Server calls socket, bind, listen and accept; client calls connect
Each accepted connection gets its own socket; servers handle many with threads or event loops

questions.modelAnswer: A socket is the operating system's endpoint for network communication, identified by an IP address, a port and a protocol, which programs use through a file descriptor. A TCP server creates a socket, binds it to an address and port such as 0.0.0.0:443, and calls listen, so the kernel starts completing handshakes and queuing incoming connections. Each call to accept takes one queued connection and returns a brand-new socket dedicated to that client, while the listening socket keeps waiting for more. The client side simply creates a socket and calls connect. To serve many clients at once, servers use threads, processes, or an event loop with non-blocking sockets.

questions.title: Packet loss and application latency
questions.prompt: How do packet loss and retransmission affect application latency?

expectedConcepts.label: TCP must detect and retransmit lost packets before delivering data
Timeouts and head-of-line blocking delay everything behind the lost packet
Small loss rates cause big tail latency; congestion control cuts throughput

questions.modelAnswer: TCP guarantees ordered delivery, so when a packet is lost, the receiver cannot pass later data to the application until the missing packet is retransmitted. The sender detects loss either through duplicate acknowledgements, a fast retransmit after about one round trip, or through a retransmission timeout, which can be hundreds of milliseconds or more. Meanwhile every byte behind the gap waits, which is head-of-line blocking. Loss is also treated as congestion, so the sender shrinks its window and throughput drops. As a result, even one percent packet loss can dramatically raise p99 latency, which is why loss on mobile and Wi-Fi networks motivated QUIC.

questions.title: Preserving the client IP through proxies
questions.prompt: How do proxies preserve the original client IP safely?

expectedConcepts.label: Behind a proxy the server sees the proxy address, not the client
X-Forwarded-For, Forwarded header or PROXY protocol carry it
Only trust headers set by your own known proxies; clients can spoof them

questions.modelAnswer: When traffic passes through a load balancer or reverse proxy, the backend sees a connection from the proxy, so the original client address is lost. Proxies pass it along in the X-Forwarded-For header, which accumulates one address per hop, the standard Forwarded header, or, at layer 4, the PROXY protocol prefix. The danger is that clients can send their own fake X-Forwarded-For header to bypass IP-based rate limits or allow-lists. So the backend should only accept the header from known proxy addresses, and take the address added by the last trusted proxy, reading from the right, rather than the leftmost value supplied by the client.

questions.title: Debugging intermittent DNS failures
questions.prompt: How would you debug intermittent DNS resolution failures?

expectedConcepts.label: Pin down which resolver, record and client fail, and when
Query directly with dig, compare resolvers, check timeouts and UDP limits
Common causes: overloaded resolvers, conntrack races, search domains, flaky upstream

questions.modelAnswer: Intermittent problems need data, so first log every failure with the hostname, the error type such as timeout versus NXDOMAIN, the client and the resolver used. Then reproduce with dig in a loop against the configured resolver and against the authoritative servers, to see whether the problem is the local resolver, the network path or the authoritative zone. Typical causes include an overloaded or rate-limited resolver; packet loss on UDP; in Kubernetes, conntrack races dropping parallel A and AAAA queries, or ndots and search domains multiplying queries; and one misconfigured authoritative server among several. Mitigations include local caching resolvers, fixing the configuration and adding retries.

questions.title: Connection draining during rolling deployments
questions.prompt: What is connection draining during a rolling deployment?

expectedConcepts.label: Stop sending new requests to an instance before stopping it
Let in-flight requests finish within a timeout
Long-lived connections need a deadline or reconnect logic

questions.modelAnswer: In a rolling deployment, old instances are replaced one by one. If you just kill an instance, requests it is processing fail and clients see errors. Connection draining means first removing the instance from the load balancer or marking it not ready, so it receives no new requests, then giving in-flight requests a grace period to complete before the process exits. The application cooperates by handling SIGTERM: stop accepting new work, finish current requests, close keep-alive connections cleanly, then exit. Long-lived connections such as WebSockets or streaming responses cannot wait forever, so they get a drain deadline after which they are closed and clients reconnect to new instances.

questions.title: Split-horizon DNS
questions.prompt: What is split-horizon DNS, and when is it useful?

expectedConcepts.label: The same name resolves differently depending on who asks
Resolvers choose views by source network or VPC
Useful for private addresses, but confusing to debug

questions.modelAnswer: Split-horizon DNS returns different answers for the same hostname depending on where the query comes from. For example, api.example.com resolves to a private 10.x address for clients inside the corporate network or VPC, and to a public load balancer address for everyone else. Cloud providers implement this with private hosted zones attached to VPCs. It is useful for routing internal traffic over private networks, avoiding hairpinning through the internet, and keeping internal hostnames from leaking. The downside is confusion: a name that works on one laptop fails on another, so troubleshooting must always ask which resolver and view a client is using.

questions.title: Works by IP address but fails by hostname
questions.prompt: Why can a service work by IP address but fail by hostname?

expectedConcepts.label: Hostname adds DNS resolution, which may fail or return another address
TLS SNI and certificate names and HTTP Host routing depend on the name
Check with dig, hosts file and curl --resolve

questions.modelAnswer: Using the hostname adds steps that using the IP address skips. First, DNS: the name might not resolve, resolve to a different or stale address, resolve to an IPv6 address that is not reachable, or be overridden in the hosts file. Second, many servers use the name itself: TLS uses Server Name Indication to choose a certificate, and the certificate must match the hostname; reverse proxies and virtual hosts route by the HTTP Host header. Accessing by IP may hit a default site, or the reverse. Diagnose by checking what the name resolves to with dig or nslookup, then use curl with --resolve to test the hostname against a specific IP.

questions.title: Network namespaces for containers
questions.prompt: How do network namespaces isolate container networking?

expectedConcepts.label: Each namespace has its own interfaces, routes, ports and firewall rules
veth pairs connect the namespace to a bridge on the host
Plugins such as CNI wire it up; overlays add overhead

questions.modelAnswer: A Linux network namespace gives a process its own isolated copy of the network stack: its own interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, firewall rules and port space, so two containers can both listen on port 80 without conflict. A new namespace contains only a loopback interface, so container runtimes connect it to the host with a virtual Ethernet pair, one end inside the namespace and the other attached to a bridge on the host. The host then routes or NATs traffic to the outside world, and published ports are forwarded with NAT rules. In Kubernetes, CNI plugins set this up, sometimes with overlay networks between hosts, which add encapsulation overhead.

questions.title: Layer 4 versus layer 7 health checks
questions.prompt: What are the trade-offs between L4 and L7 health checks?

expectedConcepts.label: L4 checks only that a TCP connection can be opened
L7 checks send an HTTP request and validate the response
L7 detects more failures but is costlier and can cascade if it checks dependencies

questions.modelAnswer: A layer 4 health check only verifies that the port accepts a TCP connection. It is cheap and protocol-agnostic, but it misses many failures: a process whose listener is up but whose application threads are deadlocked, or which returns 500 for every request, still looks healthy. A layer 7 check sends a real HTTP request to a health endpoint and inspects the status code or body, catching application-level failures. The trade-offs: L7 checks cost more and depend on a well-designed endpoint. If the endpoint also checks shared dependencies such as the database, a brief database blip can make every instance fail at once and the load balancer removes them all, turning a partial problem into a total outage.

questions.title: Investigating 502 or 504 across a proxy chain
questions.prompt: How would you investigate a 502 or 504 response across a proxy chain?

expectedConcepts.label: 502 is a bad upstream response; 504 is an upstream timeout
Find which hop generated it using headers, logs and request IDs
Common causes: timeouts mismatched, upstream crashes, connection resets

questions.modelAnswer: Both are produced by a proxy, not by the application: 502 Bad Gateway means the proxy got an invalid response or a connection error from the next hop, and 504 Gateway Timeout means the next hop did not answer in time. With a chain such as CDN, load balancer, ingress and service, first work out which hop generated the error, using response headers, the error page format, and logs correlated by request ID and timestamp. Then examine the hop behind it: for 504s, compare timeouts, since an inner timeout longer than the outer one causes this; for 502s, look for crashed or restarting upstreams, connection resets, and keep-alive timeouts where the backend closes idle connections first.

questions.title: File descriptors and descriptor leaks
questions.prompt: What is a file descriptor, and how can descriptor leaks break a service?

expectedConcepts.label: An integer handle to an open file, socket or pipe
Leaks: descriptors opened and never closed until the limit is hit
Close in finally or defer; monitor counts with lsof or proc

questions.modelAnswer: A file descriptor is a small integer the kernel gives a process to refer to an open resource: a file, socket, pipe or device. Every process has a limit on how many it can have open, often 1024 by default, set by ulimit. A descriptor leak happens when code opens files or connections but does not close them on every path, for example when an error skips the close call. The count grows slowly until the limit, then every new accept, connect or open fails with "too many open files", so the service stops accepting connections. Prevent it with structured cleanup such as try-with-resources, with statements or defer, and monitor descriptor counts using lsof or /proc.

questions.title: Buffered versus direct I/O
questions.prompt: What is the difference between buffered and direct I/O?

expectedConcepts.label: Buffered I/O goes through the kernel page cache
Direct I/O bypasses the page cache and transfers to the device
Direct I/O helps databases with their own caches but needs alignment and care

questions.modelAnswer: By default, reads and writes are buffered: data is copied through the kernel's page cache, so repeated reads are served from memory, the kernel reads ahead for sequential access, and writes return quickly and are flushed to disk later. Direct I/O, using the O_DIRECT flag, bypasses the page cache and transfers data between the application's buffer and the storage device. Databases such as Oracle, MySQL InnoDB and some storage engines use it because they keep their own buffer pool; going through the page cache too would cache everything twice and make memory use less predictable. Direct I/O requires aligned buffers and sizes, loses read-ahead, and is slower for applications without their own caching.

questions.title: CPU affinity and performance
questions.prompt: How does CPU affinity influence performance and scheduling?

expectedConcepts.label: Affinity restricts which CPU cores a thread may run on
Pinning keeps caches warm and avoids migrations; isolate cores from other work
Lower jitter for latency-critical work, but can cause imbalance

questions.modelAnswer: CPU affinity tells the scheduler which cores a process or thread is allowed to run on, set with taskset, sched_setaffinity or container CPU sets. Normally the scheduler moves threads between cores to balance load, which costs performance because the thread loses its warm L1 and L2 caches, and on NUMA systems it may end up far from its memory. Pinning a latency-critical thread to a dedicated core, ideally one isolated from other processes and from interrupt handling, gives very predictable latency, which is common in trading systems and packet processing. The cost is flexibility: pinned threads cannot move when their core is busy, so bad pinning creates imbalance and lowers overall throughput.

questions.title: Signals in multithreaded programs
questions.prompt: How do signals interact with multithreaded programs?

expectedConcepts.label: Process-directed signals go to any one thread that does not block them
Common pattern: block signals in all threads and handle them in one dedicated thread
Handlers must be async-signal-safe; avoid locks and malloc

questions.modelAnswer: Every thread has its own signal mask, but signal handlers are shared by the whole process. A signal sent to the process, such as SIGTERM from kill, is delivered to an arbitrary thread that is not blocking it, while signals caused by a thread's own fault, such as SIGSEGV, go to that thread. This makes handling unpredictable, and signal handlers interrupt whatever the thread was doing, so they may only call async-signal-safe functions: calling malloc, printf or taking a lock in a handler can deadlock. A robust pattern is to block the signals in all threads at startup and have one dedicated thread wait for them with sigwait or signalfd, handling them as normal events.

questions.title: File permissions versus Linux capabilities
questions.prompt: How do file permissions and capabilities differ in Linux?

expectedConcepts.label: File permissions control read, write and execute per owner, group and others
Capabilities split root privileges into separate units
Grant only needed capabilities instead of full root

questions.modelAnswer: Traditional file permissions answer "who can access this file?": read, write and execute bits for the owner, the group and everyone else, plus ACLs and special bits such as setuid. Capabilities answer a different question, "which privileged operations may this process perform?". Historically root could do everything; Linux splits that power into distinct capabilities, such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind ports below 1024, CAP_NET_ADMIN to configure networking, or CAP_SYS_ADMIN for many administrative actions. A web server can be given only the capability to bind port 443 instead of running as root, and container runtimes drop most capabilities by default, which follows the principle of least privilege.

questions.title: A leader crash during a replicated write
questions.prompt: What happens when a leader crashes during a replicated write?

expectedConcepts.label: The outcome depends on whether the write reached a majority
A new leader is elected with all committed entries; uncommitted ones may be lost
Clients may not know the result and must retry idempotently

questions.modelAnswer: In a consensus-based system like Raft, a leader appends the write to its log and replicates it to followers; it is committed once a majority has stored it. If the leader crashes before that, the write may exist on only some nodes. A new leader is elected, and the voting rules guarantee it has every committed entry, so committed writes survive. An uncommitted write may survive if the new leader happens to have it, or be discarded. The client usually just sees a timeout or connection error, so it does not know whether the write happened. It must retry, which is safe only if the operation is idempotent or carries a unique request ID the system deduplicates.

questions.title: Read-your-writes consistency
questions.prompt: Users edit their profile, and the page still shows the old name for a few seconds because reads go to a replica. How does read-your-writes consistency fix this?

expectedConcepts.label: A user always sees their own previous writes
Route the user to the leader or a caught-up replica after writing
Cheaper than strong consistency; matters for profiles and posts

questions.modelAnswer: Read-your-writes is a session guarantee: after a user writes something, their own subsequent reads will reflect it, even if other users may briefly see older data. Without it, replication lag produces confusing experiences: you edit your profile or post a comment, the page reloads from a lagging replica, and your change appears to have vanished. Implementations include reading from the leader for a short time after a user writes, tracking the write's log position or timestamp and only reading from replicas that have caught up to it, or pinning the session to one replica. It is much cheaper than making the whole system strongly consistent.

questions.title: Consumer lag as a user-facing problem
questions.prompt: Users complain that order emails arrive an hour late, but every service is up. How can consumer lag cause this, and what would you monitor?

expectedConcepts.label: Lag is how far consumers are behind the newest messages
Grows when consumers process slower than producers produce
Users see stale data and delayed notifications; alert on lag age

questions.modelAnswer: In a log or queue such as Kafka, consumer lag is the difference between the newest message produced and the last one a consumer group has processed, measured in messages or, more usefully, in time. It grows whenever consumers process more slowly than producers write, because of a traffic spike, a slow database, a bug causing retries, or too few consumers or partitions. Users feel it as staleness: an order confirmation email arriving an hour late, a search index missing new products, or a dashboard showing old balances. Monitor lag as time behind, alert before it violates freshness expectations, and fix it by scaling consumers, which partitions limit, batching, or removing the slow step.

questions.title: Replicated logs and state-machine replication
questions.prompt: How do replicated logs support state-machine replication?

expectedConcepts.label: Deterministic state machines that apply the same commands in the same order end in the same state
Consensus agrees on an ordered log of commands replicated to every node
Snapshots compact the log; nondeterminism breaks replicas

questions.modelAnswer: State-machine replication rests on a simple idea: if several replicas start in the same state and apply the same deterministic commands in the same order, they end up in the same state. So the hard problem becomes agreeing on that order. A consensus protocol such as Raft or Paxos builds a replicated log: the leader proposes each command as the next entry, and once a majority accepts it, it is committed, and every replica applies committed entries to its local state machine in log order. This is how etcd, ZooKeeper and many databases stay consistent. Commands must be deterministic, so no local clocks or random values, and logs are periodically compacted with snapshots.

questions.title: Consensus versus leader election
questions.prompt: What is the difference between consensus and leader election?

expectedConcepts.label: Consensus: nodes agree on values, such as each log entry, despite failures
Leader election: choosing one node to coordinate
Election alone does not guarantee safety; it needs consensus or leases and fencing

questions.modelAnswer: Consensus is the general problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a value, or a sequence of values, such that all correct nodes decide the same thing even when some fail. Leader election is a narrower task: picking one node to act as coordinator. They are related: Raft uses leader election as a step, and you can implement election using consensus by agreeing on who the leader is for a given term. But electing a leader is not enough for correctness on its own: because of network delays and pauses, an old leader may still believe it leads while a new one is elected. Safety requires that every decision goes through a majority, or that resources are protected with leases and fencing tokens.

questions.title: Tombstones in replicated storage
questions.prompt: In a Cassandra-style store, deleted records occasionally reappear days later. How do tombstones prevent this, and what do they cost?

expectedConcepts.label: A deletion marker stored instead of removing the data immediately
Prevents deleted data from being resurrected by stale replicas
Tombstones must be kept for a grace period and slow reads if they pile up

questions.modelAnswer: In eventually consistent, replicated stores such as Cassandra or DynamoDB-style systems, you cannot simply erase a record on delete. If one replica missed the delete and later syncs with the others, it would see the record as present and copy it back, resurrecting deleted data. So a delete writes a tombstone, a special marker with a timestamp that says this key was deleted, which replicates like any other write and wins over older values during reads and repair. Tombstones must be kept long enough for all replicas to learn about them, such as Cassandra's gc_grace_seconds, before compaction removes them. Large numbers of tombstones slow down reads, so delete-heavy patterns need care.

questions.title: Rolling out schema changes across services
questions.prompt: How can schema changes be rolled out safely across independently deployed services?

expectedConcepts.label: Producers and consumers deploy at different times, so versions overlap
Expand and contract: add compatibly, migrate consumers, then remove
Enforce compatibility with schema registries and contract tests

questions.modelAnswer: When services deploy independently, there is always a period when old and new versions run side by side, so every schema change, whether to a database, an API or an event, must work with both. The safe pattern is expand and contract. First expand: make only backward-compatible additions, such as new optional fields or new tables, with defaults so old readers ignore them. Then migrate: update producers to write the new form and consumers to read it, possibly writing both forms for a while. Only when nothing uses the old field anymore, contract by removing it. Never rename or change the type of a field in place. Schema registries with compatibility rules and consumer-driven contract tests enforce this in CI.

questions.title: Saga orchestration versus choreography
questions.prompt: What is a saga orchestration versus choreography trade-off?

expectedConcepts.label: Orchestration: a central coordinator tells each service what to do
Choreography: services react to each other's events without a coordinator
Orchestration is easier to follow and change; choreography is looser but harder to trace

questions.modelAnswer: A saga implements a business transaction across services as a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating action if a later step fails. With orchestration, a central orchestrator, often a workflow engine like Temporal or Step Functions, explicitly calls each service, tracks the state of the saga and triggers compensations; the flow is visible in one place and easy to change, but the orchestrator is an extra component that knows about every participant. With choreography, there is no coordinator: each service listens for events and publishes its own, such as OrderCreated then PaymentReserved. This is loosely coupled and simple for short flows, but as steps grow, the overall process becomes hard to understand, trace and debug.

questions.title: Duplicate events in analytics and billing
questions.prompt: How can duplicate events affect analytics and billing?

expectedConcepts.label: At-least-once delivery and retries produce duplicate events
Duplicates inflate counts, revenue and usage charges
Use unique event IDs and dedupe or idempotent aggregation

questions.modelAnswer: Most messaging systems deliver at least once, and clients, producers and pipelines retry, so the same event can arrive several times. In analytics, duplicates silently inflate metrics such as page views, signups or conversion rates, which can lead to wrong product decisions. In billing they are worse: a usage event processed twice overcharges a customer, damaging trust and creating support and legal problems. The defence is giving every event a unique, stable ID at the source, deduplicating on that ID at ingestion or in the warehouse, making aggregations idempotent, for example with upserts keyed by event ID, and reconciling billed totals against an independent source before invoicing.

questions.title: Testing distributed workflows under failures
questions.prompt: How would you test a distributed workflow under partitions and delayed messages?

expectedConcepts.label: Inject faults: partitions, delays, duplicates, reordering and crashes
Tools: network fault injection, simulation, deterministic testing, Jepsen
Check invariants rather than exact outputs; reproduce with seeds

questions.modelAnswer: Unit tests run in a perfect network, so distributed bugs hide. Testing them means deliberately injecting the failures that happen in production: dropped and delayed messages, duplicates, reordering, network partitions between specific services, process crashes and restarts at awkward moments, and clock skew. Tools range from proxies such as Toxiproxy and chaos tooling in staging, to deterministic simulation where the whole system runs in one process with a controlled scheduler and network, as FoundationDB does, to Jepsen-style tests for databases. Instead of asserting exact outputs, check invariants: no money created or lost, every order eventually completes or is compensated. Record random seeds so failures are reproducible.

questions.title: Database-shaped APIs
questions.prompt: What are the benefits and risks of exposing database-shaped APIs?

expectedConcepts.label: API resources mirror database tables one to one
Fast to build, but clients couple to internal schema
Design around client use cases and domain operations instead

questions.modelAnswer: A database-shaped API exposes each table as a resource with generic create, read, update and delete endpoints, sometimes generated automatically. It is quick to build and flexible for internal tools. The risks are significant for public or long-lived APIs: clients become coupled to your internal schema, so you can no longer refactor tables without breaking them; business rules end up spread across clients, which must make several calls and coordinate updates; generic updates allow invalid state transitions; and it is easy to leak internal fields. Better APIs model the domain and client use cases, such as POST /orders/{id}/cancel, with a stable contract that hides storage details.

questions.title: API composition and latency
questions.prompt: What is API composition, and when can it create latency problems?

expectedConcepts.label: One endpoint gathers data by calling several downstream services
Sequential calls add up; overall latency follows the slowest call
Use parallel calls, timeouts, partial results and caching

questions.modelAnswer: API composition is when one endpoint, often in a gateway or backend-for-frontend, builds its response by calling several services, such as fetching an order, the customer and shipment status, and combining the results. Latency problems appear when calls are sequential, so their latencies add up, or when the fan-out is wide: even in parallel the response waits for the slowest call, and with many calls the chance that one is slow rises sharply, so tail latency gets worse. Mitigations include calling independent services in parallel, giving each a timeout, returning partial results when non-essential parts fail, caching, and for heavy cases precomputing a read model.

questions.title: Handling unknown request fields
questions.prompt: What should happen when a client sends an unknown field?

expectedConcepts.label: Choose between rejecting and ignoring unknown fields
Rejecting catches typos and mass assignment; ignoring helps compatibility
Document the rule and apply it consistently; never bind unknown fields to models blindly

questions.modelAnswer: There are two defensible choices. Strict validation rejects requests with unknown fields, returning a 400 that names the field. This catches client typos, such as "emial", which would otherwise be silently ignored, and prevents mass-assignment attacks where a client sets fields like isAdmin. Lenient handling ignores unknown fields, which follows the tolerant-reader principle and helps clients built against a newer version talk to an older server. Many APIs are strict for requests and expect clients to tolerate unknown fields in responses. Whatever you choose, document it, apply it consistently, and never bind request bodies directly to internal models without an allow-list.

questions.title: Gateway authentication versus service authorisation
questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication at a gateway and authorization in a service?

expectedConcepts.label: The gateway verifies who the caller is, such as validating a token
The service decides what that caller may do with specific data
Do not rely on the gateway alone; services must check permissions and verify identity propagation

questions.modelAnswer: An API gateway is a good place to authenticate: it verifies tokens or API keys, rejects anonymous traffic early and passes the verified identity downstream. But authorisation, deciding whether this user may read this invoice or cancel this order, depends on domain data and ownership that only the owning service knows, so the service must enforce it on every request; missing object-level checks are the most common API vulnerability. Services should also not blindly trust an identity header, because anything that can reach them directly could forge it; they should verify a signed token or rely on mutual TLS between the gateway and services.

questions.title: GraphQL persisted queries
questions.prompt: What are the trade-offs of GraphQL persisted queries?

expectedConcepts.label: Clients send a hash or ID of a pre-registered query instead of the full text
Smaller requests, CDN caching with GET and an allow-list against abuse
Needs a build step to register queries and coordination with deployments

questions.modelAnswer: With persisted queries, query documents are registered with the server ahead of time, usually extracted at build time from the client code, and clients send only a hash or ID plus variables. Benefits: requests are much smaller, they can be sent as GET requests and cached by CDNs, and, if the server only accepts registered queries, it acts as an allow-list that blocks attackers from sending arbitrary expensive queries. The trade-offs: you need tooling to extract and register queries and to keep them in sync with app releases, old mobile app versions need their queries kept indefinitely, and you lose some of GraphQL's ad-hoc flexibility for third parties.

questions.title: Validation against resource-exhaustion attacks
questions.prompt: How can request validation prevent resource-exhaustion attacks?

expectedConcepts.label: Attackers send huge or expensive requests to exhaust CPU, memory or the database
Limit body size, array lengths, page size, nesting depth and query complexity
Combine with timeouts and rate limits; reject early before work

questions.modelAnswer: Many denial-of-service attacks do not need huge traffic, just a few requests that make the server do enormous work: a 500 MB JSON body, an array with a million items, a page size of one million, a deeply nested object that blows up the parser, a GraphQL query nesting friends of friends ten levels deep, a regular expression vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking, or an uploaded zip bomb. Validation defends by enforcing limits before doing work: maximum body size at the proxy, maximum lengths, counts and depth in the schema, capped page sizes, query cost limits, and timeouts on expensive operations. Combined with rate limiting, this keeps one client from consuming the whole system.

questions.title: Training, validation and test sets
questions.prompt: How do training, validation, and test datasets serve different purposes?

expectedConcepts.label: Training data fits the model parameters
Validation data tunes hyperparameters and selects models
Test data is touched once for an unbiased final estimate

questions.modelAnswer: The training set is what the model learns from: the algorithm adjusts its parameters to fit it. The validation set is held out from training and used to make decisions about the model, such as choosing hyperparameters, comparing architectures and deciding when to stop training. Because you repeatedly look at validation results, you slowly overfit to them, so a third set, the test set, is kept untouched until the end and used once to estimate how the final model will perform on new data. If you tune on the test set, its score becomes optimistically biased. The splits must also reflect reality, for example splitting by time or by user when that is how the model will be used.

questions.title: Model calibration
questions.prompt: What is calibration, and why can a well-ranked model still be poorly calibrated?

expectedConcepts.label: Calibrated: predicted probabilities match observed frequencies
Ranking metrics like AUC ignore the probability scale
Fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression; check reliability diagrams

questions.modelAnswer: A model is calibrated if its predicted probabilities mean what they say: among all cases where it predicts 70 percent, about 70 percent are actually positive. Ranking quality, measured by metrics such as ROC-AUC, only cares whether positives get higher scores than negatives, not what the numbers are. So a model can rank perfectly while all its scores are squeezed between 0.4 and 0.6, or are systematically overconfident, as boosted trees, deep networks and models trained on resampled data often are. Calibration matters whenever probabilities drive decisions, such as expected cost, risk thresholds or medical advice. Check it with reliability diagrams and fix it with Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling on held-out data.

questions.title: Linear models versus neural networks
questions.prompt: When would you choose a linear model over a neural network?

expectedConcepts.label: Linear models suit small or tabular data with mostly additive effects
They are fast, interpretable and a strong baseline
Neural networks win with large data and complex patterns like images or text

questions.modelAnswer: Choose a linear model, such as linear or logistic regression, when the data set is small or medium, the features are tabular and fairly informative, and you need speed, stability and interpretability: each coefficient shows how a feature moves the prediction, which matters in regulated fields such as credit or health. Linear models train in seconds, need little tuning and are hard to overfit with regularisation, so they are an excellent baseline. Neural networks earn their cost when there is a lot of data and the patterns are complex and nonlinear, especially for images, audio and text. For tabular data, gradient-boosted trees usually beat both before a neural network is needed.

questions.title: Online versus offline inference
questions.prompt: What is the difference between online and offline inference?

expectedConcepts.label: Online: predictions on demand per request with low latency
Offline: batch predictions computed ahead of time and stored
Online uses fresh features but is costlier to serve; batch is cheaper but stale

questions.modelAnswer: Online inference computes a prediction when it is needed, inside a request, such as scoring a card transaction for fraud in milliseconds. It can use the freshest features, like what the user just did, but requires a low-latency serving system that is always available and scales with traffic. Offline, or batch, inference runs the model on large sets of inputs on a schedule, such as nightly recommendations for every user, and stores the results for quick lookup. Batch is cheaper, simpler and can use bigger models, but predictions go stale and cannot react to recent events or new users. Many systems combine both: precompute candidates offline and rerank them online.

questions.title: Transfer learning
questions.prompt: What is transfer learning, and when does it help?

expectedConcepts.label: Reuse a model pretrained on a large dataset for a new task
Fine-tune all layers or train a new head on frozen features
Helps with little labelled data and related domains; can fail with very different data

questions.modelAnswer: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large, general dataset as the starting point for a new task. A network pretrained on millions of images has already learned edges, textures and shapes; a language model already understands grammar and meaning. You either freeze most of it and train only a new output layer on your data, or fine-tune the whole model with a small learning rate. It helps most when you have little labelled data, compute is limited, and the new task is related to the original, for example classifying medical photos with an ImageNet model. It helps less, or can even hurt, when your data is very different, such as spectrograms or sensor signals.

questions.title: Gradient clipping
questions.prompt: What is gradient clipping, and what problem can it mitigate?

expectedConcepts.label: Exploding gradients make updates huge and training unstable
Clip by norm or value so gradients stay below a threshold
Stabilises RNNs and transformers; does not fix vanishing gradients

questions.modelAnswer: During training, gradients can occasionally become extremely large, especially in recurrent networks, very deep networks and large transformers. One huge gradient causes a giant parameter update that throws the model far off course, producing loss spikes or NaN values. Gradient clipping limits this: most commonly, if the overall norm of the gradient vector exceeds a threshold such as 1.0, the whole vector is rescaled down to that norm, preserving its direction, or individual values are capped. This makes training much more stable and is standard for LLM training. It does not help with vanishing gradients, and constantly clipped gradients usually mean the learning rate is too high.

questions.title: Learning rate schedules
questions.prompt: How do learning rate schedules influence training?

expectedConcepts.label: The learning rate sets how big each update step is
Warmup then decay, such as cosine or step decay
Large steps explore quickly; small steps settle precisely; wrong schedule diverges or stalls

questions.modelAnswer: The learning rate controls how large each parameter update is. A single fixed value is a compromise: large enough to make fast progress early, small enough not to bounce around the minimum later. Schedules change it during training. Warmup starts small and ramps up over the first steps, which stabilises training of transformers and large batches while optimiser statistics settle. Decay then reduces it, in steps, exponentially or along a cosine curve, so the model makes big exploratory moves early and fine adjustments at the end, usually improving final accuracy. Too high a rate makes training diverge; too low a rate makes it slow or stuck, so the schedule is one of the most important hyperparameters.

questions.title: Building a baseline model early
questions.prompt: What is a baseline model, and why should one be built early?

expectedConcepts.label: A simple reference model, such as predicting the majority class or a linear model
Reveals pipeline bugs and gives a number to beat
Shows whether complexity is worth it

questions.modelAnswer: A baseline is the simplest reasonable solution: predicting the most common class or the average, a business rule, or a quick logistic regression or gradient-boosted model on obvious features. Building it first forces you to set up the whole pipeline end to end, data loading, splitting, metrics and evaluation, which flushes out bugs early. It gives a concrete number every more complex model must beat; a deep model that is only slightly better than a rule may not be worth its cost, latency and maintenance. Sometimes the baseline is already good enough to ship, and it remains a useful fallback in production.

questions.title: Finding subgroups where a model fails
questions.prompt: How would you detect a model that performs well overall but poorly for a subgroup?

expectedConcepts.label: Aggregate metrics hide weak performance on smaller groups
Evaluate sliced metrics by segment such as region, device or demographic
Need enough samples per slice; fix with data, features or thresholds

questions.modelAnswer: An overall accuracy of 95 percent can hide a group where the model is right only 60 percent of the time, because that group is a small share of the data. To find it, evaluate the model on slices: by region, language, device, customer type, new versus existing users, and, where appropriate and lawful, demographic groups, comparing metrics such as error rate, false positive and false negative rates. Tools can search automatically for underperforming slices. Make sure slices have enough samples, with confidence intervals, so you do not chase noise. Fixes include collecting more representative data, adding relevant features, or separate thresholds, and the slices should be monitored in production too.

questions.title: Correlation versus causation in features
questions.prompt: What is the difference between correlation and causation in feature analysis?

expectedConcepts.label: Correlation: features move together; causation: one changes the other
Confounders and reverse causality create correlations without causation
Predictive models can use correlations, but interventions need causal evidence

questions.modelAnswer: Two variables are correlated when they tend to move together; causation means changing one actually changes the other. Correlation can come from a confounder, such as ice cream sales and drownings both rising in summer, from reverse causality, or from chance. For pure prediction, correlations are fine: a feature that predicts churn is useful even if it does not cause churn. But when the business wants to act, for example "users who use feature X churn less, so let us push feature X", that conclusion requires causal evidence, because the users may simply be more engaged. Randomised experiments, or careful causal inference methods, are needed before intervening.

questions.title: A/B tests when users influence each other
questions.prompt: How can A/B testing be misleading when users influence one another?

expectedConcepts.label: Interference: treatment of one user affects outcomes of others
Examples: social features, marketplaces sharing supply
Randomise by cluster, region or time instead of user

questions.modelAnswer: Standard A/B tests assume each user's outcome depends only on their own group. That breaks when users interact. In a social network, if treated users share more, control users who follow them also see more content, so the difference between groups shrinks. In a marketplace such as ride-hailing, if the treatment gets riders more drivers, the control group gets fewer, so the measured effect is exaggerated and would disappear on full launch. This interference biases results in either direction. Remedies include randomising by clusters of connected users, by city or region, or by time windows in switchback experiments, at the cost of fewer units and less statistical power.

questions.title: Feature stores and training-serving consistency
questions.prompt: How do feature stores help training-serving consistency?

expectedConcepts.label: Training-serving skew: features computed differently offline and online
One feature definition serves both a training store and a low-latency online store
Point-in-time correct joins prevent leakage; adds infrastructure

questions.modelAnswer: A common reason models perform worse in production than offline is training-serving skew: the features used in training were computed by a batch SQL job, while the serving code reimplements them in another language, slightly differently. A feature store defines each feature once and materialises it into two places: an offline store with full history for building training sets, and a low-latency online store for serving. It provides point-in-time correct joins, so training examples only use feature values that were known at the time, preventing leakage. Feature stores also enable reuse across teams and monitoring. The cost is substantial infrastructure, so they pay off for organisations with many models.

questions.title: Model cards
questions.prompt: What should be documented in an ML model card?

expectedConcepts.label: Intended use and out-of-scope uses
Training data, evaluation metrics and results by subgroup
Limitations, risks, ethical considerations and owner

questions.modelAnswer: A model card is short documentation that travels with a model so others can use it responsibly. It should state what the model does, its intended use cases and users, and uses it is not suitable for. It describes the training data: sources, time range, known gaps and preprocessing. It reports evaluation metrics on clearly described test data, broken down by relevant subgroups, along with the decision thresholds used. It lists known limitations, failure modes, fairness and safety risks, and recommendations for monitoring. It also records the version, date, owners and how to report issues. Model cards make models auditable and help prevent misuse in contexts they were never tested for.

questions.title: System, developer and user instructions
questions.prompt: How do system, developer, and user instructions differ in an LLM application?

expectedConcepts.label: System or developer messages set behaviour, rules and context
User messages carry the end user's requests
Models are trained to prioritise higher-level instructions but can still be overridden

questions.modelAnswer: LLM APIs separate messages by role. The system message, and in some APIs a developer message, comes from the application builder: it defines the assistant's role, rules, tone, output format, tools and boundaries, such as "only answer questions about our product". User messages are what the end user types. Models are trained with an instruction hierarchy that gives higher priority to system and developer instructions when they conflict with user requests, which is how apps keep their behaviour consistent. This protection is not absolute: users and retrieved content can still try to override it through prompt injection, so critical rules must also be enforced in code, not only in prompts.

questions.title: Semantic search versus keyword search
questions.prompt: What is the difference between semantic search and keyword search?

expectedConcepts.label: Keyword search matches terms, ranked by methods like BM25
Semantic search compares embedding vectors by meaning
Hybrid search combines both; keywords win on exact codes and names

questions.modelAnswer: Keyword search, also called lexical search, finds documents containing the query's words using an inverted index and ranks them with algorithms such as BM25. It is fast, transparent and great for exact identifiers like error codes, product numbers and names, but it misses synonyms and paraphrases: a search for "car" may miss "automobile". Semantic search converts queries and documents into embedding vectors and finds documents whose meaning is close, handling paraphrases and even other languages, but it can miss exact terms and is harder to debug. Production retrieval systems often use hybrid search, running both and merging the results, followed by a reranker.

questions.title: When retrieved context is insufficient
questions.prompt: What should an LLM application do when the retrieved context is insufficient?

expectedConcepts.label: Detect weak or missing evidence instead of guessing
Say it does not know, ask a clarifying question or search again
Instruct and test the model to refuse rather than hallucinate

questions.modelAnswer: The worst outcome is the model filling the gap from its own memory and confidently inventing an answer that looks grounded. The application should detect when retrieval is weak, using relevance scores, rerankers or asking the model to judge whether the context answers the question. Then it can try to recover, by rewriting the query, searching other sources or asking the user a clarifying question. If it still lacks evidence, it should say clearly that it could not find the answer in the available documents and suggest where to look or whom to contact. Prompt the model explicitly to answer only from the provided context, and include unanswerable questions in your evaluation set to test this behaviour.

questions.title: Checking citations in RAG
questions.prompt: How should citations be checked in a retrieval-augmented system?

expectedConcepts.label: Citations must point to sources that actually support the claim
Verify cited IDs exist in retrieved context and check entailment
Models can cite real documents for unsupported claims; evaluate citation precision and recall

questions.modelAnswer: Citations make answers verifiable, but models can produce citations that are wrong: pointing to documents that were never retrieved, citing a real document that does not say what the sentence claims, or leaving claims uncited. Checks should run in layers. Mechanically, verify every cited ID or URL exists in the retrieved context, and if quotes are used, that the quoted text appears in the source. Semantically, check that each cited passage entails the claim, using a natural language inference model or an LLM judge, and flag unsupported sentences. Measure citation precision, whether citations support claims, and recall, whether claims are cited, on an evaluation set, with human spot checks.

questions.title: Limiting agent permissions and steps
questions.prompt: How should an agent limit tool permissions and execution steps?

expectedConcepts.label: Least privilege: give only the tools and scopes needed
Cap steps, time and cost; require confirmation for risky actions
Sandbox execution and log every action for audit

questions.modelAnswer: An agent decides on its own which tools to call, and it can be wrong or manipulated through prompt injection, so its power must be bounded outside the model. Give it only the tools the task needs, with narrow credentials, such as read-only database access or one specific folder. Require human confirmation for irreversible or high-impact actions such as sending emails, spending money or deleting data. Cap the number of steps, the total time and the token or cost budget, so loops cannot run forever. Run code execution in a sandbox without network access by default, validate tool arguments, and log every action so behaviour can be audited.

questions.title: Agent loops versus fixed workflows
questions.prompt: What is the difference between an agent loop and a fixed workflow?

expectedConcepts.label: A workflow follows predefined steps written in code
An agent loop lets the model choose the next action until done
Workflows are predictable and cheaper; agents handle open-ended tasks but are less reliable

questions.modelAnswer: In a fixed workflow, the developer defines the steps and their order in code, for example retrieve documents, summarise them, then classify the summary. The LLM fills in each step, but the control flow is predictable, testable and cheap. In an agent loop, the model itself decides at each step what to do next: which tool to call, with what arguments, whether to try again, and when it is finished, repeating until the goal is reached. That flexibility handles open-ended tasks, such as debugging code or researching a question, where the steps cannot be known in advance, but agents are slower, costlier, harder to test and can wander off. Prefer workflows when the task is well understood.

questions.title: Measuring hallucination rate in production
questions.prompt: How would you measure hallucination rate in a production assistant?

expectedConcepts.label: Define hallucination as claims unsupported by sources or facts
Sample conversations and label them with humans or an LLM judge
Track over time and by topic; combine with user feedback signals

questions.modelAnswer: First define what counts: for a retrieval-based assistant, a hallucination is a claim not supported by the retrieved sources; for open questions, a factually false statement. Then measure it on a regular sample of real production conversations, with privacy controls, because you cannot review everything. Break answers into individual claims and label each as supported or not, using trained human reviewers and an automated LLM judge or entailment model calibrated against those human labels. Report the rate with confidence intervals, broken down by topic, feature and model version, and watch the trend after every change. User signals such as thumbs-down, corrections and escalations are useful leading indicators.

questions.title: Changing the embedding model behind a vector index
questions.prompt: How do embedding model changes affect an existing vector index?

expectedConcepts.label: Vectors from different models are not comparable
Re-embed the whole corpus and rebuild the index
Run old and new indexes side by side and evaluate before switching

questions.modelAnswer: Each embedding model maps text into its own vector space, often with a different dimension, so vectors from a new model cannot be compared with vectors from the old one. Even an updated version of the same model shifts the space. If queries are embedded with the new model while documents still use the old one, search quality collapses silently. So changing the model means re-embedding every document and building a new index. Do it as a migration: record the model version with each index, build the new index alongside the old one, evaluate retrieval quality on a test set, switch query traffic only when ready, and keep the old index for rollback. For large corpora, budget for the embedding cost.

questions.title: What to cache in an LLM application
questions.prompt: What should be cached in an LLM application, and what must not be cached?

expectedConcepts.label: Cache deterministic, shared work: embeddings, retrieval results, prompt prefixes
Exact or semantic response caches for repeated public questions
Never share cached answers across users with private data or permissions

questions.modelAnswer: Good candidates are work that is expensive and safe to reuse: embeddings of documents and frequent queries, retrieval results, provider-side prompt caching of long fixed prefixes such as system prompts and documents, and full responses to common, generic questions, either by exact match or by semantic similarity with a high threshold. Things that must not be cached in a shared way are answers that depend on a user's private data or permissions, since a cache hit could leak one user's information to another, so key such caches by user and permission scope or skip them. Also avoid caching answers based on fast-changing data without short expiry, and respect privacy rules about retaining personal data.

questions.title: Fallback when the model provider is unavailable
questions.prompt: How do you design a fallback when the primary model provider is unavailable?

expectedConcepts.label: Detect failures quickly with timeouts and error classification
Fall back to a secondary provider or model behind a common interface
Fallbacks differ in quality and policy; test them and degrade gracefully

questions.modelAnswer: Start with fast failure detection: strict timeouts, and classifying errors such as rate limits, server errors and outages separately from bad requests, which should not trigger a fallback. Put providers behind a common interface so the application can route a request to a secondary provider, or a smaller self-hosted model, with a circuit breaker so you stop hammering a provider that is down. Fallback models behave differently, so maintain prompts per model and evaluate the fallback path regularly, not just during outages. Check that each provider meets your privacy and data-processing commitments. If everything fails, degrade gracefully with a clear message, cached answers, or a non-AI path.

questions.title: Estimating token cost before launch
questions.prompt: How can you estimate token cost before shipping a feature?

expectedConcepts.label: Measure input and output tokens per request with a tokenizer
Multiply by expected requests and provider prices
Include retries, retrieval context and hidden reasoning tokens; set budgets

questions.modelAnswer: Build a realistic prototype and run it on a representative set of inputs, recording input and output tokens for each call with the provider's tokenizer or usage data. Remember everything that goes in: the system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents and tool definitions, plus hidden reasoning tokens for reasoning models, retries and multi-step agent calls. Multiply average tokens per user action by expected actions per user and number of users, then by the provider's input and output prices per million tokens, and look at the distribution, not just the average, since long conversations dominate. Then reduce cost with shorter prompts, caching and smaller models, and set budgets and alerts.

questions.title: Managing and compressing conversation history
questions.prompt: What is context-window management, and how can conversation history be compressed?

expectedConcepts.label: Deciding what fits in the limited context window each turn
Truncate old turns, summarise them, or retrieve relevant past messages
Compression loses detail; keep key facts and instructions pinned

questions.modelAnswer: Every model call has a maximum context length, and longer prompts also cost more and can reduce answer quality, so a chat application must decide what to send each turn. Simple strategies keep the system prompt plus the most recent turns in a sliding window and drop the oldest. Better ones summarise older parts of the conversation into a compact running summary, extract key facts such as the user's name, preferences and decisions into structured memory, and retrieve relevant older messages by similarity when needed. Compression always loses some detail, so pin essential instructions and facts, and test long conversations to confirm the assistant still remembers what matters.

questions.title: Sending sensitive user data to an external model
questions.prompt: How should sensitive user data be handled when calling an external model?

expectedConcepts.label: Send only the data needed; redact or pseudonymise personal fields
Check provider terms: retention, training use, region and contracts
Inform users, get consent where required and keep secrets out of logs

questions.modelAnswer: Treat the model provider like any other data processor. Send the minimum: strip or mask fields the task does not need, such as names, account numbers and contact details, or replace them with placeholders that are restored afterwards. Choose providers and settings that do not retain prompts longer than necessary or use them for training, with a data processing agreement and an appropriate data region for regulations like GDPR. Encrypt traffic, keep API keys server-side, and avoid logging full prompts and responses that contain personal data. Tell users when their data is processed by an AI service, and get explicit consent where required, especially for health, financial or children's data.

questions.title: RED and USE metrics
questions.prompt: How do RED and USE metrics differ, and when would you use each?

expectedConcepts.label: RED: rate, errors and duration for request-driven services
USE: utilisation, saturation and errors for resources
RED shows user experience; USE finds the bottleneck resource

questions.modelAnswer: They are two checklists for what to measure. RED, rate, errors and duration, applies to request-driven services such as APIs: how many requests per second, how many fail, and how long they take, ideally as latency percentiles. It describes what users experience and suits dashboards and alerts per service and endpoint. USE, utilisation, saturation and errors, applies to resources such as CPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces, thread pools and connection pools: how busy each one is, how much work is queued waiting for it, and its error counts. Use RED to notice that the service is slow and USE to find which resource is the bottleneck.

questions.title: Metric cardinality explosion
questions.prompt: What is cardinality explosion in metrics, and why is it costly?

expectedConcepts.label: Each unique label combination creates a separate time series
Labels like user ID, URL path or request ID multiply series
Explodes memory, cost and query time; use bounded labels and logs or traces for detail

questions.modelAnswer: In metric systems such as Prometheus, every unique combination of metric name and label values is a separate time series that must be stored, indexed and kept in memory. Labels with a few fixed values, like HTTP method or status class, are fine. But adding an unbounded label, such as user ID, request ID, email, full URL path with IDs in it, or error message text, multiplies the series count into millions. That causes high memory use, slow queries, ingestion limits, and large bills on hosted platforms, and can crash the monitoring system exactly when you need it. Keep labels bounded, normalise paths into route templates, and put per-request detail in logs and traces.

questions.title: From a user-facing symptom to a backend trace
questions.prompt: How do you connect a user-facing symptom to a backend trace?

expectedConcepts.label: Start with the specific failing user action and its time
Use a request or trace ID shown to the user or captured in frontend telemetry
Follow the trace across services to the slow or failing span

questions.modelAnswer: When a user reports that checkout failed, you need to find that exact request among millions. The link is an identifier: the frontend or edge assigns a request or trace ID, propagates it through every backend call, and shows it in error messages as a short support code or records it in real-user monitoring with the user's session. With that ID, or by filtering traces by user, endpoint and time window, you open the distributed trace and follow it across services to the span that failed or was slow, then jump to that service's logs for the same trace ID to see the error. Without propagated IDs, you are guessing from aggregate graphs.

questions.title: What an incident timeline captures
questions.prompt: What should an incident timeline capture?

expectedConcepts.label: Timestamped events: detection, impact start, actions and recovery
Who did what and why, including decisions and communications
Basis for postmortem metrics like time to detect and time to mitigate

questions.modelAnswer: An incident timeline is a chronological, timestamped record, ideally kept live during the incident by a scribe. It should capture when the problem actually started affecting users, which may be earlier than detection; when and how it was detected, whether by an alert or a customer; key observations and hypotheses; every action taken, such as rollbacks, restarts or config changes, by whom and with what effect; important decisions and why they were made; external communications to customers; and when impact was mitigated and fully resolved. Recording time zones consistently matters. The timeline feeds the blameless postmortem and metrics like time to detect and time to mitigate.

questions.title: SLI, SLO and SLA
questions.prompt: How do SLI, SLO, and SLA differ?

expectedConcepts.label: SLI: a measured indicator, such as the share of successful requests
SLO: an internal target for the SLI over a window
SLA: a contract with customers and penalties if missed
Too strict slows releases; too loose hides pain

questions.modelAnswer: A service level indicator is a carefully defined measurement of user experience, for example the percentage of HTTP requests that succeed in under 300 milliseconds, measured at the load balancer. A service level objective is the target the team sets for that indicator over a time window, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days; it guides engineering decisions and alerting. A service level agreement is a business contract with customers that promises a level of service and specifies consequences, typically service credits, if it is missed. SLAs are usually looser than internal SLOs, so the team gets warned and can react long before a contractual breach. Choosing the target is a trade-off: an SLO stricter than users need slows down releases, while a loose one lets real pain go unnoticed.

questions.title: Error budgets and release decisions
questions.prompt: How can error budgets guide release decisions?

expectedConcepts.label: Error budget: allowed unreliability, one minus the SLO
When the budget is healthy, ship faster; when burned, slow down and fix reliability
Turns reliability versus speed into an agreed, data-driven policy

questions.modelAnswer: An SLO of 99.9 percent availability means 0.1 percent of requests, or about 43 minutes a month, may fail; that allowance is the error budget. It turns the endless argument between moving fast and being reliable into a shared, measurable policy. While plenty of budget remains, the team can release frequently and take reasonable risks, since perfection is not the goal. If incidents or a bad release burn through the budget, the agreed policy kicks in: pause risky launches, require extra review or slower rollouts, and prioritise reliability work until the budget recovers. Burn-rate alerts warn when the budget is being consumed quickly.

questions.title: Narrowing down a p99 latency increase
questions.prompt: Your p99 latency alert fires while p50 stays flat. How do you narrow down whether one endpoint, one host or one dependency is responsible?

expectedConcepts.label: Check what changed at that time: deploys, traffic, config, dependencies
Break down by endpoint, instance and dependency; look at slow traces
Typical causes: GC pauses, saturation, lock contention, a slow downstream

questions.modelAnswer: A p99 rise means the slowest one percent of requests got slower, so averages may look fine. First correlate with changes at that moment: a deployment, a configuration or feature flag change, a traffic spike or new client behaviour, or an incident at a dependency. Then narrow down: is it all endpoints or one, all instances or a few, one region or availability zone? Pull example slow traces to see which span takes the extra time, such as a database query or a downstream call. Check resource saturation on the affected hosts, like CPU throttling, garbage-collection pauses, connection-pool waits or lock contention. Mitigate, for example by rolling back, before chasing the full root cause.

questions.title: A service dashboard during a database outage
questions.prompt: What should a service dashboard show during a database outage?

expectedConcepts.label: User impact first: error rate, latency and traffic for key endpoints
Database health: connections, query errors, replication and failover state
Dependency and pool views show whether errors are caused by the database

questions.modelAnswer: During an incident, a dashboard should answer quickly: how bad is it for users, where is the problem, and is the fix working? So the top row shows user impact: request rate, error rate and latency percentiles for the most important endpoints and journeys, compared with normal. Next, dependency health from the service's point of view: database query latency, error and timeout counts by type, connection-pool usage and wait time, so you can confirm the errors come from the database. Then the database itself: availability of primary and replicas, active connections, replication lag, failover events, CPU, disk and locks. Annotations for deployments and failovers help correlate events.

questions.title: Synthetic checks versus real-user monitoring
questions.prompt: How do synthetic checks differ from real-user monitoring?

expectedConcepts.label: Synthetic checks run scripted requests or journeys on a schedule
Real-user monitoring collects data from actual users' sessions
Synthetic catches outages even with no traffic; RUM shows true experience across devices

questions.modelAnswer: Synthetic monitoring runs scripted checks on a schedule from chosen locations: pinging an endpoint, or a headless browser that logs in and completes checkout every five minutes. Because conditions are controlled, results are consistent, regressions are easy to spot, and you detect outages even at night when there is no real traffic or before launch. But it only covers paths you scripted from a few locations. Real-user monitoring collects measurements, such as page loads, Core Web Vitals and errors, from actual users' browsers and apps, revealing the true experience across devices, networks and countries, but it is noisier and depends on traffic. Use both together.

questions.title: Reverse proxy versus load balancer versus API gateway
questions.prompt: How do a reverse proxy, a load balancer and an API gateway differ, and why can one product such as Nginx or Envoy play all three roles?

expectedConcepts.label: Reverse proxy fronts servers; a load balancer spreads traffic across replicas
Gateway adds API concerns: auth, rate limits, path routing
Roles overlap; each layer adds a hop and a failure point

questions.modelAnswer: A reverse proxy sits in front of one or more servers and handles requests on their behalf: it terminates TLS, caches, compresses and hides the backend topology from clients. A load balancer is a reverse proxy whose main job is spreading traffic across replicas, using algorithms such as round robin or least connections plus health checks, so failed instances get no traffic; it can work at layer 4 on connections or at layer 7 on HTTP requests. An API gateway is a layer 7 proxy with API-specific concerns: authentication, API keys, rate limits and quotas, routing by path or version to different services, and request transformation. The roles overlap, so Nginx or Envoy can do all three depending on configuration. The trade-off is that every layer adds a network hop, some latency and a component that must itself be redundant, so you add only the layers you need.

questions.title: Service discovery
questions.prompt: How do services find healthy instances of each other as they scale up and down? Compare client-side and server-side discovery.

expectedConcepts.label: A registry maps service names to live instance addresses
Client-side lookup versus server-side via a load balancer or DNS
Health checks, stale entries and a highly available registry

questions.modelAnswer: In a dynamic environment instance addresses change constantly, so services look each other up by name in a service registry such as Consul, etcd, ZooKeeper or the Kubernetes API. Instances register themselves or are registered by the platform, and health checks or heartbeats remove ones that stop responding. With client-side discovery the caller queries the registry, caches the list and picks an instance itself, which saves a hop and allows smarter balancing but puts discovery logic in every client library. With server-side discovery the caller sends to a stable address, such as a load balancer, a Kubernetes Service, a DNS name or a sidecar proxy, and that layer picks the instance. Trade-offs: DNS-based discovery suffers from caching and TTLs, so clients may keep hitting dead instances; any cached list can be stale, so callers still need timeouts and retries; and the registry becomes critical infrastructure that must be replicated and highly available.

questions.title: Resolving conflicts under eventual consistency
questions.prompt: Two replicas accept concurrent writes to the same record. Compare ways to resolve the conflict: last-write-wins, keeping siblings with version vectors, application-level merges and CRDTs. What does each risk losing?

expectedConcepts.label: Concurrent writes on different replicas must converge to one value
LWW keeps the latest timestamp; version vectors detect concurrency
LWW silently drops writes; merges need domain logic
