Short sessions, rotation, revocation and re-auth for sensitive actions

questions.modelAnswer: First, mark the session cookie HttpOnly, so JavaScript cannot read it at all, which stops the most common way XSS steals sessions; Secure, so it is only sent over HTTPS; and SameSite Lax or Strict, so other sites cannot make the browser send it. Second, add a strict Content-Security-Policy: allow scripts only from your own origin or with per-response nonces, and disallow inline scripts and eval, so injected code does not run even if a template bug slips through. Third, design sessions to limit what a stolen one is worth. Keep them short-lived with rotation, rotate the session ID at login and privilege changes, store sessions server-side so you can revoke them all after an incident, and require re-authentication for sensitive actions such as changing the email address or payout details. Some teams also bind sessions to device signals and flag sudden changes. Note that HttpOnly does not stop XSS from acting as the user inside the page; it only stops the cookie leaving, so fixing the injection remains essential.

questions.title: Detecting and stopping credential stuffing
questions.prompt: Login logs show thousands of failed attempts across many accounts from rotating IP addresses. How do you detect and stop credential stuffing without locking out real users?

expectedConcepts.label: Attackers replay leaked username and password pairs
Detect by failure rates, unusual devices and known-breached passwords
Step-up challenges and MFA instead of hard account lockouts

questions.modelAnswer: Credential stuffing replays username and password pairs leaked from other sites, relying on password reuse. Because it spreads over many accounts and rotating IP addresses, per-IP rate limits and per-account lockouts do little: each account sees one or two attempts, and lockouts would let attackers lock out real users deliberately. Detect it from aggregate signals: a spike in the global login failure rate, many accounts failing from the same device fingerprint or network, traffic from hosting providers, and logins whose passwords appear in known breach corpuses, which you can check privately with a k-anonymity API. Respond with graduated friction rather than blocks: add a challenge such as a CAPTCHA or proof of work when the risk score is high, require MFA or an emailed code for logins from new devices, and force a password reset for accounts confirmed to use breached passwords. Encourage MFA and passkeys generally. Alert on successful logins that follow such patterns, because the real damage is the few attempts that succeed.

questions.title: Zero trust for service-to-service calls
questions.prompt: Your services trust any request that comes from inside the private network. What does a zero-trust approach change for service-to-service calls, and what does it cost?

expectedConcepts.label: Network location is not identity; one breached host reaches everything
Every call authenticated with workload identity and mTLS, then authorised
Costs: certificate management, policy upkeep and latency

questions.modelAnswer: Trusting the private network means that once an attacker compromises any host, through a vulnerable dependency or a stolen credential, they can call every internal service freely; that lateral movement is how many breaches spread. Zero trust says network location is not identity: every request must prove who is calling and be authorised for what it asks. In practice each workload gets a cryptographic identity, for example SPIFFE IDs issued by the platform, and services talk over mutual TLS, so both sides verify certificates. Each service then checks policy: the orders service may call payments' charge endpoint, but the recommendations service may not. User context is passed along as a signed token, so a service also knows on whose behalf it acts. A service mesh can provide mTLS and policy without changing application code. The costs are operational: issuing and rotating short-lived certificates, writing and maintaining policies, debugging failed handshakes, and a little extra latency on each new connection.

questions.title: Debugging a Kubernetes Service that returns 503
questions.prompt: Your pods show Running, but requests through the Service and ingress return 503 errors. Walk through how you find the break between ingress, Service, endpoints and pods.

expectedConcepts.label: Check pods are Ready, not just Running
Service selector must match pod labels; check endpoints
Then ingress rules and backend config; test each hop directly

questions.modelAnswer: A 503 from the ingress usually means it has no healthy backend, so work from the pods outward. First, Running is not Ready: check kubectl get pods and describe; if the readiness probe fails, the pods are excluded from the Service, often because the probe uses the wrong path or port. Second, check the Service's endpoints with kubectl get endpoints or EndpointSlices. If the list is empty, the Service selector does not match the pod labels, a common typo after renaming a deployment. If endpoints exist, check that the Service targetPort matches the port the container actually listens on, and that the app listens on all interfaces, not only localhost. Third, check the ingress: the rule's host and path, the backend service name and port, and the ingress controller's logs, which say why it returned 503. Test each hop directly, with kubectl port-forward to a pod, then to the Service, then through the ingress, so the first hop that fails shows you where to look. Network policies can also silently block traffic between namespaces.

questions.title: Terraform plans to destroy a production database
questions.prompt: A routine terraform plan says it will destroy and recreate the production database. What could have caused this, and how do you prevent a change like that from ever being applied?

expectedConcepts.label: Replacement from a force-new attribute change, a rename or state drift
Investigate state: moved blocks, import, refresh before applying
Guardrails: prevent_destroy, deletion protection, plan review in CI

questions.modelAnswer: Do not apply; read why the plan wants a replacement. Common causes: someone changed an attribute that cannot be updated in place, such as the engine, the identifier or the subnet group, so the provider forces replacement; the resource was renamed or moved into a module, so Terraform sees one resource deleted and a new one created; the state file is out of date or someone changed the database by hand, so there is drift; or a provider upgrade changed defaults. Fix the cause rather than the symptom: for a rename, add a moved block or use terraform state mv so state follows the code; for drift, update the code to match reality or import the resource; for an attribute change, find a migration path that does not recreate the database. To prevent it ever being applied, set lifecycle prevent_destroy on critical resources, enable deletion protection on the database itself, run plans in CI and require review of any plan containing a destroy, use policy checks that block destroys of tagged resources, and keep tested backups.

questions.title: Surviving an availability zone failure
questions.prompt: You run an API, a Postgres database and a Redis cache in one cloud region with three availability zones. What happens when one zone fails, and what must you design so the service survives it?

expectedConcepts.label: Spread stateless replicas across zones behind a regional load balancer
Database: synchronous standby in another zone and automatic failover
Capacity headroom: surviving zones must absorb the load
Failover drops connections and cache; cross-zone traffic costs

questions.modelAnswer: Treat a zone as a unit that can disappear. Run the stateless API replicas spread across all three zones behind a regional load balancer, with health checks, so a failed zone simply stops receiving traffic. State is the hard part. Run Postgres with a synchronous standby in a second zone, as managed multi-AZ databases do, so a committed transaction exists in two zones, and automatic failover promotes the standby in a minute or two. Redis needs a replica in another zone with failover, or the application must tolerate an empty cache. Capacity matters: if you run at 80 percent across three zones and lose one, the remaining two are overloaded, so keep headroom for losing a zone, or let autoscaling add capacity quickly. Expect side effects during failover: database connections drop and clients must reconnect and retry, the new cache starts cold, and in-flight requests fail. Cross-zone traffic also has a price, so keep chatty calls within a zone when possible. Finally, test zone failure deliberately, because untested failover often fails.

questions.title: Disk pressure and pod evictions
questions.prompt: Pods on one Kubernetes node keep getting evicted with a DiskPressure condition. What usually fills the disk, and how do you fix it and stop it happening again?

expectedConcepts.label: Kubelet evicts pods when node disk crosses thresholds
Usual causes: container logs, emptyDir, image layers
Set ephemeral-storage limits, rotate logs, ship them off the node

questions.modelAnswer: When a node's disk or inodes cross the kubelet's eviction thresholds, the node reports DiskPressure and the kubelet starts evicting pods, beginning with those using the most ephemeral storage beyond their requests, and it also garbage-collects unused images. To find the cause, check the node with df and du: the usual culprits are application logs written to stdout faster than they are rotated, data written to emptyDir volumes or the container's writable layer, such as temporary files or caches, and many large images accumulating from frequent deployments. Fix the immediate problem by cleaning up the offending pod's data or images. To stop it recurring, set ephemeral-storage requests and limits on containers so one noisy pod is evicted before it hurts others, configure log rotation in the container runtime and ship logs to a central system instead of keeping them on the node, write large temporary data to a proper volume, and size node disks for images plus headroom. Alert on node disk usage before the eviction threshold.

questions.title: Serverless functions versus containers for a spiky API
questions.prompt: Your API is idle most of the day and receives sharp bursts of traffic a few times a day. Would you run it on serverless functions or always-on containers, and what decides it?

expectedConcepts.label: Serverless scales to zero and per request; containers run continuously
Cold starts and concurrency limits versus fixed capacity
Decide by traffic shape, latency needs, run time and connections

questions.modelAnswer: For a mostly idle API with sharp bursts, serverless functions are often a good fit: they scale out per request within seconds and scale to zero, so you pay almost nothing while idle, and there are no servers to patch. Always-on containers pay for capacity all day and must autoscale fast enough for bursts, or keep large headroom. The main cost of serverless is cold starts: a new instance must start the runtime and load your code, adding from tens of milliseconds to a few seconds, which hurts if p99 latency matters; provisioned or pre-warmed concurrency helps but brings back a fixed charge. Other constraints are maximum execution time, concurrency limits, and database connections, because thousands of function instances can exhaust a Postgres server unless you use a connection proxy. Containers win for steady, high traffic, where per-request pricing becomes more expensive, for long-running or stateful work, and when you want to avoid tight coupling to one provider. So the traffic shape, latency target and connection model decide it.

questions.title: Low-level design of a parking lot
questions.prompt: Design the classes for a multi-floor parking lot with different spot sizes, tickets and payment. Outline the main classes and their responsibilities, and explain one design decision you would defend.

expectedConcepts.label: Core classes: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket
Spot allocation as a strategy; payment and pricing behind interfaces
Concurrency: two cars must not get the same spot

questions.modelAnswer: I would start from the nouns and their responsibilities. A ParkingLot has Floors, each Floor has Spots, and each Spot has a size, such as compact, regular or large, and knows whether it is free. Vehicles have a type that maps to the spot sizes they fit. When a car enters, an entry gate asks the lot to allocate a spot and issues a Ticket recording the spot, vehicle and entry time; at exit, a PricingPolicy computes the fee from the ticket, and a Payment interface handles cash, card or app payments. The decision I would defend is putting spot allocation behind a SpotAllocationStrategy interface, with implementations such as nearest to the entrance or fill floor by floor, because operators change this rule and it should not touch the rest of the design. Concurrency matters at multiple gates: two cars must never receive the same spot, so allocation must atomically find and reserve a free spot, for example with a lock per floor or a compare-and-set on the spot. Keep free spots in per-size sets so allocation is fast.

questions.title: Low-level design of an elevator controller
questions.prompt: Design the classes for a controller that runs several elevators in one building. How do you represent requests and elevator state, and which scheduling strategy would you choose?

expectedConcepts.label: Elevator state: floor, direction, door state and a queue of stops
Hall calls assigned by a dispatcher; car calls go to that elevator
SCAN-style scheduling versus nearest-car; pluggable strategy

questions.modelAnswer: I would separate two kinds of requests: a hall call, made on a floor with an up or down button, which any elevator can serve, and a car call, made inside an elevator for a destination, which only that elevator serves. Each Elevator object holds its current floor, its direction (up, down or idle), its door state, and an ordered set of stops. A Dispatcher receives hall calls and assigns each one to an elevator through a SchedulingStrategy interface, so the policy can change without rewriting the rest. The elevator itself serves its stops with a SCAN or LOOK approach, like a disk arm: keep moving in the current direction, stopping at requested floors, and reverse only when no stops remain ahead, which avoids starving distant floors. For assignment, a simple strategy picks the elevator that will arrive soonest, taking into account its direction and existing stops, rather than the physically nearest one. State changes should go through a small state machine, such as moving, doors opening, doors open and idle, so illegal actions like moving with the doors open are impossible.

questions.title: An in-memory cache with TTL and eviction
questions.prompt: Implement an in-memory cache class with get, put with a time-to-live, and a maximum size. How do you expire entries, choose what to evict, and keep it correct with multiple threads?

expectedConcepts.label: Hash map of entries with expiry times; check expiry on read
LRU eviction with a linked list or ordered map at capacity
Thread safety: a lock or striped locks; background cleanup costs

questions.modelAnswer: The core is a hash map from key to an entry holding the value and its expiry time, computed as now plus the TTL when it is put. get looks up the entry and, if the expiry time has passed, deletes it and reports a miss; this lazy expiration is cheap and always correct. Lazy expiration alone lets expired entries that nobody reads take up memory, so add either a periodic background sweep or a min-heap ordered by expiry time to remove them. For the maximum size, keep entries in a doubly linked list in recency order, as in an LRU cache: get moves an entry to the front, put inserts at the front, and when the cache is full you evict from the back, all in O(1). With multiple threads, the simplest correct design guards the map and list with one mutex; under heavy contention, split the cache into striped segments, each with its own lock and LRU list. Inject the clock instead of calling the system time directly, so tests can advance time and check expiry without sleeping.

questions.title: A thread-safe rate limiter class
questions.prompt: Implement a rate limiter class that allows each user N requests per second and is called concurrently from many threads. What data structure do you choose, and how do you keep it correct and fast?

expectedConcepts.label: Per-user token bucket: tokens, capacity and last-refill time
Refill lazily on each call from elapsed time; no timer threads
Concurrency: per-bucket lock or CAS; evict idle users

questions.modelAnswer: I would use a token bucket per user. Each bucket stores the current number of tokens, the capacity N and the time of the last refill. There is no background thread: on every tryAcquire call, compute the elapsed time since the last refill using a monotonic clock, add elapsed seconds times N tokens up to the capacity, update the refill time, and then take a token if at least one is available. The buckets live in a concurrent hash map keyed by user ID, using computeIfAbsent or an equivalent so two threads never create two buckets for the same user. The refill-and-take step must be atomic per bucket. The simplest correct way is a small lock per bucket, so threads for different users never contend; for very hot users, you can pack tokens and timestamp into one atomic value and update it with compare-and-swap in a loop. Users who stop sending requests would otherwise stay in the map forever, so evict buckets that have been idle longer than a full refill period. Inject the clock so tests can run deterministically.

questions.title: Splitting a god class by responsibility
questions.prompt: Your OrderService class has grown to 2,000 lines: it validates orders, calculates prices, charges cards, sends emails and writes reports. How would you split it, using the single responsibility and interface segregation principles?

expectedConcepts.label: Single responsibility: one reason to change per class
Extract pricing, payment and notification behind small interfaces
Refactor in steps behind tests; avoid splitting too finely

questions.modelAnswer: The single responsibility principle says a class should have one reason to change. This class changes when pricing rules change, when the payment provider changes, when email templates change and when finance wants a new report, so every change risks breaking unrelated behaviour, and merge conflicts are constant. I would extract classes along those reasons: an OrderValidator, a PricingCalculator, a PaymentGateway adapter, an OrderNotifier and a ReportWriter, leaving OrderService as a thin coordinator for the place-order use case. Interface segregation says clients should not depend on methods they do not use, so instead of one big interface I would give each collaborator a small one: the reporting job depends on an order-reading interface, not on charge and refund methods. I would do it step by step: first add characterisation tests around the current behaviour, then extract one responsibility at a time, keeping tests green, rather than rewriting. The trade-off is that splitting too finely creates indirection and dozens of tiny classes, so split along real reasons to change, not every method.

questions.title: Builder versus telescoping constructors
questions.prompt: A class needs three required fields and eight optional ones. Compare telescoping constructors with the Builder pattern, and say when a builder is overkill.

expectedConcepts.label: Telescoping constructors: many overloads, easy to swap arguments
Builder: named steps, build validates and returns an immutable object
Overkill when named or default parameters exist, or fields are few

questions.modelAnswer: With telescoping constructors you write one constructor with the required fields, another that adds one optional field, another that adds two, and so on. That leads to many overloads, and calls such as new Server(host, 8080, 30, 5, true, false) are unreadable; worse, two parameters of the same type can be swapped without any compiler error. Setting optional fields with setters instead makes the object mutable and possibly invalid between calls. A Builder takes the required fields up front, then exposes named methods for each optional one, such as timeoutSeconds(30) and retries(5), and a final build method that validates the combination and returns an immutable object. Calls read clearly, defaults live in one place, and invalid objects are never created. A builder is overkill when the class has only a few fields, or when the language has named and default parameters, as Python, Kotlin and C# do, because those already give readable, safe construction without the boilerplate of a second class.

questions.title: Drill: redirect latency rose after adding analytics
questions.prompt: Your URL shortener's redirect p99 doubled after you added click analytics. What do you check first, and how would you redesign the analytics path?

expectedConcepts.label: Analytics write is on the synchronous redirect path
Move analytics off the path: emit an event to a queue, aggregate later
Accept some lost or delayed clicks for faster redirects

questions.modelAnswer: First I would confirm what changed in the redirect path. Most likely the redirect handler now writes a click record to a database, or calls an analytics service, before returning the 301 or 302, so every redirect waits for that write and its tail latency, including lock contention on a hot counter row. Traces of slow redirects would show the extra span. The redirect should only do the essential work: look up the short code, ideally from a cache, and return. Analytics should move off the synchronous path: emit a small click event to a local buffer or a queue such as Kafka in a fire-and-forget way, and let consumers aggregate counts in batches into the analytics store. The trade-off is that analytics become eventually consistent, and a crash can lose a few buffered clicks; for most products that is acceptable, and if not, a durable local log before acknowledging still costs far less than a database round trip.

questions.title: Drill: caching a read-heavy product page
questions.prompt: A product page is read a thousand times for every update. Where would you add caching, what invalidates each layer, and what can go stale?

expectedConcepts.label: Layers: CDN for static parts, application cache for product data
Invalidate on update events; TTL as a safety net
Price and stock must be fresh; descriptions can be stale

questions.modelAnswer: I would cache at two layers. Images, scripts and the static parts of the page go through a CDN with long cache lifetimes and versioned URLs, so they are never invalidated, only replaced. The product data itself, name, description and specifications, goes in an application cache such as Redis using cache-aside: read from the cache, and on a miss load from the database and store it with a TTL. Invalidation is driven by updates: when a product changes, the write path or a change-data-capture event deletes the cache key, and the TTL is a safety net in case an invalidation is lost. The important decision is what may be stale. A description that is a minute old is harmless, but price and stock affect what customers pay and whether orders can be fulfilled, so I would keep them out of the long-lived cache, serve them from a short-TTL cache or the database, and always re-check them at checkout. Also protect against a stampede when a popular key expires, by letting only one request rebuild it.

questions.title: Drill: chat messages lost when a server restarts
questions.prompt: In your chat system, some messages disappear whenever a chat server restarts during a deploy. Where in the message flow can they be lost, and how do you make delivery reliable?

expectedConcepts.label: Messages held only in server memory before being persisted
Persist first, then acknowledge; client retries with message IDs
Graceful drain on deploy; offline delivery from storage

questions.modelAnswer: Messages are lost where the system says 'received' before the message is durable. Typically the chat server accepts a message over the WebSocket, acknowledges it or just keeps it in an in-memory buffer or queue, and then writes it to storage or forwards it to the recipient's server; if the process restarts in between, the message is gone. The fix is to persist first and acknowledge after: the server writes the message to a durable store or log, and only then sends the sender an acknowledgement with the message's ID. The client keeps unacknowledged messages and resends them after reconnecting, with a client-generated message ID so the server can deduplicate retries. Delivery to recipients reads from storage: on reconnect, each client asks for messages after the last one it has seen, so anything missed while servers restarted is synced. Deploys should drain servers gracefully: stop accepting new connections, tell clients to reconnect elsewhere, finish in-flight writes, then exit.

questions.title: Drill: estimating storage for photo uploads
questions.prompt: In about a minute, estimate the storage needed for a service that receives 100 million photo uploads a day. State your assumptions, the yearly total, and what changes the answer most.

expectedConcepts.label: State assumptions: average size and stored versions
Daily and yearly totals with replication
Biggest levers: compression, tiering, deletion and dedup

questions.modelAnswer: I will assume an average photo of about 2 megabytes after the client's compression, plus a few resized versions such as thumbnails and a medium size, adding roughly 10 percent. So 100 million photos a day times 2 megabytes is about 200 terabytes a day, call it 220 with the versions. Over a year that is about 220 times 365, roughly 80 petabytes of new data. If the storage system keeps three replicas, the raw capacity is about 240 petabytes a year, though erasure coding, as object stores use, brings the overhead down to around 1.5 times, so roughly 120 petabytes. Bandwidth is about 200 terabytes a day divided by 86,400 seconds, around 2.5 gigabytes per second of uploads on average, with peaks several times higher. The assumptions that change the answer most are the average photo size, how many versions you keep, whether old photos move to cheaper cold storage, and whether users delete photos or upload duplicates you can deduplicate.

questions.title: Drill: sizing a fleet for 10 million WebSocket connections
questions.prompt: Your chat service must hold 10 million concurrent WebSocket connections. Roughly how many servers do you need, what limits a single server, and how do clients find their server?

expectedConcepts.label: Per-server limits: memory per connection, file descriptors, CPU for messages
Rough count with headroom, for example 50,000 to 100,000 per server
Connection routing and reconnect storms after failures

questions.modelAnswer: An idle WebSocket costs little CPU, so the limits are memory, file descriptors and the message rate. Each connection needs a socket buffer and application state, often tens of kilobytes, so 100,000 connections at about 50 kilobytes is around 5 gigabytes, which a normal server handles; the operating system must also allow that many file descriptors, so raise ulimit and kernel limits. Message fan-out and TLS consume most of the CPU. A safe planning figure is 50,000 to 100,000 connections per server, leaving headroom for traffic spikes and for absorbing a failed server's clients, so 10 million connections need roughly 100 to 200 servers. Clients reach a server through a layer 4 load balancer, and a presence service records which server holds each user, so messages can be routed to the right gateway. The dangerous moment is a failure or deploy: hundreds of thousands of clients reconnect at once, so clients must use exponential backoff with jitter, and servers should be drained gradually.

questions.title: Pattern drill: group anagrams
questions.prompt: Given a list of words, group the anagrams together. Which pattern solves this, what key do you use, and what is the complexity?

expectedConcepts.label: Hash map from a canonical key to the list of words
O(n times k log k) with sorting, O(n times k) with counts
Unicode and case need a defined normalisation
Pairwise comparison is O(n squared)

questions.modelAnswer: Anagrams are words with the same letters, so the pattern is hashing by a canonical key: compute a key that is identical for all anagrams, and use a hash map from key to the list of words. The simplest key is the word's letters sorted, so 'eat', 'tea' and 'ate' all map to 'aet'. With n words of length up to k, sorting each word costs O(k log k), so the total is O(n times k log k) time and O(n times k) space for the map. For lowercase English letters, a faster key is a count of each of the 26 letters, which costs O(k) per word, giving O(n times k). Edge cases: decide whether case matters, handle empty strings, and for Unicode text define a normalisation, because sorting code units can split characters. The naive alternative compares every pair of words, which is O(n squared) comparisons; a product of primes as a key works in theory but overflows quickly.

questions.title: Pattern drill: can you reach the last index?
questions.prompt: Each array element says how far you can jump from that position. Can you reach the last index? Which pattern solves it in linear time, and why is the greedy choice correct?

expectedConcepts.label: Greedy: track the farthest reachable index while scanning
O(n) time, O(1) space
Stop when the index passes the farthest reach; zeros trap you
DP or BFS work but cost O(n squared)

questions.modelAnswer: The pattern is greedy reachability. Scan from left to right while keeping the farthest index you can reach so far. At index i, if i is beyond the farthest reach, you are stuck and the answer is false; otherwise update the farthest reach to the maximum of itself and i plus nums[i]. If the farthest reach ever gets to the last index, the answer is true. This is O(n) time and O(1) space. The greedy choice is correct because the set of reachable indices is always a contiguous range starting at zero: if you can reach index j, you can reach every index before it, so the only thing that matters is the right end of that range. Edge cases: a single-element array is already at the end, and zeros are where you get stuck. A dynamic programming solution that marks each index reachable from earlier ones also works but is O(n squared). The related problem of the minimum number of jumps uses a greedy BFS by levels, still in O(n).

questions.title: Pattern drill: word break
questions.prompt: Given a string and a dictionary, decide whether the string can be split into dictionary words. Which pattern applies, what is the state, and what is the complexity?

expectedConcepts.label: DP over prefixes: dp[i] is true if s[0..i) can be segmented
O(n squared) checks with a hash set, or bounded by max word length
Plain recursion repeats work exponentially; memoise
A trie avoids building substrings

questions.modelAnswer: This is dynamic programming over prefixes. Let dp[i] be true if the first i characters can be split into dictionary words, with dp[0] true for the empty prefix. For each i, dp[i] is true if there is some j before it with dp[j] true and the substring from j to i in the dictionary, which you check with a hash set. That gives O(n squared) substring checks, each costing up to O(n) to hash, so O(n cubed) in the worst case; limiting j to at most the maximum dictionary word length back from i cuts this to O(n times L). Space is O(n). Plain recursion that tries every split explores the same suffixes again and again, which is exponential on inputs like 'aaaa...ab', so memoisation or the bottom-up table is essential. A trie of dictionary words lets you extend from each reachable position character by character without building substrings. Returning all segmentations, rather than yes or no, can be exponential in output size.

questions.title: Pattern drill: container with the most water
questions.prompt: Given heights of vertical lines, find two lines that hold the most water. Which pattern gives a linear solution, and why is it safe to move the shorter pointer?

expectedConcepts.label: Two pointers at both ends; area is width times the shorter height
O(n) instead of checking all O(n squared) pairs
Moving the shorter side cannot lose the best answer
Equal heights: moving either is fine

questions.modelAnswer: The pattern is two pointers moving inward. Start with one pointer at each end; the water between two lines is the distance between them times the shorter of the two heights. Record the area, then move the pointer at the shorter line inward, and repeat until the pointers meet. That is O(n) time and O(1) space, instead of O(n squared) for checking every pair. Moving the shorter pointer is safe: the area is limited by the shorter line, and any container that keeps that shorter line with a pointer further inward has a smaller width and a height no greater than that same short line, so it cannot beat the area we just recorded. We can therefore discard the shorter line forever. Moving the taller pointer instead could skip the optimum. When both heights are equal, moving either one is fine, because any better container must exclude both. Arrays with fewer than two lines hold no water.

questions.title: Pattern drill: kth smallest in a sorted matrix
questions.prompt: Each row and each column of an n by n matrix is sorted. Find the kth smallest element. Compare a heap approach with binary search on the value range.

expectedConcepts.label: Heap: k-way merge of rows, pop k times
Binary search on value: count elements at most mid in O(n)
Heap O(k log n); value search O(n log range)
Duplicates and negative values in the range search

questions.modelAnswer: One approach treats the rows as n sorted lists and does a k-way merge. Put the first element of each row in a min-heap, then pop the smallest k times, each time pushing the next element from the same row. The kth pop is the answer: O(k log n) time and O(n) space, good when k is small. The other approach is binary search on the answer's value. The answer lies between the top-left and bottom-right values. For a candidate mid, count how many elements are at most mid using a staircase walk from the bottom-left corner: move right when the value is at most mid, adding the rows above, and move up otherwise, which is O(n). If the count is at least k, the answer is at most mid, so search lower; otherwise search higher. That is O(n log of the value range) time and O(1) extra space. The search converges on the lowest value with count at least k, which is always an element of the matrix, so duplicates and negative values are handled correctly.

questions.title: A service that fails under systemd
questions.prompt: Your service runs fine from your shell but fails when started by systemd, and you see no application logs. How do you find out why?

expectedConcepts.label: Start with systemctl status and journalctl for the unit
Different environment: user, working directory, PATH, env files
Sandboxing, dependencies and restart loops

questions.modelAnswer: First ask systemd: systemctl status shows whether the process exited, its exit code or signal, and the last log lines, and journalctl -u with the unit name shows everything the service wrote to stdout and stderr, which is where its logs go under systemd. If the logs are empty, the program probably died before logging, so the cause is usually the environment, which under systemd is very different from your shell. The service may run as a different user without access to its files, from the root directory instead of your working directory, so relative paths break, with a minimal PATH and none of your shell's environment variables, so configuration must come from Environment or EnvironmentFile settings. Check the effective settings with systemctl show or cat. Hardening options such as ProtectSystem, PrivateTmp or NoNewPrivileges can block writes. Ordering matters too: a service that needs the network or a database should declare After and Wants dependencies. If Restart is set, a crash loop may hide the first error, so look at the earliest failure.

questions.title: Disk full, but du shows much less used
questions.prompt: df reports a disk is 100 percent full, but du on the whole filesystem adds up to far less. What explains the difference, and how do you free the space safely?

expectedConcepts.label: Deleted files still held open by a process keep their blocks
Find them with lsof or /proc/<pid>/fd
Free by restarting or truncating; prevent with proper log rotation

questions.modelAnswer: du walks the directory tree, so it only counts files that still have a name, while df reports the blocks the filesystem has actually allocated. The usual explanation is deleted files that are still open: someone deleted a huge log file, but the process writing it still holds a file descriptor, so the inode and its blocks are not freed until the descriptor closes. Find them with lsof and look for entries marked deleted, or list /proc with the process ID and its fd directory. To free the space, restart or signal the process so it reopens its log files, or, if you cannot restart it, truncate the open file through its /proc fd entry. Prevent it with log rotation that tells the process to reopen files, or uses copytruncate. Other causes of a mismatch are files hidden under a mount point, which du cannot see while something is mounted over them, and the blocks reserved for root on ext4. Also check inodes with df -i, because a disk can be full of tiny files.

questions.title: When test-driven development helps
questions.prompt: When does test-driven development help, and when does writing tests first slow a team down? Give an example of each.

expectedConcepts.label: Red, green, refactor: a failing test drives each small step
Helps with clear requirements and logic-heavy code; shapes design
Slows exploration and prototypes; tests can lock in a bad design

questions.modelAnswer: In test-driven development you write a small failing test, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor, in short red, green, refactor cycles. It helps most when the behaviour is well defined and logic-heavy: a pricing engine, a date parser or a tax rule, where examples can be written down before the code. Writing the test first forces you to design the interface from the caller's side, keeps units small and testable, and leaves a regression suite behind, so refactoring later is safe. Bug fixes benefit too: first write a test that reproduces the bug. It slows teams down during exploration, when you do not yet know what the code should do, such as a prototype, a spike to learn a new API, or user-interface layout, where tests written first get rewritten repeatedly or lock in a design you would otherwise throw away. A practical approach is to spike without tests, throw the spike away, and then build the real version test-first, or at least with tests written alongside.

questions.title: Adding tests to untested legacy code
questions.prompt: You must change a 5,000-line module that has no tests and that nobody fully understands. How do you add tests safely before refactoring it?

expectedConcepts.label: Characterisation tests record what the code does now
Find seams to break dependencies so code can run in tests
Test only around the change; existing bugs get preserved

questions.modelAnswer: Do not start by refactoring, because without tests you cannot tell whether you changed behaviour. First write characterisation tests: tests that record what the code does now, not what it should do. Call the code with realistic inputs, often captured from production or logs, and assert on whatever it currently returns, even if it looks wrong; golden-file tests are useful for large outputs. To run the code in a test at all, you usually need seams, places where you can replace a dependency without editing much logic: pass the database or clock in as a parameter, extract a method that does the I/O and override it, or wrap a static call behind a small interface. Make these changes in tiny, mechanical steps, ideally with automated IDE refactorings. Focus on the area you are about to change rather than trying to cover all 5,000 lines. Characterisation tests also preserve existing bugs; when you find one, decide deliberately whether to fix it, since callers may depend on it.

questions.title: Recovering lost commits with the reflog
questions.prompt: After a bad rebase or a force-push, a colleague says a day of commits has vanished from their branch. How do you get the commits back?

expectedConcepts.label: Commits still exist as objects; the reflog records where HEAD pointed
Find the old commit and restore it with a branch or reset
Reflog is local and expires; prevent with force-with-lease

questions.modelAnswer: Git rarely deletes commits immediately. A rebase or reset only moves the branch pointer; the old commits remain in the object database until garbage collection removes unreachable objects, usually after weeks. The reflog records every position HEAD and each branch pointed to, so on the colleague's machine run git reflog, or the reflog for that branch, and find the entry just before the rebase or reset, for example 'rebase started'; ORIG_HEAD often points there too. Check it with git log, then create a branch at that commit, or reset the branch to it, and cherry-pick anything newer you want to keep. If the commits were lost on the remote through someone else's force-push, look for them in any clone that fetched them, in the hosting service's activity history, or in an open pull request. The reflog is local to each clone and expires, so act quickly. To prevent it, use git push --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen, and protect shared branches from force-pushes.

questions.title: Monorepo versus polyrepo
questions.prompt: Your company has 40 services, each in its own repository, and cross-service changes are painful. Should you move to a monorepo, and what would it cost?

expectedConcepts.label: Monorepo: atomic cross-project changes and shared tooling
Needs build tooling that builds and tests only what changed
Costs: CI scale, ownership rules, coupling; polyrepo gives independence

questions.modelAnswer: In a polyrepo setup, a change to a shared library means releasing a new version and then updating dozens of repositories, often over weeks, so services drift onto different versions. A monorepo puts all services and libraries in one repository: a single commit can change a library and every caller atomically, refactoring across projects is easy, and tooling, linting and dependency versions can be shared. It only works with build tooling that understands the dependency graph and builds and tests only what a change affects, with caching, such as Bazel, Nx, Turborepo or Pants; otherwise every commit runs all 40 services' tests and CI time explodes. Other costs: you need ownership rules such as CODEOWNERS so teams review changes to their code, access control is coarser, the repository grows large, and easy cross-project calls can quietly increase coupling. Polyrepos keep teams independent with clear, versioned contracts. If the pain is mainly shared-library updates, automated dependency-update bots may solve it without a migration.

questions.title: How a debugger stops at a breakpoint
questions.prompt: How does a debugger such as gdb make a running program stop at a breakpoint and let you inspect variables? Explain the mechanism and why optimised code is harder to debug.

expectedConcepts.label: Software breakpoint: replace an instruction with a trap such as int3
ptrace lets the debugger control the process and handle the signal
Debug info maps addresses to lines; optimisation breaks the mapping

questions.modelAnswer: On Linux a debugger controls the target through the ptrace system call, which lets it stop the process, read and write its memory and registers, and resume it. To set a software breakpoint, the debugger uses the debug information to find the machine-code address of the source line, saves the original byte there, and overwrites it with a trap instruction, int3 on x86. When the CPU executes it, the kernel stops the process with a SIGTRAP and notifies the debugger. To continue, the debugger restores the original byte, moves the instruction pointer back, single-steps that one instruction, puts the trap back and resumes. Hardware breakpoints and watchpoints use CPU debug registers instead, which is how you can stop when a variable changes. Inspecting variables relies on debug information, usually DWARF, which maps addresses to source lines and says where each variable lives in a register or stack slot at each point. Optimisation breaks those simple mappings: variables live only briefly in registers and appear as optimised out, functions are inlined, and code is reordered, so stepping jumps around.

questions.title: Run-to-completion versus pipeline models in DPDK
questions.prompt: Compare the run-to-completion and pipeline models for structuring a DPDK application. How do packets move between cores in a pipeline, and when would you choose each?

expectedConcepts.label: Run-to-completion: each core receives, processes and sends its own packets
Pipeline: stages on different cores linked by rte_ring queues
Pipeline adds hand-off latency and cache traffic but isolates heavy stages

questions.modelAnswer: In the run-to-completion model, each lcore owns an RX queue and a TX queue and does all the work for its packets: receive a burst, parse, look up, modify and transmit, without handing packets to another core. Packets stay hot in that core's cache, there is no inter-core communication, and scaling means adding queues and cores with RSS spreading flows. In the pipeline model, the work is split into stages on different cores, for example one core receives and classifies, several worker cores do heavy processing, and another transmits. Stages are connected by rte_ring queues, lockless rings that pass mbuf pointers in bursts, so packets are not copied. A pipeline helps when one stage is much heavier or must be serialised, such as a stateful module, or when work cannot be spread evenly by RSS. Its costs are the hand-off latency, cache misses because the packet data moves between cores, and the risk that one stage becomes a bottleneck and its ring fills up and drops. Most designs start with run-to-completion and use pipelines only where needed.

questions.title: Using NIC hardware offloads in DPDK
questions.prompt: Which work can a DPDK application offload to the NIC, such as checksums, segmentation and flow classification, and what must you check before relying on an offload?

expectedConcepts.label: Checksum, TSO and VLAN offloads and RSS hashing in hardware
Per-packet request through mbuf offload flags and header lengths
Check device capabilities; offload support varies by NIC and driver

questions.modelAnswer: Modern NICs can do some per-packet work in hardware, which frees CPU cycles. On receive, the NIC can validate IP and TCP or UDP checksums and report the result in the mbuf's flags, and compute the RSS hash, which the application can reuse instead of hashing the flow itself. On transmit, it can fill in IP and L4 checksums, insert VLAN tags, and perform TCP segmentation offload, splitting one large buffer into MTU-sized segments. Flow rules through rte_flow can steer or drop packets by header fields before they reach the CPU. Offloads are enabled at port and queue configuration, and on transmit each mbuf requests them through its offload flags, together with header-length fields such as l2_len and l3_len so the NIC knows where headers are. Before relying on any of this, query the device capabilities, for example with rte_eth_dev_info_get, because support differs between NICs, drivers and firmware versions. Keep a software fallback for missing features, and test offloads with real traffic, since a misconfigured checksum offload silently sends corrupt packets.

questions.title: Validating a DPDK setup with testpmd
questions.prompt: Your new DPDK application reaches far less throughput than expected on a new server. How would you use testpmd to check the environment before blaming your own code?

expectedConcepts.label: testpmd is the reference forwarding app shipped with DPDK
Check binding, hugepages, link speed and core placement
Compare its throughput and port stats with your app under the same traffic

questions.modelAnswer: testpmd is the test application that ships with DPDK: it initialises the EAL and ports and forwards packets between ports in simple modes such as io or mac forwarding, so it gives a baseline for what the hardware and configuration can do with minimal processing. First check the environment it runs in: the NIC is bound to the right driver, hugepages are reserved on the NIC's NUMA node, and the cores you give testpmd are on that node and not used by other workloads. Inside testpmd, show port info and stats to confirm link speed, queue counts and offloads, then start forwarding while a traffic generator sends the same traffic you test your application with, using the same number of cores and queues. If testpmd also falls short, the problem is the environment, such as wrong NUMA placement, too few queues, a PCIe slot running at reduced width, firmware or BIOS power settings, or the traffic generator itself. If testpmd reaches line rate and your application does not, the bottleneck is in your code, and per-core profiling is the next step.

questions.title: Kafka consumer group rebalance storms
questions.prompt: Your Kafka consumers keep rebalancing every few minutes, and lag grows although the consumers are healthy. What causes rebalance storms, and how do you stop them?

expectedConcepts.label: Slow processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, so the consumer is removed
Each rebalance pauses partitions and can redeliver messages
Smaller batches, cooperative rebalancing and static membership

questions.modelAnswer: A consumer group rebalances whenever a member joins, leaves or is considered dead, and during a classic eager rebalance every consumer stops processing while partitions are reassigned, so frequent rebalances mean lag grows even though nothing is broken. A common cause is processing that takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms between calls to poll: the consumer still sends heartbeats from a background thread, but the coordinator removes it from the group for not polling, it rejoins, and the cycle repeats. Other causes are session timeouts during long garbage-collection pauses and rolling deploys or autoscaling that change membership constantly. Each rebalance may also redeliver messages whose offsets were not committed, so duplicates rise. Fixes: process smaller batches by lowering max.poll.records, or hand slow work to a separate pool while pausing partitions, and set the poll interval to match real processing time; use the cooperative sticky assignor, which rebalances incrementally instead of stopping everyone; and use static membership with group.instance.id so a restarting consumer reclaims its partitions without a rebalance.

questions.title: Data contracts between producers and analytics
questions.prompt: An application team renamed a column, and three analytics pipelines broke overnight without anyone being told. What is a data contract, and how would it prevent this?

expectedConcepts.label: A data contract is an explicit, owned schema and set of guarantees
Enforced in CI and at ingestion with schema checks
Versioning and deprecation give consumers time; adds process

questions.modelAnswer: Analytics pipelines often read an application's database tables or events directly, so the producing team does not know who depends on them, and an ordinary rename breaks consumers silently. A data contract makes that dependency explicit: the producer publishes a dataset or event stream with a defined schema, field meanings, freshness and quality guarantees, and a named owner, and treats it as a public interface rather than an internal detail. Contracts are enforced by tooling, not goodwill: the schema lives in version control or a schema registry, CI fails a producer's change that breaks compatibility, such as removing or renaming a field, and ingestion validates incoming data against the contract and quarantines violations. Breaking changes go through versioning: publish a new version alongside the old one, announce a deprecation period and migrate consumers before removal. The cost is process and some loss of speed for producers, so apply contracts to datasets that other teams and critical reports depend on, not to every table.

questions.title: A service that hangs while its CPU is idle
questions.prompt: Requests to a service start timing out, yet its CPU is nearly idle and there are no errors in the logs. How would you find out what the service is waiting on?

expectedConcepts.label: Idle CPU with timeouts means threads are blocked, not working
Thread or goroutine dumps show where each thread is blocked
Check pool, queue and dependency saturation metrics
Usual causes: exhausted pool, missing timeout, deadlock

questions.modelAnswer: Near-zero CPU with timeouts tells me the threads are not doing work; they are blocked waiting on something, so a CPU profile will not help. First I check saturation metrics: active versus maximum connections in the database and HTTP client pools, request queue depth, and the latency of each dependency. Then I take a snapshot of what every thread is doing: a thread dump with jstack, a goroutine dump from the pprof debug endpoint, py-spy dump, or gdb with thread apply all bt for native code. If hundreds of threads sit in the same frame, that frame is the answer. I take two or three dumps a few seconds apart, because a thread stuck in the same place in all of them is truly blocked. Usual causes are a pool that is exhausted because connections leak or a slow dependency holds them, a call with no timeout to a dependency that stopped responding, or a deadlock where two threads each hold a lock the other needs. The fix is the specific cause, plus timeouts everywhere so the next hang fails fast instead of silently.

questions.title: Diagnosing latency spikes that repeat on a schedule
questions.prompt: A service's p99 latency spikes for about a minute at regular intervals, for example every hour, and is healthy the rest of the time. How would you track down the cause?

expectedConcepts.label: A regular period points to something scheduled
Correlate spike times across metrics and hosts
Suspects: batch jobs, backups, compaction, synchronised cache expiry, GC
Fix by spreading load: jitter TTLs, stagger or throttle jobs

questions.modelAnswer: A regular period is the most useful clue: something scheduled is competing with traffic. First I measure the exact period and duration, and check whether the spikes hit all hosts at once or one host at a time, because all hosts together suggests a shared dependency, while one host points to something local. Then I correlate the spike timestamps with everything that runs on a timer: cron and batch jobs, database backups or vacuum, compaction in a storage engine, log rotation, certificate or config reloads, and cache entries that were all loaded at the same moment and therefore expire together, sending a burst of misses to the database. A large garbage collection cycle every few minutes is another candidate. Overlaying CPU, disk, GC pause and database query graphs on the same timeline usually makes the culprit obvious. Fixes spread the load: add jitter to cache TTLs, stagger or throttle the batch job, move it off-peak, or rate limit its database usage. Afterwards I confirm that the spike is gone at the next interval.

questions.title: Rolling out a configuration change safely
questions.prompt: A one-line configuration change pushed to every server at once caused an outage. How should configuration changes be rolled out to prevent this?

expectedConcepts.label: Treat configuration as code: versioned, reviewed, checked in CI
Services validate on load and keep the last known good config
Staged rollout: canary first, watch health, widen gradually
Fast rollback; slower rollout, with an emergency path

questions.modelAnswer: Configuration changes cause a large share of outages because they often skip the safeguards code gets, and a global push changes every server at the same moment. I would treat configuration as code: stored in version control, reviewed, and checked in CI against a schema, so a typo or an out-of-range value is rejected before deployment. Services should validate a new config when they load it and keep running on the last known good one if it is invalid. Then roll it out in stages, like a deployment: a canary on a few instances or one region first, watch error rates and latency for a few minutes, then widen gradually, with an automatic halt if health checks degrade. Every change needs a fast rollback to the previous version. The trade-off is speed: a staged rollout takes longer, so keep a documented emergency path, such as a kill switch, for the rare urgent change, and log who changed what so an incident can be traced to a specific change.

questions.title: Thousands of connections stuck in CLOSE_WAIT
questions.prompt: ss shows thousands of connections in CLOSE_WAIT on your service, and it eventually fails with "too many open files". What does CLOSE_WAIT mean, and where is the bug?

expectedConcepts.label: The peer closed; our application has not closed its socket
No kernel timeout clears it: only the application can
Find the leaking code path: unclosed bodies, error paths
Contrast with TIME_WAIT, which is normal and expires

questions.modelAnswer: CLOSE_WAIT means the other side has closed its half of the connection: we received its FIN, our kernel acknowledged it, and now the kernel is waiting for our application to call close on the socket. There is no kernel timeout that clears this state, so thousands of CLOSE_WAIT sockets mean the application never closed them, and each one keeps a file descriptor until the process hits its limit. So the bug is in our code, not the network. I would use ss -tanp or lsof to see which process holds them and which remote address they point to, which identifies the client library or dependency involved. Typical causes are an HTTP response body that is not closed on some path, often only on errors, a missing defer or finally block, or a connection pool that keeps dead connections without noticing that the peer closed them. Contrast this with TIME_WAIT, which is normal: it sits on the side that closed first and expires on its own after about a minute.

questions.title: Connection tracking table full on a Linux host
questions.prompt: A busy Linux host that does NAT starts dropping new connections at random, and dmesg says "nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet". Explain what conntrack does and how you would fix this.

expectedConcepts.label: Netfilter tracks every flow for NAT and stateful firewalling
Fixed-size table; entries linger until timeouts; new flows dropped
Raise the limit, shorten timeouts, reuse connections, NOTRACK

questions.modelAnswer: Conntrack is the netfilter subsystem that records every flow passing through the host, keyed by its addresses and ports, so that NAT can translate replies and stateful firewall rules can match established connections. It is active whenever NAT or state-matching rules are in use, which includes most Docker and Kubernetes nodes. The table has a fixed maximum, set by nf_conntrack_max, and an entry stays after its connection ends until a timeout expires, so a workload with many short-lived connections can fill the table even with modest concurrent traffic. When it is full, the kernel drops packets that would need a new entry, so new connections fail at random while existing ones keep working. I would confirm by comparing nf_conntrack_count with the maximum and checking conntrack -S. Fixes: raise nf_conntrack_max and the hash table size, accepting more kernel memory; shorten timeouts such as the TIME_WAIT one; reduce churn with connection reuse and keep-alive; and exclude traffic that needs no NAT or state with a NOTRACK rule in the raw table.

questions.title: Locating packet drops in the Linux receive path
questions.prompt: A Linux server receiving heavy UDP traffic loses packets, but the switch reports no drops. Where along the kernel receive path can packets be dropped, and which counters show each?

expectedConcepts.label: NIC ring overflow, shown by ethtool -S, fixed with a larger ring
Per-CPU backlog and softirq budget: softnet_stat, one hot core
Socket buffer overflow: receive buffer errors in netstat -su
Spread load with more queues, RPS or IRQ affinity; make the consumer keep up

questions.modelAnswer: I would walk the receive path and check the counter at each stage. First the NIC: if its receive ring has no free descriptors because the kernel did not drain it fast enough, the card drops the packet, which shows in ethtool -S as missed or no-buffer counters; ethtool -g shows the ring size, which can often be increased. Next the per-CPU backlog: /proc/net/softnet_stat has a dropped column for packets dropped because the backlog queue was full, and a time_squeeze column for softirq processing that ran out of budget. If one CPU shows high softirq time in mpstat while others are idle, the hash is sending most traffic to one queue; more queues, RSS settings, RPS or IRQ affinity can spread it, though a single huge flow cannot be split. Finally the socket: netstat -su or nstat shows receive buffer errors when the application does not read fast enough and its socket buffer fills. Raise SO_RCVBUF and rmem_max, but mainly make the consumer keep up, since bigger buffers only absorb bursts and add latency.

questions.title: Testing under latency and packet loss
questions.prompt: Your service works perfectly in local tests but misbehaves on a slow, lossy mobile network. How would you reproduce those conditions in a test, and what would you look for?

expectedConcepts.label: Inject delay, jitter, loss and reordering deliberately
Tools: tc netem, a fault-injecting proxy, browser throttling
Watch timeouts, duplicate retries, partial reads, reconnects
Repeatable automated tests, plus real devices

questions.modelAnswer: Local networks have almost no delay or loss, so code paths for slow or failing connections are never exercised. I would reproduce the conditions deliberately. On Linux, tc with the netem queueing discipline adds latency, jitter, packet loss, duplication and reordering to an interface, for example tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 200ms 50ms loss 2%, and a rate limit can cap bandwidth. To inject faults for one dependency at a time, a proxy such as Toxiproxy adds latency or cuts connections between the service and that dependency, and browser developer tools can throttle a web client. Then I watch the behaviour that usually breaks: timeouts that are too short or missing, retries that duplicate non-idempotent requests, code that assumes one read returns a whole message, reconnect logic, and how the user interface shows a slow request. I would make these repeatable automated tests in a test environment, applying netem only to a test interface or container, and still check on real devices, because real networks vary more than any fixed profile.

questions.title: Catching performance regressions before release
questions.prompt: A release made a core endpoint 30 percent slower, and nobody noticed until customers complained. How would you catch performance regressions before release?

expectedConcepts.label: Automated benchmarks on every change, against a baseline
Control noise: consistent machine, repeated runs, statistical threshold
Track percentiles, throughput and allocations; canary in production
Tight thresholds cause false alarms; make failures easy to investigate

questions.modelAnswer: Performance only stays good if it is measured on every change, the same way correctness is. I would add an automated benchmark suite for the critical paths, such as the endpoint handler and its hot functions, and run it in CI against a baseline from the main branch. The hard part is noise: shared CI runners vary a lot, so run benchmarks on a dedicated or at least consistent machine, repeat each one several times, and compare distributions with a statistical test or a threshold larger than the normal variance, rather than comparing single numbers. Track latency percentiles, throughput and allocation counts, because allocation counts are stable and often reveal a regression before time does, and store results to see slow trends that no single change crosses. A threshold that is too tight causes false alarms and people start ignoring the job, so tune it and make failures easy to investigate, for example by bisecting between the baseline and the change. Finally, CI cannot reproduce production, so a canary that compares the latency of the new version with the old one is the last safety net.

questions.title: Packet rate and the per-packet cycle budget
questions.prompt: Before writing a DPDK application for a 10 Gbit/s link, estimate how many packets per second it must handle with minimum-size frames and how many CPU cycles each packet can use. What does the result tell you about the design?

expectedConcepts.label: 64-byte frames plus preamble and gap: 84 bytes, about 14.88 million per second
About 67 ns, or roughly 200 cycles, per packet
No cache misses, syscalls or locks per packet; batch and spread over cores

questions.modelAnswer: A minimum Ethernet frame is 64 bytes, but on the wire each frame also takes 8 bytes of preamble and a 12-byte inter-frame gap, so 84 bytes, or 672 bits. 10 Gbit/s divided by 672 bits is about 14.88 million packets per second, which leaves roughly 67 nanoseconds per packet. On a 3 GHz core that is a cycle budget of about 200 cycles per packet for receiving, processing and transmitting. That shapes the design. A single cache miss to main memory costs around 100 nanoseconds, more than the whole budget, and a system call or a contended lock is far too expensive, so the fast path must avoid them: process packets in bursts to amortise per-call costs, prefetch, keep lookup tables small and NUMA-local, and use no locks. If the work per packet is larger, spread flows over several cores with RSS so each core handles a share of the rate. Real traffic usually has a larger average packet size and a lower packet rate, but the worst case of minimum-size packets is what you design and test for.

questions.title: Measuring the real load on a polling core
questions.prompt: Every DPDK worker core shows 100 percent CPU in top, even at night when traffic is low. How do you measure how busy a polling core really is, and how much headroom is left?

expectedConcepts.label: Poll-mode cores spin constantly, so OS CPU usage is meaningless
Count cycles in productive versus empty polls with the TSC
Full bursts and ring occupancy show when headroom runs out; idle spinning wastes power

questions.modelAnswer: A poll-mode core never blocks: it calls rte_eth_rx_burst in a tight loop whether packets arrive or not, so the operating system sees it busy all the time and top reports 100 percent at any traffic level. CPU utilisation from the OS is therefore meaningless for these cores. Instead, measure inside the loop. Read the time stamp counter with rte_rdtsc and accumulate the cycles spent on iterations that received packets separately from iterations that came back empty; useful cycles divided by total cycles is the real busy percentage, and the rest is headroom. Recent DPDK versions can expose this through lcore telemetry when the application reports its busy cycles. Two other signals help: the average burst size, because bursts that are always full, such as 32 of 32, mean the core is falling behind and packets are queuing in the ring; and RX ring occupancy or imissed counters, which show when the headroom has run out. Spinning at low traffic wastes power, so if latency allows, an application can back off with short sleeps or switch to RX interrupt mode after many empty polls.

questions.title: Handling control-plane traffic in a DPDK application
questions.prompt: Your DPDK application owns the NIC, so the Linux kernel no longer sees ARP, ICMP or routing-protocol packets on that port. How would you handle this control-plane traffic?

expectedConcepts.label: With kernel bypass the kernel stack sees nothing on that port
Exception path to the kernel through a TAP or virtio-user interface
Or answer ARP and ICMP directly, or steer to a dedicated queue with rte_flow
Keep it off the fast path and rate limit it; KNI is removed

questions.modelAnswer: Once a port is bound to a DPDK driver, the kernel stack never sees its packets, so ARP replies, ping and routing protocols such as BGP stop working unless the application handles them. The usual design is an exception path. The fast path classifies each packet; data traffic stays in DPDK, while control-plane packets are forwarded to the kernel through a virtual interface, typically a TAP device or a virtio-user port, both available as DPDK virtual devices. The kernel and normal daemons then answer ARP or run BGP on that interface, and their replies are read back from it and transmitted on the physical port. The older KNI module did this job but was deprecated and has been removed from recent DPDK releases. Simple protocols such as ARP and ICMP echo can instead be answered directly in the application, and rte_flow rules can steer control packets to a dedicated queue served by a separate core. Whichever approach you choose, keep it off the fast path's critical loop and rate limit it, so a flood of control traffic cannot steal cycles from forwarding.

questions.title: Jumbo frames and multi-segment mbufs
questions.prompt: After enabling 9000-byte jumbo frames, a DPDK application that worked with normal traffic starts corrupting or dropping large packets. What changes with jumbo frames, and what must the code handle?

expectedConcepts.label: A jumbo frame exceeds one mbuf data room and arrives as a chain
Raise the MTU and enable scattered RX and multi-segment TX
Use pkt_len, walk next pointers, use rte_pktmbuf_read
Bigger mbufs keep code simple but waste memory

questions.modelAnswer: With default mempools each mbuf has a data room of about 2 kilobytes, so a 9000-byte frame does not fit in one buffer. If the port's MTU is raised and scattered receive is enabled, the driver stores the frame as a chain of mbufs: the first segment's pkt_len is the whole packet length, each segment's data_len is the bytes in that segment, nb_segs gives the count, and next pointers link them. Without scatter support or a matching MTU, large frames are dropped or the port configuration fails. Code written for small packets often assumes the whole packet is contiguous at rte_pktmbuf_mtod and uses data_len as the length, so it parses or copies only the first segment, which looks like corruption. The application must handle chains: walk the next pointers, use pkt_len for the total, and use rte_pktmbuf_read for headers that may span segments; on transmit, enable the multi-segment offload or linearise the packet. The alternative is a mempool whose mbufs are big enough for a whole jumbo frame, which keeps processing simple but wastes memory for small packets, so the pool holds fewer buffers.

questions.title: Limiting blast radius with cells and shuffle sharding
questions.prompt: One customer's bad traffic pattern overloaded a shared fleet and caused an outage for every customer. Explain how cell-based architecture and shuffle sharding limit the blast radius of such failures.

expectedConcepts.label: Blast radius: the share of customers one failure can affect
Cells: independent copies of the stack, each serving a subset
Shuffle sharding: each customer gets a random combination of workers
Costs: spare capacity, critical routing layer, cross-cell features

questions.modelAnswer: Blast radius is the share of customers a single failure can affect. With one shared fleet, a poison request or one tenant's overload takes everyone down. A cell-based architecture splits the system into several independent cells, each a complete copy of the stack with its own servers, queues and databases, serving a fixed subset of customers. A thin routing layer maps each customer to a cell, so a bad customer, a bad deployment or a corrupted database affects only that cell, and changes are rolled out cell by cell. Shuffle sharding applies the same idea inside a shared fleet: instead of assigning each customer to one fixed group, give each customer a random combination of a few workers, for example two out of eight. Two customers rarely share the same combination, so if one customer's traffic kills its workers, almost every other customer still has at least one healthy worker. The costs are spare capacity in every cell, a routing layer that must be very simple and highly available, harder cross-cell features such as global queries, and more units to deploy and monitor.

questions.title: Adding an enum value without breaking clients
questions.prompt: You add a new value, REFUNDED, to the order status enum in your API, and several older clients start crashing. Why does adding an enum value break clients, and how should both sides handle it?

expectedConcepts.label: Clients treat the enum as a closed set and fail on unknown values
Clients as tolerant readers: map unknown values to a safe default
Servers document enums as open; protobuf keeps unknown values
For strict clients, treat it as breaking: version or opt in

questions.modelAnswer: Adding a value looks backward compatible from the server's side, but clients often treat an enum as a closed set. A generated client may reject the whole response when strict deserialisation meets a value it does not recognise, a switch statement with no default case may throw, and business logic such as 'if not shipped, show the cancel button' silently does the wrong thing for REFUNDED. So clients should be tolerant readers: map any unknown value to an UNKNOWN or default case that degrades safely instead of crashing. On the server side, document enums as open from the start so client authors expect new values. In Protocol Buffers, proto3 enums are open and keep unknown numeric values, and the zero value should be an UNSPECIFIED placeholder. For an enum that clients already parse strictly, treat the new value as a breaking change: return it only to clients that opt in through a new API version or a capability flag, or map it to an existing value for old clients, and check how clients actually use the field before rolling it out.

questions.title: Migrating a live service to a new database
questions.prompt: You must move a live service from one database to another, for example from MySQL to Cassandra, without downtime or data loss. Walk through the migration plan.

expectedConcepts.label: Keep the new store in sync with dual writes or CDC, then backfill
Shadow reads compare results before reads move
Cut over gradually; old store stays the source of truth; keep rollback
Risks: divergence, backfill overwriting newer data; weeks of two systems

questions.modelAnswer: I would migrate in phases so that each step can be verified and undone. First, keep the new store in sync with every new change, either by dual writing from the application or, more safely, by consuming change data capture from the old database, because application dual writes can fail halfway and diverge. Second, backfill historical data with an idempotent copy job, and make sure a backfilled row cannot overwrite a newer live change, for example by comparing versions or timestamps. Third, run shadow reads: serve from the old store but also read from the new one, compare the results and track mismatches until they are close to zero and explained. Fourth, cut over reads gradually, a percentage of traffic at a time, while the old database stays the source of truth. Only then switch writes so the new store becomes the source of truth, and keep syncing changes back to the old one for a while so you can roll back. The cost is time and complexity, running two databases for weeks, but every step is reversible.

questions.title: Data layout, cache lines and structure of arrays
questions.prompt: A loop sums one field across ten million objects and is much slower than expected. Explain how data layout causes this, and compare an array of structures with a structure of arrays.

expectedConcepts.label: Memory moves in 64-byte cache lines; unused fields waste bandwidth
Structure of arrays keeps each field contiguous, so prefetching and SIMD work
Pointer chasing is worst; SoA hurts whole-object access; measure

questions.modelAnswer: The CPU does not read single fields from memory; it moves whole 64-byte cache lines. If each object is 128 bytes and the loop needs one 8-byte field, almost all the bytes it pulls through the cache are wasted, so the loop is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. It is worse if the objects are reached through pointers scattered across the heap, because the hardware prefetcher cannot predict the next address and every element can be a cache miss. An array of structures stores each object's fields together, which is good when code uses most fields of one object at a time. A structure of arrays stores each field in its own contiguous array, so this loop reads only the values it needs, sequentially, which the prefetcher handles well and the compiler can vectorise with SIMD. The trade-off is that code which touches whole objects now reads from several arrays and is less natural to write. A middle ground is splitting hot and cold fields into separate structures. I would confirm the diagnosis with perf stat, comparing cache misses before and after.

questions.title: Explaining a slowdown with hardware counters
questions.prompt: A CPU-bound function got slower after a refactor, but the profiler shows the same hot lines. How would you use hardware performance counters with perf stat to find out why?

expectedConcepts.label: Counters explain why cycles are spent, not just where
More instructions = extra work; low IPC = stalls on cache or branch misses
Same input, repeated runs; perf record on the event; multiplexing

questions.modelAnswer: A profiler shows where time goes, but hardware counters show why. I would run perf stat on the old and new versions with the same input and compare cycles, instructions, instructions per cycle, cache misses at each level, and branch misses. Each pattern points somewhere different. If the instruction count rose, the code does more work, for example because a function is no longer inlined or extra checks were added. If instructions are similar but IPC fell, the CPU is stalling: many last-level cache misses mean it is memory bound, perhaps because the refactor changed the data layout or added pointer indirection; a jump in the branch miss rate means mispredictions, often because a predictable branch became data dependent. Then perf record on the specific event, such as cache misses, shows which instructions cause them. Top-down analysis, available through perf metrics or Intel VTune, classifies stalls into front end, back end, bad speculation and retiring. When you request more events than there are hardware counters, the kernel multiplexes them and scales the estimates, so compare repeated runs rather than single numbers.
